title: I Have Universal Healthcare and It Totally Sucks/Is Awesome
content:
“How long have you been on hold?”
Across the table, Miz peers over the lip of his coffee. Beneath his feet sits Lagertha, an English Bull Terrier. Depending on who stops to pet Lagertha determines their age. For some, the dog reminds them of Willie, General George S. Patton’s dog. To me, she’s Spuds MacKenzie . To those younger than Miz and I, Lagertha is the “Target dog.” To Miz, though? She’s named after the famous Viking shield maiden. Lagertha also happens to be his service dog.

“Almost an hour so far.” I spit. “The left hand isn’t allowed to talk to the right. Red tape everywhere.”

Miz nods, then picks up his phone. “Forgot I need to set another appointment they cancelled. So far the doctor can only see me three months out, and yet they’re the ones that cancelled the appointment.”

Miz and I both fought in Ramadi, Iraq, during the surge in 2006 to 2007. Ramadi has become infamous during that time period because of the memoirs and narratives of Chris Kyle and Jocko Willink. They didn’t exaggerate, though. The city was the epicenter of hell. Always full of IEDs, constantly burning, and every building pockmarked with bullet holes like an acute case of acne.

After the war, Miz became a lawyer working with Child Protection Services and juvenile delinquents. We’ve both adjusted to civilian life, and found our callings and purpose once more in helping others. That doesn’t mean our body and minds haven’t suffered from our time in the military though.

One benefit of military service is that if your body breaks during your time in the Armed Forces — and you can prove it — you get free healthcare. I used to feel guilty about that, but if any normal job in the United States exposed you to toxic chemicals, radiation, backbreaking labor, and mental duress, you’d sue them and be a millionaire. So I no long mind getting free healthcare.

There’s a catch to our free healthcare, though. It’s handled by the notoriously inept Department of Veterans Affairs (VA).

For over a decade, I refused to use the VA because I could get better care through my job’s privatized health insurance. Regardless of whether you’re for or against the Affordable Care Act (more commonly known as Obamacare) the fact remains that while trying to do a good thing (take care of those with preexisting conditions) they broke healthcare and caused inflation at a level we’ve never seen all while making insurance companies richer. I went back through old receipts from 2013 recently and about cried seeing that I paid a mere $13 for several doctor visits.

As more employers phased out health insurance and gave stipends, it forced many families to turn to the Health Marketplace. For two years, my family used the Marketplace until it became almost as much as a house payment. Then we switched to a health sharing company, and once that became too much, I caved and went to the VA for my care. It is free, after all.

I understand why people want universal healthcare given the insane costs of insurance that don’t even cover expenses when you go to the doctor. I can’t fault anyone for their reasoning because it makes sense. But in conversations with friends and family, I carry a unique perspective on universal healthcare because I actually have it. When I clarify that I’m covered by the VA, many groan or ask what it’s like. So I tell them the truth.

It’s totally awesome. And I hate it with a passion because the care is terrible.

Not everything about the VA is as bad as people will have you believe. Much of a veteran’s experience boils down to their location and resources provided by the VA, but good things can happen inside the government entity.

First, it’s easy to sign up and get enrolled. However, there is a catch. Your care and coverage depends on a caste-based system with eight tier levels. Priority group one is the highest priority, while eight is the lowest. How the VA determines this is based on your service records, disability, and income. Because of injuries sustained in Afghanistan and Iraq, I’m lucky enough (perhaps unlucky given the circumstances?) to be in priority group one. However, I could not imagine being in a lower group, given the time it takes to be seen.

With that as the preface, the good news is that X-rays and scans are fairly easy to get. I can usually do a generic walk in for x-rays and get them done in little to no time. CAT scans to review traumatic brain injury (I got hit by a rocket) took a little longer, but still got scheduled. Blood draws, lab work, and hearing tests all go quickly as well. Anything tech related is streamlined because they have in-house technicians. As opposed to the civilian populace, you don’t have to worry about your insurance company arguing with another health provider about the cost. It’s all there and under one umbrella, so scheduling is fast and effortless.

There’s also the new Veterans Choic e option, which allows you to see outside providers (but they have to be under contract with the VA). Most of the time it’s a pain in the ass to get, but if they don’t have in-house providers like chiropractic or acupuncture, it’s a slam dunk.

Given that most veterans have major back problems due to carrying absurd amounts of equipment, getting free chiropractic and acupuncture is a god send (there’s a trade off though that I’ll address in a moment). Emergency room visits and Urgent Care the VA also handles (this, too, depends on your priority level).

Overall, there are some beneficial aspects to the VA and anyone who says differently is probably being salty if they can’t admit one good thing the department provides.

However, there are several good reasons the VA gets so much heat for their standard of care.

And that’s because the care is utterly inept.

In late 2020, Miz got COVID and had to be hospitalized. He contracted pneumonia, then caught COVID, and the combo almost killed him. Miz is the burley, athletic type who enjoys running, but when he arrived at the VA hospital in Houston, Texas, his blood-oxygen levels had dropped to dangerously low levels (52%).

Upon arrival, they locked him in a back room because of his COVID diagnosis. After laboring to breathe for hours with no one checking in on him, he pounded on a door, begging for an oxygen tank. They had no beds and told him he couldn’t sit in the hallway. When they finally gave him a bed, the linens were dirty and had holes in them. From there, things got worse.

In the military, we’re taught self-sufficiency and many of us have basic medic training. That’s what ended up saving Miz’s life — his training.

Miz changed his own oxygen liquid bags for his O2 because he could rarely get a nurse to respond. He ensured to check his medication because they almost gave him the wrong one. Miz also had to remind his nurses — when they would show up — that he needed his 5th day of remdesivir because they had forgotten. Tired of poor care, Miz took things into his own hands, and began turning down his O2 levels and working to breathe so he could convince the staff to let him leave. When he finally was discharged, the staff forgot to give him his medication and didn’t set up oxygen machines at his house, either.

When I asked if there was any benefit to the care, Miz laughed and said, “It was free. That was the only good part.”

This type of care may seem like an isolated incident, but most every veteran will tell you a similar story. If you want an appointment to see your primary care provider, be prepared to wait three months. With a recent sinus infection and severe headaches I have from a traumatic brain injury, I was told to go to an Urgent Care because they can’t see me until January 2022. Even when they outsource your care to civilian providers, you’re going to wait. I’ve spent the last few weeks on phone call after phone call because my provider has told me I need to talk to a third-party provider that handles scheduling, whereas the third party entity keeps blaming the provider.

Then there’s the mental health aspect.

Mental health within the VA is the most impersonal experience ever and you feel like a pet project as opposed to a human being. As someone who’s spent the last eight years in mental health and has certifications in Trauma Care and Suicide Prevention , half the time I’m tempted to berate the way they handle our veterans. For example, when my primary care physician called to discuss something as mundane as my physical, he stated, “Before I begin, I’m required to ask these questions. title: If California Adopts Universal Health Care, It Will Be a Model for the Whole Country
content:
After spending years voting and pledging to repeal the Affordable Care Act (ACA), when the time finally came for the Republicans to replace President Obama’s landmark health-care legislation, they hopelessly failed . Their plan would have led to skyrocketing premiums for the elderly and taken away the insurance of more than 20 million people. Only 17 percent of the public supported the GOP plan, and it never even made it to a vote.

Still, it’s clear that our current health-care model isn’t working. At 16.9 percent, the United States is an outlier in health-care expenditure as a percentage of the GDP — the second highest being Switzerland, at 11.5 percent—and the only country not to have a highly regulated universal system. There’s reason to believe that universal health care could significantly reduce total spending on health care. And Democrats and progressives need to proactively present an alternative to the ACA.

California may be the state to show the way forward. In February, Senate Bill 562 was introduced to create a single-payer health-care system that would cover all 38 million Californians. The program would eliminate copays and insurance deductibles, and “inpatient, outpatient, emergency care, dental, vision, mental health and nursing home care” would be covered. The funding specifics have not yet been provided, but this is still a significant step forward in the fight for universal health coverage.

Though governor Jerry Brown argued that single-payer would be unaffordable because California’s current system consumes 18 percent of the state’s GDP , California still has other prospects for universal health care. Gavin Newsom has promised to implement it if he becomes governor in 2018, though he’s not advocating a single-payer system. He plans to build off of Healthy San Francisco, a program he implemented as mayor in 2007. This program would fill in the gaps of the ACA by paying for those who do not have insurance, allowing them to visit community health centers and public hospitals for primary and preventative care, which has reduced overall health spending in San Francisco by catching severe diseases early and avoiding costly emergency-room visits.

Canada’s single-payer health-care system did not begin as a national program but was pioneered in the province of Saskatchewan.

While there isn’t any guarantee of single-payer happening in California, the state is taking steps in the right direction toward the goal of universal coverage. Americans need not imagine how this may occur but could look to their northern neighbor for an example.

Canada’s single-payer health-care system did not begin as a national program but was pioneered in the province of Saskatchewan. The development of universal health care took place from the mid-1940s to the 1960s and was accompanied by constant scaremongering from right-wing forces that warned that any attempt to provide government health insurance was a communist plot to take away individual freedom. They used the term “socialized medicine,” a phrase used in US health-care debates to this day. However, Canadians weren’t buying the fear campaign, as 80 percent supported a “government-funded health plan” as early as 1944.

Significant credit for Canada’s single-payer health-care system belongs to Tommy Douglas, the left-wing leader of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation (CCF) in Saskatchewan, and later the founding leader of the federal New Democratic Party (NDP). Canadians are not ignorant about what he did, considering he was voted the Greatest Canadian in 2004 for his role in establishing universal health care.

Douglas rolled out provincial hospital insurance in 1947. When the federal government responded with a plan to provide 50 percent of the funding for public hospital insurance in 1957, Douglas promised to expand provincial insurance plans to include medical services. Despite fierce opposition from doctors and medical associations, the CCF won 38 of 54 seats and 41 percent of the popular vote. Legislation was passed in October 1961 for the new publicly funded medical insurance to begin on July 1, 1962.

“What most people who favour compulsory health insurance fail to realize that it is a Trojan horse. They fail to discern that under a superficially attractive exterior it hides the forces which will destroy their freedom of choice and import a full-fledged system of state medicine into their midst.”

— William Anderson , Vice-President and Managing Director of North American Life Insurance, 1954

In 1961, doctors began holding rallies under the banner “Keep Our Doctors,” warning that many would move abroad if the government didn’t cancel its public insurance plan. On July 1, the doctors went on strike , but public opinion and the media were firmly against them . After some minor concessions, the doctors returned to work after only a few weeks of action. Around the same time, the Royal Commission on Health Services had been formed on the federal level, and the Medical Care Act was finally passed in 1966. The Medical Care Act provided funding to provinces that met the federal criteria for public health insurance: “universal, publicly administered, portable and comprehensive.” By 1971, all provinces had established systems that fit the criteria, meaning that less than 10 years after Saskatchewan had first adopted it, universal health care had been rolled out across the country, and every Canadian had public health insurance.

Canadian universal health care began as a subnational initiative, but it expanded to the national level. The same could happen in the United States. This has already happened with the legalization of marijuana and could occur if California takes meaningful steps toward passing a universal health-care plan.

The legalization of marijuana is the culmination of measures taken over the course of several decades. Efforts at decriminalization began in the 1970s, followed by California’s legalization of medical marijuana in 1996. In 2012, voters in both Colorado and Washington approved ballot measures to legalize marijuana, and its legal sale began in 2014. A total of 28 states have now legalized medical marijuana . While the federal government has not adopted state policies in this instance, it is very clear that the actions of two states have set an example that others are following.

California could do the same with universal health care. As the Saskatchewan example shows, it’s better to start somewhere than to wait for the perfect conditions that allow its implementation. Douglas started with public hospital insurance and expanded it to medical insurance when he started receiving additional funding from the federal government.

Progressives should continue the fight for single-payer whenever the opportunity arises. They should support Bernie Sanders’s federal single-payer plan and any similar initiatives on the state level, but that also shouldn’t stop them from fighting to implement and improve Newsom’s plan if that can realistically be achieved in the near term. The passing of universal health care in California in 2018 would be an important win, one that could push policy and public opinion in favor of greater expansion, moving closer to the goal of extending coverage to every American.

The development of universal  took place from the mid-1940s to the 1960s and was accompanied by constant scaremongering from -wing forces that warned that any attempt to provide  health insurance was a communist plot to take away individual freedom. They used the term “socialized medicine,” a phrase used in US health-care debates to this day. However, Canadians weren’t buying the fear campaign, as 80  supported a “-funded health plan” as early as 1944.

Significant credit for Canada’s single-payer health-care system belongs to Tommy Douglas, the left-wing leader of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation (CCF) in Saskatchewan, and later the founding leader of the federal  Democratic Party (NDP). Canadians are not ignorant about what he did, considering he was voted the Greatest Canadian in 2004 for his role in establishing universal .

When the federal  responded with a plan to provide 50  of the funding for  hospital insurance in 1957, Douglas promised to expand provincial insurance plans to include medical services. They fail to discern that under a superficially attractive exterior it hides the forces which will destroy their freedom of choice and import a full-fledged system of state medicine into their midst.”

Efforts at decriminalization began in the 1970s, followed by California’s legalization of medical marijuana in 1996. In 2012, voters in both Colorado and Washington approved ballot measures to legalize marijuana, and its legal sale began in 2014. A total of 28 states have now legalized medical marijuana . While the federal  has not adopted state policies in this instance, it is very clear that the actions of two states have set an example that others are following.

California could do the same with universal . As the Saskatchewan example shows, it’s better to start somewhere than to wait for the perfect conditions that allow its implementation. Douglas started with  hospital insurance and expanded it to medical insurance when he started receiving additional funding from the federal .

Progressives should continue the fight for single-payer whenever the opportunity arises. They should support Bernie Sanders’s federal single-payer plan and any similar initiatives on the state level, but that also shouldn’t stop them from fighting to implement and improve Newsom’s plan if that can realistically be achieved in the near term. The passing of universal  in California in 2018 would be an important win, one that could push policy and  opinion in favor of greater expansion, moving closer to the goal of extending coverage to every American.

title: Yes, Universal Health Care is a Good Idea
content:
I’ve been thinking a lot about universal healthcare. I’m not going to use the term “Medicare for All” because I’m just about to sign up for Medicare, and I’m learning about all the things it doesn’t cover.

I’m going to say “universal healthcare” and I’m going to use it to mean that our tax dollars go into a fund to pay for our medical care. Just like the systems in place in most countries around the world.

What I’ve been thinking can be summed up in one sentence:

We’ve been sold a crock of shit when it comes to healthcare.

We’ve been told that the best way to get our medical care is through a profit-based system. We’ve been told that anything else would be “socialism, Marxism, communism”, that if we abandon our private insurance companies and profit-based hospitals, our world will come to an end, people will be dying in the gutters and the economy will collapse.

But I’ve been thinking.

If businesses large and small were free of the cost of their employees’ health insurance, wouldn’t they have more money to hire new workers? And more money to expand those businesses? Isn’t that how capitalism thrives?

And I’ve been thinking about this, too.

A lot of the same people who oppose universal healthcare are deeply opposed to abortion. So I’m asking this: with universal healthcare, wouldn’t everyone have access to safe and free contraception? And wouldn’t that greatly reduce the number of unwanted pregnancies? So wouldn’t that be a good thing in your eyes?

I don’t understand. I really don’t.

If conservatives really want businesses to thrive and to have more capital to spend, then sparing them the cost of health insurance makes sense. If they want to reduce the number of abortions, the universal health coverage makes sense.

If conservatives want businesses to be able to hire more full time employees, rather than having to train and oversee a rotating list of part-timers, then they should support universal health care.

Medical care with a profit motive is by its very nature more expensive than medical care that is done at cost. That’s not exactly rocket science to figure out.

So I say it’s time for conservatives to look past the bullshit labels about “communism” and start looking at the facts.

Anyone agree?

title: The Truth About Living In A Universal Healthcare System
content:
Healthcare has proven itself to be a loaded topic for both the American left and right. It’s no secret that it’s something that polarizes our political spectrum, and it’s no secret that there is a vast amount of misinformation out there on which implications a universal healthcare system would have on our country.

The left idealizes universal healthcare like it’s the second coming of Jesus, and point to the Nordic countries as some sort of utopia that is without fault. They are quick to mention that countries like Norway are successful democratic socialist societies, when in fact it operates under a capitalist economy. It’s just not an economy that has privatized healthcare.

Meanwhile, the right demonizes universal healthcare and regularly implements scare tactics meant to instill fear and loyalty in its base. They dismiss universal healthcare as a socialist pipedream and discuss what a financial burden it would be on our economy. All while giving tax breaks to the 1% and pushing through a 1.4 trillion dollar spending bill just recently.

Both of these politicized opinions bug me to no end because neither one paints an accurate picture of what universal healthcare is actually like or what it would mean for the average American.

Being an American expat that has lived in Norway for eighteen years, I have experience in both countries when it comes to navigating the system, both good and bad. I have stood witness to the horrors of not being able to afford healthcare in the US, and the astonishment at the level of care readily available to me in Norway at a minimal cost.

Growing up, my bedroom was lined with shelves full of the most beautifully dressed porcelain dolls. I used to climb up and take them down to admire their ringlet curls and intricate details. Unlike my Barbies, who had seen better days, I handled these dolls with the utmost of care. They were special because my grandmother had given them to me.

I remember my grandmother, who I called Nannie, as a kind-hearted woman who loved her family a great deal. She kept jars full of buttons around her home (just in case she needed them), had a thing for shiny metallic shoes, and gave the biggest and warmest hugs. The few memories I have left of her are dear to my heart because, unfortunately, she was gravely ill throughout my entire childhood.

Doctors across North Texas couldn’t explain her symptoms nor her ailment. Some doctors even suggested to my grandfather, Pop, that she should be committed, as they deemed her symptoms to be imaginary. Eventually, she was diagnosed with a rare intestinal syndrome that not only made it difficult to digest food, but it robbed her body of the nourishment it needed to survive.

Taking care of Nannie and ensuring that she got the care she needed was a full-time job. A job without pay, benefits, or health insurance. Pop couldn’t work alongside taking care of Nannie, so he chose to stay home.

Without a steady source of income, bills piled high, and their funds drained. They moved from house to house, as their financial situation became steadily unstable, sometimes even resorting to living in a trailer on various family members’ properties.

My grandparents, who had the kind of love you see in movies, couldn’t see any other option than to file for legal separation. All so, Nannie could extend her Medicaid coverage and continue to have access to the medications that kept her alive.

In the last months of her life, my warm and lively grandmother became a shell of herself. Her organs started to shut down, and there wasn’t much else to do other than keep her comfortable in state-sponsored hospice services.

After decades of battling both her ailment and the healthcare system, she passed at the age of fifty-nine. I’ll never forget the sound that came out of my Pop’s mouth in the moments after her death. They haunt me to this day. I couldn’t understand why we had to lose her like that. I couldn’t understand what had just happened and why there wasn’t any more help for her to get. Even as an adult, I still can’t comprehend what my grandparents went through and how unnecessary Nannie’s experience was.

Eight months after her passing, I moved to Norway, along with my mom and younger brother. I was just twelve, and heartbroken to leave behind my family and the only place I had called home. Nannie’s passing was still a fresh wound in my young heart, and it felt surreal to leave Texas not long after she left this world.

Little did I know that I would have a similar journey with chronic health issues as my grandmother did. This time there would be a very different outcome.

In 2011 when I was twenty-one, I became ill and experienced a multitude of confusing and debilitating symptoms. I couldn’t walk more than a few feet without cold sweating all over my body, my lymph nodes visibly stuck out from my neck and chest, and my throat consistently stayed raw, swollen, and sore. Lactic acid built up in my muscles, and dizzy spells were brought on just by standing in the shower. My body went haywire during my prime.

At the onset of my illness, doctors weren’t all that sure about what had happened to me. All they knew was that my immune system was severely compromised by the perfect storm of Epstein-Barr viruses that rendered me medically disabled.

For the first three years, I bounced from specialist to specialist. Each of them ran a series of tests on me, each of them had a different theory, and each of them suggested different treatments. This period of life that was meant to be used on self-exploration, personal growth, and getting an education; was instead used on doctor visits, daily 14-hour sleeping sessions, chronic pain, and viral attacks.

Unable to work, and unable to study fulltime, I was isolated to my apartment. Days were spent resting, reading, and trying to will my body to get better. I longed for a normal life, and I longed for a normal body. Countless tears were cried as I wondered if I would have to live like this forever.

Even through all of those worries, not once did I have to think twice about affording my doctor visits or medications. I didn’t even have to worry about a steady income as I was provided with disability payments to ensure I could afford groceries, rent, and a semi-normal life.

I’ll be the first to admit that the system in Norway isn’t perfect. We have some older treatment centers and hospitals that could use serious upgrades but are locked into red-tape limbo while local politicians debate what to do and how. There are waiting lines for non-emergency/elective treatments and surgeries. And while the level of quality is good ( it placed 11 out of 36 of the best health care systems in the world ), it could be better. Tax rates are generally higher than other countries in order to pay for it all, and local GP’s are often overwhelmed with the number of patients on their lists and the amount of paperwork that’s demanded by our welfare system, NAV .

But there are plenty of amazing pros that outweigh the cons. It’s a single-payer system, so you don’t have to deal with coverage by insurance companies and a complicated payment system. It is affordable, as co-pays are around 16 US dollars, and once you hit your limit for the year, your healthcare is covered. Most hospitals are modern and digitalized. Providing you with the care you need in an efficient way.

You can choose your own GP, and whichever treatment center or hospital you want in the country. If you fall ill, then you have the right to up to 52 weeks of paid sick leave from work. If you are sick for longer than that, then the welfare system will provide you with disability benefits while they determine your working ability. The best thing for recovery is for a person to work in whatever capacity that they can, so they provide the necessary services and aids you need to get back into the workforce.

No one system has it all figured out. And while there are both negatives and positives to what it’s like in Norway, it’s nothing like it is back home in the States.

I personally don’t know anyone here who has become seriously ill or who has died due to the lack of affordable care. In the States, I know of more stories than I can count about people dying from a lack of access to affordable healthcare, people forgoing medical assistance due to their financial status, fighting insurance companies to get coverage for diseases and injuries, or having to declare bankruptcy due to medical debt.

It should be unbelievable that 69% of bankruptcies in the US are due to medical debt . Still, it’s not all that hard to believe when social media is flooded with Go Fund Me campaigns begging others to help them with their medical expenses.

I won’t claim to know the answers on what’s right when it comes to healthcare reform. I am neither a political scientist, healthcare professional, policymaker, or economist. What I do know is that my grandmother’s experience in the States and mine in Norway couldn’t be more different. Not once did I have to choose between paying rent and paying for care that would keep me alive.

And, I am happy to report that while I haven’t made a full recovery yet, I have made strides of progress. I went on to earn my degree in psychology just last year and now work fulltime for a marketing agency. I happily pay a 30% tax rate, knowing that people who were in my position are being taken care of. I gladly pay it, knowing that people like my Nannie give everything to receive a fraction of the care and services that we have available in Norway.

Even though universal healthcare has its faults, it is one that values human lives and their right to see a doctor without emptying their pockets. Whenever I check in with the latest in the Democratic Primary race, it saddens me that universal healthcare is even debatable, not to mention “controversial”.

It’s even more upsetting to hear what’s coming from the right side of the field, as Republicans spread fear-mongering about universal healthcare as if its a lingering threat to our very prosperity as a nation. It shouldn’t be a left or a right platform talking point. It shouldn’t be liberals versus conservatives. The well-being and health of our citizens and residents should be placed higher than the dollar amount hanging over our heads.

My Nannie crosses my mind almost daily. I think of how she suffered, how the last years of her life were spent worrying about medical bills, debt, and making ends meet, on top of her physical suffering. I think of how my grandparents couldn’t afford a permanent home because every penny they had was thrown at keeping my grandmother alive. Life could’ve been different for her, had she lived here in Norway.

People often ask me if I’ll ever consider moving back to my home country, the land that birthed me. I would like to move back one day, as Texas is just as much a part of me as my right arm. It’s the place where I learned compassion, lending a helping hand to your neighbor, and fighting for what’s right.

But, until things at home change and the current system is eradicated and rebuilt from scratch, I can’t in good conscience leave a system that places my life at a higher value than a buck. A healthcare system that my Nannie and Pop could have only dreamt of.

It’s no secret that it’s something that polarizes our political spectrum, and it’s no secret that there is a vast amount of misinformation out there on which implications a universal healthcare system would have on our country.

The left idealizes universal healthcare like it’s the second coming of Jesus, and point to the Nordic countries as some sort of utopia that is without fault. They are quick to mention that countries like Norway are successful democratic socialist societies, when in fact it operates under a capitalist economy. It’s just not an economy that has privatized healthcare.

Meanwhile, the  demonizes universal healthcare and regularly implements scare tactics meant to instill fear and loyalty in its base. They dismiss universal healthcare as a socialist pipedream and discuss what a financial burden it would be on our economy. All while giving tax breaks to the 1% and pushing through a 1.4 trillion dollar spending bill just recently.

Both of these politicized opinions bug me to no end because neither one paints an accurate picture of what universal healthcare is actually like or what it would mean for the average American.

Being an American expat that has lived in Norway for eighteen years, I have experience in both countries when it comes to navigating the system, both good and bad. I have stood witness to the horrors of not being able to afford healthcare in the US, and the astonishment at the level of care readily available to me in Norway at a minimal cost.

Growing up, my bedroom was lined with shelves full of the most beautifully dressed porcelain dolls. I used to climb up and take them down to admire their ringlet curls and intricate details. Unlike my Barbies, who had seen better days, I handled these dolls with the utmost of care. They were special because my grandmother had given them to me.

I remember my grandmother, who I called Nannie, as a kind-hearted woman who loved her family a  deal. She kept jars full of buttons around her home (just in case she needed them), had a thing for shiny metallic shoes, and gave the biggest and warmest hugs. The few memories I have left of her are dear to my heart because, unfortunately, she was gravely ill throughout my entire childhood.

Doctors across North Texas couldn’t explain her symptoms nor her ailment. Some doctors even suggested to my grandfather, Pop, that she should be committed, as they deemed her symptoms to be imaginary. Eventually, she was diagnosed with a rare intestinal syndrome that not only made it difficult to digest food, but it robbed her body of the nourishment it needed to survive.

Taking care of Nannie and ensuring that she got the care she needed was a full-time job. A job without pay, benefits, or health insurance. Pop couldn’t work alongside taking care of Nannie, so he chose to stay home.

Without a steady source of income, bills piled high, and their funds drained. They moved from house to house, as their financial situation became steadily unstable, sometimes even resorting to living in a trailer on various family members’ properties.

My grandparents, who had the kind of love you see in movies, couldn’t see any other option than to file for legal separation. All so, Nannie could extend her Medicaid coverage and continue to have access to the medications that kept her alive.

In the last months of her life, my warm and lively grandmother became a shell of herself. Her organs started to shut down, and there wasn’t much else to do other than keep her comfortable in state-sponsored hospice services.

After decades of battling both her ailment and the healthcare system, she passed at the age of fifty-nine. I’ll never forget the sound that came out of my Pop’s mouth in the moments after her death. They haunt me to this day. I couldn’t understand why we had to lose her like that. I couldn’t understand what had just happened and why there wasn’t any more help for her to get. Even as an adult, I still can’t comprehend what my grandparents went through and how unnecessary Nannie’s experience was.

Eight months after her passing, I moved to Norway, along with my mom and younger brother. I was just twelve, and heartbroken to leave behind my family and the only place I had called home. Nannie’s passing was still a fresh wound in my young heart, and it felt surreal to leave Texas not long after she left this world.

Little did I know that I would have a similar journey with chronic health issues as my grandmother did. This time there would be a very different outcome.

In 2011 when I was twenty-one, I became ill and experienced a multitude of confusing and debilitating symptoms. I couldn’t walk more than a few feet without cold sweating all over my body, my lymph nodes visibly stuck out from my neck and chest, and my throat consistently stayed raw, swollen, and sore. Lactic acid built up in my muscles, and dizzy spells were brought on just by standing in the shower. My body went haywire during my prime.

At the onset of my illness, doctors weren’t all that sure about what had happened to me. All they knew was that my immune system was severely compromised by the perfect storm of Epstein-Barr viruses that rendered me medically disabled.

For the first three years, I bounced from specialist to specialist. Each of them ran a series of tests on me, each of them had a different theory, and each of them suggested different treatments. This period of life that was meant to be used on self-exploration, personal growth, and getting an education; was instead used on doctor visits, daily 14-hour sleeping sessions, chronic pain, and viral attacks.

Unable to work, and unable to study fulltime, I was isolated to my apartment. Days were spent resting, reading, and trying to will my body to get better. I longed for a normal life, and I longed for a normal body. Countless tears were cried as I wondered if I would have to live like this forever.

Even through all of those worries, not once did I have to think twice about affording my doctor visits or medications. I didn’t even have to worry about a steady income as I was provided with disability payments to ensure I could afford groceries, rent, and a semi-normal life.

I’ll be the first to admit that the system in Norway isn’t perfect. We have some older treatment centers and hospitals that could use serious upgrades but are locked into red-tape limbo while local politicians debate what to do and how. There are waiting lines for non-emergency/elective treatments and surgeries. And while the level of quality is good ( it placed 11 out of 36 of the best  systems in the world ), it could be better. Tax rates are generally higher than other countries in order to pay for it all, and local GP’s are often overwhelmed with the number of patients on their lists and the amount of paperwork that’s demanded by our welfare system, NAV .

But there are plenty of amazing pros that outweigh the cons. It’s a single-payer system, so you don’t have to deal with coverage by insurance companies and a complicated payment system. It is affordable, as co-pays are around 16 US dollars, and once you hit your limit for the year, your healthcare is covered. Most hospitals are modern and digitalized. Providing you with the care you need in an efficient way.

You can choose your own GP, and whichever treatment center or hospital you want in the country. If you fall ill, then you have the  to up to 52 weeks of paid sick leave from work. If you are sick for longer than that, then the welfare system will provide you with disability benefits while they determine your working ability. The best thing for recovery is for a person to work in whatever capacity that they can, so they provide the necessary services and aids you need to get back into the workforce.

No one system has it all figured out. And while there are both negatives and positives to what it’s like in Norway, it’s nothing like it is back home in the States.

I personally don’t know anyone here who has become seriously ill or who has died due to the lack of affordable care. In the States, I know of more stories than I can count about people dying from a lack of access to affordable healthcare, people forgoing medical assistance due to their financial status, fighting insurance companies to get coverage for diseases and injuries, or having to declare bankruptcy due to medical debt.

It should be unbelievable that 69% of bankruptcies in the US are due to medical debt . Still, it’s not all that hard to believe when social media is flooded with Go Fund Me campaigns begging others to help them with their medical expenses.

I won’t claim to know the answers on what’s  when it comes to healthcare reform. I am neither a political scientist, healthcare professional, policymaker, or economist. What I do know is that my grandmother’s experience in the States and mine in Norway couldn’t be more different. Not once did I have to choose between paying rent and paying for care that would keep me alive.

And, I am happy to report that while I haven’t made a full recovery yet, I have made strides of progress. I went on to earn my degree in psychology just last year and now work fulltime for a marketing agency. I happily pay a 30% tax rate, knowing that people who were in my position are being taken care of. I gladly pay it, knowing that people like my Nannie give everything to receive a fraction of the care and services that we have available in Norway.

Even though universal healthcare has its faults, it is one that values  lives and their  to see a doctor without emptying their pockets. Whenever I check in with the latest in the Democratic Primary race, it saddens me that universal healthcare is even debatable, not to mention “controversial”.

It’s even more upsetting to hear what’s coming from the  side of the field, as Republicans spread fear-mongering about universal healthcare as if its a lingering threat to our very prosperity as a nation. It shouldn’t be a left or a  platform talking point. It shouldn’t be liberals versus . The well-being and health of our citizens and residents should be placed higher than the dollar amount hanging over our heads.

My Nannie crosses my mind almost daily. I think of how she suffered, how the last years of her life were spent worrying about medical bills, debt, and making ends meet, on top of her physical suffering. I think of how my grandparents couldn’t afford a permanent home because every penny they had was thrown at keeping my grandmother alive. Life could’ve been different for her, had she lived here in Norway.

People often ask me if I’ll ever consider moving back to my home country, the land that birthed me. I would like to move back one day, as Texas is just as much a part of me as my  arm. It’s the place where I learned compassion, lending a helping hand to your neighbor, and fighting for what’s .

But, until things at home change and the current system is eradicated and rebuilt from scratch, I can’t in good conscience leave a system that places my life at a higher value than a buck. A healthcare system that my Nannie and Pop could have only dreamt of.

title: Mugged By Reality: A Conservative Case for Universal Health Care
content:
Twenty years ago, I learned of the importance of health insurance and the role of the government in health insurance the hard way.

In November 1996, I caught the flu. At the time, I was 27 and working at a major coffee chain making $6/hour. Health care was available, but when you make only $6/hour and have to pay for various things like food and rent, health care becomes out of reach.

So, I spent a few days in bed until I felt good enough to go back to work. I felt okay for a few days, but then the illness came back with a vengeance. I couldn’t keep anything down. I started having trouble breathing. I should have gone to the clinic I frequented which offered care to the low income on a sliding fee scale. But I went to the county hospital in downtown Minneapolis. A young doctor examined me and said it was pneumonia. He gave me a five day supply of antibiotics (the usual course is ten days for something as routine as a sinus infection). I didn’t get better. Instead, I grew worse. I had a high fever and I was getting a case of thrush on my tongue turning it white. In the meantime, my parents rushed from Michigan to take care of me. I was able to see the nurse practitioner at the clinic and she took a blood test and an x-ray. She came back into the examination room and told me that I needed to be admitted to the hospital right now. My white blood cell count was 70,000, which meant my body was fighting off a massive infection. I wondered allowed how in the hell was I going to pay for this. The nurse practitioner told me not to worry.

I was in the hospital for two long weeks. My lungs had filled up with fluid so the doctors made some incisions to drain the lungs. If that didn’t work, the next route would have been a risky surgery. But that wasn’t needed. After a ton of antibiotics, I got better.

But how was this paid for? I didn’t have to face a big medical bill (or at least not so much) because that wise nurse practitioner was able to get me on to General Assistance health care, which is Minnesota’s version of Medicaid, the national program that offers health care for the poor.

It’s funny; around that time, I was moving from a liberal to more right of center, but I still believed the government had a role in providing health care because it took care of me at a point in my life when I needed it.

Conservatives believe in a limited government. It’s not because we hate the government, but because big government can easily crowd out other spheres of society. Conservatives believe government has a role in our lives, but we don’t think it should be running the show. We believe in the role of civil society and the church as institutions that can also offer help to the least of these in our society.

medium.com

So, I understand that conservatives get a little nervous when the topic of health care insurance comes up. Liberals fail to understand that conservatives don’t see government as a wholly good thing. The government’s main power is usually to compel you to do something. Knowing that power, there is always a fear of the power of government among conservatives. When you are thinking of having the feds have expanded power on 1/6 of the economy it will make a conservative feel uncomfortable. More government can seem like less freedom. This is why conservatives railed against the Affordable Care Act, especially because it mandated that people have health insurance. It’s why the American Health Care Act passed the House of Representatives because it seems to give more freedom and choice to Americans. Listen to conservatives talk, you will hear that people should be free to not have health care, that government should not impose themselves on an issue like our health.

Which is why the 2020 Presidential Race is something that gobsmacks conservatives. The idea of an American single-payer system is getting major play among Democrats. Both Senators Elizabeth Warren and Bernie Sanders have “Medicare for All” plans where private health insurance is banned (something that is not a part of the Canadian single-payer system). This is the nightmare that conservatives warn about and it is something that could put Donald Trump back in the White House.

But let’s be honest. Medicare-for-All is not going to happen. Not with all the massive disruption that would take place in the economy, if a sizable chunk of the American economy is suddenly upended.

Conservatives have too often focused so much on the fear of government controlling health care that they are blind to finding ways to use government to allow people access to affordable health care. They make bogeymen out of the fear of single-payer and ignore how regular Americans are having to skip insurance because they can’t afford it. Conservative writer and thinker John Podhoretz sums up some of the modern conservative thinking on health insurance . Here is what he said in 2017 about the American Health Care act when it went through the House the first time and the Congressional Budget Office said the new plan would cover 24 million fewer people:

The consensus headline: “24 Million Will Lose Coverage.”

As a simple matter of fact, that isn’t right. The verb “lose” suggests these 24 million will unwillingly be booted out of the system. No: The CBO says that most of those people will not be covered because they will not buy an insurance policy when it’s no longer the law of the land that they must do so.

In other words, they’ll be exercising their freedom of choice as adults to opt-out of the system — and should they try to get back in only when they get sick, they will have to pay a 30 percent penalty for their effort to game the system.

Maybe some people decide to opt-out of health care insurance and then only purchase it when they are ill. But looking at my own experience and the experience of others, it’s more likely that health care will become unaffordable and that people will forego insurance. I know of very few if any people who just opt out of insurance for the heck of it and purchase it when they become ill (which means buying more expensive insurance since you’re sick). It also ignores the fact that many people are not able to purchase insurance even though they might want it.

When the then-Republican led house tried to repeal the Affordable Care Act, they could not agree on a replacement that could come close to what the ACA offered. They were so focused on repealing Obamacare that they never really thought about what if anything fills its place. The AHCA which passed the House was based on universal access , in that people would have the opportunity to buy insurance. But this plan doesn’t even give many opportunities to get access to insurance. I had the chance to buy insurance back in 1996, but on my $6/hour salary, I couldn’t do that. Having access to buy insurance is not the same as being able to afford it. While people might be “free” to not have health care insurance, for many not having health insurance is far from freedom.

Conservatives, Republicans, libertarians should be in support of some kind of government-backed health care insurance. In the same way that we have Social Security that gives Americans peace of mind that even if they didn’t get a pension or a 401K has at least a basic stipend in their old age, we need to have a health care system where people know that there is at least some basic coverage; a safety net when things get bad. The United States needs universal health care. Now, note I said universal health care , not single-payer. When most on the right think of the government providing health insurance, their thoughts go to Canada’s single-payer model or in the United Kingdom where the state controls all aspects of health care. That is one form of coverage, but there are other ways of getting there. We could push for a system like the Swiss Healthcare System the Singaporean model , or even an update to the ACA. We don’t need to have something like Canada’s single-payer we just need some system that at as conservative Pascal Emmanuel Gobry , protects people from the “expenditures of catastrophic health problems.”

Freedom is a cherished conservative value, but there is another value among conservatives that has been ignored: solidarity. That concept, which stems from Catholic social teaching means that all of us are connected. This might seem to run counter to the more individualist ethos of American conservatism. Pope John Paul II describes solidarity as:

“Solidarity is not a feeling of vague compassion or shallow distress at the misfortunes of so many people, both near and far. On the contrary, it is a firm and persevering determination to commit oneself to the common good; that is to say to the good of all and of each individual, because we are all really responsible for all.”

We should have universal health care because we believe in the dignity of each person. We want universal health care because we believe in the words of Abraham Lincoln who said:

Mugged By Reality: A Conservative Case for Universal Health Care Twenty years ago, I learned of the importance of health insurance and the role of the government in health insurance the hard way.

In November 1996, I caught the flu. At the time, I was 27 and working at a major coffee chain making $6/hour. Health care was available, but when you make only $6/hour and have to pay for various things like food and rent, health care becomes out of reach.

So, I spent a few days in bed until I felt good enough to go back to work. I felt okay for a few days, but then the illness came back with a vengeance. I couldn’t keep anything down. I started having trouble breathing. I should have gone to the clinic I frequented which offered care to the low income on a sliding fee scale. But I went to the county hospital in downtown Minneapolis. A young doctor examined me and said it was pneumonia. He gave me a five day supply of antibiotics (the usual course is ten days for something as routine as a sinus infection). I didn’t get better. Instead, I grew worse. I had a high fever and I was getting a case of thrush on my tongue turning it white. In the meantime, my parents rushed from Michigan to take care of me. I was able to see the nurse practitioner at the clinic and she took a blood test and an x-ray. She came back into the examination room and told me that I needed to be admitted to the hospital right now. My white blood cell count was 70,000, which meant my body was fighting off a massive infection. I wondered allowed how in the hell was I going to pay for this. The nurse practitioner told me not to worry.

I was in the hospital for two long weeks. My lungs had filled up with fluid so the doctors made some incisions to drain the lungs. If that didn’t work, the next route would have been a risky surgery. But that wasn’t needed. After a ton of antibiotics, I got better.

But how was this paid for? I didn’t have to face a big medical bill (or at least not so much) because that wise nurse practitioner was able to get me on to General Assistance health care, which is Minnesota’s version of Medicaid, the national program that offers health care for the poor.

It’s funny; around that time, I was moving from a liberal to more right of center, but I still believed the government had a role in providing health care because it took care of me at a point in my life when I needed it.

Conservatives believe in a limited government. It’s not because we hate the government, but because big government can easily crowd out other spheres of society. Conservatives believe government has a role in our lives, but we don’t think it should be running the show. We believe in the role of civil society and the church as institutions that can also offer help to the least of these in our society.

title: Breaking Bad Is What Happens When You Don’t Have Universal Healthcare
content:
Breaking Bad is one of the most popular TV series of the past twenty years.

It tells the story of Walter White and his descent from high school teacher to drug lord following a cancer diagnosis. The series is a fascinating look at how an ordinary person can turn into a scheming Machiavellian sociopath in the pursuit of money and power.

This is a common narrative from the series and to a certain extent, it’s right. As the series progresses, we see Walter turn more and more sinister. From coming across as weak at the start, he becomes the complete opposite by the end. So much so, he pushes away the ones he loves.

But, there is another way of looking at Breaking Bad . One I hadn’t considered until a while ago.

It’s a tale of how broken the American healthcare system is.

Think about it for a second. A respectable high school chemistry teacher creates illicit drugs in an attempt to fund his cancer treatment. It’s an insane proposition, but this is the reality of healthcare in America today.

I only realized this after reading Breaking Bad ’s Wikipedia page the other day. I live in the UK and soon realised this series could never be made here because we have universal healthcare.

If I’m ill, break my leg, or require cancer treatment, there’s no bill. Healthcare is free at the point of use. Sure, we contribute to the system via our taxes, but this is a fee almost everyone is willing to pay because it means the healthcare system is there for us should we need it.

That’s not the case in America unless you have insurance, or you’re fabulously wealthy. Realising this made me look at the series in a whole new light.

Breaking Bad is a fantastic series, but it’s also a damning indictment of modern America.

If I need medical care here in the UK, all I have to do is ring an ambulance or go to the hospital to be treated. I can do this in the knowledge I won’t be leaving with a gigantic bill that could bankrupt me.

Healthcare is free at the point of use for all citizens in the UK. Whether you’re rich or poor, employed or unemployed, old or young, it doesn’t matter. We all have the same right to access healthcare when we need it. There are a lot of things wrong in the UK, but we’ve got healthcare right.

Now, if you live in the US, or another country without universal healthcare, you might be wondering how we pay for this. It’s a legitimate question. Nothing is free and healthcare isn’t cheap.

Our National Health Service (the NHS) is funded mostly through general taxation and national insurance contributions. These contributions are taxes we pay to fund public services, such as our state pension and the NHS. How much you pay is determined by how much you earn and the employed, employers, and self-employed all contribute to the system.

A smaller amount is raised through patient charges, related to prescriptions and dental care . But that’s it. Everything else is funded through general taxation. All those who are eligible to pay tax contribute to funding a system that ensures everyone has equal access to healthcare.

It’s not perfect, the NHS could be improved , but it works. If the NHS were to be disbanded, which some politicians want to do, the uproar would be deafening. The NHS is the closest thing we have to religion here in the UK, and it’s beloved by a majority of citizens. As much as some people would like to see it die, it’s unlikely to happen anytime soon.

This is why I look at America with bafflement when it comes to healthcare. That the richest country in the world cannot fund a universal healthcare system is confusing. Surely some of the $934 billion military budgets could be diverted to set a system up? Introducing a general taxation system similar to what we have in the UK couldn’t be too difficult either.

Watching Breaking Bad , the absurdity of the American system became clearer to me. The show wouldn’t last for five seasons in the UK, it would be over in 10 minutes.

Here’s an example of how it would look:

Walter: Hi, I’m ringing to set up an appointment with my GP (General Practitioner, akin to a Physician in the US). I haven’t been feeling well recently and I’m worried it might be something serious.

Receptionist: No problem, let’s get you booked in for an appointment and get you checked out. How does this time next week sound?

Walter: That works for me, Thanks.

Cuts to Doctor’s office

Doctor: Ok, Mr. White, I’m concerned by what I’ve observed here today. I’m going to send your case to the specialists over at the hospital so they can take a further look at you and perform a biopsy. This should confirm whether your condition is serious or not.

Ok, I've simplified the process somewhat, but you get the idea. Once Walter received his cancer diagnosis, he’d be able to start treatment soon in the knowledge he doesn’t have to worry about how he’d pay for it. He wouldn’t need to think up a crazy scheme where he produces meth, because his healthcare is provided by the state.

This might seem like paradise or a socialist nightmare to an American, depending on your point of view, but it’s normal here. No, we don’t live in a utopian paradise, nor do we salute the hammer and sickle every morning, we live fairly ordinary lives without having to worry whether we can afford to be ill or not.

Crazy, eh?

The crazy thing about the healthcare debate in the US is the popularity of universal healthcare itself. According to one report in 2016 , 58% percent of respondents were in favor of universal healthcare. That’s important because the winner of the election that year, one Donald Trump, campaigned to repeal Obamacare .

A recent poll in September 2020 found 63% in favor of the idea. Even though the policy was popular among Republican voters, 54% did say the government “should continue to provide programs like Medicare and Medicaid for seniors and the very poor.”

But realistically, were universal healthcare to be implemented and people realise the days of scrambling to find ways to fund their treatments if they're not insured were over, they wouldn’t want it scrapped. The system would be popular across the political divide.

If Americans are looking for an example of what universal healthcare could deliver, they don’t need to look much further than the vaccination effort. Millions of Americans have been vaccinated in a matter of months at zero cost to them.

Imagine a system where this is extended beyond vaccines to all levels of healthcare. No longer would Americans put off treatments for ailments due to a lack of insurance. They’d be able to access the care they needed, whenever they needed it, all by paying a little bit extra in taxes each month.

Breaking Bad is an illustration of society with muddled priorities. The popularity of the show is founded on a premise that shouldn’t be a reality in the 21st century.

Instead of lapping up the entertainment on their TV screens, Americans should be on the streets demanding better. Take it from a Brit, universal healthcare is no socialist plot , nor is it a ‘ disaster ’.

It’s simply the most humane way to organise a society and ensures everyone can access the care they need and deserve. Sure, you might not get award-winning TV series highlighting the absurdity of American life, but you’d get better public services.

Even Walter White would agree that’s better than becoming a psychopathic drug lord to fund your cancer treatment.

title: Universal Health Care — Where the need arises
content:
Here’s the thing. Money is the primary goal and whatever the corporation is hawking is secondary to the amount they can get for it using the least expensive means possible to achieve the goal.

Historically corporations due to their focus on short term goals — making money first product second, they have sacrificed everything else for that goal. This is especially true in the healthcare industry. This is a complex equation of which there are many factors.

Besides healthcare as a human right here’s something else to put into the hopper. In my early 30s I lived in Stockton, California on the central valley. There is a kind of fog there colloquially named Tule Fog (pronounced tooley). It’s a winter ground fog that can lie close to the ground or rise up to about 100 feet or so. It tends to remain blanketing the Central Valley from November to March without break — as in no sunshine. After a while the fog admits an odor — the smell of exhaust fumes in the air. I surmised that the pollutants from internal combustion engines of cars bonded with the water molecules in the air forms this noxious and dangerous pollutant trapped there. About a year later I read a study from University of California at Davis that had done a study “proving” my common-sense hypothesis. The point here is that scientific experiments can be refuted by industries that pollute to keep their profit systems running while we suffer from a toxic environment adds insult to injury.

Since industry has been increasingly focused on short term profits they tend to ignore or cover-up the toxicity of the waste products they discard. Add increasing growth in the population, more toxicity and an increasingly dangerous and inhospitable environment for human survival (thus the Climate Crisis). Corporations suppress reports about their toxic waste so they can continue to make money. Toxic producing industries contribute to acute and chronic health problems. The growth model of the healthcare industry may be to perpetually solving health problems so they can make more money on sick people, at least those sick people that can afford a treatment. Healthcare’s philosophical underpinnings is to make more money, especially by denying benefits to those who are ill. You get the idea. It’s a form of gambling with health.

Corporations that can be assumed to pollute the environment by means of their product need to have a two-fold tax applied to them since money talks. One tax would go to cleaning up the environment and one tax would go towards paying for universal healthcare.

This is why healthcare is a human right. It is because systemic predatory capitalism will either purposefully, or by willful ignorance or by accident kill off those that cannot afford health insurance.

I don’t like Medicare for All. I do like the Japanese model for Universal Healthcare because it heavily regulates insurance providers by re-educating them to care by the will of the people for the common good. It includes a different iteration of the Corporations in a solution that benefits all the people.

Government — serving all the people uses its legislative authority to mold corporations to serve All The People rather than the rich and mega-rich. I was raised thinking this was a partnership between government, industry and all of us as citizens.

title: Instead of Universal Healthcare, We’re Subsidizing Insurance Companies.
content:
Of all the reasons I supported Bernie Sanders’ run for President in both 2016 and 2020, there’s no denying that his stance on healthcare was what drew me to his campaign in the first place. It is thanks to Bernie that Medicare for All was brought to the forefront of the conversation concerning healthcare, and Americans have begun to question a system in which a profit-motivated company gets such significant influence on their care. Unfortunately, President Joe Biden infamously vowed that he would veto medicare for all if it ever came to his desk, citing “cost”, but promised the American people he would fight for a public option. Well it appears as though the public option, even in the midst of a pandemic, is going to join the list of other campaign promises Biden intends to break. He won’t even lower Medicare eligibility. Not only that, but Biden has rejected calls from other members of his party and decided taxpayer money will go towards subsidizing private insurance companies instead.

To be clear, it’s not just Joe Biden responsible for this decision.

The Washington Post reports that Biden rejected calls coming from Bernie Sanders and other Democrats to expand Medicare in favor of Nancy Pelosi ’s plan to simply cover the costs of private insurance in an upcoming bill. $200 billion that instead of going towards Medicare, will be going in the pockets of private insurance executives.

An overhaul of prescription drug pricing is also out of the bill.

If nothing else, this story is just another devastating reminder of what happens when money is allowed to corrupt our politics. Taking money does not come without expectations. Are we honestly expected to believe that donations from pharmaceutical lobbyists to Super PACs and the candidates themselves has no influence on lawmakers standing in the way of Medicare expansion? Obviously, I’m glad that lawmakers are going to be providing assistance with health insurance for people who have lost their jobs. But shouldn’t we be disgusted that the health insurance industry is making sure they can cash in, and that are lawmakers are allowing them to?

Ah, and the pharmaceutical industry as well of course. They have bribed our politicians to ensure that they cannot even negotiate on prescription drug prices, and we’re not supposed to bat an eye when suddenly that provision is scrapped from the bill almost as soon as it was put in?

At some point, when people are dying as a direct result of these decisions, it has to be considered blood money.

It’s been twelve years since the American people were promised a public option, and we’re no closer to having that now than we were then, even with demands for Medicare for All. How much longer are we expected to wait? How much longer are we going to allow them to make excuses? Democratic politicians do not fear their base the way Republicans do, and perhaps that’s what they need. But if their base does not hold them accountable and instead says “vote blue no matter who”, how will anything get done?

title: Healthcare: The Present and Future
content:
Healthcare is a universal human right. According to the World Health Organization (WHO), health includes not just freedom from disease, but prosperous conditions for the soul*. Only under those conditions can all people live the abundant lives they deserve.

HealthSapiens envisions the democratization of healthcare: creating boundary-less freedom for choice and staying true to health and wellness principles for all. We are here to stay true to the ideals of healthcare through global collaboration and the progression of humankind, one patient at a time.

Creating an incentive-driven ecosystem where all players are treated equally and rewarded properly, we’re envisioning a transparent and sustainable healthcare system that embodies the following:

We advocate the shift from a break-fix model of healthcare focused on episodic and transaction-based treatments to one focused on prevention and the overall holistic health of populations.

“The right to health for all people means that everyone should have access to the health services they need, when and where they need them, without suffering financial hardship.” Dr. Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director, 10 December 2017

Our mission is to preserve the integrity of people’s health by creating a healthcare ecosystem that covers healthcare for all individuals from cradle to grave. This in turn incentivizes preventative care, therefore driving down costs and improving health in the long term.

title: Is healthcare a human right?
content:
Is healthcare a human right? The simplest answer is yes. The United Nations (UN) adopted the Universal Declaration of Human Rights in 1948 and it includes healthcare as a basic human right as stated below:

Article 25. (1) Everyone has the right to a standard of living adequate for the health and well-being of himself and of his family, including food, clothing, housing and medical care and necessary social services, and the right to security in the event of unemployment, sickness, disability, widowhood, old age or other lack of livelihood in circumstances beyond his control. (2) Motherhood and childhood are entitled to special care and assistance. All children, whether born in or out of wedlock, shall enjoy the same social protection.

Never mind the outdated patriarchal language using the masculine pronoun. So why is healthcare coverage still a debate? Everything I know about healthcare makes me confused about this question. I’ve been working in the healthcare field for over ten years. I’ve worked in community centers, hospitals, and for managed care. Nothing I’ve seen suggests that less health coverage is good for society. So instead of repeating all the same stories about why we need coverage, I decided to look into why we don’t need universal healthcare.

The first website I went to, ProCon.org , used the headline “Should All Americans Have the Right (Be Entitled) to Health Care?” As a member of the UN, it seems we’ve already answered this question because we should be following the Universal Declaration of Human Rights. But as anyone who has gone to the doctor in the United States without health insurance or a wad of cash knows these standards aren’t being met.

There are three common arguments against healthcare for all (aka Medicare for All, Single-Payor Healthcare, and Universal Healthcare) in the United States.

Cost is the number one argument against universal healthcare. Getting a clear estimate of what it would cost to provide healthcare to everyone in the U.S. is incredibly complicated. I have not found a reliable number, mostly because there are so many considerations. Any guess is hypothetical because we don’t know what a universal healthcare plan would cost but any consideration of cost has to include decreased administrative and advertising costs that private insurances have, the savings in bankruptcies from healthcare costs, the savings from people using preventative care rather than emergency services or worse, not getting care at all.

Another concern with universal healthcare is that the quality of care that people receive may drop. The argument is that when the market pushes medical advancements, quality is driven up because companies are competing to be the best. When the government interferes with the free market there is less motivation for innovation. Johnathan Cohan argues that while it’s possible that we could create a system with these consequences, we wouldn’t have to. Universal healthcare does not inevitably limit innovation. He points out that the largest source of medical research in the world is the National Institute of Health (NIH). There is no reason it would be impacted by a change in our healthcare system because it’s funding is completely separate. He also points out that the market will focus on short term financial gains rather than long term benefits, which is one of the reasons NIH is so critical to medical advancements.

Another quality concern is that the wait time for services may increase. Many countries with universal health care have longer wait times for appointments, particularly for specialists, than the United States. For example, average wait time to see a specialist in the U.S. is less than 3 weeks, compared to the more than 8 week wait in Canada where there is universal healthcare. Physicians for a National Health Program (PNHP) asserts that wait times are a result of management techniques, not an unavoidable consequence of providing healthcare. They clarify that the wait times in other countries often quoted are for non-emergent procedures like hip replacements and that wait time for urgent matters has not been an issue. Canada has been steadily improving their system to reduce wait times even for non-emergent care. PNHP also points out that the United States spends twice what Canada does per person on healthcare, which should be enough to develop a queuing system that works.

The argument that universal health care will bring us closer to socialism isn’t hypothetical in the same way as the financial and quality arguments. The fear of socialism can be addressed right now. The general idea in the socialism argument is that healthcare is a service and people should have to pay for it. If the government pays for it then we’re one step closer to socialism. This point of view assumes that socialism is bad. That’s a topic for another day so let’s set it aside and assume that we are trying to avoid socialism. Even in our capitalistic society, there are services that we all chip in on and let the government manage. The fire department is a great example. My taxes pay for the local fire department even though I have never called the fire department. I am paying for a service that other citizens use but I don’t. We could do that differently. We could have the fire department charge you when you call them out.

“9–1–1, what’s your emergency?”

“My house is on fire.”

“Okay, before I send the truck round, do you have fire department coverage or $5000 cash to cover this service?”

Most people feel like this is unreasonable because it is an emergency service that shouldn’t be withheld because of a person’s financial status. It’s also good for the community to promptly put out a fire because fire can spread from one house to another. The same argument can be made for healthcare. If we make medical services free the way that the fire department is, people wouldn’t wait until they are so sick that it is an emergency. Emergency care is much more expensive than preventative services. When people can’t pay their astronomical emergency bills, they go bankrupt and tax payers pick up the tab anyway. It’s more cost efficient (and humane) to pay for the cheaper, preventable services upfront — just like it’s more cost efficient to put out the first house fire than it is to have to rebuild the whole block.

It’s hard to make the case that healthcare isn’t a human right by any existing definition of human rights, but it’s clear we haven’t figured out how to protect that human right. We can’t pretend that there aren’t financial and quality issues that need to be considered but I would argue that they aren’t insurmountable. We have figured out how to pay for a massive and unnecessary military. Advances in weapons development hasn’t been stymied by the being the sole provider of military preparedness. We haven’t fallen to socialism by law enforcement being paid for by taxes. It’s a matter of priority. When universal healthcare becomes a priority for the United States, we will find a way to make it work.
