title: Biden’s Remarks on Immigration Stir Controversy, Sparking Diplomatic Response
content:
President Joe Biden’s recent comments at a campaign fundraising event have caused a stir, as he seemingly grouped key allies Japan and India with China and Russia, accusing them of being “xenophobic” and hindering their economic growth due to hostility towards immigrants.

While speaking at an event marking the start of Asian American, Native Hawaiian, and Pacific Islander Heritage Month, Biden highlighted the role of immigrants in bolstering the U.S. economy. He implied that countries like China, Japan, Russia, and India were struggling economically because of their reluctance to welcome immigrants.

The remarks, not captured on video or audio, have drawn attention, especially given Biden’s efforts to strengthen ties with Japan and India since taking office. Just weeks prior, Japanese Prime Minister Fumio Kishida was hosted at the White House for a state dinner, where the partnership between the two nations was celebrated. Similarly, Biden welcomed Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi for a state visit last year, emphasizing shared values and commitments to democracy.

The timing of Biden’s comments on Japan and India, particularly amid efforts to enhance cooperation in the Indo-Pacific region through initiatives like the Quad security grouping, has raised eyebrows.

In response, the White House sought to downplay the president’s remarks, emphasizing the broader point about the importance of immigration to the United States. National Security Council spokesman John Kirby reiterated the value of alliances with Japan and India, emphasizing the president’s respect for their contributions.

Japan, known for its low levels of migration compared to other Group of Seven nations, has been gradually increasing opportunities for immigrants to address demographic challenges. Meanwhile, India, with its burgeoning population, recently passed a controversial citizenship law that fast-tracks naturalization for non-Muslims from select neighboring countries, sparking debates about religious criteria for citizenship.

While Biden’s comments may have sparked diplomatic concerns, they also underscore the complex dynamics surrounding immigration policies and their implications for global relationships and economic development.

title: The Role of Immigration in the Fall of the Roman Empire
content:
They say that those who fail to learn from history are destined to repeat it. When I learned several years back about the factors that contributed to the decline and fall of Rome, I was not surprised at the role immigration played. What did — and still does — surprise me is how the immigration issue is never brought up as something that has historical precedents.

Immigration was not the sole factor in the fall of Rome, but it was definitely one of the factors that contributed to the fall of this once-great empire. And when one looks back at that period of history, it makes sense. (Common sense is no longer common, unfortunately.)

During the later years of the Roman Empire, particularly in the 4th and 5th centuries AD, the empire faced significant challenges from both external invasions and internal unrest. Here are a couple of the ways immigration played a role in these challenges. Look at the parallels to what’s been happening in Europe and the U.S. today.

The influx of immigrants placed strain on the Roman economy, particularly as the empire struggled to provide resources and employment for its growing population. Immigrants often settled in urban areas, leading to overcrowding, unemployment and social unrest. This economic strain further weakened the empire’s ability to defend itself against external threats. (Sound familiar?)

Immigration also brought about cultural and social changes within the Roman Empire. As immigrants settled in Roman territory, they brought with them their own languages, customs, and beliefs, leading to increased cultural diversity and, in some cases, tensions between different ethnic and religious groups. These divisions weakened the sense of unity and cohesion that had been essential to the stability of the empire.

We constantly hear people extol the virtues of diversity, but how is that working out in real life over in the EU which has embraced diversity to almost a radical degree? According to British social critic and author Douglas Murray:

But the argument for mass migration on the grounds of ‘diversity’ as being a good in itself ignores one huge and until recently unspeakable issue. Just as most cultures have good things to say for themselves, all have some bad and disagreeable things about them too. And while the positives can be stressed and exaggerated from the outset, any negatives take years to admit, if they are admitted at all.

It strikes me as strange that our culture has become so polarized that we’re unable to discuss issues like this without resorting to name-calling. If people suggest that our current levels of mass immigration may not be a good idea, they are labelled as racists or xenophobes.

In the last decades of the Roman Empire there were all kinds of groups fleeing into Roman territory seeking a better opportunity. Visigoths, Vandals and Huns came because they were fleeing the conflicts in their own lands. According to historians the pressure from these migrations contributed to the weakening and eventual collapse of central authority.

Immigration wasn’t the only thing that undermined the Roman Empire. There were other causes as well, including some quite familiar to us today like overexpansion, military overspending and government corruption. Nevertheless, immigration played a part.

We have legitimate reasons to be concerned about the direction things are going. Those speaking frankly may have useful insights on this matter and ought not be dismissed outright. My gut tells me things will be getting worse before they get better unless honest discussions are allowed to take place in our communities, cities and highest levels of government. Though I feel obligated to speak up, I’m less than optimistic.

title: Democrats are Soft on Immigration, and Ice Cream Causes Murder
content:
Did you know that Democrats are for open borders? Of course you did. Everyone knows that.

How do they know? Because whenever a Democrat is president, the immigration rate goes up. Or at least that’s what the trustworthy folks at Fox News tell us.

But seriously, in this case I have to admit the right-wing pundits have a point. Just take a look at the graph below. It shows the growth in the total foreign-born population — both documented and undocumented — per year from 1990 to 2022. The y-axis is in hundreds of thousands, so 10 = one million.

As you can see, during the 1990s, when Clinton was president, the foreign-born population grew by about 1.1 million per year. It was the largest absolute increase in America’s foreign-born population ever.

During, the Bush years, on the other hand, we see that the immigrant population grew less quickly, at about 900,000 people per year for his first term. There was a spike in 2006, but then a sharp drop at the end of his term.

In 2009 — Obama’s first year — we actually see the total foreign-born population shrink. But for the rest of his term it we see it climb back up in fits and starts. Then it slows significantly under Trump, before jumping again under Biden.

So that settles it, right? Democrats really are soft on immigration. Unless… there’s another explanation?

For years, students in first-year statistics classes have confronted an odd coincidence. During the hot summer months ice cream sales spike, and so do murders. Does ice cream fill people with murderous rage? Or does the looming specter of a violent death make us hungry for one last ice cream?

Neither, actually. The two are correlated, but there’s no causal relationship between them. Instead, each one is influenced by a third factor: hot weather. When it’s hot outside we’re more likely to want a cold treat. But we’re also more likely to congregate in the kinds of social contexts where interactions might escalate to violence.

As criminology professor Steven Messner put it ,

A prime reason murder peaks during this time has to do with the routines of people’s lives…. Summer is when people get together. More specifically, casual drinkers and drug users are more likely to go to bars or parties on weekends and evenings, as opposed to a Tuesday morning. These people in the social mix, flooding the city’s streets and neighborhood bars, feed the peak times for murder, experts say.

So maybe the relationship between Democratic presidents and growth in the immigrant population is like the relationship between ice cream and murder. But if that’s the case, then what’s the third factor that explains both?

In a word: growth. Since at least 1949, the U.S. economy has performed significantly better on a host of macroeconomic indicators whenever a Democrat has occupied the White House.

That trend has been slightly more pronounced in the period from 1981 to the present. There is a clear Democratic advantage in every one of the following categories of economic performance:

First, a couple of points. The word “real” here means adjusted for inflation, so it’s not the case that people’s wages grew more when Democrats were in office, but were swamped by inflation. They really grew more. Also, the idea that Democrats are bad for business is belied by the fact that private sector job growth and business investment both grew more when a Democrat was in power. Finally, the idea that incomes only grow more under Democrats because of welfare programs is refuted. Real income grew before accounting for government transfers.

Other statistics from the same study are equally interesting. The idea that Democrats are zero-sum egalitarians — tax and spend liberals who take from the rich and give to the poor — and that working class people who vote Republican just see themselves as “temporarily embarrassed millionaires,” also doesn’t hold up.

The fact is, whether we’re looking at the top one percent, the bottom ten percent, or anywhere in between, every income level has seen their real incomes rise more when a Democrat occupies the Oval Office.

And guess what else happens when America’s economy does so well. It’s no surprise. People want to come here.

Let’s look at the data on the foreign-born population again, but now let’s add in two important economic indicators: the unemployment rate and GDP growth .

As you can see, in the ’90s unemployment trended down, GDP growth trended up, and the immigrant population grew at a high, steady clip. It grew less quickly after the dot-com bubble burst, and fell again after the housing bubble burst, only to climb back following the passage of a massive stimulus bill that pulled the U.S. out of the Great Recession. Then it dipped again during COVID, bouncing back after another round of stimulus.

So maybe immigration doesn’t grow because Democrats are soft on the border. Maybe immigration grows because Democratic policies grow the economy better than Republican ones, and a strong economy attracts people to our shores.

Some of you might be tempted to look at this data and see a worrying trend. You see foreigners coming here to take advantage of opportunities that ought to be reserved for American citizens.

But here’s the truth: immigrants aren’t just attracted to America’s economic growth. They also contribute to it.

A 2023 study by economist Madeline Zavodny of the University of North Florida found that “Immigrants boost economic growth, employment growth and economic dynamism through their contributions to the workforce, entrepreneurial activities and purchases of goods and services.”

The analysis in this study also finds that immigrants may slow the offshoring of manufacturing activity by U.S. businesses, indicating the importance of immigration to increasing U.S. domestic manufacturing production. Metro areas with a higher share of immigrants have more dynamic economies and experience faster growth in the number of jobs created and new business establishments. During 2010 to 2019, foreign-born workers accounted for up to one-quarter of employment growth and up to three-quarters of the growth in business establishments in the 248 metro areas examined.

That’s quite a contrast with the claim that immigrants displace American workers. On the contrary, immigration and economic growth are part of a virtuous cycle, one that Democratic policies foster.

And how do Democrats foster growth? Not just by spending more than Republicans. The truth is both parties spend a lot. If anything, Democrats have been the more fiscally responsible party , with deficits growing more slowly during their tenures.

title: WE NEED IMMIGRANTS: Journalist Maria Hinojosa nails it with the proper immigration narrative.
content:
Anytime I see Maria Hinojosa on cable news, I know the segment will move from rhetoric parroting shallow and Right slanted hackery to the proper real-world fact-based narrative — here on immigration.

The mainstream media, often mislabeled as left-leaning, has been under scrutiny for The United States, a nation built by immigrants, continues to grapple with its immigration policies and narratives. Journalist María Hinojosa ’s recent commentary underscores immigrants’ crucial role in the country’s economy and society. Her insightful analysis of immigration is a clarion call for a more humane and practical approach, especially as the country faces demographic and economic challenges.

Hinojosa’s perspective is vital in today’s media landscape, where diverse voices and experiences are essential for comprehensive news coverage. She highlights the economic necessity of integrating the 10 to 11 million undocumented immigrants into American society. These individuals, many of whom have lived in the U.S. for decades, contribute significantly to the economy, albeit often in the shadows. Granting them a pathway to citizenship would recognize their contributions and bolster the economy by bringing them into the formal labor market.

As Hinojosa points out, the current immigration enforcement system is marked by inefficiency and confusion. The largest law enforcement agency in the country, the Border Patrol, struggles with clear policies and humane practices. This dysfunction exacerbates the challenges faced by immigrants, many of whom now seek out Border Patrol agents rather than evade them, indicating a shift from a narrative of criminality to one of desperation and hope.

Hinojosa’s call for President Joe Biden to take decisive action on immigration through an executive order is particularly poignant. With legislative gridlock on Capitol Hill , executive action could provide the necessary impetus for comprehensive immigration reform. This would involve rejecting the fear-mongering narrative that paints immigrants as threats and instead recognizing their invaluable contributions to the nation’s fabric.

The economic arguments for immigration are robust. Immigrants fill essential roles in various sectors, from agriculture to technology. They bring skills, labor, and innovation, driving economic growth and cultural enrichment. S tudies consistently show that immigrants contribute more taxes than they consume in public services , debunking the myth that they drain resources. The aging native-born population and declining birth rates mean that immigrants are crucial for maintaining a dynamic workforce and sustaining economic growth.

Beyond economics, there are the moral and ethical dimensions of immigration. The United States prides itself on being a beacon of hope and opportunity. Yet, the current treatment of immigrants often contradicts these values. Compassion and empathy should guide immigration policies, reflecting the country’s commitment to human rights and dignity. This approach would align with American ideals and foster social cohesion and mutual respect. Our atonement for our formation demands that.

The political landscape, however, remains fraught with challenges. Any executive action on immigration will likely face immediate legal challenges, particularly from conservative factions. Nevertheless, leadership involves taking bold steps in the face of adversity. By championing comprehensive immigration reform, President Biden could shift the national narrative, emphasizing the positive impact of immigrants and countering xenophobic rhetoric.

Hinojosa’s commentary also highlights the broader issue of media representation. Diverse journalists bring unique perspectives that enrich public discourse and challenge prevailing biases . Their contributions are essential for a well-informed citizenry and a vibrant democracy. Ensuring that these voices are heard is crucial for a balanced and nuanced understanding of complex issues like immigration.

María Hinojosa’s insights on immigration offer a compelling narrative highlighting the economic, social, and moral imperatives for comprehensive reform. Immigrants are integral to the American story, and their contributions should be recognized and celebrated. By embracing a humane and pragmatic approach to immigration, the United States can uphold its values and ensure a prosperous future for all its residents. The call for executive action underscores the urgency of this issue and the need for bold leadership in these challenging times.

title: The Lesser of Evils
content:
(Before I begin this rant, I need to make something very, very clear. Almost every person that I care about is an immigrant. The most important people in my life are from somewhere else. Some are undocumented, some are not. Most work very hard to eke out a living. Some started out as immigrants, became Legal Residents, and some are becoming, or are now U.S. Citizens. My son is Bi-National. I have traveled quite a bit, seen how other people have to live, and I KNOW how good we have it here in the U.S.

So, if you’ve got strong opinions about any of these people, or believe radical shit about how they are stealing jobs, (they are not), robbing other Americans of their benefits, (they are not), or some other poppycock or bullshit, please stow that shit. I don’t have the patience or bandwidth to deal with racist, anti-immigrant bullshit, so just stow it, and keep reading. Or, if you are inclined to share your negative ideas and opinions, please fuck right off, and be blocked.)

Now, I believe that everyone, regardless of race, color and all the usual designators, deserves to have a safe place to live, food to eat, and some semblance of sanity in their lives. In a perfect world, we could travel freely throughout the world, move from place to place if we choose, and explore this amazing world at our leisure. Unfortunately, we don’t live in that perfect world. There are no unicorns, or pots of gold at the end of rainbows.

We live in a world that is rapidly collapsing into chaos. Climate change is forecast to make a large part of the world Climate Refugees, very possibly if not probably in the very near future. Look at the news, and then tell me I’m wrong. Whether it is fire, flood, earthquakes, volcanos, or various other weather or natural issues, these events are displacing people all over the world.

Economically, there are very few countries that I know of where the people are doing well, living well, enjoying all that the world has to offer, free from existential threats of one kind or another. Be it hunger, or violence, or weather events or racism or misogyny or political insanity of one kind or another, the world is metaphorically (or literally) burning everywhere. People are dying everywhere.

The world population is estimated to be eight billion people. And growing rapidly. Some people (the infamous “they”) say that there are more than enough financial resources to end hunger, but these resources are being hoarded by (again, “they” say), less than one-half of one percent of the population. Or some shit like that. More on that in another rant.

Back to this rant. The point of this conversation for me is as follows:

I agree with Biden’s move regarding immigration. I know, I know. I can hear the uproar, and I understand it. My initial reaction was to be angry at Biden.

How the fuck can he do this?

How can he send these poor sods to purgatory on the northern border of Mexico?

How can he sentence some of them to heat illnesses, sex traders or death while waiting to be processed?

But…

Life under the orange shitbag will be much worse.

If Biden loses this election, we are truly and thoroughly fucked. Immigrants will go from the frying pan into the fire. And as an ally, any one of us who supports sane and humane immigration policies will never see them. Any one of us who supports ANY sane policies, will be persecuted, along with everyone else who opposes the orange shitbag.

No matter my personal feelings around some of Biden’s policies (GAZA), he is far and away the lesser of the evils. I don’t necessarily think he’s evil. More like he is dated. Again, that is another rant.

Biden has to win this election. If he needs to implement some restrictive policies around immigration to enable himself to win the election, so be it. We can fight to change them after he is re-elected.

The fucking alternative is not an option. Not for me.

Keep it between the ditches!

Countries like Afghanistan, Laos, and Cambodia are also potentially banned even though their real transgression is that the U.S. bombed these countries into the stone age pursuing some ruthless foreign policy. Laos is still full of bombs dropped by the U.S. 40 + years ago, some of which still can detonate and injure or kill people.

Nothing is surprising about this. America’s foreign policy has been poison for many places in the world. And then there is this: the American President is a dangerous, reckless grifter. title: Are Undocumented Individuals Good for the US?
content:
In the heated landscape of American politics, the conversation surrounding undocumented individuals often becomes ensnared in the web of MAGA-driven rhetoric, painting a picture that is far from the complex reality these individuals embody within the United States.

Despite the loud voices calling for strict immigration laws and portraying undocumented people as a burden on the American system, a closer look reveals a narrative that is radically different from the one spread by some political factions.

Undocumented workers play an integral, and often overlooked, role in the American economy.

They contribute billions of dollars annually in taxes, including income, property, and sales taxes, despite their ineligibility for many of the benefits these taxes support. The Institute on Taxation and Economic Policy (ITEP) reports that undocumented immigrants contribute approximately $11.74 billion a year in state and local taxes alone.

This figure challenges the misleading narrative that these individuals take more from the system than they contribute.

Moreover, undocumented workers are pivotal in several key sectors of the economy, such as agriculture, construction, and services, where they often take on roles that are hard to fill.

Their labor is a cornerstone in these industries, supporting rural economies and ensuring the continued production of goods and services critical to American life. The reliance of certain sectors on undocumented labor underscores not only their economic contribution but also the nuanced interdependence between American society and these individuals.

The vilification of undocumented individuals as political pawns in a broader anti-immigration agenda is both unjust and counterproductive.

This strategy not only dehumanizes millions of people but also obfuscates the real economic and social contributions they make to the country. The narrative being pushed by some political groups, including prominent MAGA voices, ignores the complexity of immigration issues and the humanity of those involved, opting instead for a simplistic and divisive approach that serves political ends rather than the national interest.

It is imperative for the discourse surrounding undocumented individuals to shift towards a more balanced and fact-based conversation that acknowledges their contributions and the challenges they face.

Immigration policy should be informed by the realities of the economy and the values of fairness and compassion, rather than being driven by unfounded fears and political rhetoric.

The question of whether undocumented individuals are “good” for the U.S. is a reductive framing of a complex issue.

A more apt inquiry would consider how the U.S. can create immigration policies that reflect the economic realities and moral values of a nation built on the principles of opportunity and justice for all.

The contributions of undocumented workers to the American economy and society are undeniable, and it is high time that this reality is recognized and reflected in the nation’s policies and discourse.

title: Is immigration bad for the economy?
content:
In recent years there has been a wave of attacks against immigration. One of the biggest reasons was the case for jobs and wages. Many countries started closing their borders and made very big political campaigns against immigration from Donald Trump attack on Mexican workers, France, to Britain with Brexit, Israel on Africans refugees and immigrants and there are many more.

In this article I’m going to argue why immigration — specifically on low-skilled labor will most likely not hurt the native citizens employment and wages.

The most known argument against immigrants economically is taken from the supply-demand formula. Meaning, immigrants will increase the supply for workers and therefore wages will decrease.

However, the job market is a very different market than a regular commodity as Karl Marx has once claimed.

The labor market has many sides and you can’t just look at it as one would look at the market of Bananas for example.

1. Hiring is different from buying products like Bananas. Many times, workers have contracts and it is not so easy to fire workers. Also Keynes said long before that wages are “sticky”. Moreover, firms care about more aspects than just wages. Workers develop human relationship with employers. Furthermore, most employees for example demand experience and spend resources on finding new employees, such as time for interviews, ads, tests and time is needed for a new employee to learn the new job.

2. immigrants are also consumers. Therefore, the new immigrants will buy products as well and increase the aggregate demand in the market. The new demand for products will increase the demand for workers as well.

a. Supply Increase diagram — wages fall to S’ and W’.

b. Demand Increase — wages are rising to S’ and W’’.

3. Investments — Common production functions predict a constant capital to labor ratio, which predicts that higher L will eventually mean more investment and thus more labor demand (since the value of each worker is larger when more machines are around).

When more workers are available, entrepreneurs respond by expanding their capacity or starting new firms up. The creation of new jobs will then raise wages for both native and migrant workers.

4. Firms can reduce labor costs by hiring immigrant workers at a lower wage with respect to natives. As a result, Firms then take advantage of this cost cut by creating complementarity/support jobs largely led by native-born workers, who will not experience job losses or wage cuts.

As the Nobel laurate economists “Abhijit V. Banerjee and Esther Duflo” claimed:

“Employers may want to reorganize production to make effective of the new workers. Since many immigrants at first don’t speak the language for example, in order to hire them, the employer will need to create new roles for native workers.”

A study in Denmark checked the effects of the new immigrants and discovered that the new immigrants created new job opportunities for natives and moved from manual to nonmanual jobs and changed employers.

This is from their conclusion:

“Immigration also increased native low skilled wages and made them more likely to move out of the municipality. We do not observe an increased probability of unemployment, nor a decrease in employment for unskilled natives.”

Link to paper: http://ftp.iza.org/dp8961.pdf

What this suggests, is that natives and immigrants do not have to compete directly, they may perform different tasks. Immigrants will specialize in jobs requiring less communication, and natives in ones that do.

5. Also, the increase of the labor supply of immigrants can boost new jobs that weren’t available in large before, since native-workers don’t want to work in them for reasons other than just wage and immigrants are often less choosy. Such as cleaning, helping sick or old people, help with babies, and more. This supply boost decreases its cost for natives and therefore, lets native workers become more productive and have more time to increase their income, often high-skilled women.

6. Many times, the ones who migrate are bringing with them important skills due to the hard process of the immigration needed such as ambition and patience.

These skills will often help immigrants to raise children which will become job creators themselves.

The well-known Jeff Bezos for example, takes his name from his stepfather, the Cuban immigrant, Mike Bezos.

Before we finish,

In order to see if the theory is also true in practice, we need to check the empirics.

A review of the literature finds little evidence of a wage-depressing effect of immigration because immigrants are absorbed into the receiving economy through a series of adjustments by firms and other workers. Once these adjustments are accounted for, the wages of native workers, even workers with skills similar to those of immigrants, do not change much in response to immigration.

Borjas (2003) study is the most controversial one, as he found a large negative effect. However, economic studies found them missing. As Peri puts it: “In particular, their (Borjas) findings of a large negative impact on wages of less educated immigrants is largely driven by an imprecise and, by many economists, to erroneous estimate of the elasticity of substitution between workers with a high school degree and workers with no degree. Moreover, in Borjas (2003) the failure to account for capital adjustment in the short run adds an implausibly large negative effect to native wages in the short run.”

Indeed, “the labor demand curve is downward sloping”, as Borjas (2003) puts it, but one should not forget that the demand for each factor (type of workers) shifts when the supplies of other factors change.

Immigrants due to mostly language barriers and other necessary production skills (interactive skills) and also native school diploma are assumed as imperfect substitutes as was mentioned also by Catalina Amuedo-Dorantes. Furthermore, Borjas made a good point that if the immigrants are heterogenous to the natives, this assumption needs to be reviewed due to more similar skills. Therefore, the more comparable advantage, the better it is for the natives.

As shown in Peri and Sparber (2009), immigrants who do not speak the language of the host country are concentrated in more manual and less interactive tasks (especially among less educated groups) and tend to be paid lower salaries than natives. This increases the supply of manual-routine occupations relative to the supply of abstract-complex ones.

Nevertheless, even economists like Borjas who are negative on immigration, believe immigration impact on wages to be very small and most likely to stabilize in the future with the adjustment of new capital.

Gilad

The information I gathered was taken from economists such as “Abhijit V. Banerjee and Esther Dufloand”, “David Card”, “Giovanni Peri” and more.

Here are some empirical papers on the subject:

Reference:

Borjas (2003) https://www.nber.org/papers/w9755.pdf

title: A World With Open Borders
content:
In my last article, I argued that migration of low-skilled workers is not bad for the economy in the macro-level and could even be good. However, after my last article I felt maybe the benefits of it are not as known, if immigration is not bad in both the empirics and theory, what would happen if the whole world would enable “open borders” agenda, how big of an effect could it have? Is it just a small part in fighting global poverty and inequality or could it have a big effect?

Apparently, there has been some fascinating research on this subject, and it is a thing we as a society should definitely know better.

First of all,

To clarify, “open borders” means that people are free to move to find work. It does not mean “no borders” or “the abolition of the nation-state”.

After clarifying this notion, why would we even want open-borders?

According to the “economist”, a world of free movement would be $78 trillion richer. Yes, open borders policy would make the world richer by 78 trillion $.

In contrast, Harvard Economist Lant Pritchett, this number would be 65 Trillion$. Still a huge amount.

4 different studies have shown that, depending on the level of movement in the global labor market, the estimated growth of the world’s GDP would be in the range of 67% to 147%. Open borders will make the world around twice as rich.

How would it affect the poor countries? An economist at the University of Wisconsin has calculated that open borders would boost the income of an average Angolian by 10,000$ a year, and of a Nigerian by 22,000 $ annually.

One of the biggest questions economists face is the question of poverty. How can we end it? The capitalist world has made an amazing impact on poverty. Just from 1990 more than 1 billion more people have moved out of what the World Bank considers “extreme poverty”. And now, only 9% of the world population is considered as living in extreme poverty. The World Bank considers this kind of poverty, a paycheck of just 1.9 US Dollars a day.

In order to understand why some countries are rich and some are poor, this would take a much longer explanation, but open borders could let citizens in the countries who stayed poor get much richer, and help people from poor countries become more productive as they move from a poor country to a rich one : As they join a labor market with ample capital, efficient firms and a predictable legal system.

In order for a market economy to work well, as Adam Smith has mentioned already in the 18th century, there must be a law enforcement and legal system. Otherwise, there will be no trust, this as a result will disable investments and therefore economic growth.

Moreover, open-borders will decrease the global inequality by far and will create a much better mobility. If you were born in a poor country, you can still succeed.

We as citizens that were born in the rich world take it for granted, however, it was just luck. Why would we want a world where the biggest thing that determines our future is where and to whom we are born?

I mean, you could be thinking for yourself, opening borders would make the rich people much poorer. But as I showed in my last article, this in reality is usually not true.

In the reality of today, the poorest Billion consume only 1% out of the global consumption, where the richest 1 billion account for 72% of it.

We are so angry about inequality within our countries (within race and genders) but are so indifferent about the global inequality. We spend much more time to attack inner problems and therefore often forget the others. For example, an American worker earns three times as much for the same work as a Bolivian, even when they have the same skill level, same age etc. The economist Michael Clemens and his two co-researches conclude their research on border wage discrimination of the U.S with this: “This means that those barriers(barrier for people to move to different countries) create one of the largest distortions in any global market, create the largest form of wage discrimination observed in today’s world, and create what is apparently the largest antipoverty intervention available for people from poor countries”.

Since we dealt with the economics of immigration in the last article, and we now know the benefits of open-borders on the global poverty level and inequality, I want to tackle here some other social questions in order to further the conversation more by showing the data:

According to the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), across Europe, the average immigrant household contributes more in taxes than they take in benefit. The same conclusion was also in a study made on Britain. However, the study also found that immigrants who migrate with children and in an older age did use more.

In overall, people who migrate are in most cases young people who are looking for better lives for themselves, the ones who migrate with family are more likely to come as refugees.

Anyway, even if a country still doubts it and prefer to give less tax benefits to migrants, they can. For example, only immigrants who paid 30,000 $ in taxes will be eligible for government benefits, that’s still a win-win.

Since the economic benefits from immigration is already well researched, some people might argue that immigrants increase crime and terrorism and therefore the economic outcome doesn’t matter.

2. Before we go into seeing the evidence, there is a bigger question to ask, is terrorism really a huge threat as usually perceived? If one would have to decide by what we see in the media, the answer was probably yes. Nevertheless, according to the data, it is definitely not.

Between 1975 and 2015, the annual odds of being killed in the U.S in an attack by foreigners or immigrants was just 1 in 3,609,709. And if we remove 9.11 from the data, only an average of one a year, were killed by foreign-born terrorist in those years.

Out of a population bigger than 300 million. Therefore — 1/300,000,000

Just for perspective, the odds of being struck by a lightning in the U.S is 1/1,222,000.

Worldwide, the proportion of people dying from terrorism is 0.03% out of the total deaths, and most of the deaths are coming from the middle east, in countries like Syria, Egypt and Iraq. Not even Israel.

In comparison, 35% of the death incidents reported in New York Times are caused by Terrorism .

Are immigrants importing terrorism? This subject had many interests in recent years in some of the developing countries. Leaders like Donald Trump argue that the people who migrate are terrorists and criminals.

Is it also true in the evidence?

The evidence that checked this connection is pretty divided, depends on which countries one focus.

The ones who saw a small positive effect, was based on OECD countries alone.

However, the ones that saw no evidence checked a much wider number of countries, 170.

This was the conclusion of of the economists “Andrew C. Forrester, Benjamin Powell, Alex Nowrasteh, & Michelangelo Landgrave”:

“we find no empirical evidence to suggest that increases in the share of immigrants from abroad is significantly correlated with higher rates of terrorism. These results hold for immigrants from both Muslim majority and conflict-torn countries of origin.”

Furthermore, there is even a new research from the University of Warwick on migration flows between 145 countries shows that immigration is actually associated with a decline in terrorist acts. They conclude this, by the increase in economic development the migrants have.

So from a look on the data, one cannot really conclude if immigration lead to more terrorism. However, and more importantly, does restrict border control help to prevent terrorist attacks?

The restrict border control in the U.S started mostly after the 9/11 terror attack.

A fun fact: Not one of the 9/11 hijackers was an immigrant, and all had entered the United States on temporary visas.

Moreover, some think-tanks even argue that restrictive policy could actually increase global terrorism. “The more we act in ways that support the picture West vs Islam, the more likely it will be that al-Qaida and other groups are able to attract support for their terrorist cause. “

As Nora Demleitner (2004: 572) points out “many of the terrorism prevention mechanisms instituted in the wake of 9/11 proved fruitful in detecting undocumented aliens, but not terrorists.”

Also, from a look at the recent research that found a positive effect, when they checked what caused the immigrants to become terrorists, they found that it wasn’t because of them, and their origin. T his is from the political scientist conclusion : Richard J McAlexander (2019) — “migration does not cause domestic terrorism because of the migrants themselves, but because of reactionary elements within the host country.”

Treating certain ethnicities as “suspects” could arguably be counterproductive as it creates a more polarized society and could lead nonetheless to extremism and more terror.

In addition, the targeting of certain ethnic communities can lead to the loss of support from their home countries that is vital in the fight against international terrorism. The danger is especially acute and ironic for refugees, as those fleeing terror become the first victims of the fight against it.

Again, no. According to the data, people making a new life in the U.S commit fewer offenses and less frequently end up in prison than the native population. Even as the number of illegal immigrants tripled between 1990 and 2013 to more than eleven million, the crime rate reversed.

The evidence, based on empirical studies of many countries, indicates that there is no simple link between immigration and crime, but legalizing the status of immigrants has beneficial effects on crime rates.

W ill they never go back? Actually, open-borders promote immigrants return. The border between Mexico and the U.S for example in the 1960s, millions of Mexicans crossed it, but in time 85% returned home. Paradoxically, since the U.S militarized the border especially after 9/11, only 7% of illegal Mexicans ever go back.

Many left already before the 1965 immigration law has passed:

The number of illegal immigrants actually rose after 9/11.

The increased costs and risks led migrants to minimize the number of times they crossed the border.

Even if open-borders will be reality , lots of poor people won’t move to a different country. Lots of people just don’t want to leave their country and their communities. Furthermore, travel is expensive and moving demands some valuable skills.

Nevertheless, a huge unchecked migration wave could certainly hurt social cohesion. With that said, we must remember, migration is the strongest weapon against global poverty and inequality, and even just a small change can have a huge effect on many people’s lives. According to Clemens, the benefits are huge even for a more modest loosening of restrictions on immigration. His research suggests that allowing just 5 percent of the people now living in poor countries to work temporarily or permanently in richer countries would add trillions of dollars to the global economy. The economic gains would be greater than those from dismantling every remaining barrier to trade and investment around the world.

A World With Open Borders In my last article, I argued that migration of low-skilled workers is not bad for the economy in the macro-level and could even be good. However, after my last article I felt maybe the benefits of it are not as known, if immigration is not bad in both the empirics and theory, what would happen if the whole world would enable “open borders” agenda, how big of an effect could it have? Is it just a small part in fighting global poverty and inequality or could it have a big effect?

Apparently, there has been some fascinating research on this subject, and it is a thing we as a society should definitely know better.

First of all,

To clarify, “open borders” means that people are free to move to find work. It does not mean “no borders” or “the abolition of the nation-state”.

After clarifying this notion, why would we even want open-borders?

According to the “economist”, a world of free movement would be $78 trillion richer. Yes, open borders policy would make the world richer by 78 trillion $.

In contrast, Harvard Economist Lant Pritchett, this number would be 65 Trillion$. Still a huge amount.

4 different studies have shown that, depending on the level of movement in the global labor market, the estimated growth of the world’s GDP would be in the range of 67% to 147%. Open borders will make the world around twice as rich.

How would it affect the poor countries? An economist at the University of Wisconsin has calculated that open borders would boost the income of an average Angolian by 10,000$ a year, and of a Nigerian by 22,000 $ annually.

One of the biggest questions economists face is the question of poverty. How can we end it? The capitalist world has made an amazing impact on poverty. Just from 1990 more than 1 billion more people have moved out of what the World Bank considers “extreme poverty”. And now, only 9% of the world population is considered as living in extreme poverty. The World Bank considers this kind of poverty, a paycheck of just 1.9 US Dollars a day.

In order to understand why some countries are rich and some are poor, this would take a much longer explanation, but open borders could let citizens in the countries who stayed poor get much richer, and help people from poor countries become more productive as they move from a poor country to a rich one : As they join a labor market with ample capital, efficient firms and a predictable legal system.

In order for a market economy to work well, as Adam Smith has mentioned already in the 18th century, there must be a law enforcement and legal system. Otherwise, there will be no trust, this as a result will disable investments and therefore economic growth.

Moreover, open-borders will decrease the global inequality by far and will create a much better mobility. If you were born in a poor country, you can still succeed.

We as citizens that were born in the rich world take it for granted, however, it was just luck. Why would we want a world where the biggest thing that determines our future is where and to whom we are born?

I mean, you could be thinking for yourself, opening borders would make the rich people much poorer. But as I showed in my last article, this in reality is usually not true.

In the reality of today, the poorest Billion consume only 1% out of the global consumption, where the richest 1 billion account for 72% of it.

We are so angry about inequality within our countries (within race and genders) but are so indifferent about the global inequality. We spend much more time to attack inner problems and therefore often forget the others. For example, an American worker earns three times as much for the same work as a Bolivian, even when they have the same skill level, same age etc. The economist Michael Clemens and his two co-researches conclude their research on border wage discrimination of the U.S with this: “This means that those barriers(barrier for people to move to different countries) create one of the largest distortions in any global market, create the largest form of wage discrimination observed in today’s world, and create what is apparently the largest antipoverty intervention available for people from poor countries”.

Since we dealt with the economics of immigration in the last article, and we now know the benefits of open-borders on the global poverty level and inequality, I want to tackle here some other social questions in order to further the conversation more by showing the data:

According to the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), across Europe, the average immigrant household contributes more in taxes than they take in benefit. The same conclusion was also in a study made on Britain. However, the study also found that immigrants who migrate with children and in an older age did use more.

In overall, people who migrate are in most cases young people who are looking for better lives for themselves, the ones who migrate with family are more likely to come as refugees.

Anyway, even if a country still doubts it and prefer to give less tax benefits to migrants, they can. For example, only immigrants who paid 30,000 $ in taxes will be eligible for government benefits, that’s still a win-win.

Since the economic benefits from immigration is already well researched, some people might argue that immigrants increase crime and terrorism and therefore the economic outcome doesn’t matter.

2. Before we go into seeing the evidence, there is a bigger question to ask, is terrorism really a huge threat as usually perceived? If one would have to decide by what we see in the media, the answer was probably yes. Nevertheless, according to the data, it is definitely not.

Between 1975 and 2015, the annual odds of being killed in the U.S in an attack by foreigners or immigrants was just 1 in 3,609,709. And if we remove 9.11 from the data, only an average of one a year, were killed by foreign-born terrorist in those years.

Out of a population bigger than 300 million. Therefore — 1/300,000,000

Just for perspective, the odds of being struck by a lightning in the U.S is 1/1,222,000.

Worldwide, the proportion of people dying from terrorism is 0.03% out of the total deaths, and most of the deaths are coming from the middle east, in countries like Syria, Egypt and Iraq. Not even Israel.

In comparison, 35% of the death incidents reported in New York Times are caused by Terrorism .

Are immigrants importing terrorism? This subject had many interests in recent years in some of the developing countries. Leaders like Donald Trump argue that the people who migrate are terrorists and criminals.

Is it also true in the evidence?

The evidence that checked this connection is pretty divided, depends on which countries one focus.

The ones who saw a small positive effect, was based on OECD countries alone.

However, the ones that saw no evidence checked a much wider number of countries, 170.

This was the conclusion of of the economists “Andrew C. Forrester, Benjamin Powell, Alex Nowrasteh, & Michelangelo Landgrave”:

“we find no empirical evidence to suggest that increases in the share of immigrants from abroad is significantly correlated with higher rates of terrorism. These results hold for immigrants from both Muslim majority and conflict-torn countries of origin.”

Furthermore, there is even a new research from the University of Warwick on migration flows between 145 countries shows that immigration is actually associated with a decline in terrorist acts. They conclude this, by the increase in economic development the migrants have.

So from a look on the data, one cannot really conclude if immigration lead to more terrorism. However, and more importantly, does restrict border control help to prevent terrorist attacks?

The restrict border control in the U.S started mostly after the 9/11 terror attack.

A fun fact: Not one of the 9/11 hijackers was an immigrant, and all had entered the United States on temporary visas.

Moreover, some think-tanks even argue that restrictive policy could actually increase global terrorism. “The more we act in ways that support the picture West vs Islam, the more likely it will be that al-Qaida and other groups are able to attract support for their terrorist cause. “

As Nora Demleitner (2004: 572) points out “many of the terrorism prevention mechanisms instituted in the wake of 9/11 proved fruitful in detecting undocumented aliens, but not terrorists.”

Also, from a look at the recent research that found a positive effect, when they checked what caused the immigrants to become terrorists, they found that it wasn’t because of them, and their origin. T his is from the political scientist conclusion : Richard J McAlexander (2019) — “migration does not cause domestic terrorism because of the migrants themselves, but because of reactionary elements within the host country.”

Treating certain ethnicities as “suspects” could arguably be counterproductive as it creates a more polarized society and could lead nonetheless to extremism and more terror.

In addition, the targeting of certain ethnic communities can lead to the loss of support from their home countries that is vital in the fight against international terrorism. The danger is especially acute and ironic for refugees, as those fleeing terror become the first victims of the fight against it.

Again, no. According to the data, people making a new life in the U.S commit fewer offenses and less frequently end up in prison than the native population. Even as the number of illegal immigrants tripled between 1990 and 2013 to more than eleven million, the crime rate reversed.

The evidence, based on empirical studies of many countries, indicates that there is no simple link between immigration and crime, but legalizing the status of immigrants has beneficial effects on crime rates.

W ill they never go back? Actually, open-borders promote immigrants return. The border between Mexico and the U.S for example in the 1960s, millions of Mexicans crossed it, but in time 85% returned home. Paradoxically, since the U.S militarized the border especially after 9/11, only 7% of illegal Mexicans ever go back.

Many left already before the 1965 immigration law has passed:

The number of illegal immigrants actually rose after 9/11.

The increased costs and risks led migrants to minimize the number of times they crossed the border.

Even if open-borders will be reality , lots of poor people won’t move to a different country. Lots of people just don’t want to leave their country and their communities. Furthermore, travel is expensive and moving demands some valuable skills.

Nevertheless, a huge unchecked migration wave could certainly hurt social cohesion. With that said, we must remember, migration is the strongest weapon against global poverty and inequality, and even just a small change can have a huge effect on many people’s lives. According to Clemens, the benefits are huge even for a more modest loosening of restrictions on immigration. His research suggests that allowing just 5 percent of the people now living in poor countries to work temporarily or permanently in richer countries would add trillions of dollars to the global economy. The economic gains would be greater than those from dismantling every remaining barrier to trade and investment around the world.

Gilad

title: Is Immigration Good or Bad for The Economy?
content:
With strong opinions on both sides of the argument, immigration has been a contentious topic for decades. While some claim that immigrants hurt the economy, others insist that they are a key driver of development and innovation. So, is immigration good or bad for the economy?

In this article, I’ll cover the economic advantages and costs of immigration, evaluate the influence of immigration on taxes, innovation, the labor market, social welfare, and globalization, and answer common misunderstandings about the issue. I’ll also talk about how immigration affects a country’s cultural identity.

Let’s take a moment to define what I mean by immigration before I get into the specifics. Immigration is the transfer of individuals from one nation to another with the purpose of settling down and finding employment there. People who immigrate might come from a variety of backgrounds, including skilled workers, refugees, and asylum seekers. In recent years, the subject of immigration has attracted more attention as the number of individuals travelling to other nations has grown.

Immigration’s effect on the economy is a complicated problem with no simple solutions. To better understand the economic impacts of immigration, we can examine the data that is currently available.

Research continually demonstrates that immigration may have large economic advantages, despite the divisive discussion around it. For instance, a recent study by the National Bureau of Economic Research discovered that immigrants make a considerable contribution to job creation and economic development in the United States.

Immigrants support economic growth through innovation in addition to job creation. Immigrants have indeed started many prosperous enterprises, and they are disproportionately represented among US patent holders and innovators. For example, the co-founder of Google, Sergey Brin, was an immigrant from Russia.

In addition, immigrants contribute to the economy by paying taxes. A new analysis by the Institute on Taxation and Economic Policy (ITEP) estimates that unauthorized immigrants pay $11.6 billion in taxes annually on their own. Taxes on sales, income, and real estate are all included in this. Additionally, immigrants are net contributors to social welfare programs, which mean they provide more to the government via taxes than they do through benefits.

Despite these advantages for the economy, there are still misunderstandings regarding how immigration affects the economy. One widespread myth is that immigrants rob native-born employees of their employment. However, studies demonstrate that immigrants often fill positions that native-born employees are unable or unwilling to do. For instance, despite labor shortages in fields like agriculture, construction, and healthcare, immigrants are overrepresented in these fields.

Another fallacy is the idea that immigration reduces native-born employees’ salaries. Recent research, however, indicates that immigration has little to no effect on native-born employees’ salaries. According to a recent research by the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, for instance, the overall effect of immigration on wages is little, and any adverse impacts are mostly seen by low-skilled native-born employees.

Immigration may have a positive impact on the economy by stimulating innovation, employment growth, and tax income. Additionally, immigrants benefit social assistance programs and often fill labor gaps in important businesses. Even while there are still some false beliefs about how immigration affects the economy, research indicates that many of these worries are unwarranted.

Immigration has substantial economic advantages, but there may also be negative economic effects. The prospect for job displacement is one of the most often mentioned worries. According to the idea, low-skilled immigrants in particular compete with native-born employees for employment and may even oust them. On this matter, the evidence is contradictory, nevertheless. According to some research, immigration may have a little short-term negative impact on native-born workers’ employment, but this effect is counterbalanced by long-term gains in economic growth and productivity.

Another issue is that immigration may result in native-born employees’ wages being suppressed. According to the theory, immigrants’ increasing labor supply pulls down wages for all employees, but especially for low-skilled workers. The data is contradictory on this matter, however. While some studies have discovered evidence of negligible wage effects for low-skilled workers, other studies have discovered no effect or even positive wage effects.

Furthermore, it’s important to remember that not all groups will be equally affected by the potential economic consequences of immigration. Low-skilled native-born employees may be more susceptible to job loss and pay repression than other groups, especially those without a high school diploma. High-skilled citizens, however, may gain from immigration via more entrepreneurship and innovation.

The possible impact of immigration on social assistance programs must also be taken into account. Even while immigrants generally are net donors to social welfare programs, certain groups may be more inclined than others to use these services. For instance, immigrants with inadequate English proficiency or low skill levels may be more prone to need public assistance programs. Research, however, indicates that these expenses pale in comparison to the total economic advantages of immigration.

In conclusion, although there may be economic costs associated with immigration, especially for low-skilled native employees, the evidence for these costs is conflicting. Some groups’ employment and earnings may be somewhat negatively impacted by immigration, but there are also huge economic advantages, such as job creation and innovation. Additionally, compared to the total economic advantages, the prospective costs of immigration on social assistance programs are very low.

Through direct taxes like income taxes and indirect taxes like sales taxes, immigrants greatly increase the US tax base. In reality, according to a 2022 analysis by Boundless Immigrations, foreign-born residents of the United States paid more than $330.7 billion in federal income taxes in 2019 and more than $492 billion in total taxes (including state, local, and sales taxes). Payroll taxes, income taxes, property taxes, and sales taxes are included in this. Additionally, according to the research, immigrants are net contributors to the government’s coffers since they pay more in taxes than they receive in benefits.

The tax base is also augmented by the economic activities of immigrants. As was already established, immigrants are more likely than native-born Americans to start their own enterprises, and these companies often provide both employment and tax money. For instance, a 2019 research by the New American Economy discovered that immigrant-owned enterprises in the US employed 8 million people and created $1.3 trillion in sales.

Despite these contributions, there are worries over the expense of immigrant social programs. Some claim that immigrants are more prone than native-born Americans to utilize social programs like Medicaid and SNAP, placing a drain on the government’s resources. On this matter, the evidence is contradictory, nevertheless. While some research has revealed that immigrants are more likely to utilize certain social programs than native-born Americans, other studies have found no difference or even lower utilization rates among immigrants. A 2017 study by the Cato Institute, for instance, found that immigrants utilize Medicaid and other public programs at lower rates than native-born Americans with comparable income levels.

It’s also important to remember that the expense of social programs for immigrants is little in comparison to the total economic advantages of immigration. Immigrants, as was previously established, are net contributors to the government’s budget, which means they pay more in taxes than they do in benefits. Additionally, immigrants’ economic contributions — including their business ventures and employment creation — generate extra tax money that is beneficial to everyone.

Immigration may spur entrepreneurship and innovation, which in turn helps accelerate economic expansion and employment creation. Compared to native-born Americans, immigrants are more likely to create their own enterprises, and these companies often provide novel concepts, goods, and services to the market. In a research published in March 2016 by the National Foundation for American Policy, for instance, it was discovered that immigrants started more than half of the US startup firms with a market value of $1 billion or above, including Uber, SpaceX, and WeWork.

Additionally, immigrants have significantly influenced innovation in disciplines like STEM (science, technology, engineering, and math). For instance, a 2017 National Science Foundation survey discovered that a disproportionate number of US PhD degree graduates in STEM disciplines are immigrants. A 2018 research by the National Bureau of Economic Research estimated that immigrant inventors were responsible for almost a quarter of US patents filed between 2000 and 2010. Immigrant inventors also contribute significantly to the US patent system.

Additionally, immigrant business owners have boosted economic development and generated employment across a range of sectors. For instance, Elon Musk, the man behind SpaceX and Tesla, was born in South Africa before subsequently obtaining US citizenship. Another such is Pierre Omidyar, the creator of eBay, who was born to Iranian parents in France and eventually attained US citizenship.

Despite these contributions, there are worries about how immigration may affect employees who are citizens. Some claim that immigrants, especially in certain sectors or geographical areas, might replace native-born employees or lower their salaries. On this matter, the evidence is contradictory, nevertheless. While some studies have concluded that immigration has a detrimental impact on certain worker categories, others have found no substantial impact or even a favorable impact on native-born employees’ salaries and employment.

In addition, it’s important to keep in mind that native-born employees and immigrants sometimes have distinct skill sets and educational backgrounds, which means they may not directly compete for the same employment. Furthermore, immigrant business owners often provide new employment and possibilities for both immigrants and native-born employees.

The labor market may be impacted by immigration in both good and negative ways. On the one hand, immigrants may fill labor gaps in fields and areas where there is a lack of native-born workers. For instance, many immigrants work in low-skilled positions in the construction, hospitality, and agricultural industries, where demand often exceeds supply.

Particularly in highly skilled industries like science, technology, engineering, and math (STEM), immigrants may contribute essential skills and knowledge to the labor market. Since there are often insufficient suitable native-born applicants, many US businesses depend on foreign-born employees to fill jobs in these industries.

Concerns exist, nevertheless, over how immigration may affect native-born workers’ income and employment prospects. Some claim that immigration may lower native-born employees’ earnings, especially in low-skilled fields where there is direct employment rivalry. Others contend that, especially during periods of high unemployment or economic downturns, immigrants might grab positions that would otherwise go to native-born Americans.

There is conflicting data on these topics, and economists disagree on the overall effect of immigration on the labor market. While some studies showed no significant impacts or even favorable effects on earnings and employment prospects, others have identified detrimental effects of immigration on salaries and employment for native-born employees.

In addition, it’s important to keep in mind that native-born employees and immigrants sometimes have distinct skill sets and educational backgrounds, which means they may not directly compete for the same employment. In addition, a lot of immigrants launch their own enterprises, which opens up employment chances for both immigrants and citizens.

As a result, immigration may affect the labor market in both good and negative ways. There are worries about how immigration would affect salaries and employment possibilities for native-born employees, despite the fact that immigrants may fill labor shortages and contribute essential skills and knowledge to the economy. The research is conflicting on these problems, but generally immigration has a positive economic impact that much outweighs any possible drawbacks.

The potential expense of social assistance programs for immigrants is a widespread worry about immigration. Critics claim that immigrants may utilize social assistance like Medicaid and food stamps more often, which burdens taxpayers.

The data, however, points to immigration not being a big financial burden on social assistance programs. In reality, many immigrants cannot participate in these programs until they are citizens or lawful permanent residents. Furthermore, immigrants are less likely to utilize social assistance programs than native-born Americans even when they are qualified. According to a 2020 Cato Institute analysis, noncitizens are 25% less likely to obtain welfare assistance than Americans who were born abroad.

Additionally, immigrants make other underappreciated contributions to the economy and society. Compared to native-born Americans, immigrants are more likely to launch their own companies, resulting in the creation of employment and economic development. They also contribute to the support of social assistance programs by paying taxes, such as payroll taxes and sales taxes.

It’s also important to remember that many immigrants go to the US in order to escape poverty and enhance their chances for a better future. Supporting immigrants with social assistance may aid their integration and progress towards self-sufficiency. Long-term gains from this are possible for both immigrants and the general public.

Globalization and immigration are intertwined. The movement of people across borders is becoming more and more crucial as nations grow more interconnected and reliant on one another. Immigration may support a nation’s ability to innovate and compete in the global economy by supplying talented labor.

According to a World Bank analysis, immigration may boost economic development by filling skill shortages and introducing fresh views and ideas to the workforce. Additionally, immigrants may aid in starting new enterprises and growing current ones, which helps with employment creation and economic growth. In fact, a survey by the National Foundation for American Policy discovered that 55% of the nation’s billion-dollar firms were started by immigrants.

However, in the context of globalization, worries about how immigration may affect cultural identity are often voiced. Critics contend that a weakening of national culture and identity may result from greater immigration. The research does, however, point to the possibility that immigration might have a beneficial impact on cultural assimilation. Immigrants often bring their own distinctive cultural customs and traditions, which may improve the social cohesion of the receiving nation.

In addition, cultural interaction is reciprocal. A society that is more diversified and lively results from the mixing of cultures brought about by immigrants learning about and incorporating the cultural customs of their new country. In reality, according to research by the Migration Policy Institute, immigrant children often adapt into American society while clinging to some of their ethnic traditions.

In the end, immigration and globalization are intertwined, and immigration may support nations’ ability to compete in the international market. Despite frequent worries about how immigration may affect cultural identity, the data points to the possibility of good cultural interaction and integration as a result of immigration. Immigrants offer unique talents, perspectives, and cultural customs that may improve the host nation and promote a more dynamic and diversified community.

I looked at the many economic advantages and disadvantages of immigration in this article. While addressing worries about job displacement, wage repression, and social welfare expenses, I spoke about how immigration may help the economy thrive, create jobs, and innovate. I also looked at how immigration affects taxes, the labor market, and globalization, showing how immigrants help to fill labor shortages and promote cultural integration and interchange.

Therefore, does immigration benefit or harm the economy? The influence of immigration relies on a number of elements and settings, thus the answer is not simple. However, research indicates that, generally speaking, immigration may benefit the economy by fostering economic development, job creation, and innovation. Additionally, integration and cultural interaction may strengthen the social fabric of the host nation, fostering a more lively and diversified community.

I recommend people to educate themselves on immigration and how it affects the economy, as well as to take part in educated conversations and debates about this difficult and significant topic. We can create more effective judgments and regulations that benefit both immigrants and citizens who were born locally if we have a greater knowledge of the subtleties and complexity of immigration.
