Is Immigration Good or Bad for The Economy? With strong opinions on both sides of the argument, immigration has been a contentious topic for decades. While some claim that immigrants hurt the economy, others insist that they are a key driver of development and innovation. So, is immigration good or bad for the economy?

In this article, I’ll cover the economic advantages and costs of immigration, evaluate the influence of immigration on taxes, innovation, the labor market, social welfare, and globalization, and answer common misunderstandings about the issue. I’ll also talk about how immigration affects a country’s cultural identity.

Let’s take a moment to define what I mean by immigration before I get into the specifics. Immigration is the transfer of individuals from one nation to another with the purpose of settling down and finding employment there. People who immigrate might come from a variety of backgrounds, including skilled workers, refugees, and asylum seekers. In recent years, the subject of immigration has attracted more attention as the number of individuals travelling to other nations has grown.

Immigration’s effect on the economy is a complicated problem with no simple solutions. To better understand the economic impacts of immigration, we can examine the data that is currently available.

Research continually demonstrates that immigration may have large economic advantages, despite the divisive discussion around it. For instance, a recent study by the National Bureau of Economic Research discovered that immigrants make a considerable contribution to job creation and economic development in the United States.

Immigrants support economic growth through innovation in addition to job creation. Immigrants have indeed started many prosperous enterprises, and they are disproportionately represented among US patent holders and innovators. For example, the co-founder of Google, Sergey Brin, was an immigrant from Russia.

In addition, immigrants contribute to the economy by paying taxes. A new analysis by the Institute on Taxation and Economic Policy (ITEP) estimates that unauthorized immigrants pay $11.6 billion in taxes annually on their own. Taxes on sales, income, and real estate are all included in this. Additionally, immigrants are net contributors to social welfare programs, which mean they provide more to the government via taxes than they do through benefits.

Despite these advantages for the economy, there are still misunderstandings regarding how immigration affects the economy. One widespread myth is that immigrants rob native-born employees of their employment. However, studies demonstrate that immigrants often fill positions that native-born employees are unable or unwilling to do. For instance, despite labor shortages in fields like agriculture, construction, and healthcare, immigrants are overrepresented in these fields.

Another fallacy is the idea that immigration reduces native-born employees’ salaries. Recent research, however, indicates that immigration has little to no effect on native-born employees’ salaries. According to a recent research by the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, for instance, the overall effect of immigration on wages is little, and any adverse impacts are mostly seen by low-skilled native-born employees.

Immigration may have a positive impact on the economy by stimulating innovation, employment growth, and tax income. Additionally, immigrants benefit social assistance programs and often fill labor gaps in important businesses. Even while there are still some false beliefs about how immigration affects the economy, research indicates that many of these worries are unwarranted.

Immigration has substantial economic advantages, but there may also be negative economic effects. The prospect for job displacement is one of the most often mentioned worries. According to the idea, low-skilled immigrants in particular compete with native-born employees for employment and may even oust them. On this matter, the evidence is contradictory, nevertheless. According to some research, immigration may have a little short-term negative impact on native-born workers’ employment, but this effect is counterbalanced by long-term gains in economic growth and productivity.

Another issue is that immigration may result in native-born employees’ wages being suppressed. According to the theory, immigrants’ increasing labor supply pulls down wages for all employees, but especially for low-skilled workers. The data is contradictory on this matter, however. While some studies have discovered evidence of negligible wage effects for low-skilled workers, other studies have discovered no effect or even positive wage effects.

Furthermore, it’s important to remember that not all groups will be equally affected by the potential economic consequences of immigration. Low-skilled native-born employees may be more susceptible to job loss and pay repression than other groups, especially those without a high school diploma. High-skilled citizens, however, may gain from immigration via more entrepreneurship and innovation.

The possible impact of immigration on social assistance programs must also be taken into account. Even while immigrants generally are net donors to social welfare programs, certain groups may be more inclined than others to use these services. For instance, immigrants with inadequate English proficiency or low skill levels may be more prone to need public assistance programs. Research, however, indicates that these expenses pale in comparison to the total economic advantages of immigration.

In conclusion, although there may be economic costs associated with immigration, especially for low-skilled native employees, the evidence for these costs is conflicting. Some groups’ employment and earnings may be somewhat negatively impacted by immigration, but there are also huge economic advantages, such as job creation and innovation. Additionally, compared to the total economic advantages, the prospective costs of immigration on social assistance programs are very low.

Through direct taxes like income taxes and indirect taxes like sales taxes, immigrants greatly increase the US tax base. In reality, according to a 2022 analysis by Boundless Immigrations, foreign-born residents of the United States paid more than $330.7 billion in federal income taxes in 2019 and more than $492 billion in total taxes (including state, local, and sales taxes). Payroll taxes, income taxes, property taxes, and sales taxes are included in this. Additionally, according to the research, immigrants are net contributors to the government’s coffers since they pay more in taxes than they receive in benefits.

The tax base is also augmented by the economic activities of immigrants. As was already established, immigrants are more likely than native-born Americans to start their own enterprises, and these companies often provide both employment and tax money. For instance, a 2019 research by the New American Economy discovered that immigrant-owned enterprises in the US employed 8 million people and created $1.3 trillion in sales.

Despite these contributions, there are worries over the expense of immigrant social programs. Some claim that immigrants are more prone than native-born Americans to utilize social programs like Medicaid and SNAP, placing a drain on the government’s resources. On this matter, the evidence is contradictory, nevertheless. While some research has revealed that immigrants are more likely to utilize certain social programs than native-born Americans, other studies have found no difference or even lower utilization rates among immigrants. A 2017 study by the Cato Institute, for instance, found that immigrants utilize Medicaid and other public programs at lower rates than native-born Americans with comparable income levels.

It’s also important to remember that the expense of social programs for immigrants is little in comparison to the total economic advantages of immigration. Immigrants, as was previously established, are net contributors to the government’s budget, which means they pay more in taxes than they do in benefits. Additionally, immigrants’ economic contributions — including their business ventures and employment creation — generate extra tax money that is beneficial to everyone.

Immigration may spur entrepreneurship and innovation, which in turn helps accelerate economic expansion and employment creation. Compared to native-born Americans, immigrants are more likely to create their own enterprises, and these companies often provide novel concepts, goods, and services to the market. In a research published in March 2016 by the National Foundation for American Policy, for instance, it was discovered that immigrants started more than half of the US startup firms with a market value of $1 billion or above, including Uber, SpaceX, and WeWork.

Additionally, immigrants have significantly influenced innovation in disciplines like STEM (science, technology, engineering, and math). For instance, a 2017 National Science Foundation survey discovered that a disproportionate number of US PhD degree graduates in STEM disciplines are immigrants. A 2018 research by the National Bureau of Economic Research estimated that immigrant inventors were responsible for almost a quarter of US patents filed between 2000 and 2010. Immigrant inventors also contribute significantly to the US patent system.

Additionally, immigrant business owners have boosted economic development and generated employment across a range of sectors. For instance, Elon Musk, the man behind SpaceX and Tesla, was born in South Africa before subsequently obtaining US citizenship. Another such is Pierre Omidyar, the creator of eBay, who was born to Iranian parents in France and eventually attained US citizenship.

Despite these contributions, there are worries about how immigration may affect employees who are citizens. Some claim that immigrants, especially in certain sectors or geographical areas, might replace native-born employees or lower their salaries. On this matter, the evidence is contradictory, nevertheless. While some studies have concluded that immigration has a detrimental impact on certain worker categories, others have found no substantial impact or even a favorable impact on native-born employees’ salaries and employment.

In addition, it’s important to keep in mind that native-born employees and immigrants sometimes have distinct skill sets and educational backgrounds, which means they may not directly compete for the same employment. Furthermore, immigrant business owners often provide new employment and possibilities for both immigrants and native-born employees.

The labor market may be impacted by immigration in both good and negative ways. On the one hand, immigrants may fill labor gaps in fields and areas where there is a lack of native-born workers. For instance, many immigrants work in low-skilled positions in the construction, hospitality, and agricultural industries, where demand often exceeds supply.

Particularly in highly skilled industries like science, technology, engineering, and math (STEM), immigrants may contribute essential skills and knowledge to the labor market. Since there are often insufficient suitable native-born applicants, many US businesses depend on foreign-born employees to fill jobs in these industries.

Concerns exist, nevertheless, over how immigration may affect native-born workers’ income and employment prospects. Some claim that immigration may lower native-born employees’ earnings, especially in low-skilled fields where there is direct employment rivalry. Others contend that, especially during periods of high unemployment or economic downturns, immigrants might grab positions that would otherwise go to native-born Americans.

There is conflicting data on these topics, and economists disagree on the overall effect of immigration on the labor market. While some studies showed no significant impacts or even favorable effects on earnings and employment prospects, others have identified detrimental effects of immigration on salaries and employment for native-born employees.

In addition, it’s important to keep in mind that native-born employees and immigrants sometimes have distinct skill sets and educational backgrounds, which means they may not directly compete for the same employment. In addition, a lot of immigrants launch their own enterprises, which opens up employment chances for both immigrants and citizens.

As a result, immigration may affect the labor market in both good and negative ways. There are worries about how immigration would affect salaries and employment possibilities for native-born employees, despite the fact that immigrants may fill labor shortages and contribute essential skills and knowledge to the economy. The research is conflicting on these problems, but generally immigration has a positive economic impact that much outweighs any possible drawbacks.

The potential expense of social assistance programs for immigrants is a widespread worry about immigration. Critics claim that immigrants may utilize social assistance like Medicaid and food stamps more often, which burdens taxpayers.

The data, however, points to immigration not being a big financial burden on social assistance programs. In reality, many immigrants cannot participate in these programs until they are citizens or lawful permanent residents. Furthermore, immigrants are less likely to utilize social assistance programs than native-born Americans even when they are qualified. According to a 2020 Cato Institute analysis, noncitizens are 25% less likely to obtain welfare assistance than Americans who were born abroad.

Additionally, immigrants make other underappreciated contributions to the economy and society. Compared to native-born Americans, immigrants are more likely to launch their own companies, resulting in the creation of employment and economic development. They also contribute to the support of social assistance programs by paying taxes, such as payroll taxes and sales taxes.

It’s also important to remember that many immigrants go to the US in order to escape poverty and enhance their chances for a better future. Supporting immigrants with social assistance may aid their integration and progress towards self-sufficiency. Long-term gains from this are possible for both immigrants and the general public.

Globalization and immigration are intertwined. The movement of people across borders is becoming more and more crucial as nations grow more interconnected and reliant on one another. Immigration may support a nation’s ability to innovate and compete in the global economy by supplying talented labor.

According to a World Bank analysis, immigration may boost economic development by filling skill shortages and introducing fresh views and ideas to the workforce. Additionally, immigrants may aid in starting new enterprises and growing current ones, which helps with employment creation and economic growth. In fact, a survey by the National Foundation for American Policy discovered that 55% of the nation’s billion-dollar firms were started by immigrants.

However, in the context of globalization, worries about how immigration may affect cultural identity are often voiced. Critics contend that a weakening of national culture and identity may result from greater immigration. The research does, however, point to the possibility that immigration might have a beneficial impact on cultural assimilation. Immigrants often bring their own distinctive cultural customs and traditions, which may improve the social cohesion of the receiving nation.

In addition, cultural interaction is reciprocal. A society that is more diversified and lively results from the mixing of cultures brought about by immigrants learning about and incorporating the cultural customs of their new country. In reality, according to research by the Migration Policy Institute, immigrant children often adapt into American society while clinging to some of their ethnic traditions.

In the end, immigration and globalization are intertwined, and immigration may support nations’ ability to compete in the international market. Despite frequent worries about how immigration may affect cultural identity, the data points to the possibility of good cultural interaction and integration as a result of immigration. Immigrants offer unique talents, perspectives, and cultural customs that may improve the host nation and promote a more dynamic and diversified community.

I looked at the many economic advantages and disadvantages of immigration in this article. While addressing worries about job displacement, wage repression, and social welfare expenses, I spoke about how immigration may help the economy thrive, create jobs, and innovate. I also looked at how immigration affects taxes, the labor market, and globalization, showing how immigrants help to fill labor shortages and promote cultural integration and interchange.

Therefore, does immigration benefit or harm the economy? The influence of immigration relies on a number of elements and settings, thus the answer is not simple. However, research indicates that, generally speaking, immigration may benefit the economy by fostering economic development, job creation, and innovation. Additionally, integration and cultural interaction may strengthen the social fabric of the host nation, fostering a more lively and diversified community.

I recommend people to educate themselves on immigration and how it affects the economy, as well as to take part in educated conversations and debates about this difficult and significant topic. We can create more effective judgments and regulations that benefit both immigrants and citizens who were born locally if we have a greater knowledge of the subtleties and complexity of immigration.

title: Topic: Why Gun Control is Necessary – And Why Opposing it is Like Ignoring the Safety Features on a Car
content:
Gun control is a contentious issue in many countries, particularly in the United States, where the Second Amendment guarantees the right to bear arms. But the reality is that gun violence is a major problem that needs to be addressed, and gun control measures are an important part of the solution.

Opposing gun control is like ignoring the safety features on a car. Just as cars have seatbelts, airbags, and other safety features to protect passengers in the event of an accident, gun control measures are designed to protect people from the dangers of gun violence.

Of course, there are those who argue that gun control infringes on their Second Amendment rights, or that criminals will find ways to get guns regardless of laws. But the truth is that gun control measures can be effective, and they have been implemented successfully in other countries.

For example, in Australia, a mass shooting in 1996 led to the implementation of strict gun control measures, including a ban on certain types of firearms and a buyback program. Since then, there has not been a single mass shooting in Australia. Similarly, Japan has some of the strictest gun control measures in the world, and as a result, has one of the lowest rates of gun violence.

Opposing gun control measures may seem like a matter of personal freedom, but it can also be seen as a disregard for the safety and well-being of others. Just as we wouldn’t ignore the safety features on a car because they’re inconvenient or uncomfortable, we should support gun control measures as a way to protect ourselves and our communities from the dangers of gun violence.

In fact, opposing gun control is like driving a car without a seatbelt or airbags. Sure, you may feel free and unencumbered, but if you get into an accident, you’re putting yourself and others at risk. Similarly, if we refuse to support gun control measures, we’re putting ourselves and our communities at risk of mass shootings, accidents, and other tragedies.

Furthermore, just as we require drivers to have licenses and training before they can get behind the wheel, we should also require gun owners to undergo background checks and safety training before they can purchase and use firearms. These measures can help ensure that guns are only in the hands of responsible, law-abiding citizens who understand how to use them safely.

content:
As a retired liberal, I have always been passionate about advocating for progressive change and working towards a more just and equal society. One issue that has always particularly concerned me is gun control.

Despite the overwhelming evidence supporting stricter gun laws and the overwhelming majority of Americans who support such measures, progress on this issue has been painfully slow. Mass shootings continue to occur with alarming frequency, and yet Congress remains gridlocked on even the most basic reforms, such as universal background checks.

As a retired person, I no longer have the energy and time to devote to activism as I once did. But the thought of young people being gunned down in their schools, movie theaters, and places of worship fills me with a deep sense of frustration and despair. It seems that no matter how many lives are lost, there are always those who prioritize the interests of gun manufacturers and the gun lobby over the safety and well-being of ordinary citizens.

I know that change takes time and that progress is often incremental. But the lack of progress on gun control in this country is a moral outrage, and I can only hope that someday, common sense will prevail and we will finally see the kind of meaningful reform that is so desperately needed.

title: Gun Control Policy
content:
Update: honestly, was not expecting proof that the courts will ignore all precedent this fast. But this is a delicious example of exactly what I meant. Likely heading up to SCOTUS:

A federal judge in Virginia has ruled that federal laws prohibiting 18-to-20-year-olds from getting handguns at federally licensed firearms dealers are unconstitutional.

The National Fire Arms Act was passed in 1934 after a period of mass shootings, chiefly associated with gangsters. These happened during the 1920s and saw interesting takes from citizens. While people feared these shootouts between lawmen and gangsters, people like Bonnie and Clyde were seen as famous heroes . However, one of the triggering events that led to the need for legislation was the St Valentines Day massacre in 1929. While the people killed were not Boy Scouts, it created some panic. The most famous gun of the period, in the criminal war and law enforcement, was the Thomson Submachine Gun, You could buy it and have it shipped over the mail from both the Sears and May Company catalogs. It was as popular in certain sections of society as the AR family of rifles. At the time, these guns were shipped nationwide through the postal service, no fuss, no muss. For the record, you can still ship weapons, but it’s not as easy as before the National Firearms Act. If you are curious, here are the regulations .

One of the things the NFA did was grandfather any legal owner of these guns. If you were part of the criminal underworld, you are part of that criminal element that should not have access to weapons. In time lack of access meant that they disappeared from their hands. So yes, there are still Tommy Guns circulating. There are ways to transfer them legally; it just takes extensive paperwork. A couple of years ago, one was surrendered to San Diego Police Department during a buyback program. There were no questions asked. The owner was given a 200-dollar Walmart card. If the AR-15 and other weapons in the same family were covered under the NFA, none would remove those guns, forcefully or otherwise. Like the Thomson, selling your AR to your neighbor will take a lot of paperwork. In time the number of these weapons will go down; even if eighty years later, you can still find Tommy guns. That photo my husband took is exhibit A. That particular gun was inherited. The other choice, with a similar effect, would be a new assault weapons ban. Over the ten years it was in place; it reduced the frequency of shootings; they have since skyrocketed. This is via Pub-Med :

Assault rifles accounted for 430 or 85.8% of the total 501 mass-shooting fatalities reported (95% confidence interval, 82.8–88.9) in 44 mass-shooting incidents. Mass shootings in the United States accounted for an increasing proportion of all firearm-related homicides (coefficient for year, 0.7; p = 0.0003), with increment in year alone capturing over a third of the overall variance in the data (adjusted R = 0.3). In a linear regression model controlling for yearly trend, the federal ban period was associated with a statistically significant 9 fewer mass shooting related deaths per 10,000 firearm homicides (p = 0.03). Mass-shooting fatalities were 70% less likely to occur during the federal ban period (relative rate, 0.30; 95% confidence interval, 0.22–0.39). **Conclusion: **Mass-shooting related homicides in the United States were reduced during the years of the federal assault weapons ban of 1994 to 2004.

This was temporary, and unlike the Tommy Gun, once it was removed or let to expire, sales of AR-style platforms have skyrocketed, and we now have more than one mass shooting per day . They also sell better after each mass shooting because the companies use fear of restriction to sell more guns. It’s cynical, yes. It’s also true that most of these guns are bought by super gun owners . Some of these people own a veritable armory. No, nobody needs 140 guns. You might be able to justify seven if you are a competitive shooter, hell, even ten. 140, no, not really. What are you arming? A personal army?

We are tired of this. We are not free to go to the store, school, church, temple, farmers market, cinema, hospital, theater, or any public space without looking for cover and egress routes. This is a form of terrorism. This is not unlike the shootouts that led to the NFA:

In the 1920s and ’30s, the U.S. dealt with a different kind of gun violence epidemic: a massive increase in organized crime, fueled by Prohibition. Gangsters, like Al Capone, were making big money trafficking illegal alcohol. And a key weapon in their arsenal was the machine gun. “Those criminals from the mob took advantage of the rise of the portable machine gun, capable of firing multiple rounds of ammunition with the single pull of a trigger,” says Adam Winkler, a professor at UCLA’s school of law and author of __Gunfight: The Battle Over The Right to Bear Arms in America__.

Mind you, that was the first national gun law. The reality is that the Old West was not an open-carry area; not everybody was armed. The old West had gun control enacted by local towns. Cowboys packing heat everywhere is a Hollywood storytelling technique. Early on, it included white and black hats as well. Ironically, modern-day Texas has more liberal open carry laws than in famous locales of the old West, like Tombstone . What most of us agree on are far more extensive background checks. Getting rid of gun show loopholes. We also mostly agree on red flag laws. I am linking to the Gallup tracking poll on the issue because it is convenient. However, it is less detailed than others. As to the AR, it has the same allure, culturally, as the Tommy. We may be hitting a cultural shift. However, I don’t expect the current NRA to play a positive role. They did this in 1932 because they read the population's mood correctly. These days the NRA is part of the problem.

Armed with everything from pistols to 12-gauge shotguns, they climbed the half-dozen steps to the area around the front doors of the building. Bobby pulled out a prepared statement, and read to the students and people in front of the capitol:

“Black people have begged, prayed, petitioned, demonstrated, and everything else to get the racist power structure of America to right the wrongs which have historically been perpetuated against black people. The time has come for black people to arm themselves against this terror before it is too late.”

They then walked into the building to confront the state’s police and legislators, fully loaded guns and rifles in their hands.

Reagan was aghast, and the nearly-all-white California legislature panicked.

“There’s no reason why on the street today a citizen should be carrying loaded weapons,” Reagan said later that afternoon.

Within a few weeks Oakland’s Don Mulford (R), with bipartisan support, introduced into the California Assembly a law ( AB-1591 ) to ban people in California from carrying loaded weapons in public.

It was enthusiastically signed into law by Governor Reagan on July 28th, fewer than three months after Seale’s proclamation at the Capitol.

After a 1989 school shooting in Stockton, when a young white man wielding a semi-automatic weapon murdered five children and a teacher while injuring over 30 others, California passed a ban on assault weapons that stands to this day.

The state went on to ban private gun sales, closing the notorious “gun show loophole” that pours weapons into other states. California requires all gun dealers to be registered and licensed by the state, mandates backgrounds checks, and even outlawed the manufacture and sale of cheap “Saturday Night Special” handguns in the state.

When California put their version of “Red Flag” laws into place — laws forbidding people flagged at risk for committing gun crimes or mass murders from purchasing guns — the state followed up (it’s one of the few in the country with an agency that studies gun violence) and found them to be nearly 100% effective because of how difficult the state makes obtaining a weapon.

While in Texas a violent criminal on the federal no-fly terrorist watch list is welcome to buy a dozen assault weapons from the trunk of a car and go shoot up a school, in California you can’t buy a gun if you’ve been convicted of any violent crime whatsoever, even a misdemeanor like a bar fight.

As a result, according to New York Times correspondent Shawn Hubler, by 2019 (the last year for which we have statistics) California’s gun deaths were around 7 per 100,000 people, one of the lowest in the country.

“So there was a huge differential by 2019,” Hubler told Sabrina Tavernise on the Times’ podcast The Daily . “The chances of dying from gun violence in California were about 70 percent lower than they were in the rest of the country.”

If you live in Texas, floating around the national average at 14.2 gun deaths per 100,000, you’re far more likely to die from a bullet than in states with strong gun control laws like Hawaii ( 3.4 ), Massachusetts ( 3.7 ), New Jersey ( 5 ), Rhode Island ( 5.1 ), New York ( 5.3 ) or Connecticut ( 6 ).

When your gun-nut brother-in-law starts babbling about gun deaths in Chicago (Illinois, with reasonable gun control laws, is 14.1 gun deaths per 100,000 people), you may want to point out that nearly 60 percent of guns seized in Chicago came from out-of-state, with most coming from next-door Indiana (17.3 gun deaths per 100,000) where gun stores dot the Indiana side of the Indiana/Illinois border.

National gun control would put a quick end to that.

In the 1932 New State Ice v Liebmann decision, Supreme Court Justice Louis Brandeis famously called the states “laboratories of democracy”:

“It is one of the happy incidents of the federal system that a single courageous State may,” he wrote,” if its citizens choose, serve as a laboratory; and try novel social and economic experiments without risk to the rest of the country.”

He could have been speaking of California, Hawaii, or Connecticut. Gun control works, and we have the proof right here in the United States.

Ironically, while it was Reagan’s racism that first produced significant gun control in America’s largest state, it’s racist white supremacy in America that is today the single largest force fighting against gun control.

With very few exceptions, the entire Second Amendment Movement is made up of white people, many of them associated with white supremacy militias and politicians from former confederate states.

The NRA is greatly diminished, both in power and budget: racism continues to drive the gun control debate, this time in the opposite direction from the days Reagan was governor of California.

Today we see a knee-jerk fear of non-white people in the ongoing explosion of gun purchases in rural and suburban white communities across the country.

A recent white caller to my show went on a long rant, for example, about how he had to buy an AR-15 because, he said, “liberals” were “no longer enforcing the law and the gang-bangers are taking over our streets.” In other words, he’s terrified of Black and Brown people, which is why he “had to buy” more guns.

When America elected our first Black president in 2008, gun stores across America were so overwhelmed by white people buying guns that the “frenzy” was referred to as “the great gun and ammunition shortage.”

Scratch the surface of the most fervent “gun rights” members of Congress and you’ll find unrepentant white supremacist Republican politicians who reflexively villainize the Black Lives Matter movement and hype the Antifa straw-man at every opportunity.

On the “gun control” side, now that the Panthers are mostly just a memory on the national stage, fear of armed Black people has been replaced by fear of white children being slaughtered in public schools.

And it’s providing us with a shocking glimpse into the minds of these Republican legislators: white freak-out about Black people having weapons back in the 1960s was a stronger motivator for them than today’s slaughter of innocent children of all races.

At least so far.

title: Laughable Anti-gun Control Arguments That Will Make You Want to Cry
content:
I know. You don’t toast toast — you toast bread.

It’s a flawed statement.

Here are some more flawed statements.

If you want toast, you need to press the lever on the toaster. But it’s a damn sight easier to toast the bread if you have a toaster — in the same way, an AK47 makes it easier to toast your entire classroom.

Guns are like dildos; the lonelier the owner, the more likely they are to get used.

An umbrella? Sweatpants? Breasts? ( Bizarre murder weapons )

Let me think — why is it that the Second Amendment protects gun ownership and not kitchen spatulas?

There aren’t any mass killers who opt for something that makes their job harder. Let them find something else other than a gun. Let them be creative.

It’s like losing weight — it’s too much like hard work.

Well, change it. It’s already been amended, hasn’t it? If a law isn’t fit for purpose, legislators have the power to change it.

It’s illegal to pass wind in a public place after 6 pm on Thursdays in Florida. It’s kinda weird how that came to be a law — and it’s never been repealed. Written in the 1800s, nobody knows why it became a law, but nobody cares because it’s never enforced.

Imagine a balmy evening at Mar-a-Lago, and a cop heard President Trump trump and wrote him a ticket. How long would that law be a law?

Laws don’t change stupid laws that kill people. People change stupid laws that kill people.

Seatbelts laws won’t work. Speed limits won’t work. Air traffic control won’t work. Sunscreen won’t work. Basic hygiene won’t work. Vaccines won’t work. Antibiotics won’t work. Traffic lights won’t work.

Except they do.

The clue is in the headline: control.

Cars crash. Accidents happen. But cars aren’t designed to blow someone’s head off. But because people involved in car accidents get injured or die, they are strictly regulated.

To drive a car, you must pass a written test and prove you are competent enough to drive safely. A driver’s license can be suspended or revoked.

Cars are regulated, they have identification numbers, mandatory insurance, license plates, and safety requirements.

If you are to apply the same regulations to guns, gun owners would only be allowed to walk around with peashooters.

So you read the news, got scared, and bought a gun. Now you are safe.

Except you aren’t.

You just put yourself at more risk of being shot. Fear is a major motivation for purchasing firearms, but existing studies show that people living in homes with firearms have higher risks of dying by homicide.

Bringing a firearm into your home increases the risk to all members of your household — you can’t argue that you are only doing it to keep your kids safe when the evidence tells you otherwise.

Oh, look, I see you can. DUH.

Here’s my challenge, grow a Colt 45. Could you smuggle a rifle through customs? Could you make your own gun from the raw ingredients?

It’s not as easy as sticking a cannabis plant in your attic.

You can buy your drugs from your local drug dealer, but ask yourself why he is selling them. Service to the community? Concern for your mental well-being? The goodness of his heart?

Of course not. He sells them because he makes money.

Why do gun manufacturers make guns? Why does the NRA support gun ownership? Why do gun sellers sell guns? You got it; it isn’t because they give a rat’s backside about your safety.

Remind me again of that time.

Statistically, this is a rare event .

Despite what the people who make money from guns want you to believe, self-defensive gun use is as rare as an honest politician. That pistol in your pocket is much more likely to be used for suicide than putting holes in a homicidal maniac.

In 2018, for every justifiable homicide with a gun, there were 34 gun homicides, 82 gun suicides, and two unintentional gun deaths. — Giffords

Why? Have you no more shitty jobs for them?

Immigrants are less likely than citizens to commit crimes, especially violent crimes.

If you want to reduce the number of people killed by guns, then target the people who are statistically more likely to kill people with a gun — you know, the ones with guns.

When was the last time in American history that an armed band of citizens prevented the usurpation of rights by the Federal government?

The closest was that time Trump got on his high horse and shouted, “Infamy, infamy, they’ve all got it in for me!” And a number of brainwashed people heard this and stormed the Capitol.

Since then, at least 978 people have been charged in the Capitol insurrection. You see, laws work.

Is that a fact?

No.

It’s complete and utter bunkum. Here’s the truth. If everyone had a gun, the NRA, the gun manufacturers, the gun sellers, and the politicians who support them would be as rich as fuck.

Also, more likely to die at the hand of their customers.

“You argue a change in the law will take away the innocent pleasure of firing a gun. What about the innocent pleasure of watching a child grow up?” — Sir Sean Connery

Go on then. What is it I don’t understand?

(If your answer is it’s ‘ you ,’ I don’t understand, you are correct.)

title: Gun Control and Gun Rights — A Rational Approach
content:
The U.S. Constitution recognizes the right of an individual to own firearms.

A well regulated Militia, being necessary to the security of a free State, the right of the people to keep and bear Arms shall not be infringed. - The Second Amendment

And the Founding Fathers were clear about their intentions in their commentary.

“The laws that forbid the carrying of arms are laws of such a nature. They disarm only those who are neither inclined nor determined to commit crimes…. Such laws make things worse for the assaulted and better for the assailants; they serve rather to encourage than to prevent homicides, for an unarmed man may be attacked with greater confidence than an armed man.” — Thomas Jefferson, Commonplace Book (quoting 18th-century criminologist Cesare Beccaria), 1774–1776

As I will explain in this article, the Founding Fathers made it clear that private citizens had the right not only to own muskets but also to own ships covered in cannons. The Founding Fathers were also fans of primitive machine guns and were well aware that technology was advancing.

thefederalistpapers.org

There are those who argue that the Second Amendment was written to protect the government’s right to bear arms . “The people” here supposedly refers to the government as opposed to the citizens, as if such a declaration would ever be needed. Such an argument completely ignores the commentary from the Founding Fathers. And to say that those who make such arguments have gravel for brains would be an insult to gravel. Such people actually have negative levels of intelligence, whereas gravel has zero. It is obviously the individual’s right to arms that the Second Amendment recognizes.

But is the amendment’s prescription correct? To prove that this is the correct policy, we cannot simply say, “It’s in the Constitution” as if the Bill of Rights were brought down from Mount Sinai on tablets of stone. Perhaps our laws are wrong? Perhaps the laws should be changed to prevent guns from falling into the hands of criminals and the mentally ill.

I used to think like this, I used to think that the Second Amendment was outdated and that we should prevent people from having guns in order to prevent violence. That was until I saw the testimony of Suzanna Gratia Hupp, a woman who lost her family in a mass shooting in a gun-free zone. It is not often that one can point to one particular moment that changed his mind so drastically on any particular issue, but her testimony, which was only a few minutes long, fundamentally changed my mind on gun rights, including the right to own a machine gun.

Gun-free zones and the disarming of law-abiding citizens are not the answer to the so-called “gun violence” we see in the world today. Anti-gun laws only tip the balance in favor of tyrants and criminals, and many would argue that this is their goal. It is glaringly obvious that mass shootings tend to happen in places like schools and other gun-free zones, yet are virtually (if not totally) unheard of at gun shows.

If guns are the problem, then why do we see mass shootings in schools, but not at NRA conventions?

There is an apocryphal (probably non-authentic) quote from a Japanese military leader who is supposed to have been asked why they did not invade the American mainland. He is supposed to have responded that it is because there would have been a rifle behind every blade of grass. Whether the quote is real or not, the meaning is clear and obvious. Invade the US, and it will cost you, try to maintain an occupation and it will cost you even more.

Also, there are many well-documented cases of mass shootings being stopped by a “good guy with a gun.” Many on the Left try to dismiss these cases, but the facts are there. Covering the Sun with your finger does not make it go away.

www.breitbart.com

The Founding Fathers were not gods, they were men, but they recognized that a man has the right to self-defense — defense from criminals and from tyrants. That is why they made it clear in the Constitution that the government shall not infringe on a man’s right to own firearms.

As it stands, governments within the United States have made it difficult to purchase a firearm, completely ignoring the Constitution. This is not the answer. [See links Here and Here ]

thefederalistpapers.org

If Americans are to be serious about protecting the rights of an individual to defend himself or herself, while also keeping guns out of the hands of criminals and the mentally incompetent, the answer is obvious.

Background checks should be simple and easy in the age of the Internet. It should not take months to allow an individual to practice his constitutionally recognized rights. Such a lengthy process is clearly an infringement. As for preventing criminals from purchasing firearms, this should not be a difficult process.

Here is my solution:

A man walks into the gun store. He asks to buy a gun. The store clerk asks for his driver’s license and social security number. The customer complies. His driver’s license number and his social security number are run, showing that he has no history of criminal convictions, nor has a jury of his peers ruled him to be mentally incompetent to own firearms.

The clerk informs the customer that everything came back clear, and asks the man if he has been feeling suicidal or if he has had thoughts of murder or intense criminal violence lately. The man shrugs and says no.

The man is then allowed to buy as many rifles, machine guns, grenades, bazookas, and tanks as he wants, along with whatever else he likes that he wants to buy. Welcome to America where the government is afraid of the people, not the people of the government.

That’s pretty much it. A background check should be done in 5 minutes.

A competent government should have a registration of violent criminals. This is the day of the Internet. This should not be hard. A process like this should not take months, weeks, days, or even hours. This should be simple. And the presumption of innocence should be recognized. There is no reason to infringe on a law-abiding citizen’s rights with a lengthy background check, a waiting period, firearm taxes, or any other nonsense which clearly infringes on said right.

And by the way, the Bill of Rights does not begin at age 21 either. A competent adult should enjoy his or her full legal rights the instant he or she turns 18, including the right to the preservation of one’s life, one’s body, and one’s property.

A comprehensive database of violent offenders would not be hard to design. It might take time to upload all of the records, but if Americans are serious about curbing violent crime, this would be a major step in the right direction.

But what if a criminal wants to go buy firearms? Then the clerk should hit the button under the table and summon the police.

Also, why is this criminal not in jail? Does he live in New York where criminals are being let out without bail? Was he given a slap-on-the-wrist sentence after murdering someone? If he murdered someone already, why was he not put to death? Why was God’s death penalty mandate in Genesis 9 (for both Jewish and Gentile governments) not followed?

People talk about criminals buying guns, but far too often governments are too light on crime as it is. This seems to come from the erroneous concept that all criminals are socially ill rather than evil. If you want to keep criminals from terrorizing citizens, then prosecute the criminals. And for those who commit crimes like murder or rape, execute the criminals. Stop letting murderers out of prison after a few short years.

[Author’s note: In writing this article, one of the questions that came up was whether sending criminals to prison is the proper use of justice in the first place. Even in the Bible, we don’t see incarceration as a form of justice under God’s Law for Israel. Rather, criminals are either put to death, forced to make restitution, or exiled from the community.

But this opens up a can of way too many questions that are beyond the scope of this article. It’s definitely a topic I have been thinking about and considering, and I would have to say at the very least that perhaps incarceration is over-used. Perhaps cities of exile should be used in cases like manslaughter.

But for now, I digress on these points. Since my purpose for this article is to argue for simple and easy — yet effective — background checks, and not full criminal-justice reform, I am choosing to write this article within the context of the overall justice system that we currently have.]

The bottom line is that Democrats have no right to complain about criminals obtaining firearms when they refuse to prosecute violent criminals in the first place.

As for the mentally ill, the obvious question is: Who defines mental illness? Is someone on the Autism Spectrum to be deemed “mentally ill?” After all, many Autistic individuals are brilliant, with perfectly sound minds, but their minds work differently from those of neurotypicals. What about someone with Dyslexia, who is not violent, but confuses the spelling of words? Or someone with Tourette Syndrome who has involuntary tics but who is gentle? What about a young woman with body issues or an eating disorder who lives in a bad neighborhood and needs to protect herself?

It amazes me that some people hold to the bigotry that any mental handicap should be equated with violence. Not to mention the bigotry that any difference is automatically a flaw. It amazes me that so many people, especially those on the “tolerant” Left, stigmatize both neurodiversity and individuals with disabilities as automatically being suspects of violence. As if certain people are to be deemed second-class citizens with lesser rights. By such standards, both Albert Einstein and Sir Isaac Newton would have been deemed to be flawed or broken simply for having brains that worked differently — men with two of the greatest minds in human history.

I constantly see people in the media who talk about keeping the mentally ill from owning firearms , as if mental illness and incompetency were the same things. They are not.

www.louderwithcrowder.com

Well, what about other considerations in buying a gun? What if there is an arrest warrant? The answer is simple. This should be included in the database for when the five-minute background check is performed, and the police duress button should be pressed.

Well, what about scary machine guns like the AR-15 ? The AR-15 is not a machine gun. It’s a popular rifle for home defense and for hunting, and women tend to find it useful because it has less recoil than other firearms.

Sadly, most people who advocate for gun control do not know what they are talking about. Let’s review:

www.louderwithcrowder.com

Most on the Left, in my experience, have no idea what the difference is between a fully automatic weapon and a semiautomatic weapon. And they generally think that semiautomatic means that we are talking about a military-style machine gun. Most handguns are semiautomatic. The two categories are different. This is like wanting to make laws regulating medicine without knowing your right ventricle from your left foot.

greenslugg.medium.com

Also, the Founding Fathers were well aware of the predecessors to machine guns and were fans of such things. The Second Amendment was not just for muskets. The Founding Fathers recognized a man’s right to have a ship armed with cannons and to own fully automatic weapons .

One reviewer who gave me feedback on my article disputed whether the proto-machine guns from the time of the American Revolution could properly be called “fully automatic” because of the fact that the bullets in these weapons still had to be loaded manually one by one. That said, this same reviewer pointed out that, semantics aside, it was clear that firearm technology was making incredible advancements, yet the Founding Fathers still said that the government had no right whatsoever to interfere with a man’s right to own and carry firearms.

Keep the above in mind next time someone who knows nothing about history says that the Second Amendment was only about muskets.

With a little bit of logic and some background knowledge, the objections to gun rights fall apart.

Since basic firearm literacy is beyond the scope of this article, I recommend readers use the various resources I link to in this article to learn more. By learning a few basics about firearms, you will not only be able to better analyze this issue, but you will also be better equipped to spot politicians and news reporters who are fake. You will be able to recognize for yourself that any politician or news anchor who says that an AR-15 is a “military-style” weapon is either lying or hopelessly ignorant.

There are those who will often put out stats to claim that mass shootings and “gun violence” are especially problematic in America. A full discussion of this topic is far beyond the scope of this article. But there are several things to consider.

First of all, the abuse of a right by other people does not nullify my rights. If I as an individual have not committed any crimes, then the government has no right to infringe on any of my rights.

Also, these stats are often misleading. It is easy to cherry-pick data and change definitions halfway through an argument. I’ve seen data on the number of mass shootings in the United States compared to other countries. Yet there is no consistent legal definition of what qualifies as a mass shooting.

rumble.com

Often stats are presented that look at deaths by mass shootings but ignore the mass murder committed by governments, particularly those collectivist governments that implemented gun control.

Two of the countries I've seen presented to support gun control are China and Russia, countries where tens of millions of people were murdered by their own governments within living memory — That sort of evil is why Americans love our guns. It amazes me that anyone would be so historically illiterate as to use China and Russia as positive examples for gun control.

reason.com

When 20 people are killed by an evil gunman, it is a tragedy. There are many cases where the good guy with a gun stops this tragedy early . But compare this tragedy even 100 times over with the slaughter of tens of millions of unarmed people by an evil government.

Also, keep in mind that the charts presenting “mass shootings” and “gun deaths” tend to ignore other forms of violent crime (such as rapes and murders with a knife). It’s possible that murders with a gun decrease, while the overall murder rate increases.

There are charts that indicate an inverse relationship between gun ownership per capita and the rates of rape and murder overall.

drgo.us

Conversely, if rates of violent crime were to increase, it’s not unreasonable that more people would buy guns for self-protection. This is one example of how correlation does not indicate causation. “A” may cause “B” or it could be the other way around. Or it may be that both “A” and “B” are caused by “C”, or it could be any of a number of complex interactions.

So even if there were a correlation between gun ownership and gun crime/ overall crime/ anything else, it would not, by itself, prove a causal relationship.

As someone with a career in science, I tend to be very skeptical when it comes to statistics. Stats are easily manipulated. This does not mean that we can throw stats out the window, but it does mean that it is important to be aware of statistical fallacies and to seek objectivity in any statistical analysis.

The first rule of Stats Class: Correlation does not indicate causation. Everyone who takes a stats class learns this basic mantra. It’s also important to be aware of cherry-picking and unjustified generalizations. And it’s important to be very skeptical of stats that seem to justify the views one already holds.

It may be possible to argue whether so-called “gun control” prevents mass shootings or other forms of gun-related criminal activity. (Yet often this ignores so many other factors, such as overall violent crime rates.) But at the end of the day, private citizens have the right to own firearms to protect ourselves. Statistics by themselves do not create an argument suitable for settling questions of right and wrong — or rights and non-rights.

If one does not like the Second Amendment, then I respectfully ask that they move to another nation that better fits their philosophy of life. Alternatively, if such a person lives in a heavily Democrat region of the United States, such as New Jersey, that they petition their government for peaceful secession from the Union. This way they can enjoy their Leftist Utopia in peace, and Americans can enjoy our freedom. Millions of people have come here, and continue to come here, for the freedom that America has to offer. It is true that we are prosperous, and that people come here for that, but that prosperity is a fruit of our freedom.

Those who want gun control are free to move to shining utopias with gun control, price controls, free stuff, and “income equality,” such as Venezuela and North Korea, or to go and form their own country. Freedom has its risks, but so does dictatorship. I myself will choose to remain in the freest nation on Earth. And I will take my chances with an armed citizenry, rather than one that is unarmed.

The world is not a perfect place. Guns would have no place in the Garden of Eden, but we live in a fallen and broken world. Human beings are guilty of sin, and there are a lot of evil people out there. Law-abiding citizens have the right to protect themselves from corrupt governments and from criminals. By infringing on that right, governments only favor tyrants and criminals over lawful individuals, and, in so doing, they abdicate their authority to govern.

One last consideration. The hearts of men are corrupt. It’s been said that the wickedness of man is the most empirically evident fact, and yet also the most resisted. It’s unfashionable to talk about sin in such an enlightened age of personal incredulity. But the reality is that all of the laws in the world cannot cure the wickedness in the heart of man. Only Jesus Christ can do that .

Thank you for reading my article! If you would like to see more of my content, please subscribe to my Email Newsletter , and check out some of my other content.

title: Just What the Neighborhood Needs: A New Gun-Control Group.
content:
, Back in the olden days, meaning the 20th Century, the gun-control movement consisted of a couple of D.C.-based lobbying groups, chief among them the Brady Group which got the background-check gun bill and a ten-year assault rifle bill signed by Clinton in 1994.

The NRA, on the other hand, had connections to gun owners all over the country by dint of sponsoring shooting matches at various public ranges, as well as having display booths at hundreds of gun shows which were held in just about all 50 states.

The NRA ’s public presence and lobbying efforts were so much a part of the sporting and shooting landscape, that Bill Clinton’s declaration about how Al Gore lost the 2000 election because the NRA beat him in his home state of Tennessee went unchallenged for the next twenty years.

The NRA’s dominance of the gun debate, however, was shattered by the massacre at Sandy Hook, as well as the appearance and growth of well-financed gun-control efforts, chief among them Mike Bloomberg’s Everytown and its alliance with Shannon Watts and her MOMS group.

Almost overnight it seemed, gun-control organizations and groups started to bloom, with Gabby Giffords promoting gun control after recovering from a near-fatal shooting in 2011, and the Brady Group building membership within individual states.

You would think that with all the increased attention on gun violence generated by these new organizational initiatives, along with a weakening of NRA activities over the past couple of years, that strategies and measures would be adopted that would show some degree of a lessening of gun violence rates.

To the contrary, the per-100K rate for intentional, fatal gun injuries in 2012 was 10.45; in 2020 it was 13.58. So, in the eight years since gun-control organizational activity and advocacy began to surge after 2012, the fatal gun violence rate has increased by 30 percent! We don’t have any official gun violence numbers for the last several years, but nobody is expecting anything but further increases given the impact of Covid-19.

And what does Gun-control Nation come up with in response to a public health threat which has become endemic to a degree not experienced in any other advanced country? It’s another gun-control organization, in this case devoted to preventing or at least reducing gun violence in other countries by bringing legal actions against American gun makers whose business practices are designed to supply “the criminal gun market in Mexico, Canada, the Caribbean, and countries in Latin America and elsewhere.”

So says the website of Global Action on Gun Violence , the brainchild of Jonathan Lowy, who was Counsel for Brady for 25 years, during which time he claims to have litigated and won more than $100 million in verdicts and settlements for gun violence victims, along with all kinds of other legal victories creating ‘groundbreaking precedent’ to hold gun makers responsible for causing gun violence.

Back in 2021, Lowy evidently helped the Mexican government to develop and file a lawsuit against 6 major gun manufacturers, including Smith & Wesson, Beretta, and Glock, which was initially dismissed because of PLCCA , but apparently is now going to be reviewed by the 1st Circuit Court of Appeals. The suit alleges that these gun makers knowingly sold guns to dealers and distributors for the purpose of moving guns into the hands of Mexican criminals and therefore violating various Mexican laws covering illegal ownership and use of guns.

Before I get into the details of this lawsuit, it should be mentioned that the export market for American gun makers and dealers represents somewhere between 3% and 6% of the guns manufactured in the U.S. every year. In 2019, the most recent year for this data (from the ATF ), the gun industry manufactured 7,011,945 guns and exported 317,482 guns. In other words, gun exports represented 4.5% of all domestic gun production that year. Big deal.

Getting back to the lawsuit (which you can download here ) the complaint is nothing more than the same, old ‘rotten apple’ gun dealer narrative which has been floating around since the government started regulating gun dealers in the 1930’s and then made ATF responsible for inspecting and managing dealer behavior with the gun law passed in 1968.

We’ve been hearing this blah-blah-blah for years about how most gun dealers are ‘honest’ but there some rotten apples out there who are either not inspected by the ATF or are allowed to continue selling guns after an inspection finds that relevant laws aren’t being followed.

Back in 1999, the Clinton Administration made a deal with Smith & Wesson that would have required the company to police its dealers by physically visiting every gun dealer in the United States who sold just one S&W gun a year. I’ll spare you the details of this scheme, but the bottom line is that it would have put Smith & Wesson out of business.

Lowy’s lawsuit mentions this agreement, and states that it collapsed because S&W ‘reneged’ on the deal. Actually, it was the government which, after a Democrat named Clinton was replaced by a Republican named Bush, told S&W that the deal was dead. And by the way, had the agreement remained in effect, it would have immunized S&W from all tort suits, so bye-bye Lowy’s scheme to use tort litigation to regulate the gun business.

This new organizational effort to deal with gun violence does absolutely nothing except promote the careers and public presence of a couple of D.C.-based lawyers who are trying to carve out a new, little niche for themselves in the gun-control debate.

When it comes to reducing gun violence, this is the best we can do?

title: Gun Control Will Not Fix Gun Culture
content:
Today I read an article about a man who shot and killed his neighbor because he was using a leaf blower. The writer described the incident as part of “a string of shootings in which people have been harmed or killed over trivial matters.”

Now I, like many people, hate the sound of leaf blowers. I’m sure some who feel this way have fantasized about shooting people who use these and similar noisemakers. Some might even privately — or publicly —applaud this execution.

Here’s the thing: US-Americans shooting each other with little or no provocation is nothing new. Some have suggested that the media is currently featuring these stories to counter the narrative that the shooting of Black teen Ralph Yarl was racially motivated. “See, white people get shot for no good reason too!”

Regardless, it’s due to our gun-glorifying culture that people go beyond fantasies of ending the lives of people who irritate them to actually doing so. They do so with legally-purchased firearms as well as illegally obtained ones. They do so with pistols as well as machine guns. And they do so accidentally as well as intentionally.

funcrunch.medium.com

They do so because our media, our entertainment, and our government all promote the idea that pointing a lethal weapon at another human being and pulling the trigger is an acceptable, even honorable, thing to do. This is what needs to change.

This will not change by voting for Democrats. This will not change by banning civilian use of “assault weapons”. This will not change by imposing more restrictions on gun purchases.

To be clear, I am not opposed to gun control advocates doing any of the above things. What I am opposed to is the use of guns, period. By anyone, for any reason.

funcrunch.medium.com

funcrunch.medium.com

Am I being an idealist? Yes! Big problems necessitate radical solutions. It would be dishonest of me to support measures that might result in fewer deaths by firearm, when I believe that number of deaths should be zero. That includes those killed by police and military officers, as well. That such executions are considered legal is irrelevant to me.

funcrunch.medium.com

Am I being judgmental? Again, guilty as charged. Humans make judgements all the time, and this is literally a matter of life or death. I judge that every human life is precious, and that no one has the moral right to take away the life of another.

We need more people to proselytize peace and nonviolence. Not because God — any god — told us to, but because these values are kind and compassionate, and make good sense. The alternative is that we continue to live in fear of our neighbors, whether on the other side of the fence or the other side of the world, and act on that fear with lethal aggression.

Dare to envision a peaceful world. Not in the hereafter; in the here and now. We can make it happen.

title: Just What the Neighborhood Needs: A New Gun-control Plan.
content:
Guess what? Now that the number of fatal and non-fatal injuries may hit an all-time high for one year, a new gun-control organization has appeared. I’m talking about an outfit called 97Percent , which is basically a website touting a new piece of research allegedly proving that just about everyone in America will support laws that reduce the violence committed with the use of guns.

Well, it’s not really new research unless you define research as getting on the phone and talking to a bunch of pre-screened people who will answer questions that you believe are relevant or germane to the issue or issues being researched.

But what if the questions you ask the so-called ‘balanced’ group of respondents are full of sh*t? What if the questions exhibit a complete lack of understanding about how and why gun violence occurs?

What this new group is very good at doing is getting noticed by the national media, such as a major article in The Washington Post . The author of this piece publishes regularly in The New Yorker, The Nation, The New York Review of Books, The Times Literary Supplement, et. al. , and she has a hyphenated last name. She’s really going to know how to understand and explain the issue of guns, right?

But let’s get back to the so-called research that 97Percent believes creates a solid basis for figuring out how we can go about reducing the behavior which has killed and seriously injured at least 223 Americans over past three days — and that’s a serious undercount, believe me, okay?

Incidentally, the research being promoted by 97Percent came out of the Tufts University Medical School, so we have to take it seriously because as we all know, medical research is always supposed to be aligned with facts, or what is called ‘evidence-based’ research.

What this research shows is that there is solid support among gun owners for laws and regulations that will reduce gun violence and make America a much safer place.

Before I say something about the research, I should add that 97Percent will be holding their first annual conference on November 17, which will bring together “Members of Congress, activists and leading policy experts to discuss the current state of, and path forward for, the gun safety movement.”

Activists who are concerned about gun violence love to go to conferences. They meet their friends, they listen to a couple of interesting spiels, there’s usually something good to eat. These conferences have been going on regularly since the terrible 2012 slaughter at Sandy Hook. Know what difference they’ve made? To quote Grandpa, ‘ gurnisht helfen ,’ (read: nothing at all.)

And the reason these meetings and all these efforts to reduce gun violence have had no effect is quite simple. You can’t figure out what to do about a problem — any problem — if you continue to explain why the problem occurs by promoting an explanation for the problem which is simply wrong.

Okay, I’m repeating myself again. So now it’s time to get down to what Grandpa would call ‘ tachlis ’ (read: the real deal) and explain why gun violence actually occurs. Ready?

The United States is the only country in the entire world which sanctions the legal ownership of a product which is designed and used only for the purpose of ending human life. There is no other country anywhere on this Earth where someone can walk into a retail establishment, plunk down some hard-earned dough and walk out five minutes later with a bottom-loading, semi-automatic pistol chambered for military-grade ammunition and also have three or four additional magazines so that the gun owner can get off 50 or 60 man-killing shots in one minute or less.

There is not single word in the entire report issued by 97Percent which mentions this point at all. Nobody was asked over the phone or in some kind of ‘focus group’ whether or not Americans should be able to get their hands on such guns. Which, by the way, is the reason we have gun violence.

How do you make a Glock 17 or a Sig P320 safe? You don’t because you can’t. These guns happen to be ‘weapons of war,’ designed for military use and carried today by military troopers worldwide. And a gun-control activist is going to sit down across the table from someone who owns one of these guns and come up with a plan to make their gun ‘safe?’

Give me a break, okay?

title: Here Comes the Latest Gun-Control Bill.
content:
My friends in Gun-nut Nation are all in a tizzy because Liz Warren has re-introduced a gun-control bill that she first stuck in the legislative hopper in 2020, and now has decided to try and get it passed again. The bill is being described by the pro-gun gang as being a ‘sledgehammer’ against gun ‘rights,’ because it allegedly includes ‘national gun registration’ which has always been the biggest no-no of them all.

The doomsday reaction to national gun registration is that it will lead to national gun confiscation which has always been a strategy employed by governments to prevent the citizenry from exercising individual rights and enjoying individual freedoms — the most salient example being what happened in Germany after 1933.

Of course, it’s a well-known fact that without a gun in the home, the law-abiding citizen would be unable to protect himself against the ‘tyranny’ of the state. Which, after all, is the not-so-secret agenda of all those liberals from Communist states like Massachusetts, particularly those Communists and Jew-haters at Harvard like Pocahantas Warren, okay?

Incidentally, the previous paragraph was not just written tongue in cheek. It reflects how the GOP has managed to debase political rhetoric employed by that orange-headed asshole named Donald Trump. Anyway, back to gun and gun control.

I downloaded the actual text of the bill from Warren’s website , and when it comes to a national registration scheme, there’s no such provision in the bill at all. In fact, the bill seems to be nothing more than the gun-control law which exists in Massachusetts, and I don’t notice any gun owners in the Bay State suffering the loss of their 2nd-Amendment ‘rights.’

What the bill says is that it would establish a federal gun-licensing system “that requires individuals to obtain a federal or qualifying state-issued license to purchase or own a firearm or ammunition.” If a particular decides to implement a gun-licensing procedure, the federal government will bear the costs.

Holding a gun license doesn’t mean that you own a gun. But of course, once a national licensing system is in place, the government can send some jack-booted agents around to every house in which someone with this kind of license lives and take the place apart looking for guns. The phrase ‘jack booted’ was how Wayne-o LaPierre once described ATF agents, most of whom wear loafers or sneakers when they wander into a gun shop to conduct one of those useless inspections they perform here and there every now and again.

Notwithstanding the fact that Lizzie’s gun-control plan would allow some state and federal agencies to hire more personnel, which is always an objective of liberals and promoters of the Deep State, the real question which needs to be asked about her legislative strategy to reduce gun violence is this: since every purchase of a gun from a dealer now requires a background check, what difference would it make if law-abiding individuals went to the trouble of getting a gun license whether or not they actually owned any guns?

Right now, there are 8 states which require a gun license in order to own or purchase a gun: CA, CT, HI, IL, MA, NJ, NY and Rhode Island. In 2021, the last year for which we have data, 4,307 individuals were murdered by someone using a gun. These deaths represented 20% of all the gun homicides recorded that year in the 8 states which represent 16% of all 50 states.

From those numbers, it’s pretty difficult to believe that a national gun licensing system would make much of a difference because we have absolutely no idea how many of the shooters whose behavior accounted for those 4,307 deaths were using legal guns. Frankly, I would be astonished if the percentage of killers who were lawful owners of their weapons was higher than 5%, and I suspect that virtually all of those shootings started as domestic arguments and ended up with a — bang!

So, here we are once again finding ourselves in the middle of the endless argument about gun violence in which neither side really makes any sense.

What the hell, the argument’s only been going on for #0 years since Art Kellerman and Fred Rivara published two articles in the New England Journal of Medicine which found that guns represent a threat to health.

Thirty years? Big friggin’ deal.

She played incredible music on the amazing WXRT radio station while I sat alone scared doing bongs. It hurts me that this happened to her because she saved me with innovative music like this:

And, sadly, she sometimes spun a few Ted Nugent songs, too. Who knew?

But this Mr. Potato Head is deadly. The AR-15 was the gun used by Adam Lanza when he opened fire in Newtown, Conn., last December. Twenty-six people were killed, including 20 first-graders. Everyone was shot more than once — as many as 11 times. And that’s what the military wanted out of this gun — the ability to kill even without good aim, a weapon with high-capacity ammunition magazines that could spray bullets within close to medium range.

Would he, if he loved Mr. Potato Head as much as he loves his guns, be willing to stop playing with Mr. Potato Head if he learned that Mr. Potato Heads were exploding in children’s faces when they played with them? Would he be willing to make that small sacrifice and find other ways to entertain himself?

These guys are so dumb they can’t even get ritual child sacrifice right.

There is nothing boys with toys hate hearing more than “You are not a man.” Although I have often argued that real men don’t need to play with semi-automatic weapons of mass destruction, this typically falls on deaf ears (maybe because guns are loud and their eardrums are blown out).

The season finale should take place at a stadium full of these guys all shooting at each other for the ultimate prize of getting a little ribbon from Tucker Carlson. Sort of like World War Z, except in this case, the zombies all have guns.

Nobody wants their favorite football stadium getting all shot up by a bunch of lunatics. I understand this.

Thanks for reading!
