The law is almost 89 years old, which is still younger than current Sens. Dianne Feinstein (D-CA) and Chuck Grassley (R-IA) .

Only a month into the new Congress, freshman Rep. Eric Burlison (R-MO7) is making his mark.

His 2022 congressional campaign website touted him as a “2nd Amendment Champion,” featuring a photo depicting him brandishing a rifle. In Congress, he’s only doubled down on the issue.

GovTrack Insider recently covered the Abolish the ATF Act , a first-of-its-kind Republican House bill to eliminate the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms, and Explosives. Most Republicans want to limit the bureau’s authority or decrease its funding, but not eliminate it entirely. The bill has attracted only three cosponsors, all Republicans — but one of them is Rep. Burlison .

Now, he’s following through with a similar bill of his own.

The National Firearms Act (NFA) of 1934 was the first law enacted by Congress aiming to reduce the traffic and possession of automatic weapons and machine guns , through a combination of taxes, registration, and an application process.

Both the House and Senate passed it by voice vote, a procedure generally used for relatively non-controversial legislation. Though it was comparatively uncontroversial at the time, much of the Republican Party has moved to the right on the issue in recent years.

As a result, GovTrack Insider has covered recent Republican bills to amend or repeal select provisions from the NFA. They include the Hearing Protection Act which would declassify silencers so they’re no longer considered “firearms” under the NFA, and the Home Defense and Competitive Shooting Act which would remove short-barreled rifles from the NFA’s regulations.

Now, Rep. Burlison recently introduced the Repeal the NFA Act , which would overturn the National Firearms Act of 1934 in its entirety. It’s the very first bill that the freshman Congress member has ever introduced.

It was introduced in the House on January 24, as H.R. 450.

Supporters argue the National Firearms Act has long been unconstitutional and utilized as a measure to unjustly restrict people’s liberties.

“The federal government has used the National Firearms Act for almost a century to violate law-abiding citizens’ Second Amendment rights,” Rep. Burlison said in a press release . “The recent ATF pistol brace rule is just another example of these blatant attacks on the constitutional rights of Americans.”

Issued in January, the rule requires gun owners who own a stabilizing pistol brace to register the accessory within 120 days or else face a potential felony.

“The ATF-NFA sham needs to end. The [bill] will strip the ATF of its authority to criminalize lawful gun owners and will undo nearly 90 years of assault on fundamental freedoms,” Rep. Burlison continued. “I’m proud to stand with and support Americans nationwide as we take this issue head-on.”

Opponents counter that epidemic gun violence is a uniquely American public safety crisis which can best be solved by more, rather than less, effective government measures.

“It’s a talking point,” fellow Missouri Rep. Emanuel Cleaver (D-MO5) told the Kansas City Star of the Repeal the NFA Act. “But the fact that it’s even rising to this level of being introduced is kind of a slap in the face to all the family members of people who just got killed recently, and the thousands across the country.”

The phrase “just got killed recently” was likely a reference to two mass shootings in the prior week, which killed 11 and seven people.

As far as GovTrack Insider can determine, the only prior such attempt to repeal the National Firearms Act was just last year, with a 2022 House bill from then-Rep. Madison Cawthorn (R-NC11) .

Cawthorn had already lost the primary for his district’s Republican nomination by the time he introduced the bill, rendering it something close to dead on arrival even among his fellow Republicans. It attracted one cosponsor, a Republican — Rep. Lauren Boebert (R-CO3) — and never received a vote in the then-Democratic controlled chamber.

The current bill has attracted a larger nine cosponsors, all Republicans . It awaits a potential vote in the House Ways and Means Committee.

Odds of passage are low in the Democratic-controlled Senate.

title: Beto O’Rouke Stands up for Gun Control
content:
How one Texas Congressman openly challenged Abbott about gun control.

W atching the news briefing with Gov. Greg Abbott after the Robb Elementary massacre in Uvalde, Texas, was very telling as Abbott was flanked by all of his cohorts during his comments on the massacre of nineteen elementary school children and two teachers.

In the span of minutes, Gov. Abbott shared his sentiments regarding the loss of innocent lives but failed horribly short of calling the mass shooting the result of easy access to an AR-15, a high-capacity rifle, designed to kill a large number of victims. Also, there was no mention of needing laws to curb access to such weapons and implementing more extensive background checks.

D uring Abbott’s presentation of grief for the families and the victims of this mass shooting, he provided details about the shooting which is customary. It was at that moment that a Democratic Texas governor challenger, Beto O’Rourke, walked directly to the front and confronted Abbott on his sincerity regarding preventing these types of mass shootings with more strategic gun laws.

O’Rourke, a former El Paso congressman, U.S. Senate, and presidential candidate has in the recent past appeared on MSNBC challenging his opponent, Abbott, in the upcoming governor’s race about his honest concern for the state, its people, and now mass shootings. Abbott is seeking a third term as governor, as the people suffer under his administration which is affecting the poor and people of color.

M ost recently, Abbott was instrumental in instituting anti-voting rights bills making it more difficult for the young, physically challenged, and people of color to vote, anti-abortion laws, and signing a law giving the people the right to carry firearms in the public. These are just a recent few highlighting how Abbott has affected so many lives adversely.

The press briefing was held at the Uvalde High School’s auditorium, Abbott surrounded himself with state and local Republican officials, including Ted Cruz and John Cornyn. They all looked like a bookcase around Abbott as he talked about the 18-year-old shooter and how the AR-15-style rifle used in the massacre wasn’t due to Texas state’s lax gun laws but due to mental health illness in this community and suggested the need for more mental health support.

At that moment, O’Rourke was seen storming up to the front where Abbott was seated with his backup team and challenged him regarding gun violence being predictable when there are no laws in place to do otherwise. Meaning allowing a newly turned 18-year-old to be able to get access to an AR15 assault rifle days after turning 18 was not a mental health problem but a gun control issue.

Right or wrong in his stance, security quickly rushed to remove O’Rourke from the auditorium as the Uvalde Mayor Don McLaughlin shouted, “Sir, you’re out of line!,” and Ted Cruz told him to sit down. Also, Republican Lt. Gov. Dan Patrick called O’Rourke “an embarrassment.” Why is it that O’Rourke was out of order but Cruz, the Mayor, and the Lt. Governor’s comments were not? Could it be that they are of the same mindset as Abbott? That is a rhetorical question.

O ’Rourke was relentless in getting his voice heard as the many iPhone cameras hovered around him as he stated, “ “This is on you until you choose to do something different. This will continue to happen. Somebody needs to stand up for the children of this state or they will continue to be killed just like they were killed in Uvalde yesterday.”

Shortly after sharing his opinion, O’Rourke was escorted from the building but his words were at least heard. Abbott purposefully dismissed the words of O’Rourke and went on speaking to lessen the impact of O’Rourke’s words.

A bbott continued his dialogue about how family members were crying, hearts broken as he downplayed O’Rourke’s words claiming that they did nothing for healing broken hearts.

The Uvalde community wants action. That is why they yelled at President Biden when he visited Uvalde to do something. The time is overdue for fake promises as their kids die by bullets from a warped mind who got easy access to a high-power weapon.

W ords are useless unless acted upon. Thus far Abbott who is the governor of Texas has given words to the victims and their families and that’s where it all stopped as the Vualde Police Department hide their ineptness in delaying attacking the shooter which cost 19 innocent lives. Abbott, since the mass shooting has not suggested any plans to prevent mass shootings in the future.

At least O’Rourke continued talking outside the school’s auditorium as he stated what is needed to prevent mass shootings in the future. He advocated tighter gun laws as he railed against AR-15 style rifles that his native El Paso in 2019 had a mass shooting at Walmart, the worst shooting targeting Latinos in U.S. history.

O ’Rourke presented to the people facts about how other shootings around the country have been caused due to access to guns and mental health is not the culprit.

According to O’Rourke, there has been a number of shootings in his home state of Texas, a church in the central Texas town of Sutherland Springs in 2017, Santa Fe High School outside Houston in 2018, and Midland-Odessa in 2019. He said he talked to victims’ parents in Uvalde, El Paso, Santa Fe, and Midland Odessa.

O ’Rourke put forth a better defense for gun control than Abbott as he stated in the LA Times: “We owe those parents action,” … You want a solution? Stop selling AR-15s in the state of Texas. You want a solution? Have universal background checks. We don’t have them. You want a solution? Red flag laws or extreme risk protection orders, stop a shooting before it happens. You want a solution? Safe [gun] storage laws.”

When the governor of the state refuses to take any stance to arrest the situation, it is indicative that he does not care for the safety of children at school or their families. Otherwise, he would do something now with gun control. Like the rest of the GOP, Abbott focused on his career and his alliance with the NRA.

T he National Rifle Association held its annual convention in Houston at the end of the week of the mass shooting in Vualde, Texas Abbott Elementary Schools. Abbott did not attend but sent a video recording to convey his support. Attendance or sending a video proved where his alliance truly is.

In conclusion, the time for all voters to wake up is now. What happened in Vualde can happen anywhere. Until more gun laws are in place restricting easy access to guns, mass shootings will continue. The GOP is out of touch with reality and it is up to the public to take a stance, voting them out and putting others in place who cares about the people and not just power.

title: Clarence Thomas Is Wrong About Gun Control Laws
content:
Don’tcha just love it when a man says something incredibly stupid and a woman says “Are you sure?” with that arched eyebrow and look on her face that every man knows means that he has just stepped into very deep doo-doo?

Case in point. Everybody’s least favorite Supreme Court Justice, Clarence Thomas, writing the majority opinion on New York State Pistol and Rifle Association v. Bruen which struck down bans on concealed weapons, said that prior to 1900 concealed carry bans were not part of America’s history and traditions, and therefore they were unconstitutional.

That sounds like a dare to me.

And Moms Demand Action, a gun safety group, took him up on that dare. Members have been spending quality time in the basements of courthouses across the country researching gun laws prior to 1900 .

Guess what they found?

That prior to 1900, there were very robust gun control laws across the country banning concealed carry, open carry, shooting ranges, even gun powder kept in the home. That’s analogous to our own restrictions on ammunition.

We’re talking 18th and 19th century. Instead of worrying about protecting citizens’ rights to bear arms, local governments were more concerned with public safety by keeping guns out of public spaces.

Here’s just a sampling of their findings:

“The concealed carry of firearms was expressly forbidden in Memphis, Tennessee; Jersey City, Hoboken, and Plainfield, New Jersey; Chicago, Illinois; New Orleans, Louisiana; Olympia and Wilbur, Washington; and Denver, Colorado. More than 50 local governments outlawed the firing of any weapon within city limits. About 30 localities restricted or outlawed the storage of gunpowder. A dozen localities limited, heavily taxed, or banned shooting ranges.”

This ongoing research effort is important not just because it proves a pompous ass wrong, but it takes away a very important argument used by the courts to loosen gun restrictions. No longer can they use the excuse that any kind of restriction on the private ownership and carrying of guns is unconstitutional.

Regulating guns isn’t some new-fangled liberal idea designed to take away the constitutional rights of red-blooded Americans. It’s been with us literally since the founding of our country.

So why were there so many gun laws if the Constitution guarantees Americans the right to bear arms? Because it doesn’t. And Thomas and all the other conservative judges who seem bound and determined to arm every man, woman, and child in this country to the teeth, know this.

See, all these claims about originalism are just a smoke screen. If you truly want to read and interpret the Constitution exactly as it was written and understood at the time it was written, then you need to look at the state of the country at that time, not the delusions of modern-day conservatives.

At the time the Constitution was written, the United States did not have a standing army. The country relied on local militias to provide defense. And just like today’s militias, members were expected to provide their own guns, ammo, and combat gear.

To ensure that these citizen soldiers would be able to show up for militia duty properly armed, the framers wrote it directly into the Constitution in the Second Amendment:

“A well regulated Militia, being necessary to the security of a free State, the right of the people to keep and bear Arms, shall not be infringed. ”

Going back to the 18th century and getting into the minds of the framers, what they were thinking was that no laws should be passed banning ownership of weapons needed for militia duty. It’s right there in the beginning of the sentence: “a well-regulated militia, being necessary to the security of a free State.”

It doesn’t say anything about defending your home, carrying concealed weapons, or being able to carry a gun with you everywhere you go.

It says that you have a legal right to own a gun for militia duty. Period.

Okay, let’s say that you disagree with my interpretation of the Second Amendment. Let’s say that you think the Second Amendment means that every man, woman, and child in the country has the right to own as many guns as they want, can use those guns to defend their home, can carry them concealed, and can bring them everywhere they go.

Staying with originalism, cuz that’s the only legitimate way to interpret the Constitution according to conservatives, let’s take a look at the weapons that the framers were talking about when they used the word “arms.”

Muskets. Single shot pistols. Swords. Knives.

That’s it. There were no ARs, no semi-automatics, no pistols, no bump stocks, no machine guns, no bazookas, no anti-tank weapons.

So, if you are going to go by a strict interpretation of the Second Amendment which is what the NRA, conservative judges, and insecure MAGA morons insist on, then Americans have a legal right to own muskets, single shot pistols, swords, and knives. That’s it. Everything else is unconstitutional. Not to mention illegal.

I seem to have gotten a little off-track, haven’t I?

Getting back to my point about women going through dusty archives, I love the idea of taking an argument, and it’s a big argument, away from the gun fanatics and SCOTUS justices.

There is nothing unconstitutional about gun control laws. They have always been with us as a public safety measure.

And we need them now more than ever if we are going to feel safe in our schools, shopping malls, movie theaters, and even in our houses of worship.

title: Texas GOP Rejects Any Kind of Gun Control
content:
Today I would like to discuss gun control Texas-style. Actually, that’s an oxymoron. Texans don’t believe in gun control.

The Texas Republican Party held its annual convention the weekend of June 18 and 19, 2022. They produced a platform that consisted of more than 270 planks and a few rebukes.

In case you’re wondering, the planks included the expected stuff like “homosexuality is an abnormal lifestyle choice” and opposition to “all efforts to validate transgender identity.”

There were a few unexpected, at least by sane people, planks such as advocating secession from the U.S. and the Trump-friendly refusal to accept the certification of the 2020 election making Biden an illegitimate president.

And then there was the gun control issue. Senator John Cornyn who you may recall was part of the bipartisan Senate group working on a new gun control measure, was officially rebuked.

The new gun control measure is so bland and inoffensive to anyone , that applying it to the near-daily mass shootings the U.S. is experiencing is like applying a band-aid to an arterial bleed.

Here’s what the rebuke said and why I am so incensed:

“Whereas all gun control is a violation of the Second Amendment and our God-given rights, we reject the so-called ‘bipartisan gun agreement,’ and we rebuke [Sen.] John Cornyn (R-Texas).”

Any time a gun owner tells me that they have a “God-given right” to own guns, I always ask them to show me where it says that in the Bible. Which, as far as I know, is the only place where so-called God-given rights are spelled out.

Instead, they direct me to the Constitution which spells out rights granted by the Founding Fathers, not God, and which talks about the right to “keep and bear arms” for a well-regulated militia.

Not for use when someone cuts you off in traffic or if there are too many Mexicans at Walmart or because you were bullied in school and feel the need to murder young children.

Okay, getting off my soapbox now.

What particularly incensed the Texas Republicans was the inclusion in the Senate bill of “red flag” laws which allow the police to confiscate (i.e. take away) the guns of people who are deemed to be dangerous.

Texans live in fear of having their guns taken away.

According to Texas Republicans, red flag laws “violate one’s right to due process and are a pre-crime punishment of people not adjudicated guilty.”

Sounds good, right? Everyone is innocent until proven guilty, no pre-judging allowed. Except for that bit about people who the police feel might just want to use their guns to hurt innocent people.

Case in point. In New York, they have what they call bail reform. They decided, rightly, that bail discriminates against poor people who cannot afford to post it and thus languish in jail, sometimes for years, while they await their trials which may exonerate them.

So New York got rid of bail except for violent felonies, allowing people to walk free until they are proven guilty at a trial.

Much to everyone’s surprise, except the police who vehemently opposed bail reform, quite a few of those criminals are not sitting at home waiting for a trial. They are instead out committing more crimes sometimes resulting in the injury or death of innocent victims.

And quite a few police officers. I think New York is setting a record this year for the number of police shootings by criminals.

So, if we go back to those red flag laws, are Texans saying that they would rather wait for someone to injure or kill an innocent victim before they have their guns taken away? Doesn’t that violate the victims’ rights?

Cornyn was booed at the convention when he gave a speech trying to explain that the new gun bill in the Senate did not infringe on anyone’s Second Amendment rights.

It was the reaction of one convention goer that got my attention. She said the boos were a

“resounding strong opinion that Republicans do not want their gun rights shaved — not just taken away — but even just shaved in any form.”

That’s really dangerous when it comes to Texas. Cuz in Texas, people keep getting more and more gun rights. Now they are allowed to walk around town with a handgun, either openly or concealed, without a license or training.

I live in a blue state with strict gun laws and that just boggles my mind.

But getting back to my point. Not only do Texans object to having any gun rights taken away, they will not even tolerate small modifications like, maybe you want people to get a little training before they head to the mall with their gun?

Or how about requiring a license? Texans need a license to drive a car , so why not a license to own a gun? It seems innocuous enough.

The really sad part is that if red flag laws ever made it to the Supreme Court, SCOTUS would side with Texans. The justices are expected to overturn a New York law that strictly regulates handgun carry in the state.

In New York, it is illegal to carry a handgun openly outside of your home. If you want concealed carry, you must apply for a permit and give a damn good reason why you need to carry a concealed handgun.

New York is not the only state with such laws, so if SCOTUS strikes down the New York law, it will affect multiple states.

And nudge the entire country closer to the Texas model of all guns, all the time with no restrictions.

title: South Bay’s Concealed Carry Ordinance: Gun Rights vs. Gun Control
content:
The recent passing of South Bay’s concealed carry ordinance has caused a stir among gun enthusiasts who feel their Second Amendment rights are being disregarded. They assert that the legislation hinders their ability to carry weapons, specifically in areas deemed sensitive, such as schools, government buildings, and public parks. Those who advocate for protecting gun owners’ rights have voiced their strong disapproval, believing this policy openly undermines their right to safeguard themselves.

Gun control advocates are growing more anxious as studies reveal a troubling possibility: “shall-issue” laws that permit carrying concealed firearms may lead to a surge in both gun-related and overall homicides. Such research emphasizes that such regulations, far from deterring gun violence, may have adverse effects.

The Second Amendment and its interpretation by gun rights supporters have been called into question by South Bay’s concealed carry ordinance, causing an emotional outcry from the community. Gun control measures in California have frequently resulted in legal challenges and disputes from advocates in the past, which makes the current situation all the more volatile.

This year, San Jose faced a similar problem where the rights group contested firearm fees and insurance requirements. As a result, the future of the South Bay ordinance is still being determined since gun advocates have remained mysterious about their action plans.

Here we are again, back to discussing gun control. The South Bay’s concealed carry ordinance controversy has brought this topic front and center, igniting debates across the United States. Some people are convinced that gun control laws are necessary to reduce gun violence, but others are just as emphatic that these measures violate their Second Amendment rights. As we delve into this contentious issue, we must consider public safety and individual freedoms.

title: Don’t Care About Gun Control, Women’s Rights or Climate Change?
content:
You carry a gun, so what’s the big deal? You don’t have to worry about getting raped or having an abortion, so why care? You think climate change is, at best, an exaggeration; it’s the price of progress and soon we’ll colonize space. So why limit industry’s ability to poison the environment?

Let’s say you are that person. Let’s say you’re not angry and aching when you contemplate your children’s and grandchildren’s future. Let’s say you’re happy with the Supreme Court justices who are rolling back the rights of people who don’t think like you. You probably see gay marriage as an affront to the sacred covenant of marriage, so why not abolish that, as well? Maybe you’d like to get rid of Loving v. Virginia , too?

Well, here’s a story that even you might care about — or at least you should:

Gross v. FBL Financial Group , the case in which the 2009 Supreme Court found in favor of the company, not the 54-year-old employee who claimed he was treated unfairly after a company merger. Will Harrison notes in a 2021 piece that the decision…

…eviscerated age discrimination protections in employment and made it easier for employers to fire or demote an employee because of their age. Gross and subsequent cases also show the tangible effects that conservative judicial rulings have on the rights of everyday Americans.

Thirteen years ago, the court was split 5–4, with the conservative judges arguing that age discrimination should have a higher burden than race and sex discrimination. In other words, be careful about denying a job to a women or person of color, but the old folks…no problem.

The 2009 ruling chipped away at the 1967 Age Discrimination in Employment Act (ADEA), which was designed to protect workers and job applicants 40 and older from unfair treatment. (Pause here to reflect: this particular definition of “old” is forty !)

The 2009 decision was not under the radar and, according to Harrison, led to “widespread outcry.”

Law Professor Michael Foreman wrote that the decision “immediately impacted older workers, relegating them to second-class status among victims of discrimination . . . .” A bipartisan group of Senators introduced legislation to correct the Supreme Court’s decision and clarify that age discrimination should be decided under a less burdensome standard. Lawmakers had just taken similar action by passing the Lilly Ledbetter Fair Pay Act to correct a different Supreme Court decision that had made it harder to sue over discriminatory wages.

The Gross decision, Harrison notes, has since been used by lower courts to reject age-discrimination cases.

One of those cases was recently decided by the Seventh Circuit Court of Appeals. In 2019, all four of President Trump’s appointees to the Seventh Circuit (covering Illinois, Indiana, and Wisconsin), including future Supreme Court Justice Amy Coney Barrett, cast the deciding votes in a case that further limited protections for older Americans in the workplace.

Sound familiar? Just substitute the words older Americans workers with other recently attacked groups and causes — and, may the Force be with us — more to come.

So if you’re sitting around with friends celebrating the recent Supreme Court decisions that have nothing to do with you…know that soon they’re coming for you, too!

title: Gun Control, The Home Edition
content:
By Tim Clark

A man carrying an assault type rifle shot over thirty people in a bowling alley and a restaurant in Lewiston, Maine. At least 18 of them have died. There were standard offerings of thoughts and prayers for the fallen and their families.

Fox Television host Sean Hannity told Presidential candidate Nikki Hayley he has a plan if he is ever involved in an incident involving an armed gunman in a crowded place. Mixed martial arts. Fortunately, he didn’t elaborate on how he would throw the gunman to the ground and put him in such pain he would never try to shoot anybody again. Or, maybe he did, and I quit listening. Times of such grief and tragedy make me gloss over things I might normally find amusing.

Former House Speaker, Newt Gingrich, among many, lobbied for easier, and expanded concealed carry permits, they feel there are not enough guns. In Ohio it’s easier to buy a gun than it is to vote. It’s considerably less work to get a permit to allow you to carry a concealed weapon than it is to get baby formula.

Of course, Governor Mike DeWine had the ultimate answer, a solution so Republican I’m amazed nobody thought of this before.

He asked the legislature to approve a bill that would allow families to petition the courts to have the guns removed from people who had a drinking problem, used drugs, or had “mental health issues.” It’s almost perfect, everybody is free to carry guns unless a family member can prove to the courts that they’ve been drinking, or smoking a little dope, or maybe indulging in a few pot brownies, or trying some of the new, easy to eat gummies, or partaking in a few of the new easy to consume… Well, you understand.

“You can own and carry a gun, as long as you are willing to lay off the psilocybin, pothead!”

I’ve been known to indulge a little, sometimes a lot, and I think people who aren’t afraid to “burn a little of the ceremonial herb,” if you catch my drift, can have all the guns they want. They won’t be able to find them, anyway. And they aren’t going to want anything that loud or explosive anywhere in the same room.

DeWine, and the Ohio GOP have taken a resolute stand against background checks. Apparently, they are willing to support them as long as it is the family scrutinizing the records, checking for those little character flaws that signal a person is not healthy enough to own and carry a firearm.

DeWine’s bill has the additional benefit of adding financial and legal responsibility to the family of the shooter.

title: Do People Who Want Gun Control Know What to Say to Gun Owners?
content:
Carolyn Maloney is a House member who chairs the House Oversight Committee and is today chairing the hearing on banning assault rifles prior to a House vote on a bill thar will die in the Senate. Since 2013, she has been pushing a bill to criminalize gun trafficking, parts of which were incorporated into the gun-control bill just signed by Joe.

Maloney didn’t do groups and individuals who are concerned about gun violence and mass shootings any favors in the way she led this hearing. The witnesses were from two companies that manufacture assault rifles — Daniel Defense and Sturm Ruger — versus Ryan Busse from Giffords and a staffer from the Brady Campaign.

The fifth panelist was a young, African-American woman from the Gun Owners of America ( GOA ) nut-job gang, who claimed that Black women were the fastest-growing demographic of gun owners, a statement for which there is absolutely not a shred of real data but so what? Who needs facts to back up an argument about guns, right?

The other side, of course, has its own interesting deployment of data to bolster its point of view. In particular, there’s this whole thing about all the so-called ‘new’ gun buyers who have armed themselves over the last couple of years. The numbers come from both the gun industry and from public health research.

There’s only one little problem, however, with this argument about how the Pandemic has increased the number of Americans who own guns. Has anyone bothered to figure out how many gun owners died from Covid-19 who otherwise might be alive if China hadn’t sent us the ‘kung flu?’ And let’s not forget to mention that this virus is particularly virulent among older people, who just happen to be the demographic most likely to own guns.

Anyway, back to the hearing.

So, the Democrats on the panel tossed easy questions to the panelists from Gifford and Brady, the POS/GOP members tossed softballs to the guys from the two companies that manufacture the AR-15. Nobody on either side said anything that hasn’t been said before — the gun-control people want to ban assault rifles; the pro-gun advocates want to toss all the potential bad people with a gun into jail.

What struck me as I watched the proceedings, however, was the degree to which none of the House members nor the panelists tried to say anything that might be of interest to the other side. These two groups — gun ‘rights’ versus gun control — never (read: never) ask themselves to come up with an argument that might resonate with even one person who doesn’t agree with what they are always going to say.

I’m not expecting to hear a rational or defensible argument from the pro-gun side, because there is no rational or reasonable argument to be made for keeping an AR-15 or a hi-capacity, semi-automatic pistol like a Glock or a Sig around the house.

The reason I have those kinds of guns around my house is very simple: I like guns. Maybe it’s a case of arrested mental development, maybe I want to believe that I can be a real, tough guy if I walk around with a gun. Maybe I’m just full of shit.

Anyway, it really doesn’t matter what I think as long as I have the GOA protecting my 2nd-Amendment ‘rights.’

Several years ago, an old man came into my gun shop and bought a gun. He had trouble filling out the background-check form and started cursing ‘that goddamn Kennedy,’ even though Ted Kennedy never promoted gun-control measures in his public remarks.

Finally, I got pissed off at the guy and said: “Hey Mister, if you had two brothers who were shot to death by men who used legally purchased guns, wouldn’t you be in favor of more gun control?”

The guy stopped filling out the form, looked down, then looked at me and replied, “You know, nobody ever said that to me before.”

I am still waiting for one of the gun-control groups to come up with a meaningful way to explain gun risk to gun owners without lecturing them on being ‘responsible’ with their guns. I am still waiting for the public health researchers to discuss the same thing.

How come it’s so hard to figure out something to say to gun owners that they haven’t already heard?

title: Beyond Gun Control: A Multidimensional Approach to Preventing Mass Shootings in the United States
content:
The recent school shooting in Nashville is a tragic reminder of the ongoing issue of gun violence in the United States. Our hearts go out to the victims, their families, and the entire community affected by this senseless act of violence. It is imperative that we continue to work towards preventing such tragedies from happening in the future by implementing effective measures to reduce gun violence and support mental health initiatives.

The issue of mass shootings in the United States is a complex and multifaceted problem that cannot be solved by focusing solely on gun control measures. While gun control policies can play a role in reducing the incidence of mass shootings, they are only one aspect of a broader range of factors that contribute to this problem.

A multidimensional approach is necessary to address the issue of mass shootings in the US. This approach should include:

Predictive modeling and AI can potentially play a significant role in the early identification of individuals who may be at risk of committing mass shootings. By analyzing data from various sources, such as social media activity, criminal records, and mental health records, AI can help identify patterns and potential warning signs that may indicate a higher risk of violence.

One potential use of predictive modeling and AI is to develop algorithms that can analyze social media activity and identify individuals who may be expressing violent or threatening language or behavior. These algorithms can also analyze patterns of behavior to identify changes that may indicate an increased risk of violence.

Another potential use of predictive modeling and AI is to analyze data from criminal and mental health records to identify individuals who may have a history of violent behavior or mental illness. By identifying these individuals early, law enforcement agencies and mental health professionals can intervene and provide support or treatment to prevent the escalation of violent behavior.

However, there are also significant concerns and limitations to the use of predictive modeling and AI in this context. These concerns include issues related to privacy, bias, and accuracy. For example, the algorithms used to analyze social media data may inadvertently target individuals based on their race, ethnicity, or other factors, leading to unfair or discriminatory outcomes. Additionally, there is a risk that the algorithms may generate false positives, identifying individuals as potential threats when they pose no actual risk of violence.

Therefore, while predictive modeling and AI have the potential to help identify individuals who may be at risk of committing mass shootings, it is important to approach their use with caution and to implement appropriate safeguards to ensure that they are used ethically and effectively.

The issue of mass shootings in the United States also involves multiple stakeholders who have a role to play in addressing the problem. Some of the key stakeholders and their reasons for involvement are:

In the United States, there is no central or shared database of all gun purchases and ownership.

Studies have shown that many mass shootings involve multiple guns.

A study by the Gun Violence Archive found that between 2013 and 2021, 26% of mass shootings (defined as incidents in which four or more people were shot, not including the shooter) involved the use of multiple guns. Another study by the Center for American Progress found that in 54% of mass shootings between 2009 and 2016, the shooters had more than one gun.

Furthermore, some of the deadliest mass shootings in recent U.S. history have involved multiple firearms. For example, the 2017 Las Vegas shooting, which was the deadliest mass shooting in modern U.S. history, involved the use of 23 firearms. The 2016 Pulse nightclub shooting in Orlando, which was previously the deadliest mass shooting in modern U.S. history, involved the use of two firearms.

While the number of guns used in mass shootings can vary, it is clear that these incidents often involve the use of multiple firearms. This highlights the need for measures to restrict access to firearms and prevent individuals who may be at risk of committing acts of violence from obtaining them.

A single database of gun sales could potentially be used to flag individuals who purchase multiple firearms and identify those who may be at risk of committing acts of violence. This information could be used to conduct more thorough background checks on these individuals and to monitor their behavior for potential warning signs.

However, it is important to approach the use of such a database with caution and to ensure that appropriate safeguards are in place to protect individual privacy and prevent government overreach. Additionally, it is important to recognize that not all individuals who purchase multiple firearms are at risk of committing acts of violence, and that additional measures, such as mental health support and community involvement, are needed to prevent mass shootings.

There are arguments for and against the creation of a centralized database for all transactions on gun sales/exchanges in the United States.

Proponents of a centralized database argue that it would help prevent gun violence by providing law enforcement with more comprehensive information about gun ownership and sales. This would allow law enforcement to more effectively track guns used in crimes, identify illegal sales and transfers, and prevent individuals who are prohibited from owning firearms from obtaining them. Additionally, proponents argue that a database would help prevent accidental shootings and suicides by providing gun owners with a way to verify the safety and ownership of a firearm before purchasing or exchanging it.

Opponents of a centralized database argue that it would be a violation of the Second Amendment right to bear arms and that it would be difficult to implement in a way that respects individual privacy. They also argue that it would be expensive and difficult to maintain, and that it could be used to unfairly target law-abiding gun owners or facilitate government surveillance.

There are also practical concerns about how a centralized database would be implemented and maintained. Creating a database that accurately and comprehensively tracks all gun sales/exchanges would require significant resources, including funding, personnel, and infrastructure. Additionally, there would be concerns about the accuracy and completeness of the data in the database, as well as the security and privacy of the information.

These examples highlight the potential effectiveness of implementing measures such as gun control, licensing and background checks, and restrictions on certain types of firearms in reducing mass shootings and gun-related deaths.

Preventing mass shootings is a complex and ongoing process that requires sustained effort and collaboration among multiple stakeholders, including government, law enforcement, mental health professionals, schools, and communities. By working together and addressing the underlying factors that contribute to mass shootings, we can help create a safer and more peaceful society for everyone.

title: Where Americans Agree on Gun Control
content:
And the wildcards and court decisions that hamstring execution.

I T’S NO SECRET that Americans are divided on the personal ownership of firearms. The divide has only become sharper since the United States Supreme Court has made several decisions over the last 15 years favorable to ownership under the context of the Second Amendment of the Constitution. And other factors have thrown wild cards into the mix.

We poured over 2023 survey data from Pew Research to see if we could make sense of the divide and any wild cards. This is Pew’s first survey in the post-COVID era, in which we saw a drop in support for gun regulations and a large increase in gun purchases and first-time ownership. It provides a glimpse of where we are in the aftermath of the uncertainty and unrest in 2020 and 2021.

According to the data, 60% of Americans believe that gun violence is a “very big problem,” and a further 36% acknowledge that it is either a moderate or a small problem. That’s 96% who would use the word problem when describing American gun violence.

Other points of general agreement:

While gun violence did rise through 2021 and 2022, there are signs that the murder rate will actually fall in most places in 2023, while still remaining higher than it was in 2019.

In any case, we’re in near universal agreement that gun violence is a problem.

Currently, one is deemed ineligible to purchase or possess a firearm if determined by a lawful authority (such as a court, board, or commission) to be a danger to oneself or others, or to lack the mental capacity to manage one's own affairs as a result of “marked subnormal intelligence, or mental illness, incompetency, condition, or disease.”

A finding of not guilty by reason of insanity, or a finding of incompetence to stand trial in a criminal case also makes one ineligible.

An involuntary commitment to a mental institution by a lawful authority, including drug rehabilitation also makes one ineligible.

Many remain skeptical of expanding further than the above. For instance, there are fears that religious conservatives might deem LGBTQ as a mental defect as a pretext to disarm the community. Or that anti-gun coalitions would want to expand the definitions to include the use of certain popular prescription drugs that help people remain healthy and manage certain mental illnesses that remain safe as long as managed.

Currently, all states have laws restricting anyone under the age of 21 from purchasing a handgun. An additional seven states (California, Florida, Illinois, New York, South Dakota, Vermont, and Washington) restrict all gun sales to those 21 and over.

The wild card to this one: in May, a federal judge in Virginia ruled that such laws are unconstitutional under the precedent set by the Supreme Court’s Bruen ruling . The ruling has yet to take effect, and will certainly face a challenge from the United States Department of Justice.

Currently, the following states have restrictions on high-capacity magazines: California, Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, District of Columbia, Hawaii, Maryland, Massachusetts, New Jersey, New York, Oregon, Rhode Island, Vermont, and Washington.

There are several wild cards in this one:

The 1994 Federal Assault Weapons Ban contained a ten-year sunset provision and expired in 2004. This effectively sent the issue back to the states.

Currently, ten states have some sort of ban on assault-style weapons: California, Connecticut, Delaware, Hawaii, Maryland, Massachusetts, New Jersey, New York, Illinois, and Washington.

Recent attempts at bans failed in Colorado and Virginia, both of which had Democratic-controlled legislative and executive branches at the time.

State bans have so far survived state-level challenges, and survived emergency federal constitutional challenges. However, multiple cases are in motion to overturn some of them at the federal level.

The wild card: about 24.4 million gun owners own the most popular style of assault-style weapon, the AR-15. This is a possible boost for the “common-use” argument under the 2008 Heller decision, which stated that the Second Amendment protects “arms ‘in common use at the time’ for lawful purposes like self-defense” and arms that are “typically possessed by law-abiding citizens for lawful purposes.”

Support for stricter regulations has remained at a majority level over the years, although in 2021, it dipped as low as 53%. By 2023, it had bounced back to 58%. This still being the weakest area of agreement, there are plenty of wild cards to consider.

Gender

64% of women express support for stricter gun laws, with 51% of men in support. However, women are also known to be one of the fastest-growing demographics of gun owners. While the ownership rate is estimated at 22% for women, 33% of first-time purchases over the last few years have been by women, indicating an ownership rate that may increase in the next round of surveying.

Given that women are driving both support for stricter laws and a disproportional amount of first-time purchases, will this lead to a decrease in support for stricter gun laws in the next few years? Or are some of these women both in favor of restrictions and some rights to personal ownership?

Race and Ethnicity

A slight majority of whites (51%) support stricter gun laws. However, among other groups, the support increases significantly:

But again, minority groups are also driving first-time purchases since 2019. According to the National Shooting Sports Foundation, 2020 saw a 58.2% increase in gun purchases among Black people, a 43% increase among Asians and 49% among Hispanics.

The wild card here is that, despite the increase in purchases and ownership, so far , these groups still appear to support increased laws and regulations.

Gun Ownership

Of course, a majority of gun owners (71%) would believe that gun ownership increases safety. However, the personal gun ownership rate is estimated to be about 33% of adult Americans, about 69 million people.

Among non-owners, only 37% believe that gun ownership increases safety. However, non-gun owners make up about 67% of adult Americans, about 144.3 million people. Given this, we can assume that about 53.4 million non-owners still nominally support ownership, even if they do not own any.

Combined belief in gun safety increasing adds up to about 102.4 million people, about 49% of the adult population.

Backing this up, 36% of non-owners state that they are open to the idea of owning a gun in the future, which tracks with the 37% who believe gun ownership increases safety.

This definitely muddies the water a bit when it comes to support of stricter laws.

Supreme Court Decisions

Finally, we have the recent liberal interpretations* of the Second Amendment with which to contend.

The Heller decision in 2008 ruled that the Second Amendment protects an individual’s right to keep and bear arms. It also stated that such a right is entirely unconnected with a militia. The ruling stated that the Second Amendment protects traditionally lawful purposes such as self-defense within the home. It struck down Washington, DC’s handgun ban and requirements that other legal firearms be kept “unloaded and disassembled or bound by a trigger lock, as this effectively made them useless for self-defense of one’s home.

Heller also left an opening for restrictions beyond this, stating that the right to bear arms is not unlimited. However, the decision was notable because it was the first to decide whether the Second Amendment protects an individual right to keep and bear arms for self-defense unconnected to a militia.

The Bruen decision in 2022 ruled that the ability to carry a pistol in public is a constitutional right under the Second Amendment. The meat of the decision involved concealed carry permitting and the concepts of “shall issue” vs. “may issue.”

In a “shall issue” system, states set certain criteria, and as long as an individual meets the criteria, the state (or local jurisdiction) shall issue the permit.

In a “may issue” system, states and/or jurisdictions set criteria, but the final decision is still up to the discretion of the issuing authority. In such a system, the issuing authority could simply deny all permits, or use arbitrary reasoning to deny some while approving others.

The Bruen decision determined that states are allowed to enforce “shall-issue” permitting, but “may issue” permitting is no longer allowed because they use “arbitrary” evaluations.

However, the most consequential aspect of the Bruen decision was the new precedent to weigh gun laws against a “historical tradition of firearm regulation.” Combined with the earlier Heller decision, the precedent is now:

The divide has only become sharper since the United States Supreme Court has made several decisions over the last 15 years favorable to ownership under the context of the Second Amendment of the Constitution. And other factors have thrown wild cards into the mix.

This is Pew’s first survey in the post-COVID era, in which we saw a drop in support for gun regulations and a large increase in gun purchases and first-time ownership. It provides a glimpse of where we are in the aftermath of the uncertainty and unrest in 2020 and 2021.

According to the data, 60% of Americans believe that gun violence is a “very big problem,” and a further 36% acknowledge that it is either a moderate or a small problem. That’s 96% who would use the word problem when describing American gun violence.

Other points of general agreement:

While gun violence did rise through 2021 and 2022, there are signs that the murder rate will actually fall in most places in 2023, while still remaining higher than it was in 2019.

In any case, we’re in near universal agreement that gun violence is a problem.

Currently, one is deemed ineligible to purchase or possess a firearm if determined by a lawful authority (such as a court, board, or commission) to be a danger to oneself or others, or to lack the mental capacity to manage one's own affairs as a result of “marked subnormal intelligence, or mental illness, incompetency, condition, or disease.”

A finding of not guilty by reason of insanity, or a finding of incompetence to stand trial in a criminal case also makes one ineligible.

An involuntary commitment to a mental institution by a lawful authority, including drug rehabilitation also makes one ineligible.

Many remain skeptical of expanding further than the above. For instance, there are fears that religious conservatives might deem LGBTQ as a mental defect as a pretext to disarm the community. Or that anti-gun coalitions would want to expand the definitions to include the use of certain popular prescription drugs that help people remain healthy and manage certain mental illnesses that remain safe as long as managed.

Currently, all states have laws restricting anyone under the age of 21 from purchasing a handgun. An additional seven states (California, Florida, Illinois, New York, South Dakota, Vermont, and Washington) restrict all gun sales to those 21 and over.

Currently, the following states have restrictions on high-capacity magazines: California, Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, District of Columbia, Hawaii, Maryland, Massachusetts, New Jersey, New York, Oregon, Rhode Island, Vermont, and Washington.

The 1994 Federal Assault Weapons Ban contained a ten-year sunset provision and expired in 2004. This effectively sent the issue back to the states.

Recent attempts at bans failed in Colorado and Virginia, both of which had Democratic-controlled legislative and executive branches at the time.

State bans have so far survived state-level challenges, and survived emergency federal constitutional challenges. However, multiple cases are in motion to overturn some of them at the federal level.

But again, minority groups are also driving first-time purchases since 2019. According to the National Shooting Sports Foundation, 2020 saw a 58.2% increase in gun purchases among Black people, a 43% increase among Asians and 49% among Hispanics.

title: Why I Gave Up On Gun Control
content:
In 2018, I got a strange meeting request, “Mandatory meeting.”

I was still working in finance, in what would be my final corporate job.

I went to the small room where five other analysts had gathered. People were looking around, unsure of what was going on. My boss was noticeably absent.

An employee stood up and got teary-eyed and started talking. I got nervous, thinking something may have happened to someone. She said our boss had traveled out of town and wouldn’t be back for several weeks.

title: California Pushes Constitutional Amendment On Gun Control
content:
Governor Gavin Newsom’s groundbreaking proposal for a Right to Safety Amendment to the U.S. Constitution has been introduced as a joint resolution in the California Legislature. If passed, California would become the first state to call for a convention about amending the U.S. Constitution. This move has sparked a heated debate among gun owners and advocates for stricter gun control laws.

The proposed Right to Safety Amendment, also known as the 28th Amendment, aims to address the pressing issue of gun violence without infringing on the Second Amendment. Governor Newsom’s office has emphasized that the amendment would not revoke the Second Amendment but rather enhance it with measures designed to promote public safety.

One of the key provisions of the proposed amendment is raising the minimum age to purchase a gun from 18 to 21. This aligns with the argument that younger individuals may lack the maturity and responsibility to handle firearms safely. The amendment aims to reduce the likelihood of impulsive and reckless gun ownership by increasing the age requirement.

Another significant aspect of the amendment is the proposed ban on assault rifles for civilians. This provision has drawn both support and criticism from different factions. Supporters argue that banning assault rifles would help prevent mass shootings and reduce the availability of weapons that pose a higher risk to public safety. Critics, on the other hand, argue that such a ban infringes on their Second Amendment rights and could lead to a slippery slope of further restrictions on gun ownership.

In addition to these measures, the Right to Safety Amendment would affirm the authority of Congress, states, and local governments to enact common-sense gun safety laws that save lives. This provision recognizes the need for tailored approaches to gun control that reflect the diverse needs and circumstances of different regions within the United States. It also emphasizes the importance of balancing individual rights and public safety.

The introduction of this amendment has ignited a passionate discussion among gun owners, as it directly affects their rights and responsibilities. Governor Newsom’s diplomatic approach addresses legitimate concerns while prioritizing public safety. The proposal seeks to find common ground where gun owners can feel secure in their rights while acknowledging the need for reasonable regulations.

The outcome of this resolution in California could have far-reaching implications for the nation. If successful, California would set a precedent as the first state to call for a convention about amending the U.S. Constitution on gun control. This development could influence other states to follow suit and trigger a national conversation on gun rights and regulations.

As the debate unfolds, all stakeholders must engage in constructive dialogue respecting varying perspectives. Ultimately, the goal should be to find solutions that balance the right to bear arms and the need to ensure public safety. We can navigate this complex issue and work towards a safer future for all through open and respectful discussions.

title: Vice President Harris Advocates for Stricter Gun Control Measures: Cites Australian Model
content:
In a recent speech, Vice President Kamala Harris commended Australia’s strict gun control laws, where citizens don’t have a legal right to gun ownership and a mass gun confiscation occurred in the 1990s. Speaking at a State Department luncheon with Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, Harris emphasized that mass shootings don’t have to be a common occurrence, even in a country as large as the United States.

Australia’s approach to firearm ownership stands in stark contrast to the U.S. According to the Australian Parliament’s official website, there is no legal entitlement to gun ownership, and individuals must demonstrate a genuine reason for possessing a firearm. Notably, self-defense is not considered a valid reason under Australian law.

Furthermore, individuals acquiring firearms must obtain a license, and each firearm is required to be individually registered. This differs from neighboring countries like New Zealand and Canada, where purchasers need a license but have relatively unrestricted access to firearms once licensed.

Australia’s strict gun control measures were implemented in 1996 following a series of high-profile mass shootings. The National Firearms Agreement of 1996 banned automatic and semi-automatic firearms, introduced firearm registration, enforced stricter storage requirements, and significantly restricted non-military style semi-automatic rifle and shotgun purchases. Additionally, the government executed a mandatory gun buyback program, resulting in the collection of nearly 700,000 privately-owned firearms.

Former Australian Prime Minister John Howard, who played a pivotal role in these reforms, noted in a New York Times op-ed that the changes not only reduced gun-related homicides but also suicide rates.

The speech comes in the wake of a tragic shooting in Lewiston, Maine, which claimed at least 18 lives and left dozens injured. The suspect, Robert Card, is a trained firearms instructor with a history of mental health issues. As law enforcement agencies intensively search for him, the White House has yet to issue a formal response.

title: UNTITLED
content:
GUN CONTROL

Before I tell you why I stopped carrying my Bersa every day, I want to mention this point. I have a rule in my home that me and only me knows the whereabouts, and the specific location, I keep my Bersa (gun). Why? Because I make the decision when I use my Bersa, no one else. I am responsible for my weapon. To this day, our daughter doesn’t know that I own a gun.

Some years ago, I carried my Bersa EVERYWHERE. On my person, in my vehicle when I ran an errand or when I went on a trip (business or personal) traveling by car. On this particular day, I parked my car at the post office (not far from a military installation). I add this tidbit here because in my experience MOST military people in a military town own a weapon and sure as hell know how to fire one so I assume more people than not are concealing a weapon. Now everyone doesn’t think like me of course.

I went to the post office minding my own business. It was BUSY! There wasn’t any close parking in sight. I had my trusty Bersa with me as usual, like wearing panties (most days). As I was trekking to the main entrance of the post office, which seemed as if it would take forever, I passed a man in his parked car. For whatever reason, without warning, the man became very animated, and as I continued to walk the man began cussing even louder.

It was so bizarre! To this day, I don’t know what possessed me to stop, turn around and get closer to ask him who he was talking to but as you can imagine, he said YOU! Yep, stamp my forehead, STUPID! You know what happened next. He cussed me with such rapid fire, I barely understood the majority of what he was saying until he uttered… Why don’t you get back on the boat that brought you here and go back to your country? WTF? He was probably about 70 years old. Yep, old enough to fucking know better.

I will never forget what happened next.

I felt I was in a vortex.

I asked him to repeat what he said and yes, he stated verbatim and 10X louder for me to get back on the boat that brought me here and get back to my country…

Like a magic show, I had one hand out and in the open and oh dear fuck, the other hand was preoccupied, resting on my damn Bersa!

Mentally, now I was deep into this, I was committed to what would come next and it happened in slow motion.

I raised my voice, with added anger, and said…

Why don’t you get the fucking boat, and since you’re such a smartass, why don’t you fucking send me back to my country?

He was shocked by my response because he didn’t utter one fucking word.

He immediately placed both hands, first on his steering wheel then above his head, and started shaking and whimpering.

Did he piss himself?

Thankfully his placing his hands above his head alerted me (read snapped my stupid ass back to reality) to his decision to retreat. THANKFULLY at that moment, I didn’t further lose my grip on reality!

Crazy as it sounds, I continued my walk to the post office, calmly as if nothing had happened. Only once I returned to my car after my business was completed did it hit me what had transpired forty minutes earlier.

Reality set in.

What would have happened if this man had waited for me?

What would have happened if he had blown my brains out?

What would have happened if I had blown his stupid fuck face off for spewing hatred? You and I both know what… I would have fucked my life and I would have regretted taking the racist’s life a smidge bit early.

The conclusion I drew in that delayed moment was jail time obviously would not be worth it. I also promised I would NEVER allow myself to be MIND FUCKED EVER AGAIN!

I was disappointed in my actions that day.

I questioned why I didn’t keep walking?

Why I didn’t keep my mouth shut?

Why I didn’t use my brain? Damn, I knew better not to follow an idiot EVEN if he was a racist, down a rabbit hole.

I decided during those moments of reflection to stop carrying my Bersa. I stopped cold turkey that day .

The lesson I learned at that moment was what my parents had warned me prior, my entire life. You will meet people that have fucked up perspectives, those same people will attempt to pull you into the fray. The problem is IF you decide to remotely participate, you're done. You will be ready to stop the ride and get off (because you have responsibilities). Little do you know; their asses have packed a 12-course meal because they have been waiting for THIS moment to unleash pent-up frustrations and it’s going to be a late night of complete chaos and mayhem!

If you are wondering if my parents prepared me so well, why did I fall for the encounter with the old racist? Easy, because I had never experienced racism. Surprised? Okay but true. I grew up with hundreds of people of different nationalities ( the benefit of a military town and some traveling, thank you ). I am from a time that EVERYTHING was integrated. Interracial dating, diverse scholar clubs, schools, sports, friend groups, YOU NAME IT! Looking back now, I understand, I was inexperienced, I was naive to racism. I was barely 21 years old, and he was 70ish.

I now expect people (racists included) to attempt to hem me up therefore I avoid them and keep it moving.

I have learned to use extreme patience.

I avoid confrontation and use my brain to diffuse a situation without pulling out the ultimate equalizer .

I teach our daughter, that I don’t care what a person calls you, or calls me or anyone in our family. I don’t care if a person cusses you. She has been taught to stay out of the weeds and take swift action by notifying an adult for help and to contact Mama Bear ASAP!

I will tell ANYONE if you are not, and I repeat, if you are not (or a family member) is not in imminent danger . Call the police if you can’t avoid or defuse a situation.

Do not EVER attempt to diffuse a situation with a piece of metal. Using a gun for stupid reasons and people shooting their mouths off is a very stupid reason that you will regret on many levels while you are sitting somewhere in jail (if you’re lucky) marking the days until your release AGAIN if you’re lucky…..

Thanks for reading my story and I hope you will return for Part 2!

title: Would More Gun Control Have Prevented What Happened in KC?
content:
So, because I’m something of a gun nut myself and have published nearly 2,000 columns about guns on my gun blog , the first thing I did this morning was to click on Google News and read the lead story out of Kansas City which ‘explained’ the Super Bowl shooting as an event which reflects Missouri’s ‘weak’ gun laws.

Here’s the explanation in full:

“Missouri’s gun laws are considered some of the laxest in the country, with the Giffords Law Center calling them “appallingly weak.”

No background check is required to purchase a firearm, nor is a permit for concealed carry. There is no ban on assault weapons.

There are also no restrictions on gun ownership for people who have been convicted of violent crimes, and firearms are not required to be locked up to prevent children from accessing them.

In 2021, Missouri enacted a law called the “Second Amendment Preservation Act,” which made federal gun regulations illegal statewide, and prohibited law enforcement from enforcing any federal laws that “infringe on the people’s right to keep and bear arms.”

A federal judge later struck it down, having ruled the state law unconstitutional, and the Supreme Court upheld the decision.”

Now, let’s take this piece of ‘news’ one by one, okay?

No background check is required to purchase a firearm, nor is a permit for concealed carry. There is no ban on assault weapons . Every purchase of a gun from a dealer in Missouri requires a background check conducted by the FBI.

There are also no restrictions on gun ownership for people who have been convicted of violent crimes, and firearms are not required to be locked up to prevent children from accessing them. Nobody can pass a background check who has been convicted of a violent crime.

That’s enough. Evidently, the author of this story has never heard of the federal law passed in 1993 and fully implemented in 1998 which requires that anyone who buys a gun from a gun dealer in all 50 states must first pass a background check.

This law must even be followed in a wide-open, gun-loving state like Missouri where the two juveniles being held for yesterday’s shooting could not have had legal access to their guns.

Now granted, Missouri is typical of many states which don’t want to spend any money on supplementing federal gun laws with state laws because when a state is politically controlled by the GOP , laws which require spending any public monies on just about anything don’t usually see the light of day.

But in fact, Kansas City does have a local ordinance which prohibits kids from getting their hands on guns or ammunition without parental consent, and the reason that Missouri has a higher-than-average rate of gun violence is not because of the so-called ‘lax’ gun laws throughout the state, but because of gun violence in St. Louis, which happens to be at the opposite end of the state from Kansas City.

St. Louis is not only where about half of all gun homicides occur every year in Missouri (the city has 5% of the state’s total population) but after a dramatic decrease in shootings within the city during the Pandemic, last year the city’s Mayor referred to shootings as a “plague.” And there has yet to be any kind of explanation offered by anyone as to why gun deaths and shootings declined during the Pandemic and then jumped back up.

Incidentally, St. Louis has a program called ‘lock it for love,’ which provides city residents with gun locks at every fire station in the town. Fat lot of good that one does, right?

The story which I referenced at the top of this column is typical of the kind of disinformation which floats around the digital universe but shapes how people think and what they believe. But this lack of reality is particularly frequent when the issue in question happens to be anything having to do with guns.

title: Amend the Second Amendment to End Gun Violence
content:
Let me start by saying two things: 1) I doubt we will ever amend the Second Amendment, but I think it is necessary to have a conversation about the idea. 2) We shouldn’t have to amend the Second Amendment. It was never meant to protect an individual’s right to own a gun . The Founding Fathers clearly intended through the Second Amendment to protect the right to arm an organized militia. That said, let’s explore the idea of amending the Second Amendment to limit gun ownership to the military, police and hunters (i.e. actual hunting weapons) and why that is necessary to ensure freedom from gun violence.

Have you heard the news? England, Germany, Japan and Australia have all ended mass killings and have driven gun violence way down by banning the ownership of guns. Yet in the US 30,000 people die every year from gun violence. When will freedom from gun violence trump the freedom to own guns? The Second Amendment, as interpreted by pro gun advocates, is outdated. It is time to modernize our laws for the challenges we face today. It is too easy to obtain guns and guns are more likely to be used for criminal activity rather than self defense.

Last year the Violence Policy Center found that a gun owner is 32 times more likely to use their weapon in criminal homicide rather than in self defense . Usually the first reason a gun advocate says there is a need to own guns is the self protection myth. Now that that myth has been debunked and it has been proven that justifiable homicides are rare, we must move past the old self defense narrative and think with clearer heads when discussing gun ownership.

The second argument I hear a lot from gun advocates is that citizens need the right to be armed to protect the country from armed oppression by the government. I want to be very clear here: gun owners, your gun or collection of guns is not deterring the government for one second from an armed oppression. The US Military, the best and most powerful military in the world, would strike down an armed uprising by citizens in a heartbeat. Furthermore, most police departments are now so heavily armed that they too would make short work out of an armed uprising by citizens. We do not need guns to protect us from the government. But, more importantly, the guns we have can not protect us from the government.

Limiting ownership of guns to the military, police and hunters is a necessary step in ending US gun violence. In Australia gun buyback programs have been found to be very effective in driving down gun crime . In Japan guns must be registered with the government, are subject to inspection and you must take classes on how to properly use a gun in order for an individual to own one. And, even then, the types of guns that are allowed to be owned by citizens are severely limited. There are similar stories in England and Germany. We must modernize our laws. Why must we live with the status quo on gun ownership when so many people are terrorized by gun violence? The only way we will ever end gun violence is if those of us who care about ending gun violence are just as passionate about amending the Second Amendment as pro gun advocates are passionate about owning guns. The time is now to protect a freedom that we should all be guaranteed- freedom from gun violence.

title: I’m a gun owner. And this is the necessary next step to address gun violence in America
content:
In the aftermath of the October 1 mass shooting at a Las Vegas music festival , the national debate over gun policy has intensified. Politicians and the constituents they represent are polarized over the issue, and, in the resulting gridlock, it’s understandable that some Americans feel as though there is nothing that can be done. We spoke to Ashton Kutcher, co-founder of A Plus and a lifelong gun owner, about where we should go from here. As told to Isaac Saul.

I got my first BB gun when I was 8 years old .

I remember going out to the country for target practice and getting the safety talk from my dad when I was growing up in Iowa. He told me to never point it at anyone . When I was 12, I took a hunter’s safety course and learned the ins and outs of gun safety, then finally got my own real gun.

We’d practice shooting guns at Boy Scout camp. I’d hunt pheasants and rabbits as a 12-year-old, and I eventually started hunting deer. At 13, I worked at a gun range and pulled trap for sportsmen who came out to shoot. When I got older, I bought a handgun. I still have it locked away in a safe. In 20 years, I’ve only felt the need to take it out inside my home on two occasions.

My whole life, I never really thought of guns as weapons or associated them with self-protection. I always thought about them relative to target practice and hunting. But now, that’s changing.

What happened in Las Vegas is a travesty. I felt the same way I felt when I heard about the shooting in Sandy Hook or at the Aurora movie theater or the hundreds of other mass shootings that have happened since then. It’s an absolute misuse and abuse of firearms. As news about the shooting spread, I tweeted that we should pray and then we should change the law. And I mean that: let’s take the time to pray, let’s think about and remember that people lost their lives. People died. Families are going to be devastated. Let’s embed that in our hearts and feel it. Any change of laws we’re going to have should be about improving people’s lives, so let’s lead with compassion.

Then let’s go find a solution.

I believe I can relate to both sides of the issue. I understand the want and desire to own a gun for sport, for hunting, or for self-protection. Even after having kids, I felt more inclined to own a gun out of a desire to protect them. But let’s also acknowledge where we are: this country has a huge problem, an epidemic of gun violence we have to address. We are in a position where we have two bad choices. Either we stay the course and continue to live in the world we’re living in now — where what happened in Las Vegas is the norm — or we take a half measure and make some progress.

I believe the latter is the better of two bad choices. I believe there is some common ground we can find, and it doesn’t make sense to me that it’s not happening.

If you’re a gun advocate, understand that we can’t simply continue doing what we’re doing, which is nothing. It’s not just about protecting our rights — it’s about protecting our citizens and our children. My own thinking has shifted in terms of the right to bear arms insomuch as the founders set out to give you a tool to protect your land and form a militia to protect against a tyrannical government. But those days are gone. There isn’t a realistic militia in this country that could protect us if the government really wanted to use the weapons they have to put us down. There is no functional need for a citizen to have a semi-automatic or automatic weapon, and the risks of giving the average person access to them have clearly outweighed the rewards.

If you’re a proponent of gun control, understand that you’re not going to get everything you want. The more you advocate for “banning all guns,” the less chance you have of ever making any progress. Yes, there is data to support that bans have worked to reduce violence in other countries. If there was a new law to turn in your weapons, I’d be the first in line. But it’s not going to happen. It will always come back to the arguments that the good people are going to turn in their weapons and the bad people aren’t. That this is just one step closer to taking away all of our guns. You’re never going to win those arguments.

I think we need to start by addressing mental health and how it relates to gun laws. Any mental health professional will tell you it’s important to keep weapons out of the hands of people who want to harm themselves or others. Suicides account for almost two-thirds of all gun deaths in America . So let’s create laws that stop people who have a higher chance of hurting themselves or others from getting a gun.

Number two is addressing the procurement of weapons. It’s far too easy to get a gun on the open market in this country. Even if you want to drive an automobile, which in many ways is just about as dangerous as a gun, you have to go through stringent regulation and training to use it. You get safety courses. You get trained by someone more experienced than you. You go through a waiting period. You take a test. You get punished for misusing it or operating it when you’re intoxicated and you lose your right to drive. These are simple, sensible regulations we can apply to guns.

Third is addressing the sale of ammunition . The right to bear arms should always be protected by the Constitution, but we can tighten the regulations on the sale of ammunition. This would be a great starting point for mitigating the amount of gun violence and the number of mass shootings, like the one that occurred in Las Vegas.

The extreme sides of this argument are not and will not be feasible. We can’t continue to do nothing and we can’t ban all guns. So let’s have the dialogue and the negotiation, and let’s find the middle ground. It may hurt a little bit for both sides to sacrifice a bit of their agenda, but at the end of the day we may actually see some progress.

The next step is sitting down, together, at the table.
