title: When Your Sanctuary Is Not Necessarily a Safe Haven
content:
By Alexandra Kauffman Horowitz

T he conversation I have been avoiding having with my 7-year-old begins naturally enough. I have been procrastinating for weeks, although, in fairness, I spent one week just figuring out what to say.

“Do we tell her to run out of the building?” I had asked my husband, as I pictured our daughter alone on our synagogue’s busy urban street. Under different circumstances, it would be years before we’d let her navigate the neighborhood by herself. “She’s safer outside the building than in, if she can get out,” I had pointed out. Like most second-graders, she’d had what she called “robber drills” at school, as well as fire and tornado drills. But there was always a teacher in charge. In synagogue, she had more freedom.

We could be asking a 7-year-old to gauge whether she could escape. And where would we tell her to go if she could? The fire station across a major avenue? The shopping center across a five-way intersection? Would a child running from danger, barely tall enough to be seen above a dashboard, remember to look both ways before crossing the street?

“Unless she’s right near an exit, she should lock herself in a room and hide,” replied my husband, who had attended his share of active-shooter drills. “In a closet, if possible.”

“A closet? You’re supposed to get far away from the door. Couldn’t someone just shoot open the lock?”

“Shooters are there to kill as many people as possible. They know the police are coming. They know they have limited time. They don’t waste it breaking into locked closets.”

That sounded too rational.

“ Always? ”

“The police will be there in a matter of minutes. Then it becomes a fight between them and the shooter. Shooters know this. They know they have only so much time to kill as many people as possible.”

The strategic calculation was chilling.

“She has to stay alive until the police arrive. She should hide.”

I weighed the options and eventually agreed. At least now I knew what to say.

Our daughter considers our synagogue her second home, more so even than school, the other former safe haven. On a typical Saturday morning, she comes to the adult service for fifteen minutes, watches the Torah procession, then runs off with her friends to snack and play until the children’s service begins. Afterward, they play for another hour or so. She could be anywhere in the building, engaged in a game of tag or hide and seek. It’s a beautiful way to build community. And in this age of helicopter parenting, in which I admit participating, our synagogue is one of the few places she can run free. I don’t always know where she is in the building. But I have always known she was safe. Until now.

I will not take my daughter’s freedom away and insist she remain with an adult at all times. That would change the whole nature of our Saturday mornings. Perhaps she would be safer, but there would be a loss and maybe resistance to coming to synagogue at all. So I choose a different loss for her. I choose to lessen her innocence. And like every Jewish parent I know after Pittsburgh and Poway, I wonder how much my words will scare her and whether it’s better to say nothing at all.

For weeks I say nothing, postponing the talk I know we must have. Then one Saturday, as the two of us drive to synagogue, there is a lull in our conversation. This is my moment.

“You know,” I begin, “if you’re ever in synagogue and someone comes in to hurt people, or if you hear scary noises or see people running or screaming-–“

She cuts me off with that eye-rolling tone which younger siblings adopt far too early. She has heard me warn her brother and sister never to go off with a stranger. “I know, I know, you kick and fight and yell and make a lot of noise so people see you.”

“NO,” I say emphatically, trying to hide my alarm as I imagine her running toward a shooter. “That’s the wrong situation. That’s what you do if you’re outside and someone is trying to take you. If you’re inside and there’s someone with a gun in the building, you get away. If you’re near a door to the outside, go outside. Don’t wait for a grown-up. Run.” I pause while she takes it in. “If you’re not near an outside door, you hide. Find the closest room, lock the door, and don’t come out.”

“Like a bathroom stall?”

“No, because someone can open a stall. Like the door to the whole bathroom. There’s a lock on the door to the bathroom that you can reach. You close the door and lock it. I’ll show you later. You can try it.”

“I know,” she says with a smile in her voice so big I can hear it from the front seat. “If it’s a boy robber, I can hide in the girls’ bathroom because he can’t go in there.” So much for being scared.

I laugh. “A boy robber can still go into the girls’ room, Silly. “

We discuss other places to hide, classrooms, offices. “Try to find a room without a window in the door. But if the only place you can find has a window, go there. Lock the door, pull down the window shade and go to the other side of the room, away from the door. Don’t come out, even when you think it’s okay. Stay there until a grown-up you know comes to get you. Someone you know will come get you.”

She listens attentively, then scoffs. “This isn’t real.”

“I know,” I lie. “It’s never going to happen. But you should know what to do anyway.”

She agrees. Mission accomplished. Momentarily. Suddenly it occurs to me that there are emergencies in which you don’t want your child locked in a random closet. Many of them.

“If there’s a fire — ”

Again the eye-rolling tone. “I know. You run out of the building. You don’t take your toys or stuffed animals or guinea pigs.”

“That’s right. And if there’s a bomb, you do the same thing. You get out. You only hide if there’s a shooter.”

“Okay.” Pause. “What does a bomb sound like?”

“Like a big explosion.”

“How do you tell the difference between a bomb and a shooter?”

Good question. Not one I have considered or have any idea how to answer. I improvise. “A bomb is one really loud explosion. A shooter is a lot of smaller bangs, like a firecracker.”

“What does a firecracker sound like, Fourth of July?”

“Like — ” I grasp for an answer. “Like a series of bangs. A bomb is one giant bang. A shooter is smaller bangs but more of them … like bang, bang, bang, bang.” I cringe as I hear my words. This can’t possibly be the right thing to say. But she accepts my explanation and seems to understand.

“Okay,” she says. “Why are we talking about this now anyway?”

“No reason,” I answer. “We just had some free time in the car.”

title: Is Openly Carrying A Gun Really Necessary In The 21st Century
content:
I’m originally from the east coast of the U.S., specifically New Jersey . I moved to Arizona some 20+ years ago and to this day I still can’t get used to seeing people who are not in law enforcement carrying guns.

In New Jersey, you couldn’t carry a gun on your person openly and to get a concealed-carry permit you had to prove that you were in imminent physical danger. All I know is that it was extremely unusual to come across someone who was granted a concealed-carry permit.

This of course didn’t mean that New Jersians couldn’t own guns, you absolutely could, but you were limited in the number and type you could own. You also had to submit to a mandatory background check, get fingerprinted, and carry a firearms ID card.

In addition, when transporting a gun, say for hunting purposes, the gun had to be unloaded and separated from its ammunition. Granted this was the case 40 years ago when I purchased my first gun, but I would assume that not that much has changed.

You can openly carry a handgun, you don’t need to register it with the state or anyone else for that matter, you can own as many guns as you want, and to get a concealed-carry permit you take a course, apply, provide your fingerprints, and pay a $60 fee. Once that’s done you’re on your way carrying a concealed gun. No imminent threat required, no real need, you just need to want to carry a gun concealed.

Maybe it’s just me, but this sounds pretty loose and outright dangerous.

Before the NRA loving folks out there bite my head off, let me make it clear that I’m not anti-gun. I believe that everyone has the right to own one if, and only if, they are legally able to do so.

In my view, this determination can only come from doing a background check, not freely handing over a deadly weapon to someone with a violent criminal past and trusting that they will behave. That is just asking for trouble, and without having to submit to anything how would you know.

What brought this up is that I passed someone in the office today heading out to their car to leave for the day carrying his gun. I’ve been at this job for 15 years and I’ve know all along that he’s always done this, but it didn’t strike me as any less strange.

Sure, you can pick individual instances where a gun toting citizen pulled out his or her gun and thwarted a robbery or some other crime, but these are few and far between and certainly are nothing that one should be actively planning for in a so-called civilized society.

I can say with absolute confidence that I know of no one in all my years on this planet that has ever either needed, or had to use a gun against any other human being (military service excluded).

And maybe I’m just lucky, but I’ve never been in a situation, even with all the time I spent in New York City, Brooklyn, Harlem, and the Bronx, that I ever needed to have a gun on my person — even in the shadiest of areas. I’m talking Hell’s Kitchen, Time Square before Giuliani was mayor, and Spanish Harlem, which had a bad reputation at the time.

I’ve even gone to do something as mundane as getting an oil change and had to sit in a room with someone with a 9mm semi-automatic strapped to their hip — for what reason. Is getting an oil changes really that dangerous? Maybe I need to rethink my own safety when I go out if this is the case.

The same thoughts ran through my head that always do when I see someone like my coworker openly carrying a gun:

I have no answers to these questions, but I sure would love to know the answer to them.

All I know is that this is a very contentious topic, and pro and anti-gun advocates could each come up with a million reasons why you should or shouldn’t be able to carry a gun in public. I for one don’t think it’s necessary, but that’s just me I suppose.

Under the right circumstances wrong actions can take place simply because someone is carrying a gun. We see it here in Arizona during road rage incidents. I can’t help it, I’ve got a tragic example.

We had one on the freeway I travel everyday to go home from work. A woman driving her car down the freeway clearly upset two guys in a pickup truck. Their answer to the problem was to shoot the woman in the head as they passed her on the left. In what world would this kind of deadly action ever be justified.

I don’t know, maybe it is me just getting older, or the fact that I no longer deer hunt, or target shoot that has made me so cynical, but I think that their needs to be some national standard for owning a firearm. They aren’t toys , and in the wrong hands, they can be deadly.

Enough of my rant.

Until next time…

title: Gun Laws Need to Change
content:
“Yes, people pull the trigger — but guns are the instrument of death. Gun control is necessary, and delay means more death and horror” (BrainyQuote) -Eliot Spitzer.

Guns have been an integral part of American society since the Revolutionary era, when Colonists needed guns to defend themselves against the British. Since the 2nd Amendment was passed, guns have become a symbol of national pride and patriotism for many Americans. Throughout the years, gun control has been a highly disputed topic, as American citizens no longer need guns to defend themselves against a hostile government. The rising numbers of mass shootings and homicides with guns has sparked many new debates. One group that advocates for gun ownership is the NRA, which is a powerful lobbyist association established in 1871. The NRA is largely responsible for the fact that gun laws haven’t changed, since a large number of their supporters are registered voters who fight against any attempt to limit gun ownership rights. Current gun laws make it easy for anyone to purchase guns, including criminals and mentally ill people, as background checks are not performed at gun shows. Current gun laws also allow military-grade weapons such as AR-15’s to be sold. The current gun laws put many citizens in danger, as the failure to properly regulate guns has led to many mass shootings and homicides in America, and many more are sure to come if gun laws don’t change.

I have seen countless headlines about gun-related violence for as long as I can remember. It seems that almost everyday, there is a new story about a mass shooting in America. In many of these mass shootings, the victims are innocent people. For example, just last week, there was a school shooting in Florida that claimed the lives of 17 innocent people. “‘I knew at that point she was gone. I felt it in my heart,’ [her mom] said. ‘Alyssa was a beautiful, smart, talented, successful, awesome, amazing soccer player. You’ll be greatly missed, Alyssa. We love you so much. You’ll always, always be in our hearts’” (CNN). Alyssa was only 14 when she was killed by a school shooter, and many others also lost loved ones that day. If Congress had implemented more

restrictions on guns, then the victims of the Florida school shooting would still be alive, and tens of thousands of lives would be saved each year. But after every mass shooting, gun laws have stayed the same. The government is letting us kill each other. Congressmen care more about their gun-owning supporters than our despair. Our government has failed to protect us, and there is no telling how many more innocent people will be murdered until something changes. That is why it is the responsibility of the future generation to vote to change the gun laws.

Leah Libresco in “I used to think gun control was the answer. My research told me otherwise.” exemplifies Harris’ idea of “countering”. The popular opinion seems to be that guns need to be regulated by the NRA but Libresco counters this with a different way of thinking. The author dissents the way of thinking gun control is a necessity into eventually noting the limitations. She brings up how she is anti-gun saying, “I don’t want a gun in my home, as I think the risk outweighs the benefits.”. She is civil in her argument as she uses data to carry across her points. She identifies that lives can be saved by focusing on protecting potential victims and reforming potential killers, not from sweeping bans focused on the guns themselves. I found it interesting that she brought up how two-thirds of gun deaths in the United States were from suicides. She brings up valid points using data from other countries and their gun control laws. Libresco’s data says more people were killed in gang related homicides and from domestic violence than in mass-shooting incidents, but few policies impacted these findings. According to the data shown she right in saying that more responsibility should be put into protecting potential victims.

title: In 2015, owning a gun is about as useful as a pitchfork
content:
Amendment II “A well regulated militia, being necessary to the security of a free state, the right of the people to keep and bear arms, shall not be infringed.”

I like the phrase “well regulated militia” because I believe the founders knew this would be a solid way to beat back unreasonable demands of the British. Setting this boundary was in the best interest of a new nation and the 2nd Amendment stands pretty firmly on it’s own by endowing an incredible privilege to the citizens.

Now, keep in mind this clause was never intended to imply a federal guard; it’s meant as a provision for the citizens to rise up against an oppressive government, foreign or domestic. Power to the people, and so on.

The simple truth, however, is we don’t have anything close to a “well regulated” group of citizens who watch out for the country. At best we have a notion that guns are useful and shouldn’t be outlawed, taken away and, if so, pried from cold, dead fingers.

But, the problem is just that guns aren’t really useful for most people. I’d no sooner outlaw them than a pitchfork if we could find a real use for them aside “home defense”. Some folks like to use them for sport, others for defense, others for hunting but the majority of us…they don’t have a use. Guns just don’t serve the purpose they once did. We’re not out taming the wild anymore.

1 Corinthians 13:11: “When I was a child, I spoke like a child, I thought like a child, I reasoned like a child. When I became a man, I gave up childish ways.”

As a society we have to grow out of our need for the “boom stick”. We need to grow out of our irrational need to hit and strike in anger. Guns, both big and small, are a childish way to start or end a fight and only serves to prove that those who require their use have not evolved.

Amendments are, by their nomenclature, added on to make a document better. Think of them as the hem of shirt, the clear coat on a paint job. They added a finishing flourish to the original Constitution in a time when that was necessary.

Like other amendments added or repealed since 1791 I think it’s time to rethink our insistence on one of two things: our need for guns or our definition of a well regulated militia.

title: UNTITLED
content:
Quite rightly so, the world is discussing gun control more than ever due to the ongoing atrocities in the United States. The 2nd Amendment to the Constitution of the United States of America was adopted in 1791, 227 years ago. There are a few slightly different versions of it in existence but it generally looks like this.

“ A well regulated militia being necessary to the security of a free state, the right of the people to keep and bear arms shall not be infringed.”

The USA was very much still in its infancy at the time of adopting this amendment, having only declared it’s independence in 1776, and it was a very different time compared to today. Having just declared their independence from the English Crown, the 2nd Amendment was a way to prevent any single person rising up above the rest and it made perfect sense at the time.

The people of the USA nowadays have access to far deadlier weapons than their ancestors in the 1700s. The kind of technology in existence today wasn’t even a dream or an idea when the amendment was written. The law has to evolve with the times.

The government of the USA will never have a solid opportunity to subjugate the people and even if it did, in what world would the people of the USA, using their own firearms of varying design, be able to take on the United States Military? The people of America are so outgunned in this imaginary scenario that there’s no point in all of them holding on to their guns.

There are a few reasons for wanting a firearm. Hunting, clay pigeon shooting or target shooting with rifles and pistols are legitimate reasons. In fact, these are legitimate reasons accepted by the Police and Government in the United Kingdom, except when dealing with handguns as these were completely banned after the Dunblane shooting. (Notice we’ve never had anything like it since)

This is a picture of me using my rifle in the kneeling position. I don’t have my rifle to defend myself, it gets locked up in the club armoury when I’m not using it. I instead use it to compete in International Shooting Sport Federation (ISSF) regulated competitions to shoot at targets 50 metres away, in competition with other people doing the same thing. I have only ever shot at paper, electronic targets which use microphones and the occasional Polo mint in christmas fun shoots. I compete for my University in target shooting and I compete for myself in my country’s national Grand Prix series. Owning a firearm for sport of this kind, is the only acceptable reason. I don’t consider my rifle to be a weapon. I consider it to be like a golf club, or a pool cue. Its entire purpose is to move a projectile from point A to point B as accurately as possible. My fellow shooters here in the UK think the same.

Crime exists everywhere in the world, and we aren’t strangers to it in the UK. But we have fewer firearm offences because of our strict firearms laws. I’ll include a link to a video at the end which shows a man wielding a machete, arrested by UK police without the use of a firearm, a situation that US police would probably resolve by shooting him.

When both civilian firearm users in the UK don’t view their firearms as weapons and our police force is able to detain a dangerous individual with a weapon, without shooting and killing them, it shows without a doubt that the United States of America has a culture problem and an unhealthy addiction to firearms.

Having a firearm for home defense is an interesting concept, because it goes on the idea that there are people out there that want to harm you and your family, and by having guns you can protect yourself. The logic works but the major flaw is that if you as the “home defender” are allowed to own a firearm, then so is the “home attacker”. The law is indiscriminate and has no way of knowing whether you’ll shoot up a school/public place or keep it at home locked away in the event your home is attacked. The sensible thing to do is disarm everyone in the United States that cites home defense or the 2nd Amendment as a reason for having a firearm. US citizens should have to provide a good reason to the police force in order to obtain permission to hold a firearm and be subject to stringent background and medical checks before being allowed access to firearms.

title: Where Gun Ownership Debates Go Wrong
content:
The reality, is that the gun debate has become a diversion for the real issue. The real issue is whether or not gun control is necessary for a civil and productive society. Unfortunately any attempt to debate this is constantly derailed by the notion of gun 'rights’.

Think about that for a second. When we think about inalienable human rights, we think about the right to free expression and thought, equality, and freedom from persecution and fear. These are universal rights that are deeply rooted in human culture from earliest history.

So what makes the gun ownership rights a thing? Apperently it’s the second amendment of the US constitution — and there’s the rub. It’s a killer argument because if it’s in the constitution then it must be a right equal to the freedom of speech. It’s a completely logical argument, if you are willing to believe that a) the second amendment is correctly interpreted to mean uncontrolled gun rights (eg. standing militia?); b) the US constitution was wriiten by infallible future reading men (eg automatic weapons?); c) thay the US constitution is an infallible document (eg amendments?).

That’s a lot of bridges to cross before using the US constitution as justification for something as plainly and obviously problematic as selling weapons of mass destruction to anyone who wants them.

……..

The cold hard facts show that the lax gun laws in the US are responsible for certain types of gun crime (but not all types of gun crime).

Crime, Violence, and Mass Shootings

Firstly, and most importantly, gun control will not prevent violent crimes or homicides because these can be committed with knives and other weapons.

However, when you consider scenarios such as teens getting hold of their parents guns and rampaging their schools or accidentally killing their siblings — these are clearly not the same type of crime as drive-by shootings.

Unfortunately most of the arguments for gun ownership are driven by the overwhelming paranoia and sense of power that guns provide. The more guns in a community, the more justified you feel to own a gun to defend yourself against other guns. It’s a dark feedback loop that can only spiral downwards. When the same principles are applied internationally, it’s called an arms race, and it doesn’t work.

When looking at mass and accidental shootings, lax gun laws clearly lie at the root cause. While guns do not cause people to be mentally unstable or vulnerable, making deadly weapons easily accessible allows these people to get hold of guns they wouldn’t ordinarily get access to. The ease of acquiring guns in these scenarios initiates the steps towards the crime, and not vice versa. Instead of a person thinking ‘I want to hurt someone so I will risk my safety and spend $1000s to illegally buy a gun on the black market from organised crime’, it’s simply ‘here’s a gun I can easily, cheaply, and quickly acquire to use any way I want’.

There are high level (correlation) statistics to back this up.

A study of mass shootings (4 or more people killed) found most of these occurred with legally obtained weapons.

But the evidence doesn’t stop with mass shootings.

Lax gun laws also have a causitive impact on violent crimes. Multiple studies have found that “if guns are available, it is more likely that a violent dispute will become a deadly one, and that a criminal with the intent to kill can find the means to do so.” ( Harvard ). If someone wants to be violent they will, but using weapons other than guns would drastically reduce the fatalities of violent crimes.

Finally as a downstream effect, gun control doesn’t just remove guns from vulnerable people, but makes it easier for police to regulate and remove guns from criminals.

The Switzerland Debate (aka “a model for safe public gun ownership”)

The fact this argument is ever used demonstrates the failure of gun ownership in the US. Why look to gun ownership models in other countries if the model in your own country is working fine?

This argument states that gun ownership is compatible with safe communities because such a system exists in Switzerland. However, the Swiss example has no relevance to the US. Gun ownership is only common in Switzerland because all able Swiss citizens are required to attend military training and thereafter remain in the defense reserves. Their weapons are not owned for a love for guns or the ease of buying guns in supermarkets, and their guns cannot be used unless a war breaks out. Overall gun ownership in Switzerland is not driven by recreational or civilian use.

In the US, gun ownership is justified by the second amendment — right to bear arms. The purpose of the second amendment is to ensure that a pool of army reservists (“well regulated militia”) can be maintained. This was particularly relevant when the US army was in its infancy. Nowadays the US army is the largest in the world, and no one purchasing a gun at Walmart would ever be in danger of being confused with a reservist or fear being drafted to a militia. However, it’s clear from the second amendment that only reservists acting in defence of the State are supposed to have the right to bear arms — and not for ordinary civilian use.

The obvious irony in invoking the Swiss comparison is that it highlights how the US has departed from the original intention of supporting their initial small army, while Switzerland has correctly applied it to maintain a “well regulated militia” to protect their State.

Second Amendment Elephant in the Room

The recurring theme heard time and time again, hinges on the interpretation of the Constitution’s Second Amendment.

Until relatively recently [date], it was clear that the Second Amendment did not allow for civilians to self-arm as they independently see fit — nor did it ever imply the removal of gun control.

The law used to support a natural reading if the Constitution, in which arms were only allowed for civilians as part of a well regulated militia for the one purpose of preserving the State. It’s taken a series of individual cases, led by lobbysists, to gradually stretch the interpretations.

US politics has been under duress from corrupting forces since inception — all democracies are. In the case of the US, gun lobbyists are such a force. But this debate isn’t about corruption of the US, or its comparison with other countries, it’s simply about the clarity of a debate. Is gun control necessary for a civil and safe society?

There is only one correct answer.

Think about that for a second. When we think about inalienable human rights, we think about the right to free expression and thought, equality, and freedom from persecution and fear. These are universal rights that are deeply rooted in human culture from earliest history.

So what makes the gun ownership rights a thing? Apperently it’s the second amendment of the US constitution — and there’s the rub. It’s a killer argument because if it’s in the constitution then it must be a right equal to the freedom of speech. It’s a completely logical argument, if you are willing to believe that a) the second amendment is correctly interpreted to mean uncontrolled gun rights (eg. standing militia?); b) the US constitution was wriiten by infallible future reading men (eg automatic weapons?); c) thay the US constitution is an infallible document (eg amendments?).

That’s a lot of bridges to cross before using the US constitution as justification for something as plainly and obviously problematic as selling weapons of mass destruction to anyone who wants them.

……..

The cold hard facts show that the lax gun laws in the US are responsible for certain types of gun crime (but not all types of gun crime).

Crime, Violence, and Mass Shootings

Firstly, and most importantly, gun control will not prevent violent crimes or homicides because these can be committed with knives and other weapons.

However, when you consider scenarios such as teens getting hold of their parents guns and rampaging their schools or accidentally killing their siblings — these are clearly not the same type of crime as drive-by shootings.

Unfortunately most of the arguments for gun ownership are driven by the overwhelming paranoia and sense of power that guns provide. The more guns in a community, the more justified you feel to own a gun to defend yourself against other guns. It’s a dark feedback loop that can only spiral downwards. When the same principles are applied internationally, it’s called an arms race, and it doesn’t work.

When looking at mass and accidental shootings, lax gun laws clearly lie at the root cause. While guns do not cause people to be mentally unstable or vulnerable, making deadly weapons easily accessible allows these people to get hold of guns they wouldn’t ordinarily get access to. The ease of acquiring guns in these scenarios initiates the steps towards the crime, and not vice versa. Instead of a person thinking ‘I want to hurt someone so I will risk my safety and spend $1000s to illegally buy a gun on the black market from organised crime’, it’s simply ‘here’s a gun I can easily, cheaply, and quickly acquire to use any way I want’.

There are high level (correlation) statistics to back this up.

A study of mass shootings (4 or more people killed) found most of these occurred with legally obtained weapons.

But the evidence doesn’t stop with mass shootings.

Lax gun laws also have a causitive impact on violent crimes. Multiple studies have found that “if guns are available, it is more likely that a violent dispute will become a deadly one, and that a criminal with the intent to kill can find the means to do so.” ( Harvard ). If someone wants to be violent they will, but using weapons other than guns would drastically reduce the fatalities of violent crimes.

Finally as a downstream effect, gun control doesn’t just remove guns from vulnerable people, but makes it easier for police to regulate and remove guns from criminals.

The Switzerland Debate (aka “a model for safe public gun ownership”)

The fact this argument is ever used demonstrates the failure of gun ownership in the US. Why look to gun ownership models in other countries if the model in your own country is working fine?

This argument states that gun ownership is compatible with safe communities because such a system exists in Switzerland. However, the Swiss example has no relevance to the US. Gun ownership is only common in Switzerland because all able Swiss citizens are required to attend military training and thereafter remain in the defense reserves. Their weapons are not owned for a love for guns or the ease of buying guns in supermarkets, and their guns cannot be used unless a war breaks out. Overall gun ownership in Switzerland is not driven by recreational or civilian use.

In the US, gun ownership is justified by the second amendment — right to bear arms. The purpose of the second amendment is to ensure that a pool of army reservists (“well regulated militia”) can be maintained. This was particularly relevant when the US army was in its infancy. Nowadays the US army is the largest in the world, and no one purchasing a gun at Walmart would ever be in danger of being confused with a reservist or fear being drafted to a militia. However, it’s clear from the second amendment that only reservists acting in defence of the State are supposed to have the right to bear arms — and not for ordinary civilian use.

The obvious irony in invoking the Swiss comparison is that it highlights how the US has departed from the original intention of supporting their initial small army, while Switzerland has correctly applied it to maintain a “well regulated militia” to protect their State.

Second Amendment Elephant in the Room

The recurring theme heard time and time again, hinges on the interpretation of the Constitution’s Second Amendment.

Until relatively recently [date], it was clear that the Second Amendment did not allow for civilians to self-arm as they independently see fit — nor did it ever imply the removal of gun control.

The law used to support a natural reading if the Constitution, in which arms were only allowed for civilians as part of a well regulated militia for the one purpose of preserving the State. It’s taken a series of individual cases, led by lobbysists, to gradually stretch the interpretations.

US politics has been under duress from corrupting forces since inception — all democracies are. In the case of the US, gun lobbyists are such a force. But this debate isn’t about corruption of the US, or its comparison with other countries, it’s simply about the clarity of a debate. Is gun control necessary for a civil and safe society?

There is only one correct answer.

title: Gun Control Is More Like Abortion Than Gay Marriage
content:
By Benjamin Hart

Over the last decade, some once-polarizing behaviors have gained acceptance in American society to a degree that seemed unthinkable just a few years ago. The most prominent among these are gay rights and marijuana legalization. In both cases, the sea change in public opinion was driven by a younger cohort of Americans that proved far more open-minded than their elders; one could glance at an opinion poll in 2005 and predict with a certain degree of confidence that a more progressive generation would simply crowd out their more conservative forebears simply by virtue of demographic math.

But guns aren’t like that.

A Pew Research survey released in June found that 47 percent of Americans think it’s more important for the government to protect gun owners’ rights than it is to control gun ownership. And 51 percent favor stricter enforcement of ownership.

A timeline of responses to this question shows that, for reasons that are not clear, America has become significantly more conservative on the issue since the 1990s — despite the fact that, notwithstanding a recent uptick, crime rates have dropped precipitously since then.

Perhaps more surprisingly, a look at the differences in polling by generation found that millennials haven’t differed very much from Generation X, Baby Boomers, or the Silent Generation in their attitudes over the last few years.

The Washington Post ’s Catherine Rampell drilled into the data a bit more in 2015, and found that millennials lined up with the population at large in their views on proposed background checks for gun purchases — large majorities favor the measure — and some other provisions. But they were actually less likely than those ages 50 through 64 to support a ban on assault-style weapons, with only 49 percent of people under 30 favoring such a measure. (Such a ban was in effect from 1994 to 2004.)

Pew’s numbers have been corroborated by Gallup, which reported a similar trend in 2015. “Millennials are … less interested in gun control than those who are older, so the data suggests it’s unlike a number of other attitudes say like, gay marriage where young people are much more liberal,” Gallup’s editor in chief Frank Newport told NBC News . “We did not see that in our data on guns.”

The findings may seem like a head-scratcher, since millennials have a reputation for being more liberal than the population at large on economic and social matters.

But, as Pew found in its recent survey, gun culture is simply ingrained in many American households, especially rural ones, and especially among men. “Many American gun owners exist in a social context where gun ownership is the norm,” and “experience with guns starts relatively early particularly for those who grew up in a gun-owning household,” as the organization put it in a summary of its findings . These facts of American life have not seemed to change much in generations, leading to a frozen-in-amber dynamic.

The best predictor for support or opposition for gun control isn’t age, but party identification . The Pew survey shows a yawning divide on the issue between the two parties: 79 percent of Republicans think it’s more important to protect gun rights than it is to control ownership, with only 20 percent of Democrats concurring. The split holds even among Republicans and Democrats who both own guns. Partisanship has spiked in recent years, and the parties have major differences on pretty much every issue on the table in 2017, but guns may be the most divisive one of all:

The hot-button issue guns may resemble most is abortion. When it was legalized nationally in 1973, opinions on the issue were split along generational lines. But that schism has narrowed significantly in recent years, and the fight over access and restrictions looks to be as divisive as it is now for a long time to come.

There are all kinds of reasons Congress, and most states, never do anything to reform gun laws, from the considerable electoral clout and political access of the NRA to lawmakers’ cozy relationships with gun manufacturers to personal ideology. title: Why Gun Ownership is Necessary: Government Tyranny
content:
When I was in China, this winter break, a friend told me about the story of tens of thousands of families being kicked out of their homes in Beijing, in order to “beautify” the city . From my American perspective, I was absolutely shocked that something like this could happen. I asked him: “So you are saying that the government can just come and kick people out of their homes whenever?”

Yeah. That’s because people can’t own guns. They can’t fight back.

I was curious about this statement. I wanted to investigate whether civilian gun ownership had any effects on personal freedoms. Intuitively, it made sense to me that unfree countries like(China, North Korea..) wouldn’t let their civilians have guns. Meanwhile, United States has gun rights bolted into its constitution.

Here is a ranking of the countries with the most guns. Notice how Western/Middle Eastern Countries to have more Guns.

Here is a ranking of the most “Free” Countries

For “freedom” data I used the The Human Freedom Index 2017 , which defines three main categories for Freedom: Human, Economic and Personal. These categories encompass subcategories such as: Movement, Religion, Expression, Access to Sound Money, Freedom to Trade Internationally, Regulation of Credit… For gun data I used the Small Arms Survey 2007 .

“A well regulated militia being necessary to the security of a free state, the right of the people to keep and bear arms shall not be infringed.”

Since a government’s military is often the way a tyrannical regime imposes tyranny on its citizens, guns can be a way in which citizens protect themselves and fight in case they have to. There are many cases in history when a government disarmed their citizens then tyrannized citizens once they were disarmed. Consider the military dictatorship of Chile(1973–90) when 40,000 people were interrogated and killed, or the Holocaust when the Nazis disarmed German Jew s….or the countless other examples in history. Many of history’s worst atrocities were committed on citizens who couldn’t fight back.

Do guns protect people from government tyranny and increase human freedom? Not necessarily. There are plenty of countries that enjoy great freedoms and also have no guns(Japan/Singapore). However, in the worst cases of government tyranny, there is almost always a commonality — a disarming of civilians. That’s what the the founding fathers intended to protect against with the 2nd amendment, the absolute worst case scenario.

In the United States, a relatively free country, we enjoy more liberties and freedoms. This is why sometimes it’s hard to imagine that a government can be tyrannous. However, the usual process of government infringing on citizens’ rights is a gradual process — and in recent years there’s been more and more cases of government stepping out of bounds(Ex: Warrantless Surveillance & Snowden).

In light of the Florida shootings, my ultimate argument is not that there should be no changes to gun laws. In the dataset, the United States is an absolute outlier for how many guns we have per 100 people. However, I think social media tends to oversimplify the discussion(Ex: “guns == danger”). There’s many considerations to gun laws and I felt like the government tyranny/human freedom perspective is something we can not forget about. The United States is not even 300 years removed from government tyranny — a rather short time in history. Those who do not learn history are doomed to repeat it.

Note: The Small Arms Survey 2007 dataset has debatable validity and alot of variance between responses. I also understand that correlation does not mean causation. Moreover, it’s not necessarily true that guns allow a country to be more freedom — many of the top 30 countries are western/democratic, and thus it could be that free countries let access to guns more easily. This analysis is in no way rigorous but only serves as a data exploration, and to bring up a thought experiment.

My research for this semester is gun control and below are some of the different sources that I used throughout my research and writing. These sources are linked to many statistics and many author’s opinions about gun control, laws and even proposals. Some sources offer different perspective to see the problem and others are linked to other issues such as mental health. Also, it includes much on background information so the reader could understand better about the issue of gun control.

Background Information

Bonnie, Richard J., and Jeffrey W. Swanson. “Extreme Risk Protection Orders — Effective Tools for Keeping Guns Out of Dangerous Hands.” Developments in Mental Health Law , vol. 37, no. 2, Winter 2018/2019 2018, pp. 2–6. Recent years, there have seen a number of mass shootings in which family members or friends have been noticing warning signs that shooters were very dangerous and risking of harming themselves. In response of these tragedies, states are trying to enact laws or creating organization that can prevent gun tragedies to happen. Extreme Risk Protection Order (ERPO) laws empower families, community or officers to temporarily remove a person’s access to gun arms before they commit violence. This was created after the shooting at Isla Vista, California, where a disturbed and angry young man shot 10 people in the college town of Isla Vista. However, before the incident, the killer showed concerning behavior that his parents contacted his therapist, and alerted the police that the young man was likely to do harm to himself or others. Unfortunately, the police were unable to remove the killer’s guns or take him to custody. This articles describes that the ERPO is not a big law, but it can be use to prevent mass shootings, suicides, terrorism and others types of gun violence. This information can be helpful for my future writings about laws that are already passed to help the community. Everyone should read this article so we can stay alert and noticing people’s behavior to prevent more death tragedies.

This can be due to the exotic cultural factor in the South Region and this might have some implication for gun control proposals. However, the different opinion of gun ownership have been different because of broad support or opposition to gun control, the relationship on how specific types of gun ownership the southerners interact, the variables and the effects for the preferences of different types of gun control. The author uses a data by DMI to show how indicates that a cultural component related to the South affects the attitude on gun control and how they are the most opposed to permit laws and firearms ban. Especially southern gun owners were found the most opposed to the gun control issue. Those finding point were very interesting and that shows how we have a broad support and opinion about gun control (New York Times). Culture and history plays a big role in terms on gun control for Southerners, not to mention that they mostly own guns because it is part of their culture. title: Wh1y Is Gun Control Absolutely Necessary in China?
content:
In 1951, shortly after the founding of the People’s Republic of China, the government took steps to regulate firearms.

They implemented “Interim Measures,” requiring permits for the possession, manufacture, sale, transportation, rental, or lending of firearms. This may sound quite strict, doesn’t it?

However, in reality, firearms were still widespread among the population.

The country had just emerged from the War of Resistance Against Japan and the Civil War, with some regions still engaged in anti-bandit campaigns.

Firearms and ammunition were scattered everywhere, like beans strewn across the ground.

It wasn’t just guns; some people even had explosives, grenades, and there were those daring enough to bring home small cannons.

Can you imagine that?

At that time, every household in the village had a weapon for self-defense, just like keeping a kitchen knife at home today.

By the 1960s, due to international tensions, the entire population was militarized.

Every household was expected to be part of the militia, and everyone was required to practice using weapons.

Many of our grandparents might have handled guns when they were young.

Back then, you might see the old man next door carrying a hoe to the field in the morning.

In the evening, he could be standing guard at the village entrance with a gun.

The women, after taking care of the children and doing housework during the day, would also need to learn how to handle weapons at night.

Children coming home from school might see grenades piled up in the yard, treating them like toys.

Adults would gather and chat.

Conversations could easily shift from discussing the harvest to sharing tips on maintaining firearms.

Reflecting on this today, it seems unimaginable.

But in those days, it was the norm.

The phrase “A country vast with soldiers everywhere” perfectly captured the situation.

From cities to villages, from factories to fields, people with guns were everywhere.

Everyone had to learn to shoot, and it wasn’t a casual activity.

Each person had a militia training manual, a small book filled with detailed instructions.

It taught how to throw grenades, use explosives, and aim a firearm.

Everything was laid out clearly in the book.

Don’t be fooled by how slow those elderly folks move now; they were all highly skilled marksmen in their youth.

Pick one at random, and they could probably still shoot a perfect score.

These skills were ingrained in them, something they could never forget.

Back then, there were two villages in Hunan Province, one called Matian Village and the other Jinggang Village.

These were not small villages; each had about 2,000 residents.

The relationship between these two villages had always been strained.

Generational conflicts had created deep-seated animosity.

In 1993, things came to a head.

The trigger was some minor dispute, but the specifics are unclear now.

What is known is that a group from Matian Village, in a fit of anger, went to Jinggang Village and vandalized one of their factories.

The police intervened and mediated the situation.

In the end, Matian Village was ordered to compensate Jinggang Village for the damages.

On the surface, the issue was resolved.

However, the anger simmering in both villages did not subside.

The people of Jinggang Village felt that compensation alone was insufficient and that those responsible for destroying the factory should be punished.

Meanwhile, the people of Matian Village believed that paying compensation was already too much, so why should they face further punishment?

Thus, the conflict between the two villages deepened.

In secret, both sides were preparing, waiting for the day they could settle the score.

Eventually, one day, someone made the first move, and a full-scale conflict erupted between the two villages.

As soon as the fighting began, the situation escalated rapidly.

Just as the people of Matian Village were bringing out their artillery and mortars, Jinggang Village opened fire.

The village’s supply and marketing cooperative, hospital, and school were quickly repurposed. The counters in the cooperative were pushed aside to make room for the wounded. Doctors and nurses in the hospital were busy preparing medicines and bandages. In the school classrooms, women were preparing food and water for those fighting on the front lines. High points around the village, like hilltops and rooftops, were fortified with small cannons.

A few young men, strong and determined, crouched behind the cannons, eyes fixed on the distance, ready to fire at any moment.

The most astonishing thing was that nearly everyone in the village was armed.

Elderly villagers pulled out old guns they had used in their youth, some dating back to the Chinese Civil War.

Young men wielded hunting rifles, and some even had homemade shotguns.

Even women and children armed themselves with sticks, hoes, and whatever else they could find.

In a village of over 2,000 people, nearly everyone was mobilized.

Men and women, young and old, each had a role to play. Some took up arms and went to the front lines.

Others stayed behind to prepare food or tend to the wounded. The scene was chaotic, filled with smoke and tension. The battle between Matian Village and Jinggang Village was fierce from the start.

Every minute, more than a dozen shells flew towards the opposing side, creating massive craters.

Both sides were consumed with rage, neither willing to back down.

Villagers formed groups of three, moving through the fields like seasoned soldiers.

Each person was equipped with grenades, and they clutched their guns, ready to fight at any moment.

The scene was reminiscent of guerrilla warfare during the War of Resistance Against Japan.

“Watch out!”

A young man shouted, pulling his companion to the ground.

A shell flew overhead and exploded nearby, sending dust flying everywhere. As the battle intensified, people from nearby villages began joining in. Some joined due to family ties, others due to friendships. They brought their weapons and joined the fray.

There were 95 cannons in total, and over 4,000 firearms. This wasn’t just a brawl; it was practically a small-scale war! This is the reality of China before the gun ban. What started as a conflict between two villages escalated into a large-scale armed clash.

The county authorities quickly got wind of the situation.

They dispatched 400 armed police, and County Magistrate He Zhenxiang, along with the heads of the court and public security bureau, rushed to the scene. The command was split into two teams, each heading to Matian Village and Jinggang Village. Magistrate He led his team through the artillery fire into Jinggang Village. Amid the booming cannons, Magistrate He shouted: “Folks, stop fighting! There’s nothing to gain from this!” After repeated persuasion, Jinggang Village finally agreed to a ceasefire.

Magistrate He breathed a sigh of relief, thinking that at least half the task was done.

But then, bad news came through the walkie-talkie.

It turned out that the situation in Matian Village was even more challenging.

The villagers were well-prepared; as soon as the mediation team arrived, they immediately called for the women and children of the village to surround them.

The mediation team was caught off guard.

They couldn’t force their way through, nor could they meet with the village leaders.

Two attempts at mediation had already failed.

What could be done now?

One side had stopped fighting, but the other continued, making the ceasefire meaningless! At that moment, the sound of artillery fire was heard again in the distance. Magistrate He’s face turned pale:

“Not good! Matian Village must have learned of the ceasefire and launched a fierce attack on Jinggang Village!”

The situation was dire, and Magistrate He made a quick decision: “Order the armed police to enter the village immediately and stop the people of Matian Village at all costs!” More than 400 armed police officers and party and government officials were assembled. As the team advanced, the sound of artillery fire could still be heard in the distance. Commander Wang checked his watch and gave the order: “Move out!” The armed police team split into several groups and advanced towards Matian Village. Shells exploded around them, sending dirt flying.

Several soldiers were hit by shrapnel, but they gritted their teeth and kept moving forward.

“Fire tear gas!”

Commander Wang ordered, and more than a dozen tear gas canisters were launched into Matian Village.

Thick smoke quickly engulfed the entire village.

Under the cover of the smoke, the armed police charged into the village. Loudspeakers blared continuously:

“Lay down your weapons! Stop fighting! Government forces have entered the village; if you don’t stop now, we will take coercive measures!”

The villagers were stunned by the sudden turn of events. Some still wanted to resist, but faced with the overwhelming firepower of the armed police, they quickly surrendered.

The fighting finally came to an end.

As the smoke cleared, people began to comprehend the brutality of the battle.

More than 5,000 people had been involved, 95 cannons had been used, and hundreds had lost their lives.

The village was littered with craters and ruins, and the air was thick with the smell of gunpowder.

If such incidents had occurred across the country, the consequences would have been unimaginable.

This battle marked a turning point.

In the following years, the government intensified efforts to ban firearms and cannons. Although the process was challenging, the results were significant.

Firearms and cannons were gradually confiscated from civilians, and large-scale armed conflicts became increasingly rare.

Years later, when people look back on this history, they do so with deep reflection.

It was through such painful lessons that Chinese society gradually became more peaceful.

That brutal village conflict marked the end of an era and the dawn of a new one.

Today, Matian Village and Jinggang Village have undergone significant transformations.

The old grudges have long disappeared.

However, that battle left an indelible mark, forever changing these villages and serving as a profound lesson for future generations.

title: Topic: Why Gun Control is Necessary – And Why Opposing it is Like Ignoring the Safety Features on a Car
content:
Gun control is a contentious issue in many countries, particularly in the United States, where the Second Amendment guarantees the right to bear arms. But the reality is that gun violence is a major problem that needs to be addressed, and gun control measures are an important part of the solution.

Opposing gun control is like ignoring the safety features on a car. Just as cars have seatbelts, airbags, and other safety features to protect passengers in the event of an accident, gun control measures are designed to protect people from the dangers of gun violence.

Of course, there are those who argue that gun control infringes on their Second Amendment rights, or that criminals will find ways to get guns regardless of laws. But the truth is that gun control measures can be effective, and they have been implemented successfully in other countries.

For example, in Australia, a mass shooting in 1996 led to the implementation of strict gun control measures, including a ban on certain types of firearms and a buyback program. Since then, there has not been a single mass shooting in Australia. Similarly, Japan has some of the strictest gun control measures in the world, and as a result, has one of the lowest rates of gun violence.

Opposing gun control measures may seem like a matter of personal freedom, but it can also be seen as a disregard for the safety and well-being of others. Just as we wouldn’t ignore the safety features on a car because they’re inconvenient or uncomfortable, we should support gun control measures as a way to protect ourselves and our communities from the dangers of gun violence.

In fact, opposing gun control is like driving a car without a seatbelt or airbags. Sure, you may feel free and unencumbered, but if you get into an accident, you’re putting yourself and others at risk. Similarly, if we refuse to support gun control measures, we’re putting ourselves and our communities at risk of mass shootings, accidents, and other tragedies.

Furthermore, just as we require drivers to have licenses and training before they can get behind the wheel, we should also require gun owners to undergo background checks and safety training before they can purchase and use firearms. These measures can help ensure that guns are only in the hands of responsible, law-abiding citizens who understand how to use them safely.

title: To Control Guns, Listen To The Other Side
content:
Why do people want to have guns?

S ome people feel they need a gun for self-defense. The threats they fear come in many forms. Many fear home invasion, especially if they have small children. They fear robbery, either at home or when they are away from the house. They usually assume that there will be a lone attacker and rarely consider the possibility of a team of attackers. For home defense, a handgun is the first weapon that comes to mind, but there are certainly other possibilities such as pepper spray. An assault rifle, or any other weapon with a long barrel, will not be useful.

Let’s look at this scenario in more detail, case by case. Perhaps the confrontation is on the street, made more fearsome by the cover of darkness. You might be behind a store counter, getting into your car, or walking on a path through the woods. If you’re armed and prepared, you’ll pull your handgun from your handbag or holster and either threaten the attacker or possibly shoot them outright. This assumes that you don’t do what most people would do: either acquiesce or attempt to summon help.

The effectiveness of any armed response is chancy at best. It depends on what you’re doing at the moment of attack, and a clever attacker will choose a moment when you’re preoccupied, distracted, or half asleep. Perhaps you’ll literally be caught with your pants down.

Hunters, of course, have guns, but there’s no necessary connection between hunting and gun control. Almost all gun control advocates make an exception for hunting rifles. The interface between residential neighborhoods and hunting territory is an occasional source of conflict, especially when hunters get inebriated; there are tragic cases of people being shot by hunters in their own backyards.

Many gun advocates have multiple guns because they love the aesthetic of the gun. For self-defense, two guns are no better than one, especially if they’re stored side by side. And the type of gun does make a difference; though handguns are the cause of many deaths, they aren’t generally involved in mass shootings. For mass shootings, the assault rifle has become the weapon of choice.

The debates over assault rifles has overshadowed the debate over handguns. Handguns threaten up-close personal violence, but rarely violence at a distance or at a large scale. Handguns also need to be regulated, but the regulations would be very different from those for assault rifles. As a means of defense against assault, handguns have alternatives such as pepper sprays as even tasers.

I can appreciate the assault rifle as an aesthetic object. Its collection of intricate interacting parts is beautiful. Sadly, such a beautiful object has just one purpose: killing people efficiently as possible.

Someone might buy an assault rifle for any of several reasons: hunting, self-defense, shooting sports, collecting, just because they can — or to commit mayhem.

A different fear is that the government will be taken over by bad people and you will be outnumbered and oppressed by the Other. That fear is what motivates the Idaho militias. And given what these militia members believe, that fear isn’t unreasonable.The problem is that the kind of society they want to create is not a society that most Americans would want to live in. Certainly I would not.

And if you pay any attention to what the gun advocates are saying, you’ll see that most of them are worried about a takeover from the Left that will erase the America that they believe in, filling the country with abortionists and darkies. That the Left might win power through a free and fair election is quite beside the point to them.

title: Does Gun Control Really Work?
content:
Following the deadliest mass shooting in American history, where 59 people were killed and over 500 more injured when a lone gunman opened fire on a concert from the 32nd floor of a hotel in Las Vegas, advocates for stricter gun laws are once again calling for the heads of anyone who doesn’t agree with their authoritarian stances on firearms. But those condemning America for failing to act on gun control are either blissfully unaware or being outright dishonest about what gun control actually looks like.

Probably the most common example cited by the left as successful gun control action is the National Firearms Agreement, which were a series of laws passed in Australia in 1996, when the government decided that Australian citizens no longer had the right to possess firearms, and instituted a “buyback program”, which, as nice as it sounds, was not a buyback at all, but a government imposed confiscation. It wasn’t voluntary, there was no opting out, you either handed over your guns to the government, or you, ironically, would be facing down the business end of a gun yourself. Despite an estimated compliance of only 20% , many declared this program a success, as overall crime and murder plummeted as a direct result of confiscating just under 650,000 guns.

Or so they claim. Between 1990 and 2012, the homicide rate in Australia was declining slightly at a steady rate which continued along this trend even after the gun reform laws in 1996. In the United States, homicide as well as overall crime rate experienced similar drops, despite gun ownership increasing by almost 50% during that period. According to leftist logic, the rate of murder in the United States should have spiked dramatically and kept rising, but that’s not what happened.

Not only did the Australian buyback fail to reduce crime rates effectively, it failed to have any positive effect at all. According to a 2007 study in the British Journal of Criminology, “the NFA did not lead to a change in the rate of decline in firearm homicides”. It appears the only real and lasting effect of the passage of the NFA was the creation of an enormous and incredibly dangerous black market for firearms .

When looking to the United States, leftists love to regurgitate the long-debunked talking point of “more guns equals more crime”. Not only is this mentality incorrect, it’s actually dangerous to accommodate. Arguably the most dangerous city in the United States, Detroit has some of the strictest gun laws in the country, resulting in low firearm ownership. As a result of such “progressive” policies, the city owns one of the highest violent crime rates in the country. The reason for such an alarming, though not surprising trend, is simple; criminals don’t follow the law, they don’t register guns, and they don’t bother getting permits, which makes them all but impervious to gun control laws. The only thing gun control creates is a defenseless law abiding citizenry.

This is not an isolated example of ludicrous gun control policies doing more harm than good. in Washington D.C. in 1976, a law was implemented that allowed private ownership of guns only if they had trigger locks, which required special permission from the police to remove. As a result, the homicide rate more than doubled until the law was struck down in 2012 by the Supreme Court case District of Columbia v. Heller. To this day, D.C. still has some of the strictest gun laws in the country, consequently making it one of the most dangerous places to live in the country

One of the very things gun grabbing leftists claim they want to curb with stricter gun laws, mass shootings, are actually exacerbated by gun control laws. The Crime Research Prevention Center found that nearly 99% of public mass shooting s since 1950 have occurred in gun free zones. The reason is simple: deranged psychopaths want to kill as many people as possible, so they’ll pick a location where they’re most likely to find a defenseless group of victims

According to research from the CDC, at least 500,000 people in 2013 protected themselves or their property with defensive usage of a firearm. In the same year, there were just over 400,00 instances of illegal nonfatal firearm usage according to the National Justice Institute with 11,008 gun homicides . Even when taking the lowest figure of defensive gun uses, it is clear that firearms are used more often to prevent crime than to commit crime. That statistic is among the aspects of firearm legality that gun control advocates want to eliminate from law abiding citizens.

Thankfully, there are still some sane people out in the world. In Kennesaw, Georgia, for example, not only is firearm ownership encouraged, its mandated by law . Despite initial concerns that crime would skyrocket and there would be rampant shootings in the streets, crime has dropped 89 percent in the city since passing the unorthodox law, according to Kennesaw Historical Society president Robert Jones.

When talking about gun control, facts more often than not take a back seat to feelings and fear mongering. The left prefers to debate this way because nearly every possible study concerning or application of strict gun control laws has been a disastrous example of what happens when lies and misinformation take over in favor of objectivity and practicality. To make a long story short; no, gun control does not work.

title: UNTITLED
content:
Gun control does not work.

Presidential candidate Joe Biden said it in a tweet shortly after the Garlic Festival shootings in Gilroy, CA, “How many more families will have to lose a loved one before we fix our broken gun laws?”

Make no mistake; American gun laws are ineffectual, fragmented and pointless. At last count there were over 20,000 different gun control laws that are currently active on the books in the United States. Since local laws are not included in the official tally the actual number may be well over 30,000, possibly even over 40,000. For frame of reference, that 20,000 number was provided by Michigan Democratic Representative John Dingell’s testimony on firearms to Congress in 1965.

These laws include restrictions on possession, carry, distribution, storage, manufacture, sale, ownership, importation, use, ammunition; the list goes on and on. The bottom line is gun laws do not prevent mass shootings. In fact, it doesn’t stop senseless shootings or high crime rates.

Unsure if a gun law could work at all I decided to try an experiment. I sat down with my two sons (ages 20 and 22 — the youngest is a college student majoring in Political Science and the oldest is a veteran of the US Army) with the goal of building a gun control law from scratch. Since all three of us have very different political opinions I guessed that this would closely resemble a typical Congressional debate. The scenario was simple: we start from scratch; we cannot use any existing laws for reference; the only background available to draw upon is the second amendment.

Starting with the premise that gun control would be used to 1) regulate the sale and ownership of guns and 2) keep the populace safe from guns the three of us quickly agreed on five main points:

• Convicted felons are banned from any type of gun ownership

• If you have been institutionalized by a medical doctor for any type of mental illness you must have a signed waiver by a doctor releasing you and taking responsibility for your mental well being in order to purchase and/or use a gun

• If you are taking medication for any medical issue that prevents you from operating heavy machinery or moving vehicle you must have a signed waiver by a doctor releasing you and taking responsibility for your mental well being in order to purchase and/or use a gun

• Guns must be semi-automatic, using the definition that with each pull of the trigger one round is fired

• There must be a 10-day “cooling-off” period between the purchase and the delivery of the gun (also to be used for background check)

Things got a little sticky with the issue of education, or gun safety classes. It has always been my belief that if the government wants to control guns, then gun education must be included. If the idea is help keep the public safe, then gun safety classes in the schools should be either mandatory or at the very least, offered. If they can teach sex education classes in school, then what is the harm in adding a gun safety class?

Both of my sons were adamant that while safety classes should be included, they should also be considered voluntary and kept out of the schools. Another topic we couldn’t quite agree on was the age to introduce the safety classes. My sons thought Middle School, or 12–13 years old, would be the right age. I then asked them how old they were when they took their first gun safety course. They both responded: 16. They are correct in that they each took a course offered by the Boy Scouts of America on gun safety. Then I reminded them of the 45-minute gun safety course they each took in the first grade at the age of six before they were allowed to shot BB rifles at a Cub Scout Day Camp. They had forgotten about that, but they certainly remembered the basics of what they had been taught.

There you have it, a simple yet effective gun control plan. The mistake that is made in current gun control is that it is used as a response to crime instead of regulation. In America, where we are guaranteed our right to own arms based on the second amendment, a system like that will not work.

Part of the problem is that each state has its own system of regulating guns, and some, like Vermont, don’t have any. If caught with an unregistered gun some states have a maximum sentence of 14 years in prison, but that is rarely carried out. Other states may fine up to $210, but there are loop holes so you don’t even pay the fine and the record is expunged.

If the federal government wants to get tough on crime through the use of gun control they are going to have to make a federal law that 1) has a stiff penalty for possession of unregistered fire arms and 2) provides gun safety education. This is the key element missing in current gun laws, education. I took my first gun safety class while I was in the seventh grade. It was part of a hunting certification class that was offered after school. I learned not only what a gun could do, but more importantly, I learned how not to use it. It made an impression on me then, one that has stayed with me through the years.

American gun control laws become so unwieldy they fail to do the one thing we want them to do: keep us safe. The United States is unique in that we have the right to gun ownership written into our founding documents, specifically the Bill of Rights. We are a nation that not only allows gun ownership, but encourages it. Instead of fighting that legacy it is time to embrace it.

title: Climate Change is Real, and So is Your Money: How to Make a Difference with Green Giving 🌎
content:
You’re probably already thinking about it: climate change is a huge problem, right? We’re talking rising sea levels, extreme weather, and let’s not forget the impact on wildlife. It can feel like a mountain too big to climb, but you know what? You can make a real difference.

What if you could give back to the planet in a way that feels good, is easy, and actually makes an impact? That’s where climate-focused philanthropy comes in. This article is going to show you how to be a climate hero with your money and make a real difference. We’ll explore the growing world of climate philanthropy, learn about some amazing initiatives, and figure out how to make your investments work for a better planet.

Let’s dive in!

Just like the weather, the world of climate philanthropy is constantly changing. It’s not just about donating to the same old charities anymore. It’s about investing in innovative solutions, supporting grassroots movements, and making sure our money is working hard to tackle the climate crisis.

Think of it like this: you’re putting your money on a team. And the team you want to back is the one that’s fighting for a healthier planet. There are tons of organizations out there, and they’re all working on different aspects of climate change.

Here’s a quick rundown of what’s happening:

Let’s say you’re a huge fan of coffee, right? And you’re worried about climate change affecting your favorite beverage.

That’s where The Coffee Bean Growers Alliance comes in. They’re a non-profit organization that works with coffee farmers in developing countries to help them adapt to the changing climate. They provide training, resources, and even financial support to help farmers thrive.

Now, imagine you decide to support this organization with a donation. Your contribution could help farmers invest in new irrigation systems, plant climate-resistant crops, or even use renewable energy to power their farms. You’re not just saving your morning coffee; you’re also helping to support whole communities and build a more sustainable future for coffee.

Ok, you’re convinced. You’re ready to make your money work for the planet. But how do you actually do it?

Here are a few tips:

The world of finance is waking up to the climate crisis, too. Sustainable investment is becoming a popular way to make a difference with your money. It’s about choosing investments that align with your values and support companies that are committed to environmental and social responsibility.

Think of it like this: you’re not just picking stocks; you’re picking a future.

Here are a few things to keep in mind:

Remember, you’re not alone. Millions of people around the world are waking up to the climate crisis and using their money to make a difference.

It’s time to get involved! What are you waiting for? Start your journey as a climate philanthropist today.

title: Climate Change Is Real — I Can Smell It So Can You
content:
Climate change is a challenging topic to discuss and a tricky issue to resolve. It affects everyone, and we want everyone to chip in. Game Theory takes over as we adopt a wait-and-see attitude.

It is one hell of a dramatic global issue.

Our climate changes for the worst with each passing year, and we continue to engage in excessive debates, talking about talking about talking about talking about talking about climate change .

Even facts presented by scientists and strategic arms of the National Governments fail to move our sorry ass to do something for GAIA .

Consider the following statement from the National Climate Change Secretary (NCCS), an extension of the Prime Minister’s Office in Singapore : -

“Singapore is not insulated from the impact of climate change. From 1980 to 2020, the annual mean temperature has increased from 26.9°C to 28.0°C … Rainfall has become more intense in recent years … In 2001, the first recorded cyclone near the equator, Typhoon Vamei, swept north of Singapore and caused major flooding in the region… ”

Most general statements are clunky and long-winded. Allow me to summarize the above into bullet points.

Still unmoved?

Okay, allow me to change the official narrative, so we can understand the issue better.

Human beings have sweat glands . It helps us cool our bodies when the external temperatures rise vis-à-vis our core temperature.

You will sweat more per minute, and you will sweat more frequently. We will start to smell.

We can fix that through deodorants, of course. And that means our cost of survival just went straight up by an inch.

Serves you right, Ignoramus !

It is not just about the car.

It is the same for your apartment.

Your apartment and car will be drowned in higher water levels each time a heavy rainfall decides to pay us a visit.

Your car ceases to function, and your apartment will be flooded.

You are better off saving your hard-earned money.

Your worst nightmares will be realized, and you will go nuttier than Loony Tunes .

Your electricity expense will hit the roof because you will start switching on the air-conditioner for longer each time you do.

Your utility bill expense will hit the roof because you stink, and your clothes stink like sh*t. Plus, you shower more often and wash more often.

Your car will turn into a modern-day Jurassic Park velociraptor . It eats you alive through parking fees (since you cannot actually drive it out to go somewhere).

Thank you for growing the wealth of the nation.

Thank you for contributing to climate change (in the wrong way), asshole .

Many are unmoved by polar bears drowning .

Many think that climate change is somebody else’s problem.

Some argue that climate change is fake and unworthy of any attention.

I wish them a Pink of Health.

I sincerely hope they do not stink. I pray that their precious fixed assets are intact and they are managing their household expenditure well.

One point to note — Mother nature always wins. There is no doubt about it, and she is pretty annoyed now.

How do I know?

I am working in the living room with 2 electric fans blasting at me at full speed, half-naked, sweating non-stop, and I stink.

Have a nice stinky day.

Aldric
