title: When Your Friend Believes Climate Change Is A Hoax
content:
“H ow can two or three extra parts per million of CO2 cause climate change? Trees need CO2 and they release oxygen,” he told me. “The earth’s climate has shifted from hot to cold to hot. It is always changing. It’s nothing to do with CO2.”

I looked at Jock as if I was seeing him for the first time. What? It’s not even up for debate. Climate change is a thing and we’re causing it. I wondered if he was trying to wind me up. He wasn’t having any of it.

We got dressed and headed down for breakfast. We sat at a small table overlooking the gardens. January in Scotland is unpredictable. Jock looked out at the frost-covered ground. A flurry of snow swirled in the air, struggling to land in the bitter wind that rattled the trees. I could read his mind: He wouldn’t mind some of that global warming.

Weather and climate aren’t the same thing. The weather changes all the time; the climate is the long-term picture. “What if you are wrong?” I said. It was all I had left. “What if you are wrong?” Jock didn’t answer. “If we listen to all the tens of thousands of climate scientists and stop pumping CO2 into the atmosphere and it turns out they are wrong, it will be a waste of time and money. If you are wrong, we all die.”

It sounded like a strong argument in my head. In hindsight, Jock looked at me with pitying eyes and mirrored the exasperation I had shown him.

I’ve known Jock for thirty years. We play golf and snooker and take part in our police national championships in these events. The first time we qualified for the British snooker doubles, we won the event. It was a remarkable achievement for Jock, considering my only contribution was potting the black ball in the final to win the match. I’ve shared a room with Jock so often that it feels strange to wake up in a hotel and he’s not snoring in the bed next to me—and vice versa with my farting, I presume.

Despite being a natural leader and organizer, Jock didn’t go for promotion. He was a Police Federation rep and became the go-to guy for cops seeking advice. He’d take a bullet for his colleagues, metaphorically. He’d step between them and the bosses, no matter who they were or what rank they held. He had no reservations about telling gaffers they were in the wrong. I imagined them rolling their eyes when Jock came chapping at their doors like a bulldog with a bone between his teeth. I admired him greatly for that.

Last year, we shared a room at our indoor sports event. That morning, he voiced his opinion about climate change being a hoax. It bothered me. We’ve argued before. We have different opinions on many things and none seemed to matter much, but this bothered me. I’ve thought about it many times—and my horrified reaction. Why did I find his opinion so maddening?

Jock is a guy I respect. I didn’t work with him in the police but heard good things about him. At the latter end of his career, he worked as a detective and it was obvious the people around him held him in high esteem.

He’s intelligent. He knows how to analyze evidence; surely he couldn’t be conned into thinking climate change is a hoax. But it was true; he vehemently denied it. Jock’s argument centered on the insignificance of tiny parts per million changes in carbon dioxide concentrations in the atmosphere.

This week, I got a notification that Jock had posted something on Facebook. I’m rarely there these days. I swipe those things off my phone as quickly as they appear, but I’m sharing a room with Jock again next week, so I took a look. He was having a rant. Something he was more careful about before he retired. What you post online stays online. Jock finished his tirade with, “Oh aye and the absolute waste of money that the climate pish is!”

So much for giving, “What if you are wrong,” any consideration.

I’m worried that my irritation with his stance on climate change and other contrary views could sour our relationship. I know my opinions annoy him as much as his grate on me. My favorite saying is, “It’s okay to be uninformed; it’s not okay to be uninformed and have an opinion.”

I’d happily cite it to him about his views on climate change, but I’ll bet he thinks the same about my views. I’ve thought about why I can’t let this go and why it irks me that a friend of mine can be so blind to the facts. “How can two or three extra parts per million of CO2 cause climate change?” Just because you don’t understand something doesn’t mean it isn’t true.

It’s not as if Jock is heading up a consortium to rape the North Sea of more oil or is building a dozen coal-fired power stations. He’s not even mildly influential; his post had 17 likes and only one mentioned the climate bit of his rant—agreeing it would run its cycle. In the grand scheme of things, Jock is about as insignificant as one tiny clostridium botulinum bacterium living in your gut. Its toxin wouldn’t cause you too much trouble, but you wouldn’t want two or three extra parts per million; that would be enough to block your nerve functions and lead to muscle paralysis or even death. How many is too many?

It doesn’t matter what Jock thinks. It matters what we know. Science is like being a detective. A detective pursues the truth through a systematic methodology based on evidence. If we had a murder and set 100 detectives to investigate it and they all shared their knowledge of every fact gleaned (scientists call this peer review), they would base their case on the evidence, not some uninformed nonsensical notion. That’s what scientists have done with climate change and 99% of scientists, who have got their information from studying the evidence, are in no doubt. The recent warming of the planet is unprecedented and we’re responsible.

Of the 1% of the scientists who haven’t said it is down to humans, the majority of them are sitting on the fence while they analyze the data. To be clear, scientists are more convinced that humans cause climate change than that smoking causes cancer.

Analysis of atmospheric carbon dioxide levels from 580 million years ago reveals a correlation with mass extinction events, predating human activity and fossil fuel burning. Yet, today’s climate change is unlike anything humans have seen—it’s happening way faster and is much bigger. The speed of today’s climate change surpasses the most rapid past events by a factor of up to 50.

The fact that past extinctions were linked to CO2 isn’t good news. It’s us, not the Earth, wrecking things this time. It’s up to us to ditch fossil fuels and dodge the worst of climate change—we aren’t helpless dinosaurs.

I question where Jock is getting his information. If it’s from politicians who are funded by the fossil fuel industry, is it any wonder he is being fed bullshit? Our leaders are ignoring climate change or even denying it exists, even though there’s a mountain of evidence. Oil companies have known about the damage they are doing since the 1950s. Yet, the top polluting countries’ leaders aren’t trying to slow down climate change, much less stop it.

Yesterday, the British government issued an emergency alert in response to Storm Éowyn. I’m looking out my window at trees bending over like they are bowing to the gods and a large bucket is tossed around like a cat’s plaything. We’ve had storms before, but the frequency and strength of these are increasing. I’ve been in my house for 32 years and never had any damage until five years ago when my fence blew over. My roof has been damaged in each of the last three winters.

Climate change is bad news for the economy; we underestimate the financial dangers of climate change worldwide. Look at the cost of the recent fires in Los Angeles. With climate change, the world economy will shrink and keep shrinking. The heat is killing more people. Europe saw almost 62,000 heat deaths in 2023. Higher temperatures make the air worse, leading to more crime and cancers.

What’s the big deal? I shake my head at politicians and their fearmongering over illegal immigrants. If you think they are a problem now, wait a few years to see how many more come when the countries they live in become uninhabitable.

I worry about climate change for my children and their children. I won’t be around long enough to see the worst of what climate change will do. I fear for their health and happiness. Growing up, I advised them to save, start a pension, buy a house, and all the other crumbs of knowledge that applied to me. Maybe I’ve gotten that wrong. They might well have completely different needs and skills to survive.

I think that’s what I find hardest to accept about Jock. He has children, too. I know he loves them. He does his best for them, but he gives them no hope for the future if he thinks there is nothing we can do about climate change. His meager 17 likes on Facebook might mean something if we could change his mind. I can’t do that by asking him, “What if you are wrong?” That’s something he needs to ask himself.

title: Why Climate Change is a Hoax
content:
I feel very let down when our leaders call climate change a hoax or deny that it is a serious threat to humanity. How can they turn their back on one of the most pressing problems of our time? During my forty year history working as a conservationist and technology professional, the evidence for human induced climate change has increased substantially. Today that evidence is about as solid as it gets in science. The potential negative consequences of taking no policy and individual action are enormous whereas the consequences of taking action are likely to be highly beneficial. From a risk management point of view alone, it seems obvious that we must do whatever we can to mitigate the climate change threat.

As a scientist you are trained to be skeptical and question the validity of your conclusions. So normally I enjoy discussions with skeptics since I almost always learn something new from them. But after years of heated and fruitless arguments with climate change doubters and deniers, I’ve greatly lowered my expectations of trying to persuade them. Instead I focus on enjoying the humor on both sides of the debate while hoping I’ve planted a seed for future change. This keeps me moving forward rather than wallowing in doom and gloom thinking. It also reminds me that it is going to be the climate change believers that will have to do the heavy lifting and problem solving. Many of our leaders and friends will likely never come around, remaining under the influence of the hoaxers. Who is behind the hoax is another story, but here I thought you might enjoy these humorous but surprisingly prevalent and clearly exaggerated arguments supporting the climate change hoax.

Climate change is a hoax promoted by the liberal left

Climate change believers have liberal social values and beliefs. These people are primarily socialists who believe government owes them a living. After saving the planet, they are most interested in bigger government, universal healthcare and legalizing marijuana.

Liberals think they are cool driving electric cars

Liberals want everyone to have an electric car so they can feel justified in purchasing an ugly car with limited range. Liberals really aren’t that interested in preventing climate change and saving future generations. They only care about trendy green gadgets and looking awesome. They love to sneak up on you with their silent ugly car.

Climate change believers are hypocritical

Climate change believers still heat their homes, use air conditioning, and fly in jets. They justify their hypocritical behavior by advocating for costly environmental programs, greener technology and making greener purchasing decision if it’s not too inconvenient.

Climate change believers don’t have faith that God can take care of the planet

God created the Earth for mankind and has always taken care of it. Citing a moral obligation to combat climate change, the Pope is seriously over reaching his authority. After all, the Pope is not a scientist. Why should he weigh in on a political debate having little immediate consequence to his 1.2 billion followers?

Fox News regularly exposes the climate change hoax

This reliable news network has an unblemished fair and balanced standard that liberal news networks lack. On Fox, the 3% of under represented scientist who question climate change will continue to have an equal voice in the debate. Anyone else for that matter should be allowed to weigh in and help balance the lopsided scientific point of view.

Treating climate change as a serious problem will have severe economic consequences

If we switch to more renewable energy, Russia and other fossil fuel rich countries will have an economic advantage over the U.S. by continuing to profit from their carbon rich countries. These governments will also save billions by not having to diversify their economies. Sure the U.S. has great technological talent and leads the world in innovation, but aside from Tesla’s pure luck, what makes us think we could also lead and profit from a renewable energy revolution?

The Paris climate agreement is a global conspiracy to weaken the U.S.

Teaming up with other countries to solve a problem that doesn’t exist can only weaken our dominant economic position in the world. It takes real leadership and strength to go our own way and not follow the herd. Let the other 194 countries that signed the Paris agreement waste their money on renewable energy technology that could prevent a warmer, less habitable planet.

The free market will best solve any problem that may exist due to climate change

Government will only waste money on climate change by distorting free markets. We are blessed with an efficient free market economy based on unfettered supply and demand for goods and resources. We are also fortunate that our fossil fuel industry has a well-funded and unfettered lobbying effort to prevent pesky government interference under the guise of the public good.

Scientists are biased by government funding

Government funds the bulk of scientific research on climate change. If government funding is cut, scientists may be out of a job. Consequently, scientist will promote the research that funds them. Besides how many scientists do you know who are motivated by scientific curiosity rather than money?

When was the last time you cancelled a family picnic due to global warming?

We’ve never had to cancel a barbecue or any activity due to global warming. We haven’t even had to run our air conditioner that much more. We should worry about climate change when it’s too hot to go outside. The scientists who say the problem may take tens of thousands of years to stabilize are more interested in long-term job security.

There is significant uncertainty around the impacts of climate change

We should not take action until we know for certain how bad and where climate change impacts will occur. If our children and grand children ask us why they live in a hotter, more polluted, politically unstable world, we can tell them we would have acted sooner, but the scientist never reached 100% agreement.

Why care about polar bears?

We are tired of letting wildlife limit our economic prosperity. The dramatically shrinking artic ice cap is a myth perpetrated by bleeding heart liberals who want to save polar bears even though they’ve never seen one. I’ll be just fine if I never see another picture of a stranded polar bear, melting ice cap or receding glacier. Let’s focus on the good things climate change can do for us like new shipping lanes and new opportunities to drill for oil.

The instruments that measure climate change and carbon dioxide are in really bad places

One of the longest running climate change instruments is on Hawaii’s Mauna Loa volcano and is maintained by scientists from the most liberal State in the U.S. and the alleged birthplace of Barack Obama. Of course the instrument measured the highest CO2 levels in 3 million years — it sits on one of the world’s most active volcanoes spewing out CO2 like crazy.

My point here is simply to laugh a little at ourselves and encourage all of us to take more action and individual responsibility for climate change. For actions you can take to reduce the threat of climate change please read this .

title: If Climate Change Is A Hoax
content:
Nearly 20 years ago I left my home , family and friends . I was blind to the emotional and life changing consequences of this voluntary decision .

My naivety about living in the countryside was embarrassing and potentially dangerous, yet I did it.

I was driven by an overwhelming conviction that I was doing the right thing. I would be creating a sanctuary for my family and helping save the planet from Climate Chaos .

Now I am looking back on my hubris and ignorance, with mixed feelings from regret to gratitude .

What a joke, believing that I could help save the planet. More importantly believing that I could save my family .

Reflecting on my decision is like watching someone fumble around in the dark whilst making hilarious gaffs and also deeply hurting themselves.

The move , the hard work of creating a sustainable life ,the sacrifices all made sense when I believed in Climate Change and the imminent collapse of my civilisation .

Now I have been prompted to take stock of that major decision taken so long ago.

This is not the usual stuff from “Climate Change deniers” or “Green Washing” , that I got used to over the years and could easily be discounted .

Are we being deliberately manipulated to believe That Climate Change is real, dangerous and causing mass extinction ? Brainwashed into believing that cutting our “carbon footprint” will save us.

I totally believed in Climate Change and the coming Collapse until the so called “Pandemic “.

After the initial fear of bodies in the street. I started to question the mainstream narrative that dramatically changed most of our lives and freedoms.

I studied world events, official data and medical experts from all sides , so I could make my own meaning and sense of what was happening.

Also insightful was following the financial markets, news and different pundits. I believe these people are more interested in the money, rather than political causes . When some also started talking about The Great Reset, Davos and Klaus Scharb I knew it was time to take this crazy idea seriously .

I gained a very different view from the majority and certainly from my family. This further schism in our world views had to be compassionately managed. In the past I had been told to keep my “doom monger views to myself” , now it was my conspiracy theories.

If Climate Change is a hoax had I made a fatal past decision ?

Deep soul searching was prompted by an article written by Larry Bell from 2013 that crossed my proverbial path . It’s from Forbes magazine called “In Their Own Words , Climate Alarmists Debunk Their Science “ .

There are a number of very challenging quotes and back ground as to why Larry Bell thought the Climate Crisis science was faulty . The one that really stood out was from Maurice Strong who organised the first US Earth Climate Summit (1992) in Rio de Janeiro.

“ We may get to the point where the only way of saving the world will be for industrialised civilisation to collapse “.

Then there is this an article by J.R Flaherty about how clever marketing in the 2000’s by British Petroleum and Ogilvy made Climate Change all about us and our carbon foot print.

“ There is no proof that the current warming is caused by the rise of greenhouse gases from human activity. Ice core records from the past 650,000 years show that temperature increases have preceded — not resulted from — increases in CO2 by hundreds of years, suggesting that the warming of the oceans is an important source of the rise in atmospheric CO2 ”.

This is from a paper challenging the IPCC led by Professors William Happer and Richard Lindzen of Princeton and MIT respectively. They laid that charge, that an IPCC rule states that all summaries must be approved by governments. “ Climate science is awash with manipulated data, which provides no reliable scientific evidence ,” they said.

There are now a growing number of prominant people such as Jordan Peterson along with many scientists and ordinary folks , who are questioning the Climate Change narrative . As with many subjects , this cannot be opening debated the actual truth is impossible to find , so my doubts have not been clearly answered .

This was an emotional chasm ,

what if I had been wrong all those years ago ?

Should I have stayed in the city and been closer to my beloved

Grandchildren ?

My heartache of separation both physically and emotionally was tangible . As was the game of what if….that my busy mind had a field day with. It was a very painful process , with much soul searching.

Maybe you have the same dilemmas and are questioning everything we are being told ?

Many of us are trying to make sense of how the narratives are changing and truth is hard to find .

I sometimes have regret and sadness that I left my Daughter and Grandson, then my Granddaughter to live far away. I am not integral to their lives, only an occasional visitor.

They love their city lives and would not consider ever moving to the countryside . I now accept all this and know they will make their own decisions and future.

I have no regrets for my own evolution and transformation to who I have become as a result of the move . l have learnt many skills from growing , cooking and fermenting food. To organising community events , being self sufficient , resilient and healthy .

I love where I live , being part of a small rural community can be challenging, but is most often joyful .

Most important to me , is my loving relationship with my husband of nearly 40 years who has made this journey with me.

Then there is the Spiritual aspect of my life , which as Echart Tolle would say can only come from pain . I would not have even embarked on my spiritual quest without these challenges .

I do not know what mine or anyones else’s future will be and choose not to worry about any of it.

What I do know is that different forces in the world are conspiring to choose our future, be it as consumers, serfs , transhumans or any other version of what those in power envisage for humanity . There are lies , corruption , propaganda and malevolence at work . These are deliberately creating fear and causing harm too many.

I witness the weather and seasons changing locally. Today we are officially in a drought. I see the scarcity of butterflies and other once plentiful insects . There are increasing challenges to growing and producing food.

I know our climate is changing and that we are polluting and destroying our beautiful planetary home.

Is the deliberate attack on us , the ordinary people.

The dismantling of precious public assets such as The NHS and National Transport Systems. The manipulation and creation of wars , division and hatred to stop us collectively resisting and creating better ways to live for all. The huge price increases on energy , blamed on Russia even though apparently we only get 5% of our UK energy from there.

I used to think Governments were corrupt and mostly useless . Now I think many in Authority are cruelly focused on their own extinction agenda under the guise of saving the planet. They are using Climate Change to enforce restrictions on what we do , where we go and even what we eat.

The price we will have to pay will be dramatic loss of freedoms , our savings, our food systems, our rights and choices

This whole process has made me wiser and better informed on the mechanisms of how our world operates. How dramatically the tectonic plates of power and domination are changing daily.

In conclusion , nothing in my life has been wasted , all my decisions have taken me here. It was just my timing that was wrong about collapse . Those 20 years have been excellent preparation for the hardships that are already here for many and coming to the rest of us.

Climate Change is not a hoax , it’s just something that is being manipulated in the great power games of dying systems to create more wealth for the few and destruction for the many.

We have all or will have to make difficult life changing decisions because of the deteriorating circumstances . Rest assured this is good practise for living a meaningful life what ever your circumstances may be.

We need to see it is up to each us to prepare mentally , physically ,and spiritually.

We can be our own creators and builders of our ways of living , this I know to be true.

title: MISSING CONTEXT: This Nature article on Antarctic ice does not prove global warming is a hoax
content:
A claim that a research paper published in Nature shows global warming to be a hoax is MISSING CONTEXT.

The story, published by the Canada-based Centre for Research on Globalization, claimed that the paper demonstrated Antarctic ice is expanding, “proving that the man-made global warming narrative is entirely based on fraudulent data.”

The study is authentic . However, the inference that it proves global warming to be a hoax is misleading.

The article states that its focus was on East Antarctica, where it observed a general increase in ice and the growth of 21 glaciers. However, the paper also acknowledged rapid ice loss in other regions of Antarctica, particularly the Peninsula and West Antarctica.

It also notes that “ the East Antarctic ice sheet is more vulnerable than previously anticipated and has made a considerable contribution to the continent-wide mass loss during the past decades.”

The net ice gain in the East does not offset the overall losses due to global warming. Between 1992 and 2017, the continent lost 2,720 ± 1,390 billion tonnes of ice. Ice loss in the West and Peninsula is many times more than the ice gained in the East, approximately 5 ± 46 billion tonnes per year.

The overall stability of ice sheets in East Antarctica compared to the West and Peninsula has been well documented, for example here , here , and here .

However, some studies suggest that this may not last with the increase in global warming. Some areas of the East Antarctic ice sheet are already experiencing melting. Other researchers have warned that this could increase with more warming, which shows no sign of abating .

Likewise the rapid and increased melting of ice sheets in both the Peninsula and West has been well documented here , here , here , and here . The dramatic loss of sea ice around Antarctica has been underscored by numerous studies, here , here , and here .

Scientific research is unanimous that global warming and climate change are happening and are caused by humans, principally through the emissions of greenhouse gases. This view is shared by science academies and the United Nations Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change ( IPCC ).

PesaCheck has previously shown that both sea ice and ice sheets in Antarctica and the Arctic are melting due to anthropogenic global warming. This has numerous negative consequences, mainly through sea level rise .

PesaCheck has examined a claim that a Nature paper about Antarctic ice shows global warming is a hoax and finds it to be MISSING CONTEXT.

title: “Climate Change” is a Hoax: The Truth From a Climate Change Denier
content:
Author note: I’m only calling myself a climate change denier because I think that’s what people would call me, I don’t actually know what it implies.

Honestly, I’m not even sure what the phrase “climate change” means. I have a few cro-magnon friends/peers that believe themselves to be intellectuals who like to go around scoffing at straw-man arguments and making vague comments about how climate change deniers are nut-cases (I never liked people use of the phrases like “straw-man” in a debate because I feel like its a diversion from any true meaning and dialogue. Here I use the phrase to specifically suggest that climate change proponents (again what does that mean?) are choosing to argue against ACTUAL idiots rather than an intelligent person that simply doesn’t share their own view).

I’ve never heard an actual argument from Climate Change “protesters” (I don’t know what to call them because I don’t know what their stance actually is). Here I’m not suggesting (yet) that their argument is not fact based or even that I haven’t heard any facts (a lot of statistics and graphs get thrown around but with no proper context), rather what I am suggesting is I have never heard an actual thesis or “point” to the climate change proponents cries.

It always seems that the people that are the most vocal about climate change feel that their argument and especially the thesis for it, implies itself. I think perhaps this is a not so clever way of simply avoiding giving a statement that can be refuted (such as we will all die in 10 years because of climate change).

And so we come across one of my first major points in regard to the battle versus ignorance. It is the previous paragraph that sheds light on what it means for something to be scientifically based, and that is that the claim must be falsifiable. I know that some of these vocal proponents of climate change (?) would now present a bunch of graphs and facts and suggest that they are falsifiable claims, but graphs and data do not make claim-the are (supposed to be) objectively collected observations.

That if climate change becomes an urgent threat of immediate and impending doom, then we will simply use it as a focal point for co-operation. Some people might argue that is exactly what is happening with the “debate”, that people are finally waking up to the impending doom. That movement doesn’t at all tell me that climate change is getting serious and real. It tells me that most people were too lazy to do their homework, and that our school systems don’t teach us what science is.

If climate change is a problem, then technology and entrepreneurship, discovery etc. is the solution. This happens to be my same recommendation to a world in which climate change also ISN’T problem. What is more likely “impending” and “worrisome” to the people is procuring security for the future, as we do that we can THEN begin to discuss long term and bigger issues.

Running around like “chicken little” sending memes about how the sky is falling (or snow is melting) is not attending to any social problem that is useful to solve.

title: Trump 2.0 Un(der)covered: What This Really Means For The Climate — And the World
content:
So “climate change is a hoax” Donald Trump is set to reclaim the reins of the world’s largest historical greenhouse gas emitter.

Unsurprisingly, neither Trump nor Kamala Harris made the climate crisis a prominent feature of their campaigns, daring to confront the elephant in the room. This oversight occurred even as the US was pounded by weather disasters supercharged by an unusually warm Atlantic Ocean that claimed 232 lives across the southwest in a merciless display of climate change’s growing wrath.

And here’s the most ridiculous irony: nearly half of those deaths occurred in the swing state of North Carolina, which, believe it or not, moved decisively behind Trump. In the state’s still-recovering western region, voters lacking proper polling stations cast their ballots in tents .

Meanwhile, global temperatures have been so high through the first 10 months of 2024 that only an implausibly sharp drop in the final two months would prevent a new record from being set.

According to Samantha Burgess , Deputy Director of the Copernicus Climate Change Service (C3S), “It is now virtually certain that 2024 will be the warmest year on record (surpassing the current record of 1.48C, which was set only last year ) and the first year of more than 1.5ºC above pre-industrial levels according to the ERA5 dataset”.

The most recent analysis by Carbon Brief supports this claim, marking a symbolic and ominous milestone as we breach the 1.5ºC threshold for the first time.

It’s crucial to note that while 2024 may breach the 1.5C limit, this doesn’t mean the Paris goal is lost, as it refers to long-term average temperatures. However, each year we exceed this threshold brings the world closer to permanently surpassing the 1.5C mark.

With levels of greenhouse gases in the atmosphere still rising, our civilization faces unprecedented challenges in a climate warmer than any we’ve experienced. This inevitably pushes our ability to respond to extreme events — and adapt to a warmer world — to the absolute limit.

Drill, baby, drill , right?

During his first term, Trump made his disdain for climate policy a cornerstone of his politics, turning the United States into a global environmental outcast. His second term will unfold in a different context — one where the U.S. has enacted meaningful climate legislation, but China has taken a commanding lead in crucial zero-carbon technologies. Consequently, Trump’s climate decisions will have remarkable implications for the country’s economic policy.

So, what might a second Trump administration mean for climate action?

For that, we have Project 2025 to answer. The “book” published by the conservative Heritage Foundation is more than a radical political manifesto. It’s a blueprint to dismantle environmental protections, obliterate climate policies, and gut any institutional checks on presidential power.

After going undercover to meet one of Project 2025’s masterminds, Russell Vought , the Center for Climate Reporting (CCR) uncovered the detailed plan for the upcoming administration — one that could push the US closer to authoritarianism and kill any hopes of keeping global temperatures under the 1.5 C° mark.

The first few steps were easy to predict. That is, basically, a seismic shift in U.S. energy policy, steering the country away from green initiatives and setting the stage for an unrestrained Big Oil feast.

Trump will likely withdraw the United States from the Paris Agreement again, approve a new wave of liquefied natural gas export terminals under the banner of “unleashing American energy,” and begin dismantling the Environmental Protection Agency’s climate rules and emission standards. He could place the agency under direct presidential control, transforming it into a puppet for fossil fuel interests. Trump might also “dismantle” and “privatize” much of the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) — described as “one of the main drivers of the climate change alarm industry.”

Vought’s team has been drafting executive orders and secret directives aimed at reversing Biden-era climate policies, completely erasing “climate change references from government documents.” Their vision is clear: a government that answers only to the president, with agencies transformed from watchdogs into enablers of mass drilling, mining, and deforestation. Even federal support for renewable energy, crucial for U.S. climate resilience, could be stripped away.

The most terrifying part? This isn’t just about climate. Vought even boasted about crafting policies for “the largest deportation in history” and readiness to use military force against protesters, revealing the plan’s authoritarian ambitions. And Trump’s public denial of the project? Nothing but smoke and mirrors, according to Vought.

And the secrecy is deliberate. The CCR’s hidden cameras captured Vought proudly describing how the entire Project 2025 blueprint is kept “very, very close hold” — meaning journalists and the public would never see the full extent of it. By avoiding freedom of information laws, Project 2025 intends to hide every detail of its climate-wrecking agenda until it’s too late to stop it.

If Project 2025 unfolds as the investigation suggests, the US could be dragged into a reality where power is absolute, accountability is gone, and opposition is crushed. Essentially, the country risks becoming a fossil-fuel sanctuary with little regard for climate impact and the worldwide people affected by it. In fact, according to a study by Carbon Brief , policies to encourage more drilling and burning of oil and gas would add four billion tons of greenhouse gas emissions to the atmosphere by 2030 that could cause global climate damages worth more than $900bn. For context, this is equivalent to the combined annual emissions of the European Union and Japan, or the combined annual total of the world’s 140 lowest-emitting countries.

The impact of these rollbacks won’t be immediate. Take the Environmental Protection Agency’s (EPA) clean car rules — they apply to vehicles through model year 2026. Automakers have already invested to meet these standards. However, vehicles in the latter half of this decade will likely face much weaker rules, if any at all.

Then come the weightier climate policy questions.

First up: Will Trump attempt to repeal or hinder the Inflation Reduction Act (IRA), Biden’s landmark climate incentives law? This bill, a major climate policy victory, allocated $369 billion for clean energy investments. Today, the U.S. electric vehicle (EV) market is booming, with sales surging over 50% annually. But Trump has dismissed EVs as a “scam,” vowing to “terminate” IRA spending and “rescind all unspent funds” under the law.

Yet Trump’s crusade against clean energy could backfire spectacularly. The IRA’s investments, primarily tax credits, have predominantly benefited Republican districts. A Washington Post analysis reveals that Trump-supporting districts from 2020 have received triple the IRA funding of Biden-backing areas. New EV, battery, and solar panel factories have sprouted across purple and red America, thrusting 18 House Republicans to ask not to repeal the law.

This is the IRA’s built-in defense mechanism. Like the Affordable Care Ac t before it, the climate law aims to safeguard itself by intertwining with local economies nationwide. But will this strategy succeed? Can the IRA weather Trump’s first 100 days? And will Trump eventually muster enough House votes in the chessboard for outright repeal? Even if the law stands, Trump might seek alternative ways to undermine it. His threat to “rescind the [IRA’s] unspent funds” raises the specter of impoundment — the legally questionable way for a president to delay or refuse to spend congressionally authorized funding.

Only time will tell.

Beyond the IRA, the second Trump administration’s climate and environmental policy harbors several lurking fissures. Because an unlikely coalition aided his second ascend to the White House: Elon Musk, an EV and defense contracting billionaire, and Robert F. Kennedy Jr., an environmental lawyer turned anti-vaccine crusader and roadkill enthusiast — yes, a simmering cauldron of contradictions. Trump has promised Kennedy control over public health policy , while Musk will oversee a new Department of Government Efficiency

While these men find common ground on some policies, their views diverge significantly, particularly in energy policy. Trump’s victory speech provided a taste of the fireworks to come when he playfully warned Kennedy to “stay away from the liquid gold” — a not-so-subtle nod to the administration’s fervent embrace of domestic oil production.

Nuclear stirs the cauldron, too. Kennedy, a lifelong opponent of nuclear energy, counts shutting down New York’s Indian Point nuclear reactor among his greatest career victories. In stark contrast, Musk champions nuclear energy, deeming reactor closures “total madness.” The incoming vice president JD Vance quietly aligns with the pro-nuclear camp, while Trump (as always) dances in contradictions — officially advocating for a nuclear renaissance while simultaneously voicing skepticism about its future.

The fault lines deepen. Kennedy’s crusade against the chemical industry clashes violently with Trump’s vision of a refinery-studded America. Meanwhile, Musk has claimed that repealing the IRA could benefit Tesla by hindering its competitors. Yet, today Tesla thrives on regulatory credits born from the climate policies Trump seeks to obliterate.

The backdrop to these disagreements is the permanently altered landscape of climate policy geopolitics. Gone are the days during Trump’s first term when climate policy was a quaint environmental footnote. Today, clean energy — encompassing renewables, batteries, and EVs — is pivotal to modern economic development and geopolitical strategy.

And there is the dragon, getting stronger by the day.

As Trump’s America retreats from the global climate stage, China will surge forward, assuming greater global leadership — ironically fueled by Trump’s own past policies . Over the past decade, China has secured a commanding lead in zero-carbon technologies, now dominating the electric vehicle production , offering cheaper and technologically superior models compared to global competitors. Should the US withdraw its EV support, China stands ready to twist the knife and capture the remaining global market share from U.S. automakers — a process already underway .

So, while the upcoming Trump White House deals with this internal policy schizophrenia, on thing stand clear: This isn’t just about policy; it’s about power, profit, and the very future of our planet.

Even before Trump’s re-election, the 1.5°C target was hanging by a thread. According to a recent United Nations emissions report , most countries are cutting emissions far too slowly to stabilize warming at safe levels. And in all truth, even a climate champion couldn’t have steered the U.S. back on track to meet its climate goals.
With that said, the ripple effects of Trump’s election will not only affect the US, but also send shockwaves across the global climate landscape.

His victory comes just days before (the failing) representatives from nearly 200 nations gather in Azerbaijan for COP29 , the annual United Nations climate summit. The two-week meeting, starting November 11, will unfold under the shadow of a Republican president-elect who has promised to lead another withdrawal from the landmark 2015 Paris Agreement.

António Guterres, the UN secretary-general said that “The Paris Agreement can survive, but people sometimes can lose important organs or lose the legs and survive. But we don’t want a crippled Paris Agreement. We want a real Paris Agreement. It’s very important that the United States remains in, and more than remain, that the United States adopts the kind of policies that are necessary to make the 1.5 degrees still a realistic objective.”

A fresh exodus by the world’s largest economy and second-biggest emitter , echoing Trump’s first term, would signal that the U.S. is out of the climate fight, further eroding faith in global climate cooperation and potentially encouraging other countries to follow suit. Without U.S. engagement, efforts to cut emissions in an already strained global system could stall during this critical decade for curbing Earth’s rising temperatures.

The diplomatic world is already reeling. With the U.S. delegation to COP29 reduced to lame-duck status with diminished credibility and leverage, the vital climate finance for developing nations — a key focus of this year’s summit — hangs by a thread. Meanwhile, ambitious carbon-cutting pledges risk being watered down or abandoned altogether.

But make no mistake: Trump will never be above the laws of physics, and neither will the country he leads. Climate change doesn’t give a damn about politics or party lines. The U.S. (and the world) will face fiercer storms, more intense heatwaves, and deadlier wildfires as long as we keep burning oil, coal, and gas. No amount of denial or policy rollbacks can alter this harsh reality. So, ifTrump follows through on his threat to ditch the Paris Agreement, the biggest loser will be the United States itself.

So, yes, the 1.5 C° target might be dead but even with all this threatening context, the path to limiting global temperature rise to 2 degrees Celsius remains open. It all depends on the actions of state governments, local governments, other countries, and ultimately, in our own.

It’s time to step up and fill the void.

So be loud.

Thank you for your thorough reading and support!

title: FALSE: ChatGPT did not say climate change is a hoax
content:
Claims that ChatGPT has said climate change is a hoax are FALSE.

Various tweets — here , here , and here — alleged that the Artificial Intelligence (AI) language model said climate change is a hoax or is not real.

According to its developers, ChatGPT is an AI language model trained to interact with users through conversation.

“The dialogue format makes it possible for ChatGPT to answer followup questions, admit its mistakes, challenge incorrect premises, and reject inappropriate requests,” they say .

The technology uses data from the internet to respond to queries conversationally, simulating human responses.

The claims that ChatGPT is sceptical about climate change are not true. PesaCheck asked ChatGPT questions (see screenshots below) and it consistently answered that climate change is real. It based its answers on “scientific consensus” and the “vast body of scientific research and evidence”.

It reiterated that as an AI model it does not “have personal beliefs or opinions”, and responses are based on available information and data. It denied saying climate change is a hoax, not real or happening, and that it does not believe it is real.

An environmental advocacy group quizzed ChatGPT about climate science and found it “demonstrated decent accuracy responding to very specific questions”, although there were omissions. It answered that greenhouse gas emissions by humans caused climate change.

Journalists and researchers asked ChatGPT about climate change — here , here , here , here , here — where it reaffirmed its position about climate change and never referred to climate change as a hoax or that it is not real.

The developers admit that ChatGPT has certain limitations. There are “plausible-sounding but incorrect or nonsensical answers”, it can be confused by question phrasing, it can be “excessively verbose” and overuse some phrases, it relies on guesswork for ambiguous questions, and can occasionally “respond to harmful instructions” or produce biased content.

The developers add : “We’d recommend checking whether responses from the model are accurate or not”.

PesaCheck has examined whether ChatGPT has disparaged climate change and finds it to be FALSE.

This post is part of an ongoing series of PesaCheck fact-checks examining content marked as potential misinformation on Facebook and other social media platforms.

By partnering with Facebook and similar social media platforms , third-party fact-checking organisations like PesaCheck are helping to sort fact from fiction. We do this by giving the public deeper insight and context to posts they see in their social media feeds.

Have you spotted what you think is fake or false information on Facebook? Here’s how you can report . And, here’s more information on PesaCheck’s methodology for fact-checking questionable content.

This fact-check was written by PesaCheck climate change fact-checker Christiaan van der Merwe and edited by PesaCheck senior copy editor Cédrick Irakoze and acting chief copy editor Francis Mwaniki.

The article was approved for publication by PesaCheck’s managing editor Doreen Wainainah .

PesaCheck is East Africa’s first public finance fact-checking initiative. It was co-founded by Catherine Gicheru and Justin Arenstein , and is being incubated by the continent’s largest civic technology and data journalism accelerator: Code for Africa . It seeks to help the public separate fact from fiction in public pronouncements about the numbers that shape our world, with a special emphasis on pronouncements about public finances that shape government’s delivery of Sustainable Development Goals (SDG) public services, such as healthcare, rural development and access to water / sanitation. PesaCheck also tests the accuracy of media reportage. To find out more about the project, visit pesacheck.org .

PesaCheck is an initiative of Code for Africa , through its innovateAFRICA fund , with support from Deutsche Welle Akademie , in partnership with a coalition of local African media and other civic watchdog organisations.

Citizens need accurate information to make sound decisions. PesaCheck is Africa’s largest indigenous fact-checking organisation, debunking misleading claims and deciphering the often confusing numbers quoted by public figures in 16 African countries.

Are they lying? Kenya’s 1st fact-checking initiative verifies statements by public figures. A @Code4Kenya and @IBP_Kenya initiative, supported by @Code4Africa.

title: Don’t Read This If You Think Climate Change Is a Hoax
content:
According to Jane Goodall, the three greatest problems facing the world in terms of its ability to sustain us are (1) extreme poverty, (2) the lifestyle most of us adopt once we cease to be poor, and (3) the sheer size of the human population.

Notice I framed the problem around us humans, not around the numerous species that have recently become extinct due to our actions. It’s too late for them. Even if we all suddenly had the will to make the changes needed to reverse course, they will not come back. Ever. And more are certain to have the same fate, even if we act.

It’s hard for us to take responsibility for what our species has done when we fail to see how so many things around us that we view as normal are part of the problem. We hardly think about how our entire human environment and personal choices, regardless of whether we’re poor or rich, when added up, are unsustainable.

We all can do something about poverty, lifestyle and the size of the human population. There’s no valid excuse other than ignorance of the problem. Here are some ways we’re all living an illusion when it comes to our impact on our planet. All you have to do is open your eyes and mind.

“How can we even try to save these precious famous chimpanzees while people living around the borders of their park are in this terrible situation?” Jane Goodall , in Masterclass

Extreme poverty (set by The World Bank at living on less than 1.90 dollars a day) entails enormous human suffering for close to 700 million people.

Many people ask, in good faith, How can we even expect the very poor to change any practices, however harmful to the environment? They’re right, we can’t. The main responsibility rests on the rest of society, institutions, and policymakers simply because those who live in extreme poverty harm the environment because they have to.

The task of poverty reduction is rendered even more complex by the fact that reducing poverty goes hand in hand with preserving the environment. They are interdependent, as the United Nation report Poverty and the environment/climate change explains:

title: Energy Savings, not Warming, will Sell Renewables
content:
Often, I meet climate change deniers who argue that global warming is a “hoax”. I counter that apart from CO2 release, renewables and electrification are more efficient, representing a more economical future in addition to a cleaner and simpler one. But what is the evidence for this?

There are two competing arguments that you often see in print, regarding the efficiency of electric cars versus gasoline cars. Left-leaning articles “rightly” state that electric cars are 60%+- efficient, while gasoline cars are 20%+- efficient (efficiency being measured by the amount of onboard “fuel” utilized while the rest is “wasted”). Right-leaning articles say that when the efficiency of the electricity source is considered (usually around 33%, in the conversion of natural gas or coal), electric cars are often not more efficient than gas cars. Some quick math reveals there is a partial truth to that last statement, since for electrics 0.33 x 0.60 = 0.20 which equals the gas car efficiency. However, gasoline production has efficiency issues too (it requires energy to be brought from the ground and processed) and increasingly electricity is being produced by renewables (with much higher efficiency rates) while electric cars are getting more efficient, so it is an evolving argument. Let’s examine some of the details. ( Hanley,2018 ),( Skowron,2019 ),( Deb,2016 )

The chart below is one of my favorites. It shows the various energy sources by percentage in the US (as of 2017), and how much of that energy is utilized or wasted. Since renewables are getting ever better, cheaper, and more efficient, while fossil fuel is getting ever harder to get out of the ground (not to mention harder to clean up), there seems to be a growing efficiency advantage to non fossil-fuel options (it depends on your efficiency sample points). However, energy utility is not always about energy efficiency. The easiest way to explain this is to examine fuel densities. Energy density is sometimes needed to make a fuel portable, and so a trade-off is made between efficiency and portability. A rocket ship, for instance, uses liquid oxygen which is very energy dense, portable, and expensive. A jet fighter or tank may use kerosene and diesel, respectively, and we are a long ways from battery-powering either one of them (batteries currently have a relatively low energy density and energy/weight problem). Hydrogen is one of the best bets to power these jets or tanks cleanly, due to a decent energy density and especially a high energy/weight ratio. However, hydrogen takes a fair amount of energy to produce, and is thus not highly energy efficient or even cost effective. Ethanol made from corn is also a notoriously inefficient process (it takes more energy to make it than it produces), but other societal values are at work (the processing of biomass waste to make a clean/portable fuel). ( Roberts,2018 )

Internal combustion engines are relatively complex and will probably never be highly efficient. The combustion needed to power them produces heat, which is typically wasted. If this heat could somehow be recovered (there have been attempts to use this heat to augment the power train or alternator, called exhaust heat recovery ), cars would be more efficient, but it may be a losing battle. Fossil fuel burning at a power plant, on the other hand, can (and does) use this waste heat more effectively (called cogeneration ), plus is in a much better position to “scrub” CO2. All this is pretty much why burning natural gas and coal at the plant are 30% efficient and cars 20% efficient. Remember that internal combustion engines were designed around the relative abundance of fossil fuels 100 years ago, which were at the time practically leaking out of the ground. Now that fossil fuel is getting harder to find ( and fracking tends to pollute groundwater or create unintended methane releases ), it is getting less efficient to produce all the time. Renewables, on the other hand, are getting more efficient by the day, especially as photovoltaics are producing more with cheaper materials and manufacturing processes, and batteries are becoming more energy dense and less pricey. Economy of scale and public interest will continue this trend.

At this point, we need to point out that electrification is not always efficient either. Electricity travelling over long distances through traditional HVAC (High Voltage Alternating Current) wires (plus the transformers that step down the voltage) can create up to 50% line losses. Electric motors (which power electric cars or home heating/cooling systems) can also produce waste heat. There are four major avenues being explored/implemented that could greatly reduce this electrical waste: 1) Electric cars with regenerative braking (where the energy used to “brake” is fed back into charging the batteries, or some other onboard utility) 2) HVDC (High Voltage Direct Current) power, direct current (often from renewables) that suffers much less energy line loss than HVAC, and can be used to “share” energy between regions and offset “time of use” problems (renewables generally produce during the day, and expanding their daytime markets reduces the need to store energy in expensive devices) 3) Air-source heat pump s are the hope of electrifying heating/cooling in a highly efficient manner, so as to replace relatively inefficient gas heat (these heat pumps “draw” hot or cold out of ambient air, and can be highly efficient) 4) Electrified light rail and high speed rail could be much more energy efficient than air or car travel, if filled to capacity with riders. Maglev high speed rail is extremely energy efficient (because it rides on an air cushion and has little resistance), but is expensive to build. Of course there are other electrification applications too numerous to mention, but the general idea often involves direct DC transfer from renewables to the application, with some kind of energy storage (battery or fuel cell) if necessary. This eliminates the relatively inefficient AC power delivery and standby waste heat (like when your internal combustion engine idles at a stop light). The holy grail of electrification is superconductivity , in which there is no waste heat and potential 100% efficiencies (sounds too good to be true, but they have recently engineered superconductive materials that operate at room temperature, quite a breakthrough). The next challenge is to make these relatively brittle materials into some kind of wire! ( Molina,2019 ),( Daware,2016 )

It’s best to conclude that energy efficiency is something to strive for when possible, such as in controlled conditions like ordinary transportation, energy delivery, and home heating. In situations where a large load is being moved in a remote place (such as a truck, jet, rocket, or tank), energy densities come into play and efficiency may take a back seat, but over time (and with new technology) these should become the exceptions. So now that you know all this, the next time you’re at a cocktail party and some ignoramus says “global warming is a hoax!”, tell them “no, it’s not…but even if it was, switching from fossil fuels to renewables and electrification generally offers greater efficiencies that are already proving to save energy, while being easier, and cheaper to use. At the same time, society should acknowledge that hydrogen may be the less efficient, more energy dense and portable fuel for remote/high horsepower needs such as jets and tanks”.

See how all that rolls off the tongue?

title: My Plan To Tackle Climate Change
content:
We can’t afford to gamble with our future. Climate change is not a visible enemy, and sometimes it can feel like it moves so slowly that it will never affect us. Sadly, that doesn't seem to be the case. The vast majority of scientists agree that the risk of climate change is significant and that human activities largely contribute to it . However, the few skeptics of climate change are very vocal and challenge overwhelming scientific evidence. I believe that we should always remain vigilant in our pursuit of the truth, but skepticism and dogmatic opposition should never be the defining feature of policymaking. The consensus of scientific research has made it clear to me that we can’t afford the risk of inaction. It’s time we take concrete steps to prevent damage from climate change, while also protecting our jobs and our way of life.

Often when people think of the effects of climate change, they think of warming. By 2050, Oklahoma could see more than dangerously hot 90 days annually, t he fifth greatest number of dangerous days among the lower 48 states . However, climate change poses risks to Oklahoma beyond warming. We may see both extremes, hot and cold. According to the director of the Oklahoma Climatological Survey, we’ve set one record cold in the last 30 years and 14 different days at record highs since 2000. Climate change could cause heavy downpours that result in severe flooding in Oklahoma. Severe flooding can cause a lot of damage. In fact, when OKC was hit by a historic downpour in 2015, meteorologist Damon Lane reported that someone’s tornado shelter had floated above ground .

In Oklahoma, we know that droughts can be devastating to some of our most important industries. Ignoring climate change will undoubtedly increase the years when droughts occur. By 2050, the severity of widespread summer drought is projected to almost double in Oklahoma. We also know that extreme summer heat and droughts can increase the risk of wildfires, which have hurt Oklahomans in the past. In fact, more than 38 percent of the state’s population is living in areas at elevated risk of wildfire. This will affect the entire Oklahoma economy.

Oklahomans are proud of our energy economy. We often worry that addressing climate change in Oklahoma will be devastating to our flourishing oil & gas industries. However, natural gas is an essential transition energy. Natural gas has been incredibly effective at reducing emissions, in fact, sometimes even more than renewables. This is because the renewable energy economy is still in development. As one of Oklahoma’s senators, I will not punish the natural gas industry for being in high-demand as a clean and efficient source of energy. We need to take the issue of climate change seriously so that our state isn’t left behind as new energy projects emerge.

Oklahoma must take the lead in the clean energy transition. As we transition to a clean energy economy, Oklahoma has the opportunity to become the silicon valley of energy. We have the capacity to produce and export massive amounts of renewable energy. We are a state of innovation. Oklahoma City was ranked №1 by CNN Money for being a business friendly city. Oklahoma has played a crucial role in maintaining American energy independence, which is essential to preventing devastating foreign conflicts. As senator, I will support our state’s innovative businesses including increasing federal investments in research and development for new energy projects.

To innovate, we need a high-skilled workforce to do the jobs that will be created. That’s why I will push for job training for Oklahomans so that we can fill those jobs. Oklahomans are smart, and we deserve the opportunity to compete in our changing economy. And it is a great opportunity for job growth; the two fastest-growing jobs in the nation are solar panel installer and wind turbine technician. It’s important that we re-establish dedicated programs for green industrial and construction job training and placement under the Workforce Innovation & Opportunity Act (WIOA). We need to expand opportunities for young people entering the workforce to develop skills that will allow them to adapt to a changing energy economy.

We must revamp our nation’s public transportation system, especially in Oklahoma. The U.S. ranks 37th in the world for our railway system. Improving our railway system could create jobs and help people get to the jobs they already have easier. Relying entirely on individual vehicles is not only bad for our climate, it also limits the ability for low-income people who lack car access to participate in the economy.

Oklahoma can be at the forefront of the sustainable agriculture industry. Oklahoma has a growing agriculture business. In 2017, our state sold $7.5 billion of agriculture products. But, climate change puts that industry at risk because it threatens to devastate our family farms with changing temperatures, grassfires, and drought. That’s why we need to revamp the Conservation Stewardship Program (CSP), which provides funding for farmers to transition to sustainable practices and delivers returns to taxpayers. I’m determined to ensure that our agriculture sector isn’t left behind.

This is a moral issue. I spent a lot of my childhood in two places: my grandparents’ farm and Sunday school. Spending time on the family farm taught me the moral imperative of being stewards of the land. And while we couldn’t predict every change in the weather, my grandpa was always on the cutting edge of being a true steward of the land, like the time he built a first-of-its-kind irrigation system that ran uphill in the middle of the drought that no one thought would work. It worked. And his crops survived season after season. The other place that shaped me was my upbringing in the Nazarene church. I listened attentively as my Sunday school teacher read from Matthew 7:24 and explained that everyone who heard Jesus’s word built their home on a rock, but those who didn’t built their house on sand. And then, when the winds and the floods came, they destroyed the houses built on sand. Scripture also told us the man who built his house on sand did so because he thought God would save him. But, God had already tried to save him by warning him of the devastation to come.

As a kid, I learned the same lesson parents across our state still teach our kids: how to determine what’s right and wrong. Life would certainly be a lot easier if we could call God on the phone with our questions. That’s why we have to have faith in the character and integrity of the people who lead us — faith that they know what’s right and wrong and make informed decisions when warnings are staring us in the eye. I worry that the partisan gridlock that’s driven Washington for so long has left us as a nation built on sand. As we refuse to heed warnings of a threat to the world that God gave us, we may be putting that world at risk. Because, the floods and winds and many other devastating events will come, and it appears we are ignoring this impending moral crisis because of partisan politics.

I will fight for you. As we are faced with the imminent threat of climate change, I am committed to ensuring that Oklahoma is protected from the floods, fires, or droughts that will occur. I am also committed to ensuring that our state is at the forefront of the shifting economy. With the right policies, our state and nation will thrive.

I will fight for you. As we are faced with the imminent threat of climate change, I am committed to ensuring that Oklahoma is protected from the floods, fires, or droughts that will occur. I am also committed to ensuring that our state is at the forefront of the shifting economy. With the right policies, our state and nation will thrive.

title: I’ll Admit Climate Change is Real if You Admit Fight Club Is The Best Movie of All Time.
content:
I feel like we’ve reached an impasse. You want me to, as you say, “believe the science” and admit that Climate Change is the greatest threat facing the world today, and I want you to recognize David Fincher’s 1999 magnum opus Fight Club as the classic it is. Surely we can find some common ground.

Look, I know that the jokes about not talking about Fight Club get annoying after a while. But if you can look past all the surface fandom bullshit, you’ll see that underneath Fight Club is a fantastic movie. A movie about … fighting and… clubs? Ok, so I can’t break down and analyze movies like a film school nerd. I still know a good movie when I see it. Kind of like how you’re not a scientist, but you still think melting ice caps and cow farts are bad.

Fight Club gets a bad rap. We both know that toxic masculinity is a made-up concept like greenhouse gasses or carbon footprints, and yet plenty of people — primarily libs — use the term to stigmatize Fight Club unfairly. Is it toxic to beat the shit out of your best friend to avoid having to talk about your feelings? Of course not! Is it toxic to spend all night making love to a beautiful woman only to pretend you’re a completely different person in the morning? Hell no! Fight Club is about as toxic as clean coal.

Of course, it’s hard not to have your opinion about Fight Club tainted by all the video essays. You know, the ones on YouTube where a young woman calling herself something dumb like The Groovy Moovy Slut says that Ed Norton’s character has a mental illness and that he conjures up Brad Pitt to replace the dad that abandoned him? I mean, yes, Brad Pitt is a daddy, so that part tracks, but everything else is just a bunch of dumb theories. Seriously, most of the analysis is so bad it almost makes An Inconvenient Truth look believable.

All I’m asking you to do is ignore whatever the pasty white chicks on YouTube have to say and form your own opinions about Fight Club . If you can do that, I can do my best to ignore all the evidence that the Earth is actually cooling and consider replacing my SUV with a hybrid. No promises, though.

Because despite what every halfwit cinephile on the internet would have you believe, Fight Club is not some clever allegory for being queer. There’s no subtext about being transgender or anything like that. It’s not secretly about trauma, abuse, or abandonment. Fight Club is simply about a guy trying to get another guy to stop acting like such a pussy and be a man. He does this by starting a club where guys can beat the shit out of each other. Oh, and the first guy is actually the second guy, but you don’t find out until the end. They also make soap for some reason, but like super masculine soap, not the kind that smells all flowery.

That’s it, that’s all that the movie is about. If there is any deeper message in Fight Club , I have willfully ignored it for over twenty years and will continue to do so for the foreseeable future. Just like global warming! Speaking of which, in honor of Fight Club’s infamous third act twist, here’s one of my own: I know climate change is real; I just don’t care. Why should I? I’ll be long dead before it gets truly awful. Let my grandkids worry about it.

Meanwhile, I’m just going to keep on jerking off into a pile of styrofoam while covering myself in aerosol deodorant and watching my DVD copy of Fight Club . Call me Jack’s selfish indifference.

title: Those the Gods wish to destroy…..they first make mad…
content:
President elect Trump says, repeatedly, that he thinks climate change is a hoax. He belongs to a mystical madness sect whose adherents, increasing daily, refuse to accept scientific evidence. It is not possible to find out if Trump is merely pretending to agree with the entire mystical madness belief system. This is capacious indeed, and extends to any belief which has no evidence to support it. Often, members claim to believe certain propositions just because they like the other people who believe them. Or because, whilst they know them to be false, it is in their interest or to their advantage, that everyone else believes them.

In Trump’s case, he knows a lot of his supporters depend on cheap fossil fuels. So he says we don’t need to worry about the effects of CO2 in our delicate and vulnerable atmosphere. As long as you can still breathe it without coughing up blood, you are good to go. So is Trump. He gets his votes, his money from the oil companies and another chance to pretend to be a tough guy, Genghis Kahn type Prince of Peace. Plus stable genius. And make another fortune for himself! ( Don’t do it Vladimir, don’t do it…the scriptwriters are on it already )

Maybe he’s thinking he won’t be around by the time it gets really emphysema out there. Trump Junior can sort it out.

Take a look at the chart at the top here. There you have the evidence that mass emphysema and global warming are on hand. CO2 will catapult us all into the age of polycrisis. Meaning that a lot of close to insurmountable problems are likely to emerge all at once : war; a multi-polar nuclear armed planet, climate breakdown; famine; drought; civil insurrection; chaos generally on a planet of eight billion. Planet earth has had tons of CO2 swirling around before now — but that was when the dinosaurs ruled the roost. Volcanic eruptions filled the ether with lung clogging smoke and tropical jungle hid the sun from less long necked creatures than T Rex and friends. This time, it’s us that are the source of the invisible, toxic, chemical recipe that will poison our grandchildren.

CO2 and the climate change it is causing is the central casting villain here. Trying to sort out everything else whilst, like the devil disguised as a snake, this deadly but invisible airy stuff slithers around our feet or descends down upon us, is what is meant by the term Polycrisis. The age of Polycrisis is upon us, unfortunately.

Back to the madness dispatched by the Gods.

Trump has an unelected secretary of state. This secretary has a knack for making money but has decided that he can make even more if he is running the USA. His name is Elon Musk. The world has had many very rich men and none have lived forever. Some have even died for money, but not for love.

But most have left something beneficial behind, and we, the poor toiling masses, have still been able to live and love when our turn came along. But the way Musky the Mad is cavorting around….waving his arms and kicking out, he is likely, unintentionally, to smash the Ming vase of the world into a thousand irreparable pieces. ( I didn’t mean to, Don) Which seems to go against the public positioning of his nominal boss The Prince of Peace himself, Trump.

After all, when a grown man starts whooping and jumping up and down in front of adoring crowds you know something is wrong. But when he starts creating the foreign policy of the USA all by himself, calling British government ministers mass rapists, or genocidal, or accusing his former friends on the right of being weaklings, well, you know something is seriously wrong. Here is a boy-man who is incapable of self government. A kind of arrested adolescent. Autistic, perhaps, which might account for his brilliance at business. But not someone to be let out onto the playing fields of politics.

Talking of self — government, how much longer can we accurately describe the United States as a democratic republic? It must be more accurate now to apply the term plutocracy — the rule of the rich. A billionaire buys his way into a secretary of state position. Appoints himself. He makes the once august republic look and sound ridiculous in the eyes of the world. He also makes it look as if it’s got a madman at the wheel. This madman stares at his X tweets and screeches with delight, like a little boy who watches in amazement as his remote control car, a present, whizzes off and drives itself into the village pond, spoiling Christmas for everyone.

This sort of thing has happened before : Nixon was a drunk. He decided to bomb North Viet-Nam back into the stone age. But at least then, there were some responsible adults around who hid him away and didn’t let him anywhere near the big bad button.

Musky makes the Prince seem clever too. Two genius dudes, hanging out. And Trump needs Musky’s money too.

That’s a worry. Worse still, Trump seems to have no control over him. The remote control isn’t working. Well, adolescents can be difficult. As Bob Dylan sang, ‘ Your children are beyond your control, and it’s a hard rain’s a gonna fall’

Once again I am indebted to Adam Tooze’s Chartbook for the chart which pictures CO2 emissions. He is not responsible for any of the opinions I base upon it!

title: Eldoris: The future of fuel
content:
40

Listen

Share

More

Unless you live under a rock, or your one of those people who believe that climate change is a hoax, most of you have probably heard about climate change and think we should do something about it.

But basically, our Earth is dying. According to a recent report, scientists predict that we have 12 years, till the damage on our planet is irreversible. After that our planet is on a fast track (yes faster than now), to destruction. Now seeing that we probably won’t be able to pack up our bags, and do a mass evacuation to Mars or another planet soon, we should probably start considering how we can stop or reverse the effects of global warming. Notice that I said probably because you can expect the unexpected from Elon and others.

But anyways assuming that we have to fix things up in 12 years, and that we all don’t want us humans and every other living thing on this planet to go extinct, its mostly up to our generation to figure this one out, because unfortunately there aren’t many people in older generations working on this, and its unlikely that they’ll start working on this, because when you’re an adult you have responsibilities, so its probably best to do something that gives you a stable income, instead of working on problems like global warming, unless you’re already a billionaire.

Well ok enough chatter. How are we going to address climate change? A wide variety of factors cause climate change, but one of the biggest is our use of fossil fuels. 63% of all carbon emissions are due to our reliance on fossil fuels.

They also have a variety of other adverse effects like land degradation (basically destruction of ecosystems for land), water pollution from runoff, and ocean acidification (basically changes in the PH level, and this has adverse affects on organisms that require a certain PH level.)

Yeah but you’ve probably heard this a thousand times before, and already know that fossil fuels are bad, so I won’t keep going on about it. So well how are we going to solve this.

We need to find widely available resources on our planet, that can be used as a renewable form of energy.

Well one of the most abundant and almost totally unused resources on our planet is… drum roll

Seawater.

And thats where Eldoris comes in. Eldoris is a moonshot created by Kritik Kaushal , John Redmond , and I.

Our mission at Eldoris is to drastically decrease the effects of global warming by sourcing fuel from seawater.

71% of the Earths water is ocean water, and now we can use this untapped resource for carbon-neutral fuel. Wait but how would we do this?

How are we going to do this

In 2007, John Kanzius accidentally found out that a 13.56 Mhz could be used to split the hydrogen and oxygen in water.

Salt water consists of sodium chloride and hydrogen and oxygen. A radio frequency generator (RFG) set to 13.56 Mhz can break the bonds holding these molecules together. This releases the volatile hydrogen molecules and the heat output from the RFG ignites them and burns them. We can then produce energy from the burning hydrogen molecules.

The only problem here was that the radio frequency generator takes up more power, than it produces through this process.

In order to make it more efficient, we can add nano super capacitors to it. The nano super capacitors would allow it to store energy much much more efficiently, and also charge must faster with less energy consumption.

Humans are really good at procrastinating, believe me I know from experience. But we only have 12 years and we can’t afford to procrastinate this anymore. 12 years is around the time when all of us high school kids will be going into the job force, whats would we be working for, if we know that our species is probably going to go extinct anyways.

We need more people working on this problem. I mean whats the point of working on anything else, because if we don’t solve this problem we’re probably going to go extinct, and nothing else will matter when we’re about to go extinct.

The first step is to stop waiting for other people to solve the problem, and to start solving it yourself..
