title: Why Banning Abortion Affects Every Woman
content:
Content warning: stillbirth, pregnancy, baby loss, abortion, bodily autonomy.
T he US federal election is in our rearview, and so I feel compelled to excavate old pain, because if I can make even one person understand more about this fight, it will have been worth it.

I will preface this by saying that I am Canadian. Had my older sister not been born with complex medical needs, promoting my parents’ move from Montana to Alberta, I would not be. As so very many of my family and friends are American and will be directly affected by the election results, I believe it is my duty to use my platforms to speak on women having rights to our own bodies.

My first child died while still sheltered inside of my body. I was 27 years old, engaged to and living with the man who would become my husband. I was also 38 weeks pregnant. For those who do not know, 38 weeks is considered full term. On March 10, 2009, I headed off to an appointment with my doctor. My hospital bag was packed and waiting by the door. I wondered if that day would be the day. When I returned to my home, would it be with a baby in my arms?

That day was the day, but it was a nightmare rather than a sweet dream. You see, when I saw my doctor, I learned that my baby had died. In addition to receiving the most painful news of my life, I still needed to give birth. Inducing labor was necessary. We didn’t know when our baby had died, you see, and the longer a dead child resides inside the mother, the greater the risk to the life of that mother.

Induction for a stillbirth is not the same as induction for a live birth. For a live birth, the mother will typically be given an IV drip laced with hormones to kick start the birthing process. A stillbirth like mine is induced via prostaglandin tablets or gel inserted vaginally. It is a zero-to-sixty, rough, incredibly painful process designed to empty the body as quickly as possibly. This is the exact same method used during induction abortion, a procedure which may be done for many reasons, the well-being of the mother included.

It is the same. It is the same process. It is the same.

On top of losing my child, had I not had access to this induction, I could have died

Without this induction, some women whose infants have died in utero go into labor on their own. Some do not. Those who retain the infant without medical intervention are at risk of severe blood loss, severe infection, and death.

On top of losing my child, had I not had access to this induction, I could have died.

In the aftermath of the US Supreme Court’s 2022 decision in Dobbs v. Jackson Women’s Health Organization , which overturned the Roe v. Wade constitutional right to abortion, each state now holds the power to decide on abortion legality. This allows states to regulate abortion as they choose, including outright bans for any reason. Alabama, Arkansas, Idaho, Kentucky, Louisiana, Mississippi, Missouri, Oklahoma, South Dakota, Tennessee, Texas, Utah, and Wyoming have already implemented bans on abortion.

But Lacie , you say, you did not have an abortion, you had a stillbirth. Surely that’s an entirely separate matter.

Not as separate as you’d think. Banning abortion means that access to services such as the stillbirth induction I required are severely limited. And the trouble doesn’t stop there — the road is now clear for women who experience pregnancy loss, stillbirths included, to be prosecuted for the death of the fetus and/or child.

Yes, you read that right. A woman can experience this tremendous loss and then be charged. You see, there is now space for lawmakers to decide that, should your child be stillborn, you did or did not do something to cause it. Did you take drugs? Did you stop taking drugs? Did you drink? Did you smoke? Did you quit smoking? Did you take anti-depressants? Did you ignore your depression? Did you dye your hair? Did you exercise? Did you stay sedentary? Did you drink coffee? Did you change kitty litter? Did you jump on a trampoline? Did you accidentally eat a bologna sandwich that contained nitrates? Did you sit next to someone who had blue cheese on their salad?

The road is now clear for women who experience pregnancy loss, stillbirths included, to be prosecuted for the death of the fetus and/or child

Yes, I’m fully aware of how ridiculous some of these things seem, but the fact remains that this happened even before the overturning of Roe vs. Wade, and now the path is clear for any of the above and more to be offered up as an argument that you are guilty of the homicide of your child and to be charged. Don’t believe me? Google Brittany Watts , Brittney Poolaw , and of course Regina McKnight , who served eight years for the stillbirth of her child.

Any woman can be charged for their pregnancy loss, but marginalized women, especially women of color, are at extra risk for this treatment. In a world in which Donald Trump can be president, I will never again be able to think of the loss of my child without reflecting on my privilege. I am a white middle-class woman who lucked into having parents who moved to Canada before her birth, and these are privileges that allowed me medical intervention and kept me from being subjected to criminal action.

She died despite my best efforts and my substantial privilege

Not everyone holds this privilege, but let’s be clear on one thing: Trump round two does not care about your privilege. No woman is safe in this dedication to creating an American Gilead.

No woman. None.

I wanted my daughter. I will never know why she died, but I do know that, despite the intrinsic, suffocating guilt felt in the wake of such a loss, I did everything I was supposed to do to support my pregnancy. She died despite my best efforts and my substantial privilege.

The gaping hole this loss left in my life means that I’m not likely to ever choose an abortion for myself , unless it was medically necessary. Despite my views for myself, I am so thankful to have access to that medically necessary intervention. I also fully support a woman’s right to make decisions for her own body, a body she knows infinitely better than any of the people seeking to control it.

Access to vital health care procedures and a basic understanding of the fact that humanity has never and will never be able to overcome the inherent fragility of our mortal bodies is a basic human right

I will forever be grateful that I had access to induction. I will forever thank my lucky stars that nobody looked at me after, as I flailed to stop myself from sinking in the quicksand of guilt and grief and shame, and decided that my child dying was my fault and that I should pay.

I should not have to be grateful for either. Access to vital health care procedures and a basic understanding of the fact that humanity has never and will never be able to overcome the inherent fragility of our mortal bodies is a basic human right.

If you voted for Trump, or didn’t vote at all, then you denied people this fundamental right. Don’t be surprised when people fight back.

Think about it.

Behave or be blocked. The loss of my child is not troll fodder.

Why Banning Abortion Affects Every Woman Content warning: stillbirth, ,  loss, abortion, bodily autonomy.
T he US federal election is in our rearview, and so I feel compelled to excavate old pain, because if I can make even one person understand more about this fight, it will have been worth it.

I will preface this by saying that I am Canadian. Had my older sister not been born with complex medical needs, promoting my parents’ move from Montana to Alberta, I would not be. As so very many of my family and friends are American and will be directly affected by the election results, I believe it is my duty to use my platforms to speak on women having rights to our own bodies.

My first child died while still sheltered inside of my body. I was 27 years old, engaged to and living with the man who would become my husband. I was also 38 weeks pregnant. For those who do not know, 38 weeks is considered full term. On March 10, 2009, I headed off to an appointment with my doctor. My hospital bag was packed and waiting by the door. I wondered if that day would be the day. When I returned to my home, would it be with a  in my arms?

That day was the day, but it was a nightmare rather than a sweet dream. You see, when I saw my doctor, I learned that my  had died. In addition to receiving the most painful news of my life, I still needed to give birth. Inducing labor was necessary. We didn’t know when our  had died, you see, and the longer a dead child resides inside the , the greater the risk to the life of that .

Induction for a stillbirth is not the same as induction for a live birth. For a live birth, the  will typically be given an IV drip laced with hormones to kick start the birthing process. A stillbirth like mine is induced via prostaglandin tablets or gel inserted vaginally. It is a zero-to-sixty, rough, incredibly painful process designed to empty the body as quickly as possibly. This is the exact same method used during induction abortion, a procedure which may be done for many reasons, the well-being of the  included.

It is the same. It is the same process. It is the same.

On top of losing my child, had I not had access to this induction, I could have died

Without this induction, some women whose infants have died in utero go into labor on their own. Some do not. Those who retain the infant without medical intervention are at risk of severe blood loss, severe infection, and death.

On top of losing my child, had I not had access to this induction, I could have died.

In the aftermath of the US Supreme Court’s 2022 decision in Dobbs v. Jackson Women’s Health Organization , which overturned the Roe v. Wade constitutional right to abortion, each state now holds the power to decide on abortion legality. This allows  to regulate abortion as they choose, including outright bans for any reason. Alabama, Arkansas, Idaho, Kentucky, Louisiana, Mississippi, Missouri, Oklahoma, South Dakota, Tennessee, Texas, Utah, and Wyoming have already implemented bans on abortion.

But Lacie , you say, you did not have an abortion, you had a stillbirth. Surely that’s an entirely separate matter.

Not as separate as you’d think. Banning abortion means that access to services such as the stillbirth induction I required are severely limited. And the trouble doesn’t stop there — the road is now clear for women who experience  loss, stillbirths included, to be prosecuted for the death of the  and/or child.

Yes, you read that right. A woman can experience this tremendous loss and then be charged. You see, there is now space for lawmakers to decide that, should your child be stillborn, you did or did not do something to cause it. Did you take drugs? Did you stop taking drugs? Did you drink? Did you smoke? Did you quit smoking? Did you take anti-depressants? Did you ignore your depression? Did you dye your hair? Did you exercise? Did you stay sedentary? Did you drink coffee? Did you change kitty litter? Did you jump on a trampoline? Did you accidentally eat a bologna sandwich that contained nitrates? Did you sit next to someone who had blue cheese on their salad?

The road is now clear for women who experience  loss, stillbirths included, to be prosecuted for the death of the  and/or child

Yes, I’m fully aware of how ridiculous some of these things seem, but the fact remains that this happened even before the overturning of Roe vs. Wade, and now the path is clear for any of the above and more to be offered up as an argument that you are guilty of the homicide of your child and to be charged. Don’t believe me? Google Brittany Watts , Brittney Poolaw , and of course Regina McKnight , who served eight years for the stillbirth of her child.

Any woman can be charged for their  loss, but marginalized women, especially women of color, are at extra risk for this treatment. In a world in which Donald Trump can be president, I will never again be able to think of the loss of my child without reflecting on my privilege. I am a white middle-class woman who lucked into having parents who moved to Canada before her birth, and these are privileges that allowed me medical intervention and kept me from being subjected to criminal action.

She died despite my best efforts and my substantial privilege

Not everyone holds this privilege, but let’s be clear on one thing: Trump round two does not  about your privilege. No woman is safe in this dedication to creating an American Gilead.

No woman. None.

I wanted my daughter. I will never know why she died, but I do know that, despite the intrinsic, suffocating guilt felt in the wake of such a loss, I did everything I was supposed to do to support my . She died despite my best efforts and my substantial privilege.

I also fully support a woman’s right to make decisions for her own body, a body she knows infinitely better than any of the  seeking to control it.

Access to vital health  procedures and a basic understanding of the fact that humanity has never and will never be able to overcome the inherent fragility of our mortal bodies is a basic human right

I will forever be grateful that I had access to induction. I will forever thank my lucky stars that nobody looked at me after, as I flailed to stop myself from sinking in the quicksand of guilt and grief and shame, and decided that my child dying was my fault and that I should pay.

I should not have to be grateful for either. Access to vital health  procedures and a basic understanding of the fact that humanity has never and will never be able to overcome the inherent fragility of our mortal bodies is a basic human right.

If you voted for Trump, or didn’t vote at all, then you denied  this fundamental right. Don’t be surprised when  fight back.

Think about it.

title: Changes in Brazilian Abortion Laws Will Harm Children
content:
Trigger warning: this post talks about upsetting issues, including abortion, sexual abuse, and rape. Read with caution.
The Brazilian House of Representatives (Câmara dos Deputados, in Portuguese) sanctioned this past week a state of urgency on voting in a bill that criminalises abortion after the twenty-second week of pregnancy.

The vote took only 24 seconds.

As House President Arthur Lira declared, it was only a symbolic vote, but the repercussions are very real. The bill won’t need to go through the very lengthy process of deliberation that is the norm in the Brazilian House of Representatives; because it’s now urgent, it can be voted on quickly.

If the bill is approved, a woman who gets an abortion after the twenty-second week of gestation, as well as all those who help her, will face a prison time of 6 to 20 years, equivalent to the penalty in homicide cases.

The bill, officially named PL 1904/2024 , has been nicknamed Rape Bill, Abortion Bill, or more adequately, Childhood Pregnancy Bill.

The bill changes the Brazilian legislation on abortion, but only after the twenty-second week of gestation.

At five months pregnant, most women have a bump, although it might be almost imperceptible, especially if it’s her first pregnancy. I could barely see any bump until I was well into my seventh month while pregnant with my eldest.

Most women can feel the baby moving at that stage, too, though it could take as long as 24 weeks for the baby to settle into a pattern. I could feel my eldest moving at eighteen weeks, but I couldn’t feel her sister at all until I reached twenty-three weeks, even though that was already my third pregnancy, and I knew very well what to look for.

It’s hard to deny that at 22 weeks, the baby is more than just a bunch of cells. The foetus will measure almost 28 cm long , or if you’re keen on the grocery store comparison that all pregnancy apps and magazines seem to subscribe to, the size of a sweet potato.

Although the foetus already resembles a baby, it won’t be viable until 24 weeks . That’s when there’s a good chance of survival if you go into early labour. So, at 22 weeks, you’re just short of that mark but still really close.

In Ireland, women can get an abortion up to the twelfth week of pregnancy. In the UK, up to twenty-four weeks , when the foetus becomes viable. Things are more complicated to ascertain if you live in the US, where abortions are banned in fourteen states and under hostile laws in another eleven. But you can still get access to abortion in most states, up to the point of viability in many.

So, perhaps you’re thinking that it’s not too bad that Brazil will only criminalise abortion after twenty-two weeks. It’s better than Ireland; less complicated than the United States. Women will have several months to decide.

Right? Not quite.

Abortions are already illegal in Brazil in most cases and for most women.

In Brazil, abortions are illegal.

Unless, of course, you’re rich enough to pay to get an abortion abroad. In which case, you deserve all the care your money can buy. Sorry, I’ll try to keep my cynicism in check.

As it currently stands, the abortion laws in Brazil are very strict. Women who get an abortion can get one to three years in prison, and those who help her can get from one to four years of incarceration as punishment. Abortion is considered a crime against human life under the Brazilian constitution.

I almost forgot to add that if a Brazilian citizen gets an abortion in a country where the procedure is legal, she won’t face criminal charges . I said I would keep my cynicism in check, so I’ll leave the snarky remark to your imagination.

However, there are three particular circumstances in which a woman can get a legal abortion:

Although in these cases abortion is legal, that doesn’t mean it is easy to obtain. Brazil has only 111 centres that perform legal abortions. For a country that spans over 8 million km² and has a population of 203 million , that’s not a lot of clinics.

Considering the stringent access to legal abortion, such a low number of abortion centres is enough to attend to the population, as long as they can get there. In many cases, women must travel over one thousand kilometres to a clinic where the procedure can be done.

Currently, the woman just needs to go to a hospital that offers the procedure, and all documentation will be completed there. In medical cases, either anencephalic foetus or a threat to the mother’s life, the woman also needs a doctor’s note. In the case of rape, the doctors will take her word for what happened, although they have to notify the police. However, that could change, as there is another bill proposing that a woman will have to have a police report and a medical examination prior to requesting a legal abortion.

If you still think they’re trying to protect life, I applaud your mental gymnastics.

In 2021, there were 1,823 legal abortions in Brazil. That’s not a very high number, considering the country’s population. Even when taking into account the restrictions to legal abortion, the number is still staggeringly small.

Especially when we put into perspective the numbers on sexual assault and, more disturbingly, the data on children giving birth in the country.

“If we think only of girls that get pregnant before 14 years old, who would automatically have the right to abortion for being victims of statutory rape, there are over twenty thousand births. The abortion isn’t mandatory for them, but they have the right to get one. Do you think all these girls wanted to keep their pregnancies?”, says the doctor Helena Paro .

Even though sex with children younger than 14 years old is statutory rape, over seventeen thousand girls under the age of fourteen gave birth in Brazil in 2021. The figure doesn’t include girls who might’ve had their babies at home, girls who turned fifteen during the pregnancy, or girls who lost their babies.

Sit with that figure for a minute, if you can. It makes me extremely uncomfortable, but sometimes you just can’t ignore reality.

Let me make you a bit more uncomfortable — around 30% of girls haven’t had their menarche (first period) at this age, either, which means they couldn’t be impregnated, although they’re often violated.

In Brazil, one woman is raped every 8 minutes .

This data point reflects only the cases that are reported to the authorities. I can only imagine how many children are still in very vulnerable situations, unable to report what’s going on with them, especially when the perpetrator is also their legal guardian.

Almost 90% of children who are victims of sexual abuse know their abuser; 64.5% are the children’s own family.

Shockingly, 61.4% of sexual abuse victims in Brazil are children, thirteen years old or younger. If these children end up pregnant, for now, they have the legal right to terminate their pregnancy.

I can’t help but wonder how many of these children actually have any choice at all. It saddens me to see any of it taken away from them for political smoke and mirror acts.

Let’s be very honest here. Who does this change in law affect?

It affects only women who have been raped, over 60% of which can’t even be called teenagers, let alone women. They’re children, girls aged thirteen and younger.

The law won’t affect those women living in penthouses overlooking the beautiful Rio de Janeiro beaches. No, it affects the ones a few blocks away, living in the favelas, often poor and black. Or those living in rural communities, unable to afford to travel to a clinic unless they save for months.

If these women can’t feed or care for their children, for they’re children themselves, the poor babies might end up in orphanages, where they’re likely to remain their whole lives.

The changes in the law won’t affect any of the house representatives or their family members. If they need (or want) to terminate their pregnancy, they have the means to hop on a plane and do it in a country where abortion is legal.

Those supporting such bills want votes, and they do not care about the repercussions for women. Politicians only care for lives that can get them elected.

The law should protect the most vulnerable. I fail to see how that’s not the woman carrying an unwanted baby, especially in the few cases that have access to abortion in Brazil. Especially when the “woman” is only a child herself.

Look, I’m not trying to say that women should be waiting for over twenty weeks to decide if they want the baby or not. But if you think that’s what happens, you’re ignoring reality again. Women who seek an abortion at such a late stage are only doing so because of delays caused by bureaucracy , the lack of means to get to a clinic, or because they failed to notice the pregnancy earlier.

I don’t know about you, but when I think about eleven-year-old me, I’m not sure I’d know what to expect from a pregnancy. I was not sexually active at eleven, but I was fertile. Had I been the victim of sexual abuse, I can’t help but think of how scared and ashamed I’d be. How innocent, too. I would probably have no clue I was pregnant until very late.

I’m proud of being Brazilian. Most of the time.

But not now. I’m not proud of this backward legislation trying to harm women and girls, after they have already been harmed beyond imagination.

Because the bill is now considered urgent, it won’t undergo the usual bureaucracy that such a project would face — it can take the Brazilian House of Representatives over a year to discuss a bill and present pros and cons before it gets the final vote. Now, this bill can be voted on quickly.

If this bill becomes law, girls who terminate their pregnancies will face jail time from six to twenty years. Their rapists? At the most, they’ll get fifteen years in jail.

The proposed bill is in the name of life, fairness, and justice. Just not for women, or for the children after they’re born.

All over the internet and on street protests, Brazilians shout, “Children aren’t mothers; they’re victims”. I hope the Brazilian people can be loud enough to prevent such an unimaginable and atrocious bill from becoming law.

If this bill becomes law, girls who terminate their pregnancies will face jail time from six to twenty years. Their rapists? At the most, they’ll get fifteen years in jail.

The proposed bill is in the name of life, fairness, and justice. Just not for women, or for the children after they’re born.

Shortly after moving into my home, I realized the business next door was an All Women’s Health Facility that specializes in family planning, and is also a provider of abortions. Oddly, it wasn’t the sign in front of the business that keyed me in — it was the protestors.

This isn’t a fact I have ever shared, or one I share lightly. But that is what happened and I don’t regret it. It was the right decision for us. I suspect it is also that experience that has made me quite bothered by the protestors. And it’s not like I can look away.

Even when I’m leaving, traffic frequently backs up in front of this facility, so I’m forced to watch whatever ridiculous scene is unfolding. Very often, protestors form this silent wall facing the clinic with their backs to the street, as a deliberate act of collective symbolism:

Recently, I saw a woman getting out of her car, walking into the facility, while people shouted from the sidewalk, “Jesus loves you!”

And, “It’s not too late!”

These are the moments I get upset. I know from experience that this woman is already having a bad day, and these people are only making it worse. It’s also possible she isn’t even getting an abortion. But if you dare pull into that lot, you’ll be yelled at or have lines of scripture dropped on you.

I have repeatedly made promises to myself not to react to their presence, as it genuinely puts me in a bad mood. But yet again, my face got hot yesterday as I saw a sign reading, “Love them both.” It had a caricature of a woman, with a baby inside her.

“Yeah, cause ya’ll do such a good job of that,” I muttered sardonically.

The thing that frustrates me even more — is that these protestors have already won. Recently, Florida fell just short of passing Amendment 4 , which would afford protections to abortion care in the state, reaching only 57% voting yes (60% is needed for it to pass). And while I’m actually proud that we demonstrated a pro-choice majority, I’m also troubled because abortions are now outlawed at eight weeks in this state.

It’s clear that these activists won’t be happy until they have total victory. Consequently, I’ve taken to a grim curiosity in them.

I love taking walks each day, usually sometime mid-afternoon. It’s a way to break up my writing schedule and see the neighborhood. Very often, I’ll pass the backside of this clinic. One house shares an actual backyard with it— which must be an interesting way to live.

Each week, I purposefully walk along the sidewalk where the protestors stand and take mental notes as I pass.

What’s striking is that the majority of them are visibly tied to a church. They have Christian or Jesus oriented shirts on. They are loudly and proudly announcing their affiliation.

On one occasion, I saw a priest standing halfway up on a ladder with a megaphone, shouting at the clinic . It was then that I realized how unpleasant it must be to work inside this clinic. The windows are all understandably blocked with blinds.

Imagine starting your day knowing you’ll arrive to an ocean of hostility. The signs, shouting, cursing — the ever-present wall of noise and judgement. Despite this animus, I’ve never seen staff break composure. They go in and out with a quiet resolve, as though they’ve become immune to the daily barrage.

The ringleader protestor is a man I call “Angry Tom”. He usually has a fold out chair, and will be there alone on the slower days, never seeming to have a job. He also has this big rack with pamp hlets on it. It looks heavy, like he’s hauling a dresser out to the sidewalk each day.

As I passed, he held his hand out for me to take a pamphlet. I nodded no and kept looking forward. He called out from behind me, “Have a blessed day. God loves you.”

I winced with irritation. I’m not a particularly religious person, and I don’t like being showered with unsolicited blessings — especially from such a confrontational presence. It made me briefly consider if the first amendment was a mistake.

What drives me nuts is the hypocrisy of it all. I’ve made the mistake of engaging with them a few times in mostly cordial conversations. I always make it a point to ask them how many unwanted babies they’ve adopted. I’m still waiting for my first yes. Sadly, I’d wager many would oppose gay couples adopting these unwanted babies.

The king killer hypocrisy comes right back to Angry Tom. I did a bit of research and asked around, and learned his real name, and it turned out: Angry Tom is an appropriate nickname for him. There were multiple mugshots of him from over the years (Florida has a policy of releasing these). He’d been convicted of assault and domestic violence (twice). He’d served time in prison.

And yet here he is, on his high horse, shouting at young women. It reminded me of an old phrase my mother said, “It’s always the loudest ones that have something to hide.”

Perhaps it explained his fervor. Sitting outside of a clinic and calling other people murderers to make him feel a notch higher.

Are the other protesters there for the reasons they claim? Or is it some subconscious desire to feel morally sound in the eyes of god? To feel like a holy warrior?

The point I’m making is that getting or not getting an abortion is a deeply personal experience, and it should be respected as such. I learned firsthand that it’s not a decision someone makes on the fly, like a flippant impulse purchase at a gas station. There’s often significant turmoil in their life. In my view, this decision should justifiably rest in the woman’s hands, as she carries this ultimate burden.

I feel sad for young people today who have to face this issue, while people who aren’t childbearing or of childbearing age are making all of these laws that restrict what women can do with their bodies. It’s easy to sit on the outside and feel moral righteousness. But that doesn’t mean it’s the right thing to do.

title: I Asked 4 Women Why They Had an Abortion—Their Answers Shocked Me
content:
It started as an experiment. I was curious —I am always curious . I wanted to explore a topic thats been a point of contention for many years now.
Abortion
Why do women do it? What leads them to make that choice? I wasn’t looking to judge or debate; I just wanted to understand.

So, I decided to ask. Two of the women were former colleagues, people I’d once worked with but never truly known beyond office walls. Our conversations changed how I saw them and many other women.

The other two were friends of friends, acquaintances who were kind enough to share their deeply personal stories. There’s nothing a heartfelt conversation won’t bring out.

What they told me shocked me— not because their reasons were dramatic or unbelievable, but because they were so painfully real. Made me feel connected to many many women out there, making tough choices everyday.

A not so fun fact by the way — In 24 countries, abortion is still completely banned, even in cases of rape or when the mother’s life is at risk. In dozens more, it’s so heavily restricted that it might as well be illegal.

It’s heartbreaking. These are decisions no one makes lightly, yet so many women are denied agency over their own bodies. Hearing these four stories made that injustice even more real to me.

She was my former colleague, around 30, someone I’d worked closely with for two years. We hadn’t spoken much since I left that job, but when we reconnected recently, our conversation drifted into territories I didn’t expect. She told me she’d had an abortion three years ago, and the reason shook me.

“I had to choose between the baby or myself,” she said quietly, her hands clutching her coffee cup. She’d been diagnosed with a serious health condition early in her pregnancy. Her doctor told her that continuing the pregnancy could endanger her life. She didn’t want to believe it, but after second and third opinions, the reality sank in.

“I didn’t want to make the decision,” she said. “But I also wanted to be alive. It was my family, my husband… everyone wanted the baby, but I wanted to live. So I chose … me”

title: Anti-Abortionist Video ‘Meet Baby Olivia’-related Legislation Passed in North Dakota and Tennessee for Inclusion in Sex Education in Schools Said to Include Inaccurate Information
content:
Widespread changes to the landscape of abortion have occurred in the wake of the overturning of Roe v. Wade.
Politicians interested in promoting the anti-abortion agenda are using the reconsideration of constitutionality to advance their message.

Several states, in fact, are changing laws to accommodate interests seeking to establish anti-abortion rhetoric into all sex education curriculum.

“Meet Baby Olivia ” legislation is the latest attempt to warp the minds of young people into believing a myopic narrative of “life” that is intended to weigh heavily enough on the emotions of young mothers and fathers that they opt out of terminating their pregnancy.

This type of all or nothing thinking misses certain situations like, for example, when a pregnancy results from a forced sexual encounter.

One young woman was forced to carry the pregnancy that was caused when she was raped by a stranger in the yard of her family home. She was 12.

We are seeing the use of media like “Meet Baby Olivia” pop up in curriculum discussions across the country in a concerted effort by anti-abortion activists to mandate the inclusion of anti-abortion content.

In a fundamentally American way, it makes sense to include all sides of the story in the context of education. We are, after all, one of the few places in the world where you can freely share ideas without filter…although not entirely void of consequence.

Part of the controversy surrounding the “Meet Baby Olivia” curriculum is centers on a lifelike resembling human baby (re: white baby) in utero with music and other related imagery intended to be emotionally evocative and persuasive. It is produced by the American anti-abortion group Live Action. The video depicts “human embryonic and fetal development” in a manner that invites and/or encourages the viewer to take the perspective that personhood starts with the first cell division.

North Dakota became the first state to pass a law mandating the screening of “Meet Baby Olivia” or a similar video in schools. Following North Dakota’s lead, Tennessee enacted its own law mandating that anti-abortion content be shown to students within the sex education framework, again emphasizing human development from the point of conception.

At least ten other states have introduced similar bills, often specifying that the video should show every stage of human development inside the uterus, noting significant markers in cell growth and organ development.

From a medical standpoint, the content of “Meet Baby Olivia” includes controversial claims that life begins at conception and that fetal heartbeats can be detected three weeks after fertilization . Both assertions are contested by medical professionals who argue that the video spreads misinformation and emotionally manipulative content rather than providing scientifically accurate information.

The American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG), among other medical experts, has criticized the video, stating it is “designed to manipulate the emotions of viewers rather than to share evidence-based, scientific information about embryonic and fetal development.”

Critics point out that there is no scientific consensus on when life begins and that the video’s depiction of a fetal heartbeat is not medically accurate, as the embryo does not have a fully developed heart at that stage.

Broader implications related to these bills are manifesting within the broader context of post-Roe v. Wade America, where anti-abortion activists are seeking new avenues to influence public opinion and policy. Observers have noted this as an expansion of the anti-abortion movement’s focus, indicating a strategic shift to include sex education.

Organizations like the Guttmacher Institute and ACOG have voiced strong opposition to these bills, citing concerns over the dissemination of misinformation and the emotional manipulation of students.

Much of the language in these new pieces of legislation include language that also reduces attention to ideas related to abortion. Offering students a balanced perspective on any topic is important. “Meet Baby Olivia”-type legislation exemplifies the ongoing cultural and political battles over abortion, sex education, and reproductive rights in the United States .

By embedding anti-abortion content in school curricula, these bills aim to shape young people’s views from an early age…and when the educational experience is myopic…bias is born.

Despite significant opposition from medical and advocacy groups who criticize the video’s scientific accuracy and emotional manipulation, the legislation continues to gain traction in several states. This movement highlights the broader strategy of anti-abortion activists to influence public opinion and policy through education, reflecting a significant shift in their approach post-Roe v. Wade.

Wade America, where anti-abortion activists are seeking new avenues to influence public opinion and policy. title: If Americans Talked About Guns The Way They Talk About Abortion
content:
We should outlaw self-defense all together. No one should be allowed to buy guns to defend their houses with. I know people keep saying they have a right to own a gun, but why should we allow them to have that right when shooting someone else is murder?

People keep trying to claim self defense isn’t murder, but it is murder. Just because you’re doing it to protect yourself doesn’t make it not murder.

I mean, people have souls, even when they’re breaking into your house. I’m pro-life and a Christian, so I don’t think people should have a right to murder people because God gave them souls.

The constitution gives burglars a right to life , liberty, and the pursuit of happiness. Shooting them, even when they’re breaking into your house is violating that right.

I know people say there should be exceptions if your life is in danger or if there is rape, but those aren’t good excuses to actually murder someone else. I mean, just because you might die if you don’t defend yourself doesn’t make murdering someone else okay.

And only like less than 1% of self-defense cases involve rape or violence. Most burglars want to get in and out of the house peacefully without hurting anyone, so why should we make laws based on that the small amount of exceptions there are?

Most people just want to use self-defense as an excuse because they can’t afford to be robbed at this time in their life or because they don’t like having all their stuff stolen, but none of those are good excuses to murder people. They’re selfish.

I mean, people keep saying, “It’s my house, my choice.” They keep insisting that they shouldn’t have to keep a burglar alive in their house if it’s being done against their will. But I think the government has a right to step in and decide things about your house for you in situations like this. You have to help keep someone who breaks into your house alive for as long as they’re there, even if you feel violated by it.

Maybe we can make some exceptions for people to defend themselves if they catch the burglar before he actually breaks in. The burglar has to be caught early enough. No glass can be broken or locks picked yet. And maybe they need to prove that they would have actually died if the person broke in.

We should leave it up to the states to decide whether people should have a right to a gun or not. I mean, it’s a violation of states rights not to. What’s right for your state is not necessarily right for mine.

And in the end I’m pro-life and self-defense is murder, so if you defend yourself when someone breaks into your house, then it’s always murder. People pretend it’s more complicated than that, but it’s really not.

title: How Black Woman’s Preventable Death Exposes Danger of Abortion Bans
content:
As the battle over women’s rights is waged on America’s political battlefield, a Black woman has become the first reported casualty. Women’s rights advocates warned healthcare would be compromised if state-wide abortion bans went into effect. Now, we’re seeing this play out in real-time as doctors hesitate to provide life-saving care due to their fear of being held criminally liable. For instance, “at least two women in Georgia died after they couldn’t access legal abortions and timely medical care,” according to a ProPublica repor t. Amber Nicole Thurman, a 28-year-old Black mother and medical assistant, has been named as the first “preventable” death resulting from an abortion ban.

How did this tragedy happen? After taking abortion pills at home, Amber suffered a rare complication, as the fetal tissue did not naturally expel from her body. She sought help from doctors at the Piedmont Henry Hospital, where they could perform a dilation and curettage procedure. However, a new Georgia law characterized the procedure as a felony. Any doctor who provides abortion care in the state could serve up to a decade in prison. While the facility had well-trained staff, doctors there felt powerless to help. This is precisely what medical professionals warned would happen. Dr. Melissa Kottke, an OB-GYN, told state lawmakers in 2019 that doctors “would feel the need to wait for a higher blood pressure, wait for a higher fever — really got to justify this one — bleed a little more.” In other words, abortion bans would make doctors hesitate instead of focusing on providing quality care, and this could endanger women’s lives. And that’s precisely what happened in the case of Amber Thurman.

In the hours leading up to her death, Amber shared concern for her 6-year-old son. As she waited for treatment, the infection continued to spread, compromising her organs. One of the most heartbreaking elements of the story is that Amber’s death was deemed “preventable” by Georgia’s maternal mortality review committee. A group of experts, including ten doctors, reviewed patient care data and found the hospital’s decision to delay the procedure had a “large” impact on her death. Doctors waited 20 hours, almost a day, to operate. Sadly, by then, the procedure was too late to save her life. While ProPublica uncovered the stories of two women who have died following Georgia’s abortion ban, reporter Kavitha Surana noted they are likely many more. Amber’s case shows why abortion bans are dangerous — they make doctors weigh their careers and freedom against their professional oath to save lives.

In Georgia, the maternal mortality rate is “ almost twice the national rate,” and Black women are nearly three times as likely to die compared with White women. However, researchers suggest many of these deaths are preventable. Amber Thurman was physically healthy before the complication and would likely still be alive if doctors hadn’t waited so long to operate. The fact that a Black woman has become the first documented casualty of abortion bans is significant given the legacy of racial discrimination targeting Black women.

James Marion Sims, the so-called “father of modern gynecology,” conducted painful experiments on enslaved Black women throughout the 1840s without their consent or the use of anesthesia. Thus, the development of this specialty originated from an unfair tradeoff, where a doctor sought to expand medical knowledge while disregarding the humanity of Black women. It’s a tragic irony that doctors knew how to save Amber Thurman but refused to do so. And it’s reminiscent of the medical racism that launched the field of gynecology in the first place. Abortion bans put doctors between a rock and a hard place, as some feel they need to wait until a woman is on the brink of death before rendering aid to justify any actions they take to save her life. However, beyond considerations for a doctor’s career, one mustn’t forget women are the ones whose lives are on the line.

The fact that doctors in states where abortion bans are in effect feel unsure of how to proceed and are waiting until women are in critical condition to perform life-saving care puts their lives in jeopardy. Of course, there is no quick fix to this social problem, as Georgia doctors who deny care to women will likely continue to do so to follow the law. It’s also a reminder that not all women have the money and social support to leave the state they live in to seek reproductive healthcare. While some believed women would be able to mitigate the fallout by traveling to another state or acquiring abortion pills they could take at home, Thurman’s death dispels the myth that this strategy is a viable solution to the systemic problem. Some may not have the money to travel, lack the time away from work, or the social support they need to access reproductive healthcare. Only federal legislation securing women’s rights could correct the injustice.

There are consequences to banning abortion, namely that women seeking healthcare may not receive lifesaving care in time. In depriving women of a choice and disregarding the wisdom of medical professionals, states like Georgia are openly disregarding women’s right to emergency medical treatment. In a statement about Thurman’s death, V.P. Kamala Harris said, “This young mother should be alive, raising her son, and pursuing her dream of attending nursing school,” adding that “Women are bleeding out in parking lots, turned away from emergency rooms, losing their ability to ever have children again. Survivors of rape and incest are being told they cannot make decisions about what happens next to their bodies. And now women are dying,” arguing, “These are the consequences of Donald Trump’s actions.” Harris is referring to Trump’s role of stacking the Supreme Court with conservative justices who struck down Roe v. Wade. While some Republicans support a national ban, the former president has supported a “your state, your decision” policy. Those who study the chattel slavery era will see the problem here — of states individually being able to extend or retract citizens’ rights at will.

T o those who are locked into the topic of women’s reproductive rights, the death of women resulting from abortion bans was expected. As Mini Timmaraju, the president of Reproductive Freedom for All, said, “We actually have the substantiated proof of something we already knew that abortion bans can kill people.” Given that pregnancy-related deaths disproportionately impact Black women, it could even be expect ed they would be among the first casualties. However, this is fresh news for some, something they never considered or believed would happen. The real question is what we do about this social problem. Women’s rights advocates warned healthcare would be compromised if state-wide abortion bans went into effect. Now, we’re seeing this play out in real-time as doctors hesitate to provide life-saving care due to their fear of being held criminally liable. For instance, “at least two women in Georgia died after they couldn’t access legal abortions and timely medical care,” according to a ProPublica repor t. Amber Nicole Thurman, a 28-year-old Black mother and medical assistant, has been named as the first “preventable” death resulting from an abortion ban.

How did this tragedy happen? After taking abortion pills at home, Amber suffered a rare complication, as the fetal tissue did not naturally expel from her body. She sought help from doctors at the Piedmont Henry Hospital, where they could perform a dilation and curettage procedure. However, a new Georgia law characterized the procedure as a felony. Any doctor who provides abortion care in the state could serve up to a decade in prison. While the facility had well-trained staff, doctors there felt powerless to help. This is precisely what medical professionals warned would happen. Dr. Melissa Kottke, an OB-GYN, told state lawmakers in 2019 that doctors “would feel the need to wait for a higher blood pressure, wait for a higher fever — really got to justify this one — bleed a little more.” In other words, abortion bans would make doctors hesitate instead of focusing on providing quality care, and this could endanger women’s lives. And that’s precisely what happened in the case of Amber Thurman.

In the hours leading up to her death, Amber shared concern for her 6-year-old son. As she waited for treatment, the infection continued to spread, compromising her organs. One of the most heartbreaking elements of the story is that Amber’s death was deemed “preventable” by Georgia’s maternal mortality review committee. A group of experts, including ten doctors, reviewed patient care data and found the hospital’s decision to delay the procedure had a “large” impact on her death. Doctors waited 20 hours, almost a day, to operate. Sadly, by then, the procedure was too late to save her life. While ProPublica uncovered the stories of two women who have died following Georgia’s abortion ban, reporter Kavitha Surana noted they are likely many more. Amber’s case shows why abortion bans are dangerous — they make doctors weigh their careers and freedom against their professional oath to save lives.

In Georgia, the maternal mortality rate is “ almost twice the national rate,” and Black women are nearly three times as likely to die compared with White women. However, researchers suggest many of these deaths are preventable. Amber Thurman was physically healthy before the complication and would likely still be alive if doctors hadn’t waited so long to operate. The fact that a Black woman has become the first documented casualty of abortion bans is significant given the legacy of racial discrimination targeting Black women.

James Marion Sims, the so-called “father of modern gynecology,” conducted painful experiments on enslaved Black women throughout the 1840s without their consent or the use of anesthesia. Thus, the development of this specialty originated from an unfair tradeoff, where a doctor sought to expand medical knowledge while disregarding the humanity of Black women. The fact that doctors in states where abortion bans are in effect feel unsure of how to proceed and are waiting until women are in critical condition to perform life-saving care puts their lives in jeopardy. Of course, there is no quick fix to this social problem, as Georgia doctors who deny care to women will likely continue to do so to follow the law. It’s also a reminder that not all women have the money and social support to leave the state they live in to seek reproductive healthcare. While some believed women would be able to mitigate the fallout by traveling to another state or acquiring abortion pills they could take at home, Thurman’s death dispels the myth that this strategy is a viable solution to the systemic problem. Some may not have the money to travel, lack the time away from work, or the social support they need to access reproductive healthcare. Kamala Harris said, “This young mother should be alive, raising her son, and pursuing her dream of attending nursing school,” adding that “Women are bleeding out in parking lots, turned away from emergency rooms, losing their ability to ever have children again. title: SCOTUS Punts on Abortion Again
content:
So SCOTUS did it again. Avoided the whole abortion mess by passing it off to someone else. They did it with the Dobbs decision which said there was no constitutional right to abortion and sent the issue down to the states.
That worked out really well, didn’t it? Women are dying. Doctors are afraid to treat them. It’s real medieval shit going on. Next thing you know, they’ll be bringing back the Inquisition.

Now we have their non-decision on Mifepristone, which is used for abortions, saying that the plaintiffs have no standing . That wasn’t the question guys. The question was about the FDA’s approval of the drug that the plaintiffs said was dangerous.

But the justices were too busy taking luxury vacations and flying controversial flags to be bothered to actually do their job . Seriously. This is their reasoning:

“The plaintiffs do not prescribe or use mifepristone. And F.D.A. is not requiring them to do or refrain from doing anything. A plaintiff’s desire to make a drug less available for others does not establish standing to sue.”

Um, yes it does. That’s what the whole abortion issue is about. Pro-life people want to deny abortions to everyone whether they agree with them or not. That includes the so-called abortion pills which can be ordered by mail in states where abortions are banned.

Get with the program, guys. You were put on the court specifically to deal with this. Ban abortion completely and that includes mail-order pills. It doesn’t matter that none of you have ever had an abortion or ever will have one. Cuz if it did matter, then you wouldn’t have standing to decide the case, would you?

Wait, now we’re getting back to that whole argument that only people with uteruses should be making decisions about uteruses. Nope, only old white men (and one token Black man) are making important decisions about uteruses.

I can’t wait for the issue of contraception to reach the court. What will their reasoning for avoiding that whole issue be? States rights? Standing? Gotta help the wifey pick out a flag to fly? Away on a luxury vacation?

Ya know what? They’re all cowards. There’s not a single backbone amongst all of them. They talk a good game, but when it comes time to actually make a decision, they fob it off on someone else.

The whole lot of them should be impeached and removed. Well, maybe not the liberal justices. They, at least, are willing to take a stand on issues whether you agree with them or not. But hot button cultural issues like abortion … the rest of them want to keep us comfortably in the 50s, where women and Black people knew their places and gay people did not exist at all.

So, here’s a question that often bothers me. Why the hell does Clarence Thomas want so badly to go back to the 1950s? Doesn’t he realize that he would be thrown off the court and his marriage dissolved?

No more luxury vacations. Just a life filled with manual labor until he was too old and broken down to work anymore. Then he could live out his remaining years occupying a street corner begging for change.

How much do you think that Ginni would throw in his cup?

Or would she even stop at all?

title: Witch hunts replaced by abortion hunts and trials
content:
In a sweeping interview with Time magazine, Trump painted a startling picture of his second term, from how he would wield the justice department to how he would surveil pregnant women to enforce abortion laws. On abortion, he said that all decision-making power over reproductive rights had been handed to the states following the supreme court’s overturning of the right to a termination in Roe v Wade. He said he might contemplate Republican states putting pregnant women under surveillance to monitor whether they had abortions beyond the state’s designated ban. “I think they might do that,” Trump said.

25% of women have a miscarriage. States monitoring who is pregnant but does not deliver will arrest the woman who miscarriages. It is impossible to prove the pregnancy ended by miscarriage not abortion. Up to 25% of women will be innocent but convicted.

An illustration or perhaps a prediction, An abortion trial in Alabama.

It was a hot Alabama August, just weeks after strict abortion laws were passed. Jury selection had just started, and the DA asked perspective jurors the same questions. Do you favor or agree with abortion laws recently passed? Do you view abortion as a sin? Have you or your spouse ever have an abortion? All the selected members of the jury answered yes, yes, and no. The defending attorney in this small town was planning on running for DA next year. His questions were simple. Can you fairly judge the guilt or innocence based on the evidence? Have you ever served on a Jury and convicted someone of the white race? All the selected jury members answered Yes and Yes.

The individual on trial was charged with endangering the life of a minor and manslaughter. The mother of 3 children, working at minimum wage jobs was unmarried, 35 years old and visibly upset. Her court appointed attorney assured her that justice would prevail.

The DA’s opening statement did not look good for the defendant. Ladies and gentlemen of the jury, the state of Alabama will prove the defendant placed the life of an unborn child at grave risk and took steps to end her pregnancy. Against doctor’s advice, she continued working late into her pregnancy. A police search of her computer showed that she looked up abortion and pregnancy risk factors. In the third trimester her pregnancy ended at home. The woman called 911, explaining that she was bleeding and in tremendous pain. On arrival at the hospital the doctors pronounced the baby had died and removed the fetus. The doctors also filed a suspicious end of pregnancy report with the police, who immediately took her computer and cell phone, a requirement for all potential abortion cases. This led to the discovery of computer searches related to pregnancy and to her arrest while in the hospital.

After the trial, the jury foreman provided some insights into how the jury quickly reached a verdict. His recollection: “The first step in our process was to pray for God’s guidance. Then we each discussed our point of view. Many of the jury members noted that the doctors would not have filed a report of a potential violation of the law, nor would the DA have filed unless the evidence was strong. All of the jury agreed that the internet search followed by the death of the unborn child was the strongest evidence. A few members stated they had wished the prosecution had brought in doctors to testify but they were sure of their verdict in any case. Especially when the women gave her testimony and claimed she had a miscarriage but offered no proof that she had a miscarriage. On cross examination she admitted that the father of the child had been from a rape, by a co-worker who had left the state. That pretty much proved her motivation and guilt.”

The woman was sentenced to 5 years in prison and lost custody of her three children. They were placed in foster care. It was a shame that the oldest committed suicide and that the two young children became so depressed their grades went from passing to failing in their schoolwork. Folks in town knew the sins of the mother were on her children. Some people spoke about how important parents are in the development of a child and how the loss of a parent can be so hard.

The jury, all men, meet every year to pray and remember their role in the fight against abortion. They pray for the children of the woman convicted and remind each other of their role in the fight for the unborn.

The author wonders how Alabama ranks in the US and in the world for foster care and health care support for low-income mothers. What is the death rate during birth for both mothers and babies in Alabama compared to other states and other countries? Perhaps an internet search would shed some light.

title: At the Abortion Clinic
content:
The pick combed outward from my scalp through wiry brown tresses and into the air. It raced to a nearby spot on my head, the last of a hundred repeated motions. Born was an Afro hairdo, a hip symbol of racial brotherhood. Glancing in the mirror, I addressed a newly formed pimple with a dab of Clearasil , then turned around to my closet, grabbing and popping on a print-polyester disco shirt.

The heat had just begun in Coconut Grove. It was late March 1975.

Back in front of the mirror again, I buttoned the shirt, standing tall in platform shoes, which made my feet look like Wonder Woman’s. My violet hip-hugger, extra-wide bellbottoms, and a purple haze that matched the world around me took my whole body by surprise. I was on my way to the abortion clinic with Gwen.

It was two years after the decision on Roe v. Wade was made by the Supreme Court on January 22nd, 1973.

Gwen, my best friend, one year younger than me, had been underage. She was pregnant; I could see it, though I didn’t know how far along she had been.

Since I had been a good listener, Gwen, who I bonded Platonically since we were babies, confided the details of her romantic experiences. In fact, that’s all we talked about.

S everal weeks before, I learned about Gwen’s affair with a muscleman. She told me about an experience with a guy named Kurt, whom she had broken up with after a few rendezvous with him.

“You met him,” Gwen shouted while we walked past the Florida Pharmacy in the middle of the Grove.

“I did? When?” Suddenly, my mind came to. I stopped in my tracks.

“Come on, Marv,” Gwen ordered as she walked quickly past me.

I ran up to her.

“Why you walking so fast?”

Gwen ignored me. She walked even faster. I jogged to keep up.

Then she spoke fast.

“He was a friend of my brother’s… the guy had been a bodybuilder who had competed with Arnold Schwarzenegger a few years ago,” Gwen explained.

“Wow!” I responded. “That’s cool!”

Gwen had a brother a decade her senior. On Christmas Day of 1974, Gwen’s mom threw a party. That’s where I recalled I had seen Kurt. I had been so stoned it was all a fog.

“Oh… I remember! Did he have dark hair and look as if he had been a bodybuilder? He was a stud!” I babbled, and my heart rattled as I thought about him and all of her brother’s friends.

Gwen’s eyes grew dreamy.

“Yeah, I went for him,” she detailed. “He took me out for drinks, and then we went to his house on Tigertail. It was quick because it was a school night.”

“When did this happen?” I asked.

“It was on my birthday, Oct. 22nd. I was at Big Daddy’s in the Grove.”

“How did you get in there?”

“Bev…Bev and I have fake IDs. I had no idea he had been friends with my brother until he arrived at the party. He didn’t even acknowledge me.”

“Oh, shit!” I commented. “I had no idea.”

I was running out the door of my house when I heard Gwen honk; my mother ran and pecked me on the cheek. “Have fun, Marvin!”

“I will!” I said, breathing heavily.

Gwen’s mom’s car, a baby blue Mustang, parked in the driveway as I ran to it waving with glee at seeing her. we peered at each other. Now I understand how it happened.

After I hopped into the bucket seat, I glued my eyes to Gwen’s mid-section. I saw a tiny baby bump. I figured out the pregnancy was a couple of months along since it was March already.

“I’m really lucky because my girlfriend, Marge, set me up with an appointment at a new clinic that had just opened,” Gwen proclaimed.

“Oh! Marge! She sat next to me in government class last year. She’s super smart.”

“Yep, Marvin, that’s for sure. She’s already been through this and knows all the ropes. I found out that abortions have been legal for a while,” Gwen had snapped back.

“I’m nervous, Marvin. I’m so nervous. You don’t know how nervous I am.”

“It’s gonna be alright, Gwen. You made an appointment, right?

Gwen stepped on it. It took 15 minutes to get to the Coconut Grove Pregnancy Center.

We parked in the large lot adjacent to the building, shaded by a huge banyan tree.

I held the door to the center open for Gwen. She rushed to sit down. She was shaking.

“I called this place yesterday. I had a million questions. They were very nice. They told me everything I wanted to know. But I’m still afraid. I feel ashamed. I can’t even look at my mother.”

I kept quiet, only providing gentle nods. I had no idea what she was going to go through. I hurt too in some odd way, a way I couldn’t explain.

The nurse greeted us. She took Gwen to an examination room after welcoming me and telling me it’d be about a three-hour wait.

“Fuck!” I said to myself. “What am I going to do here for three hours!”

After Gwen left for her procedure, I spotted another woman.

“I know that woman, I groaned out loud. “It’s my mother’s friend, Milly. Milly Barnes.”

Two hippies sitting adjacent to me laughed at my conversation with myself.

“Small world. Groovy world,” one of them blurted out to me.

“Yeah, I guess so,” I replied.

Milly glimpsed at me with a quick smile and a wink. Milly was playful. She didn’t care much except for peace and happiness for herself and those around her.

Milly put her finger up, letting me know she’ll talk to me when she can. As my drowsy eyes fell into slumber, I felt exhausted at the thought of the doctor taking out a live baby from Gwen’s stomach. I decided to fixate on Milly; I pondered the last time I saw her.

Milly, one of my mom’s best friends swam at our house frequently. Her daughter had gone to school with Gwen. I often did yard work at her sizeable two-story home on Tigertail in Coconut Grove. I had been an ape working there, climbing trees to rip out the dead branches and palm fronds.

I dozed for a long time when Milly sat next to me.

“I know why you are here,” she remarked, smiling and reaching out for my hand.

“You do?”

“Not only me,” she confided. “Your mother; Gwen’s mother, Gwen’s brother, and my husband. Just about everyone.

My eyes popped open, and my neck pulled my head back.

“Really! I chirped.

Yes, honey. We all knew.

I was confounded, upset, and suspended in disbelief.

“How did everyone find out?”

“Gwen’s mom told us she wanted Gwen to work this out herself. She only helped a little.

“What?” I said.

She phoned the clinic yesterday, telling them her daughter would be coming in today.

“What?” I asked again.

“I do want to let you know that you’re an angel…”

“Why?” I asked.

“You’ve been such a good friend to Gwen. It’s not easy for a young man to come here to support his friend.”

title: Let’s Talk About Male Abortion Trauma And Pro-Choice Policies
content:
Lately, I’ve started to notice a pattern about men who are anti-choice in my circles. For the most part, the vast majority of the men I speak to are pro-choice, either because they are childfree or because they realize it’s ultimately the birthing person’s body choice.

But, I’d be lying if I said that I didn’t know at least a handful of men who were anti-choice. I don’t talk to them much, but I do overhear what they said. Such was the case with Biffo*.

Biffo was a guy in the rock industry who was fairly popular. I was surprised to hear it, but he’s actually a conservative voter. Moreover, he was not as pro-choice as one would think he’d be for a guy who’s hit it with over a hundred women.

Biffo had a girlfriend at one point. She got pregnant, he was elated, he prepared to marry her, but she was in school and decided to abort. She wanted to focus on becoming a doctor, which she later accomplished.

This actually traumatized him. From what I heard, he wasn’t okay for a good six months. As I heard him tell my friend, “ I felt like my future got ripped out with that fetus.”

He used to be pro-choice up until then. He broke up with her, then became pretty vehemently anti-choice. He never quite was the same after that breakup.

I was shocked to hear this until my husband clued me in: this kind of reaction is a lot more common than we as a society want to admit.

Most of the time, the fight for a woman’s right to choose is focused on women — as it should be. However, there’s something to be said about talking about how abortion affects men.

A lot of men really do want to become fathers for one reason or another. Sometimes, those reasons are altruistic. They want a kid to take care of, and they want that loving family unit.

Other times, it’s because they want to baby-trap a woman. (Sorry, guys, women are very well aware that men can do reproductive coercion as well. For the sake of this article, I won’t bother with talking about them.)

Men tend to get attached to the idea of having an unborn child. It’s not unusual to hear dads gushing about having a kid, fantasizing about playing catch with their sons, or working on a new nursery for their kids .

I know it’s weird to hear, especially if you’re a woman who had a guy ditch them post-pregnancy announcement. However, it’s a legit thing. Guys get very emotional when they find out their significant other is pregnant.

Those first couple of months with a pregnant woman get a lot of men’s hopes up in a way that’s hard to explain. They see this white picket fence, life on easy street, and a future that reminds them of a past that never existed.

For men, particularly men who don’t really think about their partner’s needs or desires, it’s easy to get caught up in the whirlwind of the fantasy of having a kid. They tend to forget that:

Simply put, you and your partner might not be in the right place or time to have a kid. It’s foolish to assume that “God will provide,” and even more foolish to think that pushing for a child your partner doesn’t want will save a relationship.

Though I can remind men that it’s a woman’s choice and that having a baby doesn’t always turn out well, that doesn’t remove the sting of hearing that you lost that future you thought you were going to have.

When you feel like you’ve had something taken from you , it’s normal to want that to never happen to someone else again. That’s likely why a lot of men who experienced their partners getting abortions become anti-choice.

They’re still hurting from a future that never came to be. And unfortunately, we live in a society that tells men to just “suck it up” because it’s the woman’s choice — never giving them an opportunity to grieve and feel validated.

I mean, it’s not a future that would have been tenable in most cases. In most cases, the woman is right to choose to terminate a pregnancy, especially if the relationship is going bad or if she doesn’t want a kid. Even so, it still can hurt, you know?

It can be extremely hard to make a decision that benefits society when you have your emotions screaming at you. That’s why it might be time to talk about the trauma that men can have when their wives have an abortion.

I mean, we can’t really expect men to want to side with women when they’re hurting, and no one pays attention to them. They feel hurt, and their feelings are valid.

So far, most of the therapy groups that discuss abortion-related trauma are pro-life. I’d go so far as to say that these groups have been a major driving for in the indoctrination of hurt men at risk of radicalization.

Anti-choice “support” groups like this validate men’s feelings, but they also encourage men to invalidate women’s feelings. They work by weaponizing trauma they claim to help men heal from.

The men never heal. They’re just taught to lean into the hurt and anger they feel, channeling it into slut-shaming, controlling behavior, and toxic spirituality.

The pro-choice movement has patently ignored their trauma. Is it any shock, then, that so many men end up turning anti-choice after their partners have an abortion?

If the pro-choice movement is ever going to take men by storm, we have to actually help them feel supported as well. Maybe it’s time pro-choice support groups start stepping up their support of men.

A lot of therapy can help overcome this type of anti-choice reactionary trauma. It can help guys realize that they may have a right to feel upset, but that doesn’t give them the right to demand women hand over rights to their bodies.

The solution to this might be more simple than we’ve been thinking. We’ve been witnessing an extreme rise in male radicalization, often caused by men who feel like they’re being pushed out or replaced in society.

Maybe it’s time we actually take a cue from the groups trying to radicalize them and give them a way to direct their anger into something. Just, you know, make it a healing force rather than a destructive one.

It’s a thought.
