title: Is Abortion OK if it Saves the Mother’s Life?… Nope!
content:
And you thought all the crazy, hardcore fundamentalist Christians lived in the red states of the USA?!
Nope.
Introducing Pastor Tom Foord — the young pastor from Australia who leads the ironically named Hope Reformed Baptist Church. Yes, Pastor Tom offers hope to the world by reminding the world that it is depraved, wicked, and hopelessly lost and perishing, apart from a small group known as “the elect” who God predestined before the creation of the world to be “saved.”

So much hope in that message, isn’t there?

Occasionally, Pastor Tom runs Q&A forums, which he helpfully posts on YouTube. I think he does this to protect his flock from those wicked liberal Christians with their woke theology, keeping them firmly inside the echo chamber of reformed theology.

I had a friend who deeply objected to one of Pastor Tom’s YouTube Q&A answers, so he posted his reasonable (and well-researched) objections to Pastor Tom’s position.

And Pastor Tom deleted it.

So, my friend reposted his objections.

And Pastor Tom deleted it again.

So, my friend reposted it again.

And pastor Tom deleted it for the third time.

For over an hour, my friend kept reposting his comment, and Pastor Tom kept deleting it. I can imagine Pastor Tom sitting in his office, refreshing his browser over and over again as if that were a good use of the time that the people of his congregation were paying for with their tithes and offerings.

The offending Q&A Forum included the following question: “Is abortion okay if it costs the mother her life?” As the interviewer asks the question, Pastor Tom repeatedly interjects, “No! No! No!” so you pretty much know exactly how this is going to end.

Here is what Tom says:

“I am unapologetically pro-God, and God says if you’re a mother, you owe that child your life.

Now, does that sound rich, coming from a husband who’ll never get pregnant and never have to give my own life? Maybe.

But women aren’t allowed to be preachers, so I gotta say it for them.”

If you think that smacks of arrogance, then just wait until you watch the video from YouTube. Here it is:

If you’re anything like me, you probably had a moment of disbelief when Pastor Tom delivered his resolute answer to a question that’s anything but straightforward. While “confidence” might seem like an appropriate term at first glance, “arrogance” feels like a better fit for his demeanor.

The type of mindset that simplifies everything into just two options, where one is deemed right and the other wrong, is referred to as dualism. Dualism essentially operates on a binary system, where choices are seen as either/or. It thrives on comparisons, contrasts, and drawing clear lines between opposing ideas. This mindset often uses terms like good/evil, black/white, or in/out, failing to recognize the vast spectrum of possibilities that lie between these extremes.

While dualistic thinking may serve its purpose in making things easier to grasp, it falls short when it comes to uncovering truth and appreciating the intricacies of real-life experiences. To put it simply, this kind of thinking takes no account of the individual person, which is precisely the opposite approach to that of Jesus Christ.

Pastor Tom’s world is black and white. He knows the answers. There is no room for nuance or even humility because he knows the truth. If he didn’t believe that was so, he could have prefaced it with, “This is my opinion,” but instead played the trump card, “ This is what God says.”

But I think Tom is a bit mixed up…

I am sure that if you tried to argue with Tom about matters of theology, he would require you to quote scripture accurately. I could imagine him saying to his opponent in a debate, “Where does it say that in the Bible? Show me the scripture!”

Because, in the Reformed Church, the Bible IS the word of God.

So, when Tom says: “God says if you’re a mother, you owe that child your life,” I am left wondering where exactly God said that. Because it’s not in the Bible. There is nothing even similar to that in the Bible.

I think it is more likely that Tom put those words in God’s mouth based on Tom’s interpretation of the Bible. So, really… it’s what Tom thinks. It’s a dangerous thing when a pastor confuses his own words with God’s words, isn’t it?

What right does a twenty-something-year-old pastor with a theology degree have to tell women what to do with their bodies? Well, in a system that elevates men above women, he has every right. In fact, men in the church have been policing women’s bodies for millennia.

For so long, women in the church were expected to cover up their bodies — for fear that somehow this would lead men to sin — as if men were incapable of being able to control some kind of animalistic urge. Yes, men in the church shamed women’s bodies by making out that women were the cause of their sexual temptation — and the chief cause of any occasion where they fell into sexual sin. Adam was the first to blame Eve, and in all the millennia since, men still haven’t yet taken responsibility for their own actions. What is more, men held back Christ’s affection for women because of their own insecurities and fears.

In patriarchal churches such as the one Pastor Toms leads, women are expected to submit unilaterally and unquestioningly to men, fathers, husbands, and pastors — even if those men are not worthy of such submission. This creates fertile soil for the objectification, devaluing, and even abuse of women.

A man forbidding a woman from having an abortion is another example of the coercive control men have exercised over women in the church for far too long. It’s high time that it stopped.

Call me woke if you like, but I happen to believe that the way of Christ is always the most life-giving way. When a mother’s life hangs in the balance due to complications during pregnancy, the decision to terminate the pregnancy can be fraught with anguish.

Yet, in many cases, choosing to prioritize the mother’s life is not only a compassionate decision but also the most life-affirming one. Imagine if the mother had other children, for example. Do we rob those other children of their mother for the sake of an unborn child? And It’s hardly a clear-cut decision.

Yet, surely, the only person who ought to have the final say in such a decision is the mother herself. Not the pastor. Not the Bible — or rather someone’s interpretation of it — and not the church.

In such challenging circumstances, the most life-giving approach is always the one that seeks to minimize harm while maximizing compassion.

But compassion doesn’t seem to enter the equation in Pastor Tom’s rigid stance.

Tom says he is unapologetically “Pro-God,” which means he believes a mother should die rather than abort her fetus.

So, if we follow that line of reasoning, anyone who doesn’t believe that a mother should die rather than abort her fetus must be anti-God.

Or, to put it another way, the only possible way that you can be pro-God is to believe what Tom believes about abortion. Thus, in Tom’s head, pro-God and pro-Tom are essentially the same things. Therefore, anti-Tom must also be anti-God.

I guess I must be anti-God.

Let’s imagine for a moment that Tom’s views on abortion are right. I don’t think they are, but let’s imagine. Do you suppose that his delivery would have won anyone over?

Do you think that anyone watching would have thought, “Gosh, Tom! You’re right! Women shouldn’t preach, and I’m so glad I have a man like you to speak the truth for me?!”

I doubt it.

I’m not opposed to Christians having alternate, counter-cultural, or even unpopular views. After all, Christianity is a counterculture, so it will not be everyone’s cup of tea. What I am opposed to is Christians ramming their views down the throats of others as if their “views” are the truth. Show some humility.

As for Pastor Tom, even if the things he had to say were true — which I don’t think they are — his delivery is, well… “unloving” would be a generous way of describing it. If Christians are commanded in the Bible to “speak the truth in love,” then Pastor Tom fails on both accounts.

He neither speaks truth nor love.

Dan Foster is the author of “ Leaving Church, Finding God: Discovering Faith Beyond Organized Religion . ”

title: Should Abortion be Legal or Illegal?
content:
Abortions have been a subject of debate for many decades. Women feel they should have the right to choose if they continue with an unplanned pregnancy or if they should abort the pregnancy. However, there are many women who think that having an abortion is linked to murdering a child. Then there are women that feel they are a good person for not having a child for their own reasons. The

The chart above shows many different reasons that women will have an abortion. The highest reason on the table is that they are not ready/poor timing with 27% and not being able to afford a baby at 25%. The main reason debated about why abortion should remain legal is due to cases of rape which according to the chart above is only 1% of the reason why women choose to terminate the pregnancy.

In the diagram above it shows the process of an abortion conducted at 23 weeks. This shows a depiction of a fetus being removed from the women’s womb in pieces. The first step to this process is to grab the body parts of the fetus and remove them from the body, followed by the head. After all the remains of the fetus have been removed the placenta and remaining contents will be removed from the uterus. This diagram could be used as an anti-abortion tactic to show why having an abortion is wrong. What they dont show is that most of all abortions are terminated before 10 weeks and are not performed in this manner. This gives women an unintentional fear of terminating an unplanned pregnancy and will possibly lead to an unhappy life and a budgeted future for the child.

The women in the picture above are protesting the right to choose if they can have an abortion. Pro-abortionist believes that by making abortions illegal women will result in having back alley abortions which is extremely dangerous. Back alley abortions are usually performed in a home with a under qualified health professional. These abortions lead to over bleeding and often kill many of their patients due to the low sterile environment. Protest rally in front of the White-house in Washington in hopes that no law is passed to make abortions illegal.

Many people set up to protest abortions in front of planned parenthood clinics which provide legal abortions and outreach for women who are raped and abused. The protesters make the women that need the outreach from going to these clinics because of the judgment and embarrassment protesters cause. Planned parenthood also provides counseling services and birth control options so that another abortion will not occur. Even though these clinics provide abortion services their main goal is to prevent a second abortion.

Women have the right to do as they please with their bodies. It is not fair for others to judge or cause ridicule for a decision based on the best outcome for the mother herself. However, women also have many birth control options to choose from and safe sex is the best way to avoid any termination of life and ultimately any diseases.

title: Why Abortions Should be Legal
content:
One of the most heated and debated subjects in the world.
All political parties use it to garner support based on being for, or against.

Roe v. Wade gives women the right to legal abortions. There are a handful of states trying to change this through restrictive laws. They are doing this in an attempt to end up at the Supreme Court and overturn Roe v. Wade.

Let’s discuss this from a scientific viewpoint, rather than a religious one, because, at the end of the day, this is about the law . Religion may impact how you feel about the issue but it should not play a part in determining the law.

The science isn’t that complicated. Modern medicine makes it possible for a fetus to exist outside of the womb at 24 weeks. The survival rate at this point is between 25–30 percent. Of course, survival is more likely with each week longer that the baby incubates.

Only 1.2 percent of abortions occur after 24 weeks and then only in extreme circumstances.

Ninety-two percent of abortions occur before 13 weeks or during the first trimester. At this point the brain is not formed enough for complex thought. I would still not consider this a child because of this.

There are those who would drag religion into the debate of deciding at what point life begins. I won’t deny that there is life as soon as the cells begin to divide. Yet this life is no different than any other microscopic life. Because it can develop into something more, should not alter one’s choice to end it.

Everyone who does not agree please take a deep breath.

To be honest this point is the only one that matters in this entire discussion.

Many people will argue that a mother can not end her pregnancy. That to do so is committing murder.

Yet there is this thing called body autonomy,

A person has control over whom or what uses their body , for what, and for how long. It’s why you can’t be forced to donate blood, tissue, or organs. Even if you are dead and even if it would save the other person’s life.

By not allowing a woman access to an abortion you are breaking this fundamental right and law.

Finally, my biggest issue is with those who oppose abortion and believe it should be illegal.

I won’t call them pro-life, as that would imply they cared for life as a whole. The vast majority that I have encountered do not. Once the child is born, the woman is on her own,

For many children that is a life of neglect and abuse. If they came to be out of violence such as rape or incest, they often end up in the overloaded foster system.

I understand that most of these women got themselves into this situation. I understand that everyone should take responsibility for their own actions.

Some take responsibility by making the decision to abort. For me, it was adoption. Still others opted to have their babies and raise them. Not everyone can walk down the same path but all the options should be there and available.

No woman should perish because of a coat hanger.

title: The Abortion Debate is Being Undermined. Part One: Personhood.
content:
“I can’t believe that in this day and age, we are still discussing whether abortion should be legal or illegal. What world are we living in?”
So began a conversation with a close friend of mine last week. I nodded in agreement, presuming to agree with his pro-choice stance. I never had an opinion on abortion to be completely honest. I felt the conversation was polarizing at best. I’m not religious. I do not have a significant other who has or had a pregnancy concern. I’m a man. For these reasons, I was automatically disqualified from having an opinion on abortion. Or at least that’s what I felt.

I wouldn’t be shocked if many feel the same.

It’s odd to think that my gender would determine my position on a very controversial topic. But my bigger issue in the abortion debate is the very topic being whittled down by celebrities chastising men and celebrating women, which does not lead to a fruitful conversation. This discourse does not treat you as a competent, rational individual. It presumes that your opinion is based on your gender .

There is a grave injustice celebrity culture is doing to perhaps one of the greatest debates of our time. And I worry this injustice will spawn discourse not rooted in fact. But rooted in emotion and conjecture. Abortion requires a serious examination of both sides of the debate.

This is why I’ve decided to create a mini-series on this topic. I’d like to examine a multitude of areas surrounding this debate, from being curious above all else. I do not believe that either side has all the answers. Nor do I believe that one side is more right more of the time. I’m legitimately curious and want to use this curiosity to share my learnings with you.

Maybe together we can have a more shared understanding of this very pressing topic.

Bringing up abortion as a topic of conversation is perhaps rarely a good idea in a social setting. I suggest treading with caution when talking in groups because you never know what someone may have been through.

I began researching this topic believing myself to be pro-choice 100 percent of the time. Of course, the woman must have a say. But, I am understanding the pro-life debate more. I guess you could say I am part of the very small minority of people ( 11 percent in Canada ) who are not sure about laws governing abortion. I understand both sides of the debate, but I don’t know where I stand.

…Do I have to pick a side?

And no matter where you stand, understanding that this debate will never be over is a very important point to mention. Polls conducted on abortion have always had the same result: people are divided, generally speaking. A small majority seems to be pro-choice on some aspects of abortion, but not all.

In 2018, approximately 58 percent of Americans believed abortion should be legal in all/most cases. While this can be seen as a majority, it is not a convincing majority. To me anyway. The poll also found 37 percent of Americans polled believed abortion to be illegal in all/most cases.

37 percent is not a small minority.

But I do believe all of us can learn more on the topic.

Understanding the abortion debate rests almost solely on the definition of personhood. What constitutes human life is a question steeped in morality, religion and personal beliefs. But personhood has a very legal connotation. There are rights and freedoms associated with this definition. And it does not help that the highest courts have not defined whether or not an unborn fetus constitutes personhood.

The Supreme Court in the United States in its Roe v. Wade decision continuously bracketed ‘personhood’. The Court ruled not on the definition of personhood, but that each state be allowed to decide the legal status of an embryo or fetus. Perhaps this is the greatest travesty of the debate. Personhood, with its legal implications, with its rights and freedoms, is left bracketed with quotations, leading to ambiguity. And ‘personhood’ has rights and freedoms enshrined not only at the State level, but the federal one too.

Many researchers argue that human life is not up for debate. Yes, the embryo or fetus either has human life or the potential for human life.

But does the embryo or fetus contain the legal status of personhood?

Conservatives have indirectly indicated that indeed an unborn fetus constitutes as a person. Kind of.

Many US Republican politicians have compared the fetus and embryo to an ‘unborn child’. This understanding is important because specific states have enacted legislation treating the embryo and fetus as if it contained the legal understanding of what we consider personhood to be. For example, some states have brought on laws on behalf of the fetus for their unborn death. Caitlin Borgmann’s “The Meaning of ‘Life’: Belief and Reason in the Abortion Debate,” is a wonderfully-researched article. In it, Borgmann states the following:

Wisconsin allows the state to incarcerate pregnant women during pregnancy in order to prevent harm to the fetus…States have passed laws that require abortion providers to anesthetize the fetus before an abortion if the woman consents. Doctors who provide abortions have been sued for malpractice for failing to tell the woman that her embryo is a ‘complete, separate, and unique human being’. (pg 559)

This distinction is critical to understanding part of the pro-life debate on personhood. It is steeped in legal consequences and extending the legal definition of personhood to an embryo and fetus aligns with what many laws are already doing.

Despite this, many conservative politicians have skirted the issue of personhood. Instead of addressing whether an unborn fetus constitutes personhood, the focus is placed on when a woman can abort. For example, John McCain stated the following:

After a lot of study, a lot of consultation and a lot of prayer, I came up with a position that I believe there should be an exception for rape, incest or the life of the mother…[the Abortion issue] is one of the most difficult and agonizing issues that I think all of us face, because of our belief — yours and mine — that life begins at conception.

While conservatives believe ‘life’ begins at conception, ‘personhood’ may. Or may not. It’s confusing.

Judge Judith Jarvis in the 1970s argued that indeed abortion should be allowed even if the definition of Personhood extends to an embryo or fetus. The reasoning rests on self-defence and self-preservation of the woman. In both instances, the woman would be undertaking abortion to protect her own rights and self-interests in the face of an external threat (e.g., rape, incest). And trumping the woman’s right for self-defence and self-preservation should not be the answer.

But when it comes to defining ‘Personhood’, pro-choice advocates are less clear on where this should be established. In fact, many argue the definition of personhood should be left to the woman based on moral, religious and personal beliefs. It should not be the responsibility of the State to provide this definition. And perhaps, this is where the great divide of the abortion debate begins.

John Kerry, during the 2004 Presidential debate reiterated this point. Kerry claimed to ‘deeply respect’ the view that a fetus is a person, while also saying this view should not be imposed on everyone.

What we have seen is that human life is not for debate. Yes, the embryo and fetus has either human life, or the potential for human life. However we want to define human life is up to us, but there is no denying that an embryo or fetus has the potential for human life.

Personhood is less clear.

If we are arguing in favour of abortion being legal, we are effectively okay with stating the embryo or fetus, while containing human life (or the potential for human life), does not contain the legal status of personhood. As well, by the courts bracketing ‘personhood’, the legal system has effectively determined that no, the embryo and fetus does not contain personhood. And in fact, it is up to the States to determine this definition.

This can get very confusing again.

When discussing abortion, we cannot subtract the legal entity of the rights and freedoms we are all guaranteed. Authors like Borgmann have cited examples used by other scholars when discussing Personhood. One example resonated with me: slavery. A human being lacking the protection of rights and freedoms is what legally allowed for slavery to exist. There was no denying that a slave was a human life. But did a slave contain the rights and freedoms of a ‘person’ as defined by the Constitution? No. And if a slave owner were to kill a slave, would the slave owner be charged? Personhood must lay the groundwork when discussing the abortion debate.

In subsequent articles, I’ll examine other aspects of the abortion debate that are very necessary.

title: Should Abortion Be Legalized?
content:
Let us get rid of the political, social, economic, religious, and emotional aspects of the debate and look at abortion dispassionately from a purely medical point of view first.
A woman seeks an abortion when:

A 13-year-old is brought to a gynecology clinic because someone in her family or her boyfriend raped her. She didn’t tell her parents until she started vomiting severely when it was discovered that she was 10 weeks pregnant.

An 18-year-old has consensual sex. Her partner uses a condom. She misses her periods three weeks later. A pregnancy test at 6 weeks turns out positive.

A 25-year-old married woman is in her first pregnancy. At 16 weeks she finds out that the baby has a severe congenital defect. She has to decide between an abortion or delivering a mentally and physically challenged child.

A 30-year-old woman with severe heart disease conceives for the first time. Even at three months gestation, she is breathless and her face turns blue. Her doctor strongly advises her not to continue with the pregnancy as it would pose a considerable risk to her life. Her only recourse — abortion.

A 45-year-old woman with two children had an intrauterine device inserted three years ago. She and her partner come to the clinic horrified to learn that she is eight weeks pregnant. There is no way they can afford to look after a third child.

These are not make-believe cases. They are real-life situations occurring day in and day out in any gynecologist’s clinic anywhere in the world. I have seen hundreds of such cases in my 30 years of clinical practice.

What can these women do? There is no contraceptive that does not fail, even tying the tubes. The failure rates vary from 0.1 (1 in 1000 cases) for oral contraceptives to 150 for condom usage.

Is it the woman’s fault if the contraceptive method she is using fails? If we cannot provide 100% failproof contraception, we have no right to ban abortions.

Should we tell all women to go around wearing chastity belts and hijabs? Should they abstain from sexual intercourse altogether just because they do not want a child at that point in time?

And what are the men going to do? Who is going to tell them to take a hike and head for the Himalayas and practice celibacy?

Women seeking abortion are not doing it for fun. The vast majority have a valid reason for terminating their pregnancy. More than 90% of cases fall in scenarios 1 to 5.

It is a very painful process for the woman. Right from finding out that she is pregnant when she least expects it, to making a decision to terminate the pregnancy.

It is absolute bullshit to say that women seeking abortion are murderers. They do not come dancing with joy to a gynecology clinic asking for an abortion.

The emotional and mental agony is compounded by the actual process of abortion. Regardless of the method used, there is severe pain and cramping in the lower tummy accompanied by bleeding that may sometimes be severe.

Surgical procedures used for abortion have their own risks of anesthesia, bleeding from incomplete emptying of the womb, and pelvic infection.

Perforation of the womb by instruments used for the procedure can lead to damage to other internal organs and even death.

Added to this is the more worrying complication for the young woman of inability to conceive due to blockage of the fallopian tubes following repeated abortions and/ or infections.

This is why in countries where abortion is legal, there are strict criteria as to when one should and should not terminate a pregnancy. As per the MTP Act of India (1971), pregnancies can be terminated when:

Let us not make the women suffer more than they already are by forcing them to continue their pregnancy.

Who will look after the unwanted baby of a 13-year-old?

Will the courts hand the child to the rapist?

Who will care for a severely physically and mentally challenged child?

Or the child born due to failure of contraception?

If you want to ban anything, ban pornography.

Ban pedophiles.

Ban the religious fanatics who try to put their spin on everything to score brownie points for themselves and their followers.

Ban the extremist politicians who create these situations just to secure votes for themselves.

Distribute the unwanted and challenged children among the social activists and ask them to take care of these children.

These people are totally devoid of common sense. It is amazing that a so-called developed nation like the USA cannot understand the health implications of banning abortions.

title: Yes, Abortion Should Be Legal in the Ninth Month
content:
Let’s talk about one of the most contentious aspects of the abortion debate: Late term abortions.
For Republicans, it sounds like an easy slam-dunk to prove that they’re on the right side morally. Late term abortions — especially in the final weeks before birth — take place when the fetus much more resembles a baby, and are likely to survive outside of the womb. It doesn’t make sense to terminate the pregnancy at that point.

But that argument is based on a fundamental misunderstanding of the reality of late-term abortions like that. And I’m giving the benefit of the doubt here by calling it a misunderstanding, because the alternative is that Republican politicians fully understand the reality and the lives they’re endangering with their abortion bans, but want to either score political points with their base, or punish women (or both).

Let’s be clear: No one is getting abortions in the final weeks of pregnancy because they

…and then just decided, actually, no, I’ve changed my mind.

People are getting abortions that late because they are forced to make an awful decision, usually because someone is going to die regardless.

And sure, the anti-abortion laws could include language excepting those conditions. But if there is a law that allows abortion only if the pregnant person’s life is at risk:

You don’t know, do you?

Neither do the doctors.

Neither do the lawmakers.

When abortion is only allowed under certain, ambiguous or undefined circumstances, the doctors end up with two choices:

And it’s not like they can go to court to figure it out before making a choice. It’s a decision that has to be made in that moment. They can’t wait until the legal system confirms their choice.

Think that sounds unlikely? It’s already happening.

Or, another instance when an abortion in the final weeks may happen: The baby is pretty much guaranteed to suffer immensely and die soon after birth.

The parent then has to make a choice:

Do they have an injection that stops the fetus’s heart before birth, giving it a relatively peaceful death in utero?

Or, do they go through a birth that will be traumatic for both parent and child, to a baby that will be in extreme pain, and allow death to occur naturally?

And contrary to what former President Trump has repeatedly claimed , in no state is it legal to kill a baby after birth, nor is anyone advocating for that.

I gave birth to my daughter at the end of 2017. It was a completely normal pregnancy, until it wasn’t. I ended up diagnosed with pre-eclampsia right at 37 weeks, had to be induced, and ended up having an emergency c-section because she wasn’t tolerating labor.

It was scary, but I count myself lucky that my odds for survival and hers were both good. I never had to make a choice of what would be the most humane path for my baby’s inevitable death. Ican’t begin to think what I would do in that situation.

But I can tell you I would want the decision to be mine and my doctor’s, not the government’s.

THAT is why most Democrats push for abortion at any time during pregnancy with no restrictions. THAT is why, yes, in some places abortion is legal up to the ninth month, and it needs to be, nationwide. Because anyone faced with these kinds of decisions needs to be able to have the medical care they need, quickly, legally, and safely.

title: Abortion Rights: Why Abortion Should be legalized Worldwide Without Restriction
content:
An in depth look into the legal status of abortion throughout the world
Studies have shown that abortion has been legalized in most countries. When it comes to the rights of women and abortion, overtime, there has been great changes, and around 50 countries removing certain restrictions in their laws on abortion. Although this is great news, not much change has happened since then, but still gives women access to abortion with restrictions such as a threat to their life or where the pregnancy was a result from rape. Roughly 59% of women and girls who are fertile, live in countries where abortion is commonly allowed, while 41% of women and girls live in countries where they are expected to obey the restrictions. The lack of having proper access to safe abortion not only affects women, but roughly 23,000 per year have died from the process of unsafe procedures. These numbers could decrease significantly if there was safe and legal access worldwide for all women without restriction.

While some countries have some limitations on their laws on abortion, there are three countries around the world that not only have the most restrictive laws, but also criminalize women. Ireland, El Salvador and Chile are the top 3 countries where abortion is still illegal. All three countries ‘ governments have introduced restrictive and discriminatory abortion legislation that threatens women and girls ‘ lives. In Ireland, they have not completely banned legal abortions, but there is not much hope.This makes it difficult for a woman or girl to access safe and legal services. The laws in Ireland treat women and girls as criminals, and any individual who supports them faces up to 14 years in prison and a fine up to £4,000 for violating the PLDPA ( The Protection of Life During Pregnancy Act 2013). Because of Ireland’s criminalization of abortion, roughly 4,000 women and girls between 20 and 34 travel out of the country every year for an abortion. El Salvador and Chile still have full bans on abortion, even if the life or health of the individual is at risk, the pregnancy is non-viable or a result from rape or incest. Women who had miscarriages were charged with aggravated murder, and could result in a prison sentence of up to 50 years. in El Salvador. There are even consequences for doctors who try to protect their patients life — a 6–12 year sentence in prison. In Chile, most women and girls are using illegal abortions that could jeopardize their lives. Looking for medical treatment may result in a sentence of 3 to 5 years imprisonment. Those that are able to afford leaving the country, do so to have safe procedures done. With all that being said, El Salvador, Chile and Ireland are not meeting their expectation in regards to the law on human rights. The lack of providing useful services for abortion in these countries has been made aware globally and is currently fighting for the rights of women and abortion laws to change.

With any major decision, there are pros and cons. In this case, I believe there are a lot of benefits from legalizing abortion. One of the reasons that really stands out to me is pregnancy resulting from rape. In girls aged 15 and under, over 90% of pregnancies are due to rape by family members — yes, incest. Estimates have shown that rape conception happens in the U.S. alone between 25,000 and 32,000 times a year. The United States has the benefit of having legal abortion upon request, but given the information on the countries that have illegal abortion, it is heart breaking to know that they do not have these privileges. In other cases, an individual could be incapable of giving their baby a proper life. Let’s say for example the person who becomes pregnant is living in poverty or is homeless, under these circumstances, it sometimes is best to consider to abort an unwanted pregnancy. As stated in the La Times article ‘ Op-Ed: Restricting access to abortion makes poor women poorer’ , “ It’s important to think about pregnancy and abortion in the context of real women’s lives, rather than as fodder for political debate”. Lastly, another benefit is the age of the person who has become pregnant. A young mother can be a difficult role to fill, especially if there is no adult help. Being a teen mom and having a child while still having to attend high school is not a simple way of life. When it comes to teens and sexual intercourse, there are circumstances where they do not really understand the practice of safe sex and can lead to unwanted pregnancy. In this case, it is no ones fault, but there are solutions other than adoption, which would mean a full pregnancy for a minor.

In conclusion to what I have stated, I believe that all countries could benefit from legalized abortion. Given the facts, the numbers, the criminalization of women due to abortion, and the benefits from having it be legalized, there should be more concern for the rights of women. This is only a sliver in the rights we women have in this world. Yes, we have more say than we did those years ago, but even then, there is still a right to fight! If we all come together and fight for one another, there is no greater power than forming an alliance. We have the privilege of digital technology; it’s literally at our fingertips. Together, we can make a change in history.

title: Should Abortion be Legal?
content:
One of the most polarizing issues in our nation today is abortion. Should it be legal or illegal? At what point in the pregnancy should it be deemed immoral or illegal? Both are very important questions, but the fact of the matter is that all women should have the right to make that decision themselves. Pregnancy happens in a woman’s body, so why would that power be put in someone else’s hands? Making abortion illegal is unsafe and unjust.

An article from The New York Times by Michelle Oberman discusses what would happen if abortion became illegal. Over the past decade, Oberman traveled to several Latin American countries and studied the result of making abortion illegal and found that even in places where it was illegal or almost illegal, abortion still remained common. She then explained this as very problematic, giving her readers insight into what would happen if abortion became illegal in their own country.

In the article, Oberman shares that even when abortion is illegal, women find ways to have abortions despite the laws. This results in very poor decision-making because women are unable to get help from their physicians so they turn to unsafe solutions. Oberman found that the most common illegal way to get an abortion in many Latin American countries was a drug called misoprostol. Misoprostol is most commonly used to treat ulcers, so when women take the wrong dosage or even the wrong drug because they don’t have guidance from doctors, they can end up in the hospital.

Another large issue with making abortion illegal is that doctor-patient relationships would be severely impacted. Women that are in search of ways to have an abortion no longer feel like they can trust their doctors because their doctor-patient confidentiality can be broken at any time. Oberman shares how she has witnessed this being in issue in many of the countries she visited. The article states that “Government officials there have toured the country’s hospitals to inform doctors of their duty to report women suspected of having induced their miscarriages.” (Oberman). When doctors are expected to report any suspicions of women trying to have an abortions, women are less likely to visit them or look for professional help. When a woman is scared about being accused of such a crime, it causes issues in the doctor-patient relationship, which is very dangerous because it leads many women to postpone or forgo necessary care.

A pregnancy happens inside a woman’s body, therefore, it should be the woman that decides whether or not she wants to give birth to it. This power should not be put in anyone else’s hands. It is her choice. In 1973, the Supreme Court made a decision that would affect women everywhere. This was the Roe v. Wade decision, which established women’s right to abortion and addressed criminalization issues of and access to managing fertility. Recently, this decision has been put in jeopardy by President Trump, who is attempting de-fund many family planning organizations that promote abortions or refer patients to clinics that provide them. In his third presidential debate, he affirmed “he would appoint only pro-life justices to the Supreme Court and that Roe v. Wade would be ‘automatically’ overturned.” (Chang). This is a huge issue because the Roe v. Wade decision was put in place for a reason and has been very beneficial to making countless lives better. With this decision in danger, it leaves many women worried for the danger the government will put them in.

Abortion is a choice and a right that all women should have. It influences a woman’s whole life; from relationships to jobs; from dreams to responsibilities, childbearing has a huge impact on a woman’s life. A mother, psychologist and author named Valerie Tarico wrote an article about abortion and why it should never be made illegal. She writes “being able to delay and limit childbearing is fundamental to female empowerment and equality. A woman who lacks the means to manage her fertility lacks the means to manage her life.” (Tarico). Any professional woman wouldn’t be able to get to where she is without access to manage fertility. Any young woman with aspirations of becoming a professional woman would not be able to reach those goals without reliable means to limit or delay childbearing.

Despite what people negatively think about abortion, well-timed pregnancies give children a better start to life. Abortion can help to plan pregnancies so they are there when wanted and not when unwanted. A child born in a household that has prepared for its coming can be healthier because of prenatal care and fundamental to getting out of poverty. Women who have timed their pregnancy can take part in prenatal and postcontreception care. If this happens, the baby will have better and more nutrients to be healthier and have an easier start in life. Having many children due to lack of fertility management can be detrimental to wealth and economy. When families have access to these means, they can have fewer children, boosting economic opportunity and ending multigenerational poverty. This is critical to the modern industrial economy.

The health and safety of all women in America should not be carelessly put into the hands of a few powerful men in Washington. Not only is the issue of abortion about a political and cultural hurdle for our nation to eventually grasp and overcome, it is most importantly about any person’s universal rights to safety and to seek medical attention if they require, or desire, it. Making abortion illegal would be effectively taking away a fundamental freedom for all women; not being able to safely manage their fertility and their lives takes away a women’s right to live freely. Abortion gives women the choice of making their own decisions, empowering them and their bodies. Abortion can eliminate unwanted and unplanned pregnancies that can lead a child to a neglected household and lifestyle. It can also immensely help developing economies by controlling the population and boosting opportunity, overall improving our world. Abortion is a choice, and it is a choice only a woman can make for her own body.

title: Most People In America Agree Abortion Should Be Legal — So Why Can’t We Find Common Ground?
content:
I have had a horrendous time sleeping recently, and I’ve blamed it on Mother’s Day earlier this month. Less than a year ago today, my mother passed away in an automobile accident. I try not to dwell on it, to live my life and move forward, as I know she would want for me, but I am still devastated — daily, indescribably. I remind myself to be thankful for what I do have. I remind myself human suffering and misfortune have far greater victims than me. To wit, one has to look no further than the news cycle over the past couple weeks. Multiple states have passed some of the most radical anti-abortion legislation in the history of this country. Here in Louisiana, the House and Senate approved an amendment which will deny abortion rights statewide if a heartbeat can be detected. Gov. Edwards has already stated he will sign the bill if it comes across his desk.

My mother was in college in the late 1960’s when abortion was illegal, sex education and birth control were taboo, and the proliferation of the pill was in its infancy. She saw firsthand the impact illegal abortions had on women. She knew women who had illegal abortions that almost killed them; women who were left sterile for the rest of their lives; women who were forced to give up promising jobs and education paths, because they had no other choice. The criminalization of abortions did not prevent abortions. It served only to make the procedure more expensive and dangerous for the women having them, and further enabled a highly patriarchal society.

1960 wasn’t that long ago, yet here we are in 2019 looking to repeat our old mistakes. Let’s be clear: what’s happening right now with abortion across the country is a systematic, calculated plan by one side to dismantle Roe v. Wade. According to Planned Parenthood, before abortion was legalized in the US, 1 in 6 pregnancy-related deaths were due to illegal abortions. The idea that making abortions illegal will stop abortions is short-sighted and totally contrary to the actual evidence.

When it comes to social issues, I’ve always appreciated a utilitarian explanation over an ethical one. We may not always agree on the nuances of the latter, but I think the former is often fairly obvious. Abstinence doesn’t prevent pregnancy, and criminalizing drugs only makes safe drug use an uphill battle for users. That’s why it’s so important to teach our young people about sex, and provide treatment and support for drug users and addicts. Abortions are going to happen, whether it’s illegal or not, and arguing over ethics is missing the point.

The media paints the divide on this issue in broad, contentious strokes. Finding common ground doesn’t spin as well for ratings, I guess. According to recent research , American voters’ stance on abortion is less of a stalemate than the media and politicians would have you believe. According to a nationwide survey, 73% of voters believe Roe v. Wade should not be overturned. 67% would make abortion legal in “most” or “all” cases. Yet there are billions of dollars being poured into this issue on both sides. Let’s reverse the model — how can we reallocate the money and energy poured into the perpetuation of this decades-long battle and instead put it towards practical, realistic solutions and common ground?

I think most of us would agree that getting an abortion is not an ideal circumstance, nor a decision to be taken lightly. Whether it’s your religion, moral code, or just plain empathy — most of us appreciate the magnitude of the decision and the procedure itself. So we want to build a system wherein abortions are safe and available for those that need them, but which also proactively integrates solutions for curbing them. Sex education is key here, and I don’t think I have to point to any hard data to convince you that teaching people about sex ,and empowering individuals to take control of their own bodies and desires is a good thing. I know, I know. You’re going to say that the same people that want to ban abortions also want to abolish real sex education. This may be true to an extent, but I believe it is more of a fringe stance at this point. There are always going to be radicals on either side, but there is also, for instance, a huge universe of pro-life ardent voters that have no problem with real life sex education. These are the people that will absolutely vote pro-life, but encourage the use of condoms and birth control. Even most moderately conservative religious groups these days are not opposed to practical and safe utilization of birth control.

I truly believe that the majority of the country can come together on this issue, and that it can have impactful and far-reaching ramifications. The fringe groups that oppose sex education are not big enough to be a relevant factor in this movement. Or — they shouldn’t be. Some of those people are currently in political positions of power. In my time serving on the Orleans Parish School Board, I butted heads more times than I’d like to recount on the simple issue of being honest with our kids about sex and sexuality. The good thing about politicians, of course, is that if they aren’t acting in interest of the majority, they can be voted out.

In conjunction with standardizing and dispersing sex education, we must make birth control more accessible to everyone in America. The no-win situation that women of my mother’s generation found themselves in was perpetuated by a lack of resources and access. Unfortunately, while we’ve made strides since then, we still have a ways to go. We have to make birth control available to people where they are — in their communities, without hassle or stigma attached. Easy access is key. Condoms should be available for cheap, happily displayed at stores. They should be free at schools and community centers. The pill should be easily attainable from doctors and clinics. There should be no judgement from nurses or doctors, and certainly no woman should ever have to cross an angry picket line outside a Planned Parenthood just to fill their prescription. Other modern alternatives to the pill, like IUDs or vaginal rings, should be just as available, and taught about in sex education. Many women do not like how they or their bodies respond to the pill, and these alternatives provide great options for protecting themselves and taking control of their body without negative side effects.

Finally, I think that we have to build better infrastructure around adoption. We need to provide a realistic and proactive alternative to abortions for those who may want it. Again, education is key here. Not only should the systems in place be fine-tuned and pared down from a technical and bureaucratic standpoint, but we must also provide useful, honest, and practical education about this option — no more scare tactics and overt moralizing. This will require government money to improve the healthcare system, as well as money and cooperation from the private organizations offering adoption. It’s an investment, both in terms of time and money, but an important one, and I believe if done right it can go a long way toward weaving that middle ground between voters on this issue.

I know I’m not reinventing the wheel here with my suggestions, but as I’ve stayed up way too late watching the news cycles the last week or so, I’ve been astounded and discouraged by the lack of productive talk about this issue. There’s so much vitriol and divisiveness. I guess that makes for good TV right? I think we need to change the conversation, and do it fast. The fact of the matter is, if Roe v. Wade is overturned, nearly one third of women in this country will lose access to abortion rights . It won’t stop abortions, it will only make them much more dangerous.

This is a death sentence for women. We may not all agree on the right or wrong of this issue, but we can all agree that something has to be done. We can’t let people die while we wave signs and drown in semantics. I think, particularly in our age of social media and the 24 hour news cycle, combatting some of those narratives that can be so pervasive starts with organizing at the local level. We need coalitions of people from both sides coming together to constructively reduce abortions, yet make sure they remain available to those that need it. Yes, maybe that’s a centrist approach. I prefer to think of it as a rational one. It’s building trust and common ground that doesn’t exist in the media, to jumpstart a change from the bottom up. I will include some organizations below that are doing important work during this difficult time. If you can, give to their funds, or get involved. For me, I hope to honor the memory of my mother by supporting a woman’s right to choose, and to open a conversation for a brighter future where we don’t have to recreate the sins of our past. It won’t be easy, and it will take time and continued effort, long after the news cycle moves on. With that in mind, I’m going to try to get some sleep.

title: I’m Pro Life…and I think abortion should be legal.
content:
by Karen McKenna
When I was in my twenties I owned a house with my first husband, an over 100 year old farmhouse in rural Massachusetts. Like all houses of its age, this house had some mice living in it. At night they would come into the kitchen and get into the food, so I decided to buy some mousetraps, the old fashioned spring type. The theory was that the mouse would stick its head in to grab the bait and the spring would pop, breaking its little neck quickly and painlessly. I will admit, I didn’t think much about it. It was a solution to a problem.

One night I set the traps and then went into the living room to watch some TV. Suddenly I heard a thwap sound…and then the most horrible scream I had ever heard. I ran into the kitchen where I saw a mouse running around the kitchen floor with the mousetrap on its head, screaming in pain and desperately trying to get it off. I tried to help, but it was too late. The poor animal died of exhaustion, pain and probably a broken back. As its cries finally subsided and it’s little body went limp, I carried it outside, went up to bed, and cried myself to sleep. I still cry when I think of it.

That little mouse did not die in vain. I count that experience as the beginning of the awakening of my conciousness. I considered myself a “good” person, but I began to realize that as a human being, a spirit of God in a human body, it was my duty and responsibility to live my life as much as possible in accordance with God’s love, and that included the desire to live a life that caused as little pain and fear to other beings as was humanly possible.

It led me, eventually, to where I am today. I believe in the conscious spirit of all beings. I believe everything is a reflection of God’s love, and for that reason deserves reverence and respect.

So I would consider myself to be quite pro life.

And yet, it’s obvious to me that abortion must not only be legal, but must be a choice that any person can make if and when it’s necessary.

Abortion isn’t about killing babies. Every woman is hard wired to protect and nurture a baby. That’s biological. Why would a woman want to kill a baby? Anti abortionists would say it’s because babies are inconvenient and the women are selfish. I just don’t find that to be true about the women I know.

Men are out there shooting children, but so far I haven’t heard of a woman going into a school or a children’s parade and opening fire, have you?

No, in general women feel the need to protect and defend babies and children. Abortion is not a woman giving birth and then taking a hammer and smashing her baby’s head in.

It’s not killing babies.

You might say, but what’s the difference if you abort a baby a few weeks before it’s born? Isn’t that just smashing it with a hammer in utero?

If that’s what abortion was, you might be right. But only a tiny percentage of abortions are done after the 5th month, and only when there’s a very good reason. For example, the pregnancy is threatening the mothers life. Or the baby is found to be not viable, in other words it will not be able to live…and this usually goes along with threat to the mother.

Another reason is because the baby is already dead. Pregnancy is fraught with peril, and not every conception results in life…far from it. How devastating is it for a woman to be forced to carry in her body a child that is already dead. I can’t imagine the heart break.

You might notice that in the last few paragraphs I have referred to the unborn as a “baby” or “child”.

Because I am not one of those who believe life begins at birth, or first breath.

If you’ve ever been pregnant, you know that there’s a point where that life, well, comes alive. And it’s long before the actual birth.

But how long before? For me, with both my children, it was around the fifth or sixth month. That’s when you start to feel movement, “kicking”, and it’s around the time that a baby can be born prematurely and possibly survive. Possibly.

But probably not.

Because central to this issue is the FACT that that babies must grow inside of their mothers’ bodies.

Mothers are necessary for there to be babies at all. And pregnancy is a dangerous undertaking that requires the mother to literally give up her body, and maybe her life, to create a new being.

If that being is under 3 months in utero, it is not a separate, viable life.

(And, by the way, Roe only allowed abortion without a medical reason before 3 months.)

Because the mother is taking ALL the risk, and suffering all the discomfort, the decision to carry the pregnancy should be hers and hers alone. There are a million good reasons for a woman to terminate a pregnancy. Maybe she’s been raped. Maybe she’s ten.

Maybe it’s just not a good time.

Because not having a baby because it’s inconvenient is not selfish, it’s responsible. Because pregnancy IS inconvenient. It changes your life irrevocably and if you’re not ready for that, you shouldn’t do it. Period.

I’m old enough to remember the discussion about Roe when it first became law. I remember hearing, and agreeing with, the argument that legal abortion could be used by men to pressure women into getting rid of a “problem”, even if the woman wanted the baby. Or that women would be inclined to use abortion that way, as a form of birth control. But this didn’t happen. Abortion rates went down under Roe.

Because in the end women, and men, are not monsters. No one wants to kill a baby. No one wants to terminate a pregnancy, even an unwanted one.

But sometimes it is the right thing to do.

Even if you’re pro life.

title: Abortion — Why it should be legal?
content:
To start, abortion is not a dirty word. There are many people and groups that disagree with abortion being legal, now they are entitled to their own opinion, but no one deserves to be told they are wrong for feeling a certain way. Abortion is the deliberate termination of a human pregnancy, most often performed during the first 28 weeks. (Oxford Dictionaries | English, 2017) Just to put it out there, I would personally never believe in getting an abortion for myself, but for other women, they deserve the choice. It is their body and they deserve their rights, just like men have control over their bodies.

I can understand religious aspects meaning some people can never accept the idea of abortion. However they still have that decision, the choice to follow a faith. Just to clarify with what it takes for a woman to be able to get an abortion. They need to go through a process where she get’s authority from at least 2 different doctors. Most women will have to visit their GP, where they will be asked if it is what they 100% want. They will then be referred to a health clinic where again, they will be asked the daunting question again. “Is this what you really want?” They have plenty of time to be swayed against their decision to get an abortion. (Anon, 2017) “Women are given an opportunity to talk things through, and offered extra support, including counseling, to help them make their decision.” It’s not as quick as people may think. In contradiction to the argument that abortions can either seriously harm the woman or have affects on planned pregnancies in the future. When in reality, the affects are very minimal and the percentages of their actually being a problem are very low. Damage to the uterus happens in less than one in every 1,000 medical abortions carried out after 12 weeks of pregnancy. There are always going to be risks with everything. People do not think differently when unnecessary body surgery is undertaken. The chances are miniscule, and for someone making the decision that is right for them, I am willing to fight for that small risk.

There are some instances when abortion is illegal, but that’s when the mother was to go to someone unprofessional and when the procedure is taken after a certain amount of weeks. Doctors do take the wellbeing of the child into consideration. Abortions are legal when it comes into the topics listed below and others that are not listed. (Anon, 2017)

· Abortion for the sake of the mother’s health

· Abortion where a pregnancy is the result of a crime — such as crimes like rape, incest, or child abuse

· Abortion where the child of the pregnancy would have an unacceptable quality of life.

Now from my point of view, they are reasons very much worthy of a woman having an abortion. I can only imagine the impact it would have on someone’s life if they were sexually assaulted and then had to carry and give birth to a result of that crime. Yes, she is ending a life, but she is helping herself to keep her life.

Victims can experience both short and long-term psychological effects of rape. This includes the victim blaming him or herself. — There are so many affects but this is a huge one. (Healthyplace; Anon; 2017) Due to this, the woman is not going to be able to take care of herself properly, let alone a new child. The implications could be devastating for both lives. Would this not also be punishing a child for a crime it did not commit? Yes the argument of ‘the child not having a choice’ is valid. In this instance, life may not be very long without the protection of a fit mother or father.

Abortions are not only due to having unsafe ‘consented’ sex. This is the viewpoint many anti-abortion groups take into consideration. Not every aborted pregnancy was an accident and I really think this should be taken into consideration. Abortions are safe and only legal to a certain point in the pregnancy. However, if made illegal, there are other ways of getting an abortion. The question is, are you willing to let a woman go to extreme lengths and possibly end up ending her own life? That to me is the opposite of conserving life. A valid point to think about.

title: Why States Matter: Abortion & Gerrymandering in Ohio
content:
Here’s a conundrum for you: 30 percent of our fellow Americans believe abortion should be legal in all circumstances. Add in “most” circumstances, and the number goes to 63 percent. (I know, not great, but at least it’s a majority.) Only nine percent believe abortion should be illegal in all circumstances , per a recent poll of 20k+ Americans by The 19th News .

So how is it that a majority of American women of child-bearing age — 58 percent, according to the Guttmacher Institute — now live in states “hostile” or “extremely hostile” to abortion rights? (For purposes of this article, I use “women” to include “anyone capable of pregnancy.”) In a nation where abortion was legal for half a century, how is it that over 8 million women of childbearing age now live in one of the 14 states that ban abortion completely?

One obvious answer, of course, dates to June 24, 2022, when the US Supreme Court threw women under the bus and overturned Roe v. Wade. Abortion, a constitutional right for 50 years, was now a matter for “the people’s representatives,” according to Justice Samuel Alito. Safeguarding the fundamental human right to healthcare and bodily autonomy was now up to the states.

Another answer dates to June 27, 2019, when the US Supreme Court threw democracy under the bus and ruled that courts had no role in settling disputes over partisan gerrymandering. “For the first time ever,” according to dissenting Justice Elena Kagan, the Court was refusing to “remedy a constitutional violation because it thinks the task beyond judicial capabilities.” Safeguarding the fundamental American right to equal representation was now up to the states.

NB: “Gerrymandering,” a funny word with very un-funny consequences, refers to the practice of drawing legislative maps to favor one party or class of people over another, usually by “packing” (concentrating as many of the opposing party’s supporters into as few districts as possible) or “cracking” (diluting opposing supporters’ votes by spreading them among several districts). Partisan gerrymandering enables the majority political party to consolidate disproportionate power that does not reflect or represent constituent demographics, after which said party can ram through unpopular policies, voters’ wishes be damned.

See where this is going?

Case Study: Ohio

… where both abortion and gerrymandering have made national news. Things to know about Ohio, other than its renowned Cincinnati Chili:

The Supreme Court Ohio’s seven Supreme Court Justices are elected by voters. Elections were non-partisan until 2021, when GOP lawmakers changed the law (soon after Republicans lost three of four Supreme Court judicial seats, coincidentally enough); now, prospective Justices run according to party affiliation. Current makeup: 4 Republican, 3 Democrat.

The State Government Way to go, O-hi-o! You’ve made the top-11 list of the nation’s Most Gerrymandered States, according to the World Population Review.

The state GOP has worked hard to maintain solid trifecta control over the House, Senate, and Governorship since 2011. Most recently, state legislators submitted post-2020-census redrawn maps that were challenged in court by voters’-rights organizations as “extreme partisan gerrymanders that favored Republicans in violation of the state constitution” (this per the superb Democracy Docket ).

In the first months of 2022, the legislature proceeded to submit five — five! — separate new maps, all of which were struck down by the OH Supreme Court as unconstitutional partisan gerrymanders. The seven appointed members of the GOP-majority Ohio Redistricting Commission (yes, ORC ) also failed to submit workable maps, leaving Ohioans to vote on unconstitutional maps in the November 2022 midterms.

Sixth Time Is The Charm?

In September 2023, the ORC adopted legislators’ sixth set of legislative maps, which were immediately called out by election experts as… illegally partisan gerrymandered. The long-suffering plaintiffs asked the OH Supreme Court for permission to file objections, whereupon the Republican Secretary of State and allies filed motions asking the Court to dismiss the lawsuits, and — the cherry on the top — to void the Court’s own five previous decisions. The Court’s 4–3 Republican majority granted the state officials’ motion to dismiss, although not the voidance (there are some bridges still too far, thank goodness).

An effort is underway to gather enough signatures to get a voter-approved constitutional amendment on the 2024 ballot, which would void the maps and create an independent, citizen-led redistricting commission. If it fails, OH voters are stuck with the current maps until 2031.

So What Does Gerrymandering Mean for Women’s Health?

Nothing good. Ohio abortion law was already far from perfect — patients must make two trips, for example, one for in-person counseling and another 24+ hours later for the procedure, while numerous unnecessary Targeted Restrictions on Abortion Providers (TRAP) laws hinder providers at every turn — but at least abortion was legal in the state up to 22 weeks. That changed in 2019, when the GOP legislature and Governor pushed through a six-week ban, with no exceptions for rape or incest (not that any woman seeking an abortion should be subjected to a hierarchy of need, but, good god). The ban was tied up in court until June 24, 2022, when SCOTUS overturned Roe, at which point the ban became law, and *poof*, just like that, the majority of women seeking autonomy over their own bodies were out of luck.

Eighty-two days later, a judge issued a preliminary injunction on the ban. Abortion was now… legal? Maybe? For how long? Did women have control over their own reproductive organs or not? In response, Republican Secretary of State Frank LaRose and State Representative Brian Stewart unveiled the “Ohio Constitution Protection Amendment,” which would raise the amendment-passing threshold from 50 percent to 60 percent, and raise minimum signature requirements to encompass all 88 counties instead of the established 44.

While the timing of this amendment might appear suspicious to the untrained eye, LaRose swore otherwise: the amendment was “designed to help protect the Ohio Constitution from continued abuse by special interests and out-of-state activists,” he assured voters. “There’s no time like the present to make a good government improvement to our state system here in Ohio.”

Except that he was caught several months later at a public event admitting that, actually, yes, the amendment was “100 percent about keeping a radical pro-abortion amendment out of our constitution.” His similarly logorrheic co-sponsor complained to House colleagues that, unless the amendment threshold were raised, “liberals” would gain the power to draw legislative districts, “affecting not only the Ohio legislature, but control of the United  House of Representatives as well.” (“And gerrymandering is our prerogative, dammit!” he might have added.)

Legal, Shmegal

Failing to obtain enough legislative votes, supporters missed the May 2023 primary deadline for getting the amendment onto the ballot. Normally, that would be the end of it for the year, but GOP lawmakers proposed a special election for the issue. The only problem: lawmakers had passed a law outlawing such elections  months earlier.

Awkward… but nothing a little magical thinking couldn’t solve.

“Yeah, the legislature has the constitutional authority to create an election day,” fantasized then-House Speaker Jason Stephens.

Er, nope: according to Steven Steinglass, Dean Emeritus of Cleveland State University’s Cleveland-Marshall College of Law, and a foremost expert on the Ohio Constitution, “the Ohio Supreme Court said, and I quote, the statute law of the state can neither be repealed nor amended by a joint resolution of the General Assembly.”

Details, details. Lawmakers forged ahead nonetheless and scheduled an (illegal) special August election, counting on the historically low voter turnout that had prompted them to eliminate special August elections in the first place. The move was challenged in court, but in yet another 4–3 decision, the OH Supreme Court allowed the scheduling — essentially blessing the legislature’s decision to break its own, newly-passed law.

While this travesty was unfolding, abortion advocates, medical professionals, and other  who cared about women had gathered enough signatures to get their own constitutional amendment, aka Issue 1, onto the November 2023 ballot. While approving most of the amendment, the OH Ballot Board ordered the language on the actual ballot to be changed from “” to “unborn child,” a clear effort to pave the way toward fetal “legal ”; once again, the OH Supreme Court upheld the change.

Fortunately, an army of activists hit the ground to educate voters about the August power-grab, er, election (let’s hear it for grassroots organizations on the ground! And for concerned citizens across the country, who wrote postcards reminding Ohioans to vote! And for voters themselves!). The GOP’s plan to capitalize on August apathy backfired, and on August 8, 2023, OH voters defeated the proposed amendment 57 percent to 43 percent.

Three months later, by the same resounding 57 percent, voters approved Issue 1, aka “The Right to Reproductive Freedom with Protections for Health and Safety.” The amendment provides critical constitutional protection to both women and doctors, stating, “Every individual has a right to make and carry out one’s own reproductive decisions, including but not limited to decisions on: 1. contraception; 2. fertility treatment; 3. continuing one’s own ; 4. miscarriage ; and; 5. abortion.” Abortion cannot be prohibited “if in the professional judgment of the pregnant patient’s treating physician it is necessary to protect the pregnant patient’s life or health.”

The  have spoken!

Yes, But…

You knew that was coming, right? Yes, but GOP legislators didn’t like what they heard, so they set out to silence constituents by other means. Following the election, 27 state legislators signed a press release condemning the “vague, intentionally deceptive language of Issue 1” and vowing to do “everything in our power to prevent our laws from being removed” (huh?). The OH State Senate President and his far-right GOP allies floated a potential 15-week abortion ban.

It was only a matter of time before someone proposed a straight-up legislative coup, and GOP State Representative Jennifer Gross stepped up to the challenge, separation of powers be damned. Blaming “foreign election interference” for Issue 1’s success, Gross has introduced the “Issue 1 Implementation Act,” which stipulates, “The Ohio General Assembly shall have exclusive authority over implementing Ohio Issue 1… All jurisdiction is hereby withdrawn from and denied to the Courts,” with any judge hearing cases regarding Issue 1 subject to impeachment and prosecution for a misdemeanor. In other words, judges would be jailed for enforcing what is now a constitutional right in the state.

You know who else will be in jail with them, besides doctors,  of color, and other miscreants? Women. Right now, a grand jury is deciding whether an Ohio woman who miscarried a nonviable  in her bathroom should face criminal charges. If so, she could face up to a year in prison.

Assuming *weak laugh* we still have a democracy in which to vote, even the most power-mad party will begin to crack under an influx of sane, humane, brave legislators. This means SUPPORTING great candidates at all levels, established and upcoming, up-ticket and down; EDUCATING voters about the candidates, issues, and ballot measures; and GETTING VOTERS TO THE POLLS, so they can vote all the way up and down the ballot… three things Sister District Project does really well.

title: Abortion — Should it be legal? Decide for yourself
content:
Religion reinforces the negative perception of murder as being labeled as a sin and as the worst thing that a person can do. I do not believe in religion, but even if you do, is murder always an immoral act? For example, would it have been a bad thing to assassinate Adolf Hitler? Or Osama Bin Laden? Jeffery Epstein? The person who murdered your mother, a pedophile who molested your children? Is murder always a bad and immoral act that should lead to a negative outcome? Can it be justified? People clearly do justify murder because murder happens and those murders are usually justified by the perpetrators, even if the justification does not make sense to us.

Maybe murder is still bad to you.

But what happens when a rape victim is impregnated by her perpetrator, does she have to have this baby? Why? Are there not enough people on the earth? We only have so much resources to support so many people. Is it just because murder is bad? How can we determine when an organism is officially alive and why do we get to make that determination in the first place? Does life start in embryo even though you don’t have any recollection of this? You don’t have any recollection of the first year of your life either.

Let’s say that life does start immediately upon fertilization. But then how come we are perfectly fine with consuming chicken embryos (eggs) and fish embryos (caviar)? Yes, these animals are not humans. But are humans not also animals? Mammals to be specific. Why do we deem our species’ lives to be so much more valued than other species lives? What actually makes us more important than every other organism on the earth when we are actually just organisms ourselves? I am not a vegan and not advocating for everyone to stop eating animal products, I am just trying to figure out this dilemma. It seems contradictive that murder is always bad and then we are fine with murdering plenty of other species, especially insects.

Are human embryos that much more important than other animal’s embryos? Why? Did these animals have the decision to have a life before we took it from them? Or do only the human ones deserve that?

Let’s say that humans are more important than other animals and that people should always have every child that is conceived.

The victim from before is forced to have the child that she had with her rapist. The child is born, the mother is forced to change every aspect of her entire life to now care for this baby that she never even wanted. Yes, she will love her baby, but they will remind her of her rapist every day. They will cost her a fortune. They will cost her plenty of social and professional opportunities. She decides to keep it to make sure they stays out of the foster care system because she is aware of the negative behavioral and psychological effects associated with foster care. She does her very best to give this child the best life that she can. This is obviously an optimistic example of this situation and very unlikely to be an outcome in reality.

If this woman never wanted to have this child in the first place, did we not just sentence her to a life sentence of motherhood? Compare it to prison. One thing deemed negative by society happens and you end up forced to serve a very precise role for the remainder of your life with no ability to escape it.

How do we justify enslaving someone to the task of parenthood? Is parenthood an obligation to being human? Is promoting life an obligation to being human?

What exactly are the moral things in society rather than socially agreed up constructs from previous generations? All of which are largely corrupted by religion, wealth, and power.

We need to start thinking for ourselves.

So what do you think?

Should abortion be legal?
