title: Imaging the Fetus
content:
A hot topic issue in today’s politics is abortion. A contributing part to the controversy over whether or not abortion should be legal relates to visual rhetoric. In the article “Constructing visions of the fetus and freedom” one of the main arguments is that the war on abortion might not be going on today if it were not for the dissemination of photos that displayed dismembered fetuses post abortion. This argument it intriguing, and I partly agree with it.

My issue with this argument is that abortion and Roe v. Wade is a dynamic argument that the Supreme Court has been in constant controversy over for the past several decades. The American Public also feeds off more than just the visual aspects that are circulating through the media. People form their own opinions based on many factors including gender, race, identity, values, culture, etc, and are also influenced by outside sources. However, I do believe images of dismembered fetuses has a great impact on how people think about abortion.

“Because visual images are inexplicit, (one picture is potentially a thousand different words), an image can function in an argument only if its meaning is actively focused” (Condit).

“Because arguments based on images are completely dependent on tropes, they are open to the dual possibility of persuasive potency and argumentative inaccuracy” (Condit).

By framing abortion through the use of dismembered fetuses, it may change the political agenda to thinking of abortion as murder. One of the main arguments in the abortion controversy is that every human life matters, and many Catholics and other Christian faiths believe that human life begins at the moment of conception. Not to discount anyone’s belief systems, however, I think a portion of pro-life believers have been deprived of the information they need to make an informed decision.

I am very familiar with this issue as I come from a Catholic family who always pushed the idea of being Pro-Life in front of me. Every year, the Catholic high school i attended would send a bus of girls out to Washington D.C. to participate in the annual March for Life. My grandpa, being a devout Catholic himself, sent me on this trip every year that I was in high school, and I was not given much of a choice. Throughout the four years that I went I was able to view one side of this issue up close, and would gather different perspectives each time I marched through the streets of D.C.

There is a section of the march that displays warning signs that some images may be disturbing for the next portion of the march. Images of bloody, dismembered fetuses sitting on doctors trays with bloody tools would be blown up on to large screens displayed for all to see. At first I was very upset by these images, disturbed, in fact. Through the years I was in D.C., I noticed something. With each passing year i marched, the number of disturbing images shown during the march kept increasing. There were many more being displayed from the first year I went, to the fourth year I went. Thinking about this now is causing me to ask the question: Why?

The answer can be found in the Condit article: “these fetal pictures are persuasive.” Fetal images have the power to change one’s mind about abortion. This may be the case for the more undereducated members of the population who do not know the other effects that making abortion illegal would have on the population of women. However, these fetal images are still powerful. Why else would they have to be censored?

It is important for any kind of sensitive image to be censored for the main reason that someone should get the choice of whether or not they are exposed to certain messages. If a young child was marching in D.C. and saw the sensitive images and the parent or chaperone was not warned, the child could become afraid and become terrified to see images like this in the future. Simply put, people should have a choice. People should have a choice of what kinds of media they consume, and people should have a choice in the matter of whether or not they are going to bear a child.

Images of dismembered fetuses or abject things in general are using a fear tactic to scare the public into thinking a certain way or to be afraid think another. Some may argue that the images are meant to educate, not scare, however I believe otherwise.

It is easy for me to say that growing up as a Catholic, my family pushed Catholic ideals onto me and forced me to go to mass every Sunday, causing me to grow up in a faith I felt was forced upon me and was not mine. I have different views now, as a result of growing up and being allowed to choose the things i believe in and don’t believe in. My stance on abortion has also changed after experiencing the pro-life side to the abortion argument up close and extensively. I think images of fetuses have the potential to change opinions and stir up conversation as well as controversy, however there is more to the argument than just the censored photographs we are being fed.

A contributing issue to the pro-life argument is that by making abortion illegal, many women would feel trapped into either becoming a parent when they aren’t prepared or financially stable, as well as women resorting to alternative methods to terminate their pregnancy that are unsafe. According to Condit, the most used image used in pro-choice movements is a bloody coat hanger. This also uses the fear tactic, but in a different way. People see the coat hanger and feel scared or saddened that a woman would feel like that method is her only option. However, the hanger in itself is not a very persuasive image, certainly not as persuasive as the images of the disembodied fetuses. “The hanger — even with its drops of blood — was not, in itself, a tremendously moving visual depiction.

The images can be harmful to both pro-life and pro-choice supporters — and while I think it is important that images of dismembered fetuses should be censored, they should not be unavailable should people wish to seek out this type of information. Images contain powerful messages and are a large part of shaping the rhetoric of today’s society, which is why it is important to have images like this available so that the public is able to make a more informed decision on controversial issues.

Abortion does not just affect the fetus, it affects the mother as well, and women should all have a say in how our bodies are being treated. This is why many supporters of pro-choice are also women. If a woman tried to tell a man how to make the most important decision of his life, the man would also feel a sense of fury as many women do when told they have to bear a child. This argument over pro-life v. pro-choice (Roe v. Wade) could go on forever. America is notorious for being split in opinions on many relevant topics. However, through the circulation of sensitive images, people are able to see the reality of abortion, what tolls it takes physically and emotionally. I think for America to gain a better informed understanding on the pro-life pro-choice debate, every resource should be available on the realities and consequences one may face when making the decision to abort or not abort — this way, at least, the opinions others have on the issue can be respected.

title: Why Abortion Should Be Legal Everywhere
content:
As many of you have probably noticed, this post-covid era has become one of the most retrograde moments for many powerful countries, like Russia with its invasion decision, or the US, as the Supreme Court has removed the constitutional landmark right to abortion and returned this issue at state level.

For most people this decision was no surprise since it has been leaked since May , when a draft opinion was published.

Though the anti-abortion movement is deeply rooted in the US political and cultural structure , the Supreme Court decision was largely unexpected. Because Roe vs Wade had been in effect for over 5 decades, and it seemed that women in America had gone so far ever since.

However, it was never too late for the women’s reproductive right and freedom to be banned. On June 24th, Roe v Wade was officially overruled, and women in several states are going to be surely affected by this decision, at least 26 states have or are going to take some restrictive measures, or even totally prohibit abortion.

Whereas many people see the abortion as a cruel decision a person can make, but sometimes it can be inevitable. And when it is illegal, the drawbacks can be considerable for the woman, her child (or children), her family, her community, and the overall society.

Many people think that abortion would suddenly disappear when some officials decide that this right is going to be banned, but it is not what would happen at all. Women will continue to terminate pregnancy, but secretly and, most often, without any medical support, which would probably affect the woman’s life.

The right to abortion was never exclusively about allowing women to choose whether to bear a child or not, but instead regulating and making safe and secure something that existed long ago .

The protection of the rights to abortion is not only about protecting women but also protecting families and children. Oftentimes some people feel that they are obliged to create a family when they get pregnant, even though they are not ready financially and mentally to take care of their children.

When abortion is banned, more children will be born in vulnerable conditions, and we would have many poor and toxic families. And yes, this would affect the whole society, and the future generations.

It is sure that there would be more cases of emergency in hospital because some people would perform their abortion on their own, or with the help of unprofessional individuals.

Nevertheless, there will be some other complications while pregnancy continues, because of the misuse of some abortion pills, as well as possible self-boycott of the pregnant person.

Besides, agglomeration in some places could create chaotic situations where providers would probably feel stressed and burnt out.

Under these circumstances, the mental health of the woman, her family, friends, and partner could not be steady. That is, there will also be more mental health diseases, disorders, and fatigue within our society. The psychological and mental issues will also provoke other physical illnesses.

And the list will go on and on…

How many hours do we need to take care of a child? How much money do we need? Taking care of a child is a lifetime payless job and would probably cost (if not both parents) at least the mother many hours off her paid job. As you probably know, less people working also mean less productivity.

Maybe in the long run the population growth might help gaining more workforce, but still, there is no way to prove what an unborn child is going to be, or whether they would be good for our society.

Besides, the future of any child depends on their environment, and the way they have been raised. Therefore, when a person thinks they are not ready to have kids, no one should force them into changing their mind, or otherwise criminalize their choice.

Most often their choice to not bear a child is going to be beneficial for both themselves, and the overall society.

title: Should Abortion be Legal?
content:
As to any argument, there are two opposing sides when it comes to the matter of abortions. These two opposers usually refer to themselves as “pro-life” and “pro choice”. Pro-life supporters maintain that abortion is wrong and pro-choice believe that it is a woman’s freedom to choose her pregnancy decisions. When it comes to the topic of abortions, most of us will readily agree that it’s a woman’s choice to decide what her reproductive decisions are, i.e. pro-choice. Where this agreement usually ends, however, is in the question of whether or not abortion is a fundamental right granted to women by the Constitution. Whereas some are convinced that a fetus is considered alive at conception, usually citing the word of God, others maintain that women’s right to choose is a fundamental right of the U.S. Constitution. While some insist that the issue of abortion is about when life occurs, leading to arguments about murder and the defiance of God’s word, others would say that the issue is the rights of women and protecting those rights, I argue that it is a woman’s right to choose what she wants to do with her body

The General Board of Church & Society of the United Methodist Church, the General Assembly Mission Council of the Presbyterian Church, and the Unitarian Universalist Association of Congregations all acknowledge that it’s a woman’s choice to decide her reproductive decisions (139, 140, 141) . Rick Lowery, PhD supports this claim by arguing that The Bible doesn’t explicitly portray that killing an unborn fetus is the equivalent to killing a human being ( 33 ). In making this comment, Lowery and the churches mentioned above argue that it is a woman’s right to choose what decisions she make regarding her reproductive system. While I agree with the churches’ sentiment that is mentioned above and the author on the basis that it is included in women’s liberties to choose what she does with her reproductive system. Having just argued that is should be a woman’s right to make her reproductive choice, it is more important that it has already been established to be a fundamental privilege given to women to have an abortion that is given to us by the Constitution. In other words, women are given the right to their own privacy to decide whether or not they want to continue their pregnancy. As agreed upon in the case of Roe v. Wade , this right is a part of our Constitutional rights in a 7–2 Supreme Court decision.

Here many other conservative religions would object the claim that the option of abortion is a fundamental right given to women by the Constitution. Those that are “pro-life”, such as Sivaya Subramuniyaswami, argue that life begins at conception, therefore defies the word of God and strips the unborn babies away from their right to live by murdering them ( 15, 16, 23, 126, 148 ). These opposers attempt to demonstrate that unborn babies are considered human beings by the government. Unborn babies are protected by the Unborn Victims of Violence Act, which ensures protection to unborn children from assault and murder. This act punishes people for intentionally killing or the attempt to kill a “human being.” The essence of the arguments from those that are pro-life is that life begins at conception because upon fertilization, genetic identity is given to a human. Because of this, the individual is given a fundamental right to live, therefore abortion would be murder. Murder is not only illegal, but also immoral. Many of the people that agree with that would argue that by deliberately destroying a life, abortions defy the word of God. Just because the unborn child has not yet been officially “born”, does not mean that they do not already have genetics and are breathing human beings. These unborn babies are recognized by good the moment they are fertilized and conceived, therefore they are living humans. Moreover, each human being is given the same unalienable rights presented by our Founding Fathers. No matter if the fetus is born or not, they still need to be given the same rights as any other human because they are still considered life. Denying these right would just be blatantly unconstitutional.

Although I concede that aborting an unborn baby is the ultimately murder, I still insist that every woman is granted their own right to choose how they proceed with their pregnancy on the basis of their fundamental rights of the Constitution. In the same way, I recognize that opposers of abortion argue that unborn babies are given those same unalienable rights. Although I agree with Sivaya Subramuniyaswami up to a point, I cannot accept her overall conclusion that aborting an unborn baby is the equivalent to killing that baby’s parents. I would argue that a fetus is considered lively upon birth, when a baby can survive outside the womb on its own when not dependent on the mother for life. I do agree that abortion defies the word of God, however I do not believe that the religions of others should be implemented onto other people. There is an invisible line that separates church and state, as it should be considering that not every person in the U.S. practices the same religion. Yet, there isn’t a solid line that dictates the morality of laws. Therefore, laws cannot be forced upon a person based solely on the fact that it defies the religion of a totally different person. Favoring a religion over others by passing a law because it goes against that religion is prohibited by the Constitution solely for the reason to keep people’s free religion amendment protected. At the end of the day, the rights of the U.S. people is what needs to be protected, not the religion of others and protecting their morals.

Although abortion may seem of concern to only a small group of conservative religions, it should in fact concern anyone who cares about their rights given to us by the Constitution. Not only is the right for women to choose their decisions for their reproductive system a fundamental right granted to them by the Constitution, but also protecting us from the establishment of a law based on the favoring of another religion.

While some insist that the issue of abortion is about when life occurs, leading to arguments about murder and the defiance of God’s word, others would say that the issue is the rights of women and protecting those rights, I argue that it is a woman’s right to choose what she wants to do with her body

Having just argued that is should be a woman’s right to make her reproductive choice, it is more important that it has already been established to be a fundamental privilege given to women to have an abortion that is given to us by the Constitution. In other words, women are given the right to their own privacy to decide whether or not they want to continue their pregnancy. As agreed upon in the case of Roe v. Wade , this right is a part of our Constitutional rights in a 7–2 Supreme Court decision.

Unborn babies are protected by the Unborn Victims of Violence Act, which ensures protection to unborn children from assault and murder. This act punishes people for intentionally killing or the attempt to kill a “human being.” The essence of the arguments from those that are pro-life is that life begins at conception because upon fertilization, genetic identity is given to a human. Because of this, the individual is given a fundamental right to live, therefore abortion would be murder. Murder is not only illegal, but also immoral. Many of the people that agree with that would argue that by deliberately destroying a life, abortions defy the word of God. Just because the unborn child has not yet been officially “born”, does not mean that they do not already have genetics and are breathing human beings. These unborn babies are recognized by good the moment they are fertilized and conceived, therefore they are living humans. Moreover, each human being is given the same unalienable rights presented by our Founding Fathers. No matter if the fetus is born or not, they still need to be given the same rights as any other human because they are still considered life. Denying these right would just be blatantly unconstitutional.

Although I concede that aborting an unborn baby is the ultimately murder, I still insist that every woman is granted their own right to choose how they proceed with their pregnancy on the basis of their fundamental rights of the Constitution. In the same way, I recognize that opposers of abortion argue that unborn babies are given those same unalienable rights. Although I agree with Sivaya Subramuniyaswami up to a point, I cannot accept her overall conclusion that aborting an unborn baby is the equivalent to killing that baby’s parents. I would argue that a fetus is considered lively upon birth, when a baby can survive outside the womb on its own when not dependent on the mother for life. I do agree that abortion defies the word of God, however I do not believe that the religions of others should be implemented onto other people. There is an invisible line that separates church and state, as it should be considering that not every person in the U.S. practices the same religion. Yet, there isn’t a solid line that dictates the morality of laws. Therefore, laws cannot be forced upon a person based solely on the fact that it defies the religion of a totally different person. Favoring a religion over others by passing a law because it goes against that religion is prohibited by the Constitution solely for the reason to keep people’s free religion amendment protected. At the end of the day, the rights of the U.S. people is what needs to be protected, not the religion of others and protecting their morals.

title: Why Abortion should be Legal in Nigeria
content:
If you didn’t already know, inducing an abortion is illegal in Nigeria except when the woman’s life is at risk. It is governed by two laws, the Penal Code, for the North and the Criminal Code for the south. The sections concerning abortion are 228, 229 and 230 in the Criminal Code Act of the Constitution of the Federal Republic of Nigeria. It states that

228. Any person who, with intent to procure miscarriage of a woman whether she is or is not with child, unlawfully administers to her or causes her to take any poison or other noxious thing, or uses any force of any kind, or uses any other means whatever, is guilty of a felony, and is liable to imprisonment for fourteen years… more

So, if you are seeking abortion or already sought it, you are liable to 7 years in prison, but if you are the provider of abortion, you are liable to even greater punishment, 14 years in prison.

Data on provision of abortion & post-abortion care were collected from a sample size of 772 health facilities by Nigerian researchers at the Guttmacher Institute, New York to estimate the incidence of abortion and unintended pregnancy in Nigeria in 2012. An estimated 1.2 million induced abortions occurred in Nigeria in 2012. This is equivalent to 33 abortions per 1000 women. Estimated unintended pregnancies were 59 per 1000 women between ages 15 & 49. About 56% of those unwanted pregnancies were resolved by abortion. About 212,000 women were treated for complications of unsafe abortion, representing a treatment rate of 5.6 per 1,000 women. A staggering 285, 0000 women experienced serious health consequences but did not receive the treatment they needed. All of this, in a country where abortion is illegal. So what gives?

*Fun Fact : Did you know, that Nigeria and Ghana have the highest online search for abortion pills despite ban?

It’s not a question of whether women will try to procure an abortion or not regardless of the law, whether we like it or not, it’s going to happen, no matter if it is safe or not. The data has shown this. It’s a question of whether they get to have these abortions safely under close monitoring of quality health professional. It’s a question of whether they are not afraid of getting help when things go terribly awry from inducing an abortion.

No woman should have to go to jail because they don’t want a pregnancy. A pregnancy which if carried to term, would solely be her responsibility for a major part of her life ! By the way, the government doesn’t care if you can’t afford to take care of that baby, but they are going to try and force you to keep that baby. No such thing as welfare/aid for you if you are a poor mother in Nigeria. The closest you are going to get to welfare in this country is rice or money shared by political aspirants during election season.

With the high cost of living and low income plaguing the country, raising an unwanted child is very expensive. It is time consuming, it drains you financially and emotionally. The onus is on the woman to bear the burden of taking care of the baby alone in majority of the cases of unwanted pregnancies. If she’s lucky, the baby’s father or family members help out.

Poor mothers with unwanted pregnancies are usually the ones who bear the brunt of the abortion ban. They are more likely to be desperate for an abortion than women of means, because of their low/zero income and the potential future cost of raising a new child and as a result, are more likely to seek the help of a quack doctor or even worse do it themselves because they can’t afford a better specialist willing to perform the illegal procedure; which may or may not lead to abortion complications and in extreme cases, future infertility or death.

Teen moms are not left out. There’s a huge social stigma around sex out of wedlock, talk less of pregnancy. A pregnant young teen, because of the stigma and shame from society, will try to prevent people, most especially her parents from finding out she’s pregnant. There’s even a saying used to shame unmarried ladies with unintended pregnancies; “Belle don come, shakara don end”, meaning “Pregnancy has come, thus posing/showing off has ended”. This stigma is strong enough to drive most girls to get an abortion at all costs. I’ve heard horror stories of pregnant boarding school girls aborting their baby by using an iron cloth hanger to pull the fetus out. There’s a kind of desperation that makes a woman insert an hanger into her body, regardless of bleeding to death or facing prison. Social pressure is hard. No woman should have to face that.

There are some common arguments people give against why abortion should be illegal all over the world.

People will say things like, you should have used a condom, you should have kept it in your pants, you should have used Postinor 2. That logic is faulty. You might as well tell someone who contracted HIV/AIDS that they don’t deserve to get treated for it because they should have been more careful. These people are forgetting that contraception does fail. Contraception failure doesn’t discriminate against married or unmarried women. So, when contraception fails, what happens then? In your opinion, do they deserve to have an unwanted pregnancy?

Apart from that, not everybody knows what they are doing when it comes to sex, especially teenagers. In Nigeria, sex education from parents to their children is nothing to write home about. Most parents try to avoid it or even sugar-coat it. You won’t hear the average Nigerian father tell his son to use a condom, because they don’t want it to seem like they are encouraging their kids to have sex, so they avoid the conversation all together.

Doesn’t a woman with five/six/enough kids, who has an unwanted pregnancy deserve an abortion? Should a naive, immature fifteen year old girl with an unwanted pregnancy who made the mistake of having sex without condom have to pay for that mistake for the rest of her life? Should a woman who gets pregnant after being raped have to be reminded of this humiliation forever by keeping that child? Should a university student that can’t fend for herself have to keep an unwanted pregnancy by a man who could not care less? Should a career driven woman who is not emotionally/psychologically ready to care for a baby have to keep her pregnancy?

Well the government thinks they should, by keeping that law in place, and preventing medical practitioners from openly helping these women exercise their human rights over their own body. Abortion is an issue that most people feel doesn’t concern them, until it does.

Not to mention, we have a population problem in Nigeria. The fact is, Nigeria is lacking a concrete population control plan, since we are depending on family planning alone to curb our population explosion. The government of China uses abortion as a family planning tool and also as a remedial measure for controlling their population.

Some give religion as a reason that abortion should continue to be illegal. A lot of people believe that God is against abortion. Personally, I challenge the belief/argument that abortion is forbidden by religion, but that’s a story for another day. Abortion is not treated anywhere in the christian/Islamic scriptures; you might then give a rebuttal, saying thou shall not commit murder is a part of the ten commandments and that a fetus is a living human. Is it though? At what point do we draw the line between an unborn’s right and the mother’s rights.

I believe we should let the woman decide herself, if she wants to commit the sin of abortion (since we are discussing something that affect her person) , the same way condoms are provided to the general public and people are left to decide if they want to commit the sin of premarital sex, after all, thou shall not fornicate is a law in religion.

The matter of whether abortion bans should be removed should be decided by conscience and reason, not by religion. The woman is the closest one to the decision. She is the one who has her life on the line, whose body and future are at stake. She should be left to decide what she wants.

So called killing of the unborn child is a lesser evil compared to not giving a woman the sole right over her body. We don’t get to force people to have a baby earlier than they are ready to or at all.

A lot of people believe that abortion can cause a woman to die or can lead to future infertility. They are not wrong. But so can pregnancy. The risks referred to, do happen when abortions and pregnancies take place in unsafe ways without close monitoring by qualified health professionals. According to a study by Obstetrics & Gynecology , the risk of death associated with childbirth is approximately 14 times higher than that with abortion. This actually makes sense, because as the fetus grows bigger, the placenta gets stronger, and the baby depends on the mother more, delivering a baby that has come to term comes with larger risks.

Abortion has a scary reputation, and rightfully so, but this believe is based on outdated and unsafe techniques of abortions being carried out in the country. Abortions are unsafe in Nigeria, because people don’t have access to safe procedures; they don’t have access to safe procedures because there’s a ban on it. If the ban remains, the procedure remains unsafe. We can’t have one without the other.

It’s the government’s job to make sure women don’t die unnecessarily from unsafe abortion. The right way for the government to reduce abortion is to make it less necessary instead of less available. Programs should be made available to educate people on the use of various means of contraceptives. Also, parents should be encouraged to educate their children on premarital sex and contraceptives. Another way is to make sure, women have the financial means and access to health care should they choose to keep the baby. This is by far, a better way of reducing unintended pregnancies.

Women should also have access to safer abortion procedures. They can make sure of this by lifting the ban first and then training professionals who can carry out the procedure safely on a world class level.

***************************************************************

In Nigeria and around the world, organizations have been set up to help women who want an abortion. So if you are a girl/woman and you wants an abortion you can get help from the likes of WomenOnWeb and Miss Rosy . Also, if you want to read about other people’s abortion stories, read this site and this site .

title: Abortion Should Be Legal
content:
It was 4am here and I was sleepless so I checked my email. There was one from my mother that I thought would be a description of her new home. Instead, she told me about the leaked draft of a Supreme Court paper about overturning Roe v Wade.

For the love of G-d, America. Just look at yourself. What the hell are you doing?

We all knew this was coming when you idiots voted for Trump. We all knew this was coming when Mitch McConnell stalled a fair hearing of Democratic Justices. I have a ninth grade education and I could see this garbage coming down the chute. What did you think was going to happen with evangelical devils near the throne?

Every woman has the right to decide what happens to her body and through her body. I am absolutely livid that this paper has been drafted. My mother is in some kind of shock, and the world seems a lot darker. In the face of a nation of people who claim to be a beacon of freedom whilst trying to maintain essentially the same balance of power that existed during slavery, I can only gasp in astonishment.

What would Miss Manners have to say about these gaslighting bunch of cockknuckles? Nothing nice, I can tell you that. Miss Manners would be writing a long, perfectly punctuated letter to her representatives, toot-friggin-suite. That idea has merit but mere letters and votes will not stop the beastly thievery that is afoot.

I can’t get involved as a voter in the USA anymore, but I can beg you all who can to do something, anything . Just do not let this shit go down. My mother also tells me that the language of this draft indicated to her that gay marriage could be under threat next. Do you see how this ends? Did you read The Hangman ? Is this thing on?

Long ago, My ex husband and I drove for four hours to a state near our state. We parked and walked through a crowd of chanting, screaming anti abortionists to reach the clinic. We were not ready or able to be parents at that time. It was not an easy decision, but it was the best one for the child. I like to think the child’s spirit came back to me in one of my two children now.

Would I have chosen differently if life had been different? Probably. I can’t ever know. What I do know is that G-d is in control. This fight to control our bodies by people who think they can speak for G-d merely whets my appetite for battle. Sound the horn! Circle the city and march until the walls come crumbling down.

No petty tyrants can take back autonomy from their mothers, their sisters, their wives and daughters. We have rights and you can’t take them back. You want to see how far our patience can be stretched? Fuck around and find out.

title: My Fat Opinion on Abortion
content:
The debate over whether or not abortion should be a legal option continues to divide Americans long after the US Supreme Court’s 7–2 decision for the case of Roe v. Wade on Jan 22, 1973. This decision declared the procedure as a “fundamental right” for women to have access to. But even if it is supported by law, is abortion right?

Let me begin by clearly stating, I am not for abortion. In the case of rape (i.e. when a woman did not have a choice over how she got pregnant), incest, or health of the mother, I believe abortion should be allowed to be done quickly and prayerfully. When it comes to abortion in any other case I am strongly opposed.

One of my favorite arguments against abortion was given by Ronald Reagan, the former president of the United States. Reagan once simply stated, “I’ve noticed that everyone who is for abortion has already been born.” Is this not true? Every person who is directly affected by abortion has absolutely no say in it, while on the other hand, every person who is for abortion has never been directly affected by it.

To answer my own question, “is abortion right?” I find the resolution is as simple as “treat others how you would like to be treated.” Just imagine you are in your own mother’s womb, on no fault of your own, with a possible future as bright or brighter as yours is today. Knowing all of this, you are killed, having never even been given the opportunity at living. When we put ourselves in the place of an unborn person, it is not hard to justify that the unborn within a woman have a right to live because we ALL would want to live.

Now here come the pro- choice advocates(sadly, they didn’t give 54 million people a “choice”) who will respond saying, “But a woman deserves the right to choose what occurs within her own body!” And to that I say emphatically, yes! A woman deserves the right to choose what occurs in her own body, but her rights end where another human’s right to live begins. All people deserve a right to decide what to do with their own bodies, the unborn included. A women chooses to risk creating a child within her when she consensually agrees to have sex. The decision was already made and cannot be taken back.

Pro-choice advocates have also used the rallying cry, “Abortion should be safe, legal, and rare!” But why must it be “rare?” If it is something that they hope does not happen often, it must also mean it is something they should hope never happens at all. Stating that abortion should be “rare” only proves that there is truly something morally wrong with abortion!

Margaret Sanger, the founder of Planned Parenthood, is praised as a hero by the community who is for the legalization of abortion. Yet, the same community ignores Margaret Sanger’s history rooted in eugenics. Eugenics is the science of “improving” a human population by controlled breeding to increase the occurrence of “desirable” heritable characteristics.

On December 10th, 1939, in a letter to Dr. Clarence Gamble, Sanger explained her idea for what she called the “Negro Project.” She wrote, “It seems to me from my experience… that while the colored Negroes have great respect for white doctors they can get closer to their own members and more or less lay their cards on the table which means their ignorance, superstitions and doubts. We should hire three or four colored ministers, preferably with social-service backgrounds, and with engaging personalities. The most successful educational approach to the Negro is through a religious appeal. We don’t want the word to go out that we want to exterminate the Negro population , and the minister is the man who can straighten out that idea if it ever occurs to any of their more rebellious members.” Not many know that Sanger hoped to partner with African American religious leaders to help coerce African American woman into having abortions.

Sanger saw abortions as a way to sterilize minorities, especially African Americans. Even today most abortion clinics are still located in minority areas. Today in New York City more African American children are aborted than born. The effects of the racist history of abortion is still evident.

In the past Americans said they needed slaves to lead better economic lives, slaves weren’t really whole people anyway, and the majority of people would allow slavery so it must be okay. Slaves have no rights, and besides, they are my property. The same arguments are made today by pro-choice advocates. They claim they need abortion to live an economically better life, that fetuses aren’t really whole people anyway, and abortion is legal in so many places, so it must be okay! An unborn person has no rights, and besides, it is “ my body, my choice.” And just like slavery, in the future, our country will look back on abortion with the same horrific remorse, especially when there was scientific proof an unborn fetus is so clearly a living human being.

In a study by Dr. Brenda Major, a Professor of Psychology and Communications at the University of California, it recorded that approximately 21 percent of American women who receive an abortion believed that their abortion did more harm than good. This percentage grew to 28 percent within two years of the abortion. This means of the one million women who have abortions each year in the U.S., more than 280,000 of them believe, within two years, that their abortion did more harm than good. Dr. Priscilla Coleman, a professor of human development and family studies at Bowling Green State University in Ohio, published a study in the August 2011 issue of the British Journal of Psychiatry. Her study concluded that “women who had undergone abortion experienced an 81 percent increased risk of mental health problems.”

In the documentary film Hush , by Punam Kumar Gill, she records the devastating personal experiences of women who suffered emotional and psychological trauma from their abortions. The women all reported suffering many different effects like depression, anxiety, self-deprecation, sexual dysfunction, PTSD, suicidal tendencies, and substance abuse. However, the voices of the women harmed by abortion are treated like they don’t exist. As Dr. David Rearden says in the film, “blanket claims that there are no psychological effects of abortion are deliberately misinformed… its really calling every woman who says, ‘I felt grief after my abortion,’ a liar.” The emotional scars of the quarter of a million hurting women are unacknowledged by the media, policy makers, and the medical community. These women have been labeled as statistically insignificant by those who wish to protect abortion in America.

Today, women who get an abortion are not being told all of the side effects of getting an abortion by medical professionals. This is due to the Supreme Court’s ruling which took down Texas laws that enforced abortion providing clinics to give informed consent, where a person has the right to accurate and unbiased information prior to receiving medical care. For any other medical procedure doctors are required to inform their patients of any risks involved, but now in the case of abortion, this is not true. The majority ruled the Texan law’s requirements pose a “substantial obstacle to women seeking abortions” and place an “‘undue burden’ on their constitutional right to do so.” The Supreme Court has chosen to protect abortion clinics ability to operate rather than protect women in the U.S. deprived of their right to the information of their own health risks.

After listing all of these grievances against abortion, and believing that woman would have access to at least some of this knowledge, then why would a woman ever think to get an abortion? As for me personally, I believe people are generally good, so the answer is not that the women getting abortions are evil or selfish. If that was the case I believe abortion would be much less prevalent.

When I try and put myself in the shoes of a woman who has gotten an abortion and I try to discern within myself why I would ever do it, I come to the conclusion that I would have to be very, very scared. The abortion rates within minority groups in the U.S. are two to three times greater than that of white people in our country. White people today typically have support from family and feel financially secure. If a white woman accidentally gets pregnant she often has family that will willingly be able to support her and she knows that she will not have to raise the child alone. As for minority groups in the U.S. this is not as often the case. Minority groups struggle much more with support from family. Only 38.7 percent of African-American minors live with both of their parents. It is an undeniable fact that minority groups struggle much more financially than most white Americans. Some people do not know where their next meal will come from. Some people do not have any family at all to fall back into if an unexpected pregnancy occurred. Abortions biggest advocate is the lack of support given to pregnant women leading them to feel scared and alone.

People need to take responsibility for their actions. Having sexual intercourse, even when contraceptive methods are used, carries with it the risk of a pregnancy. An unborn baby should not be punished for a mistake made by its parents. If women are unprepared to care for their children, they should do their best to put them up for adoption. However, demonizing a woman for getting an abortion is almost always wrong. Woman who receive abortions are scared and feel alone. It is all pro-life advocates’ duty to support all women, helping them not feel alone in raising their child. As we offer love, support, and security to women who are afraid, we can strike down abortion at its source.

title: Abortion, A “Sin”?
content:
The argument that abortion should be illegal or legal is dull. This topic is not one that should be up for debate regarding it’s legality. In regards to religion, specifically Christianity, there is no such thing as true sin or even the opposite, a truly righteous act. What Merriam Webster states as the definition of sin is “an offense against religious or moral law”. This contradicts almost every claim that sin is definite and those who follow the law of religion are “right”.

Both religion and the concept of morality, things that both define “sin” are up for more debate on their true meaning than the sin itself. why should people have an exact definition of what “sin” is when there are only obscure notions about the ideas that birthed them. For example, Christianity defines ‘sin’ as “a transgression of the law of God” (Merriam Webster). This by example over the ages has been mostly set as a rigid and unwavering set of rules that in some circumstances is impossible to follow and yet the offender of such laws is still punished even if it is unjust. An example of this is Cyntoia Brown who killed her captor and receive a harsher charge than the person responsible for her pain.

Abortion should at the very least, under this specific set of laws (Christian and the United States) be called forth as an abstract idea of something that should really be assessed as “by situation” and not pertaining to the public as a judge or jury.

The Bible was written thousands of years ago and just as the concepts within society have changed over time, so should the morals and concepts in the text. I will concede, some of the laws in the Bible and other such texts should be taken literally such as the assumption that “you shall not murder” (Exodus 20:13). However, the concept of murder in itself has changed from the simplicity of taking a life to include circumstance. An example of this could be the commonly known term “manslaughter” in which the definition is “the unlawful killing of a human being without express or implied malice” (Merriam Webster). This could easily be applied to the overarching topic in this paper, abortion.

The statement that “children are a heritage from the lord” (Psalm 127:3) claims that yes, children are precious to the human existence and one’s life should never be taken but this was never the argument that was up for debate. The question was not when is it OK to kill a child, the question was when does the fetus become developed enough in the mother’s womb to warrant the title at all.

One argument is that the fetus inside the womb should be considered a child from the moment of conception. Another idea is that the fetus should not be considered a sentient being until several weeks or even months after said conception.

Around the time that holy texts such as the Bible (used again due to the renown of this text and its relation to many others) were created, again thousands of years ago, scientific advancements regarding pregnancy were nowhere near where they are now. As such we should again consider the possibility that God or who/whatever might be out there did not intend us to take the interpretations of the Bible as seen from the past and transfer those same ideas without change through history, but rather alter the same core concepts shown through the majority of literature and human experience and morphe it to continue to advance along with our understanding of the world and how it works.

The other concept that is involved is morality. The concept that our own thought and consciousness prevent instances from happening or inspire other moments to happen. This is even more up for interpretation than religion in my opinion. These set rules for what may seem like the entirety of a society or even the world but truthfully every single individual has their own set of morals and follows them according to their own standards and in some cases the standards around them.

These two broad ideas of morality and religion can intertwine. In some cases, they can become the same thing or idea within a person or group. Morality is the code of life that one lives by and that can be individualistic expectations of one’s self that could conflict with their religious beliefs or it could be a code that harmonizes perfectly with the more holy, as some would say, aspects to their belief system.

The choice of whether an abortion is to be considered ‘sin’ in conclusion is not a decision for a group of people to make because there is no “right” answer. It is completely up to the individual person to decide on their own, with the knowledge they have (and this can change at any point), what they believe, and with that knowledge what they think is right for themselves and their own sense of righteousness. I think that it is within a person’s rights to exercise this decision whether permanent or not how they wish (within reason).

Pregnant women considering an abortion should be able to make an informed choice based on their beliefs and knowledge and should not be forced one way or another by pressure from another person or the legal situation binding someone into something. I also think however, that doctors with the qualifications to perform said operation should be able to make the same choice in a different manner and decline performing the procedure. Although they should help the patient to get the assistance they need in other places if they are not willing to do it.

This could be talked about until everyone changes their minds and it becomes an entirely different ordeal but I hope that sometime in the near future, humanity will realize that it is not our decision to make as a whole but rather as individuals.

title: Some Adults Should Never Be a Parent, Abortion Should be Legal.
content:
After I wrote the article about having maternal instincts doesn’t mean you need to be a mother , some readers asked for my views on abortion. I can only tell you my personal opinion as I’m not a family planning expert or a scientist.

I was furious when places like Poland and Alabama made it illegal for women to abort, and citizens are rightfully standing up for their rights.

www.ft.com

visegradinsight.eu

My argument is simple — not everyone can be a parent . I think it’s a given that women who’ve been raped or incested shouldn’t be punished for keeping the child but provided it’s safe medically to do so and enough guidance and discussions have been made with the ‘mother’, abortion should be plausible in any circumstances.

I don’t think this is a philosophical or religious question, I think it’s common sense and logic and clearly, not everyone with power has them.

The question as to when the physical material dimension of a human being begins is strictly a scientific question, and fundamentally should be answered by human embryologists not by philosophers, bioethicists, theologians, politicians, x-ray technicians, movie stars, or obstetricians and gynecologists. The question as to when a human person begins is a philosophical question. - WHEN DO HUMAN BEINGS BEGIN? “SCIENTIFIC” MYTHS AND SCIENTIFIC FACTS , paper by Dianne N. Irving, M.A., Ph.D.

If you write abortion into the law, you should expect there are an infinite amount of exception clauses under it. Because every situation is different, and the law will only make it rigid and more problematic than it already is.

The principal for pregnancy and abortion should be holistic. Have institutions and educational bodies done enough on sex education, and correctly? What’s the actual fact pattern for each case? Why does the mother want an abortion? What’s the role of the father? Has she received enough objective and professional guidance and support? Is it medically safe to abort?

It’s a potential life we’re talking about. We should think about it as rationally as possible. Your emotional attachment to a child at the wrong time can’t possibly be enough to ensure the wellbeing of the baby and it can actually be selfish.

This is not to make abortion easy and waste taxpayers’ money. It’s to give choices and power to women (and men equally) as we have advanced scientific understanding for this to be a choice.

There are credible resources online and offline to help a pregnant person making this tough choice. The first question they usually ask is: are you ready to be a parent?

Whether a woman is ready or not to be a parent is as subjective as it is objective. Some women, including myself, will never be ready to be a mum because of their career aspirations, value systems and own experience; some women, are simply not in the position to be a parent, such as if they are very young or if they have been traumatised. Please note that I’m not here to pretend I know everything, or to reduce anyone’s experience.

The point of this question is for the mum- and dad-to-be to consider should be: Is giving birth the best outcome for the baby?

I’ve seen so many mothers (and fathers) who are literally children themselves. They are carrying wounds and pain from their parents, ancestors and society that all they’re doing is to disrupt their children’s development and happiness.

A woman who can’t deal with criticism healthily, for example, have counteract her low self-esteem by controlling and criticising her daughter to prove her superiority.

A woman who was spoiled by her parents, another example, feels entitled, acts narcissistic and lacks practical skills of survival. I’ve seen a mother keeps asking her children for money because she can’t control her shopaholic desires. I’ve seen a mother claims that when a child is grown up, it’s her divine right to depend on them physically, materially and psychologically.

A even more common example is when women get pregnant in an attempt to save a relationship. Babies are not a tool to spice up your failing marriage, this is plain selfish.

This has nothing to do with physical age, but everything to do with one’s upbringing and wounds. It might seem that maturity comes with age, but that’s not true, it comes with exposure. An older person is more likely to have more life experience, but it’s equally possible that a person lives their own life in a well.

I’ve seen so many parents (my generation or older), who really could live a much happier life without kids and these kids are suffering, badly.

If a law must be enacted then it should be that everyone who wants to become a parent must’ve done therapy to clear their wounds (I know that doesn’t seem possible), and understand the responsibility involved in child caring.

My mother is a psychologically wounded woman, you can tell by observing my grandma. Until today, as I’m talking to my therapist and doing everything to help myself, she’s still inflicting pain on me. There’s no way I can avoid that until the day she dies.

This means the only option I have is to keep protecting myself, setting boundaries and creating distance from my mother.

title: How Georgia’s gerrymandering threatens reproductive rights
content:
You’ve probably heard us talk a lot about how All On The Line ’s fight for fair maps will directly affect our progress on the issues that we care about: Health care. Climate change. Economic opportunity. Preventing gun violence.

But we want to show you, too.

So we’re going to start bringing you Deep Dives into what’s happening in states across the country: How gerrymandering allows for extreme legislation, or stands in the way of progressive ideas, or how a state with fair districts is able to actually represent the will of the voters.

First up? Georgia , where House Bill 481 — otherwise known as the “Heartbeat Bill” — is threatening reproductive rights, thanks to a gerrymandered state legislature.

What is the “Heartbeat Bill”? HB481 is a proposed new law pushed through by a gerrymandered majority in the state legislature that would prohibit abortions after doctors can discern a fetal heartbeat — something that happens around six weeks of pregnancy, before some women even know they’re pregnant. If passed, it would be one of the most restrictive abortion laws in the country.

Is that what Georgia voters want? Not even close. Almost 7 in 10 Georgia voters believe abortion should be legal, and 56% of Georgia voters — a 2-to-1 margin — say they’re less likely to vote for a politician if they support legislation that criminalizes abortion.

So why did state representatives push it through? Because Georgia’s legislature has been gerrymandered to the point where its elected officials are no longer responsible to the people in their districts. They know they can’t be held accountable for extreme votes like these.

How did it pass? By a single vote (92–78 in the State House, needing 91). Imagine that vote in a state where just one more representative had to answer to a non-gerrymandered district — one that was moderate like the state itself, and not like the far-right policy he or she voted for.

What happens now? The bill will go to the desk of … new Governor Brian Kemp, who won the election last November by shamelessly suppressing votes: closing polling places, purging voter rolls, and stopping voter registration applications.

These are the consequences of our unfair system and unfair elections. It’s time to fix the system.

Angry? Us, too.

For all the progress we’ve made — electing better representatives, passing “fair maps” ballot initiatives, spreading the word about legal victories in states like Pennsylvania — there is a long way to go.

And every day we go without fair districts is a day that allows policies like these to become law and threaten basic rights and hold us back from progress.

That’s why we’ll keep shining a light on places like the Georgia state legislature, and work tirelessly to change things.

Visit allontheline.org to join the All On The Line team today.

title: 5 AI Tools to Screen Resumes Without Losing Your Mind
content:
Hiring is tough.

And by “tough,” I mean wading through 500 resumes to find the 10 people who actually read the job description.

Resume screening is somehow both the most important and the most soul-crushing step in hiring.

But here’s the thing: you don’t have to manually scroll past 17 versions of “Team Player, Hard Worker, Go-Getter” to get to the good stuff.

Most Applicant Tracking Systems (ATS) rely on basic keyword matching.

And that’s a problem…

…because it’s easy to game the system with buzzwords and clever phrasing.

Just sprinkle in the right jargon, and even an underqualified candidate can rise to the top.

What ATS tools miss is depth.

They can’t tell the difference between someone who mentions a skill and someone who’s actually mastered it.

The AI-powered tools I’m about to share look at how skills are applied, the context of experience, and patterns that signal real expertise.

Let’s get into it!

Fabric uses AI to analyze resumes, detect keyword stuffing, and highlight top candidates based on real skills.

What sets it apart is its flexibility. It can match candidates’ past projects to the day-to-day work described in your job description, making the screening process far more relevant.

You can even customize what you’re looking for by describing your requirements, similar to writing a prompt in ChatGPT.

Workable’s Screening Assistant uses semantic matching and doesn’t overindex on phrasing and keywords

Manatal is designed for speed and relevance.

Hirebeat offers a simple way to evaluate candidates with AI scoring.

Rchilli focuses on resume parsing and works well for global teams.

Keyword-based screening is often worse than reviewing resumes manually.

Why? Because at least when you read a resume yourself, you can pick up on context, nuance, and actual relevance.

ATS just tallies buzzwords, giving you false positives.

AI tools are built to detect keyword stuffing and look for depth of experience, helping you cut through clutter effectively.

If you’re serious about hiring better, faster, and more fairly, these tools are a solid place to start.

title: Practical cases of AI Ethics applied.
content:
Three practical cases of applied AI and their ethical considerations will be considered: AI in hiring processes, AI in healthcare and AI in public security. With this three examples, we re going to find out the key points to consider in general to create “more ethical” AI systems.

Algorithmic Hiring Bias

Several companies and platforms have faced criticism for using AI algorithms in their hiring processes. These algorithms may inadvertently discriminate against certain groups based on historical hiring data or biased training datasets (Dastin, 2018).

The discrimination, inequity and lack of diversity might be perpetuated in the job market. Even companies which are using these technology, are in reputational risk in case of the algorithms apply any kind of bias on the Human Resources selection.

For example, Amazon has reevaluated and adjusted the hiring algorithms to reduce the bias, recently categorised as “sexist” (Gonzalez 2018)… even when according to some authors, these algorithms are better than human bias (Lavanchy, 2018). Another case is Pymetrics, (Flores, 2020) a good example of a startup which focus is to provide an ethical AI to assist in the hiring processes.

Impact of AI in healthcare diagnostics.

The impact of AI in healthcare diagnostics analysing symptoms, medical history and test results to determine the cause of a medical problem and make an accurate diagnostic is clear (Al-Antari, 2023). However the ethical concerns lie in issues like data privacy, patient consent, transparency of algorithms and the potential of the AI of make life-altering medical decisions without oversight.

To minimise the impact of misdiagnosis, data breaches and erosion of trust between patients and healthcare providers, it’s essential to ensure that the usage of AI is transparent, accountable and respect the patients rights.

The National Academy of Medicine (NAM) impulses the adoption of the Artificial Intelligence Code of Conduct (AICC) as a framework to ensure the AI algorithms applied in health care perform their tasks in an ethical way, addressing the concerns previously before. It’s a working in progress, and anyone can register for updates (NAM, 2021).

The Coalition for Health AI (CHAI) is a community of organisations, experts and academic health systems with the aim to harmonise standards to avoid algorithmic bias and develop health equity to facilitate AI adoption in health care (CHAI, 2023).

Bias in Facial Recognition Technology applied to public security.

The use of facial recognition technology by security forces and other organisations raises new ethical concerns. For example, research has shown that these system exhibit racial and gender bias, leading to potential discrimination and wrongful arrests. The reason under this behaviour is the way these systems are trained and maintained with images from arrested people (Najibi, 2020), perpetuating and making deeper the bias.

On top of that, the accuracy of these systems, according to a report from University of Essex (Fussey and Murray, 2019) is not greater than 65%.

Thus might result in unfair treatment and infringement in civil rights. San Francisco (Van Sant and Gonzales, 2019) and Massachusetts (Ryan-Mosley, 2023) have imposed bans on the use of facial recognition technology by police and city agencies.

The concerns, not on the AI itself but on the way the data and the results are used:

• Which is the current and future use of the collected data? Clearly not today to improve the public security (a 19% of accuracy means not a clear impact on security)

• Even in the cases where this technology were useful, the low rate of accuracy and the known biases might invalidate it as trial: instead of helping to fight against the crime, will be a tool in hands of criminals to avoid prosecutor processes.

At this moment, IBM, Microsoft and Amazon have put a halt or imposed moratoriums on their facial recognition technology at the same time they are working to develop unbiased AI systems for facial recognition (Feiner and Palmer, 2021).

title: AI Algorithms in Hiring Processes
content:
AI has entered enterprise decision making processes for a while now. Human Resources, or the People Function with its new name, is late in the game adopting AI in their processes.

The exact market size of HR Tech is debatable at best, going between 17bn USD and 24 bn USD for 2021 globally, and possibly having 6% to 12% annual growth (CAGR) until 2028[1]. This growth is mainly fueled by AI based applications, promising companies efficiency and effectiveness. The HR tech will come in form of Chat Bots, automated payroll processes, learning management systems, talent development applications, career management, hiring and in all other areas of HR. According to SHRM[2], “Eighty-eight percent of companies globally already use AI in some way for HR, with 100 percent of Chinese firms and 83 percent of U.S. employers relying on some form of the technology.” And that was in 2019.

AI in Hiring decision making processes is the most debated AI usage in HR. Since the famous discrimination incident with Amazon’s hiring AI in 2018[3], the topic increasingly received attention and many academics and regulators have been raising concerns. In the last months of 2021, New York City, US is putting in place legislation that requires employers to inform job applicants if and how they are using artificial intelligence (AI) technology in hiring decisions[4], followed by the U.S. Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC) announcing their focus on the topic[5].

After this introduction, I will iterate the main problem areas of AI usage in hiring and try to articulate ways to avoid bias and discrimination that might arise through AI.

The context: How is AI used in Hiring

Hiring, or Talent Acquisition has some fundamental steps. Talent attraction, talent sourcing, screening, interview and offer process are the six stages of hiring. Even though AI can be used in all those stages, HR tech has focused on talent sourcing and screening as the primary AI use areas.

AI for Talent Sourcing:

Talent sourcing is the stage where companies source the best fitting profiles to their vacancies. Talent sourcing can be reactive, where it only ranks and filters the applications or pro-active where it searches passive candidates and approaches the best fit. AI based tools are used in in both cases. With AI tools, the companies aim to go:

1. Go through the vast number of applications in short time and filter out “irrelevant” profiles faster, without human interaction. Creating huge efficiencies.

2. Decrease bias during the sourcing of best fit, as in theory AI should provide consistent, fair, and objective selection.

3. Reach out to and identify talent that would most likely be missed by humans.

AI includes several different research areas, such as machine learning (ML), speech and image recognition, and natural language processing (NLP), face expression processing (FEP) (Kaplan and Haenlein 2019; Paschen et al. 2020). Most of the hiring AI mechanisms are in reality Machine Learning algorithms, which learn from data presented and predict or suggest an outcome for new cases. Machine Learning algorithms learn in three ways: Supervised, unsupervised or reinforced learning. Supervised and unsupervised learnings are based on set input data and a defined set of desired outputs. The algorithm learns looking at the input data it is provided and the outcomes that were desired. Having built logical correlations between the data and outcome, the algorithms set out to solve new cases. In reinforced learning, the algorithm doesn’t have a defined input, it is “let loose” in a data environment and learns trends and correlations with a defined rewards mechanism[6].

Hiring or Talent Acquisition algorithms learn mostly in supervised or unsupervised fashion. The machine learning is fed thousands of CV’s of candidates as input and also the ones that “got the job” as the desired outcome. Learning from those cases the machine learning devises its own algorithms and decides which profiles are best fit for given vacancies.

This is where the concerns start. Learning from the past practices, the algorithms will learn from the “biased” decisions of the past. And repeat and amplify those biases in large scale. This is what happened with Amazon’s AI hiring in 2018, it decided to favor men over women when deciding on the final candidates.

Even though hiring software companies state that their algorithms are “ethical” and do not discriminate any minority groups, there is good reason to doubt that statement.

Let’s look at the selection criteria closer. AI algorithms look at a few criteria to match the candidates to the vacancies:

1. Skill match. Stated skills of the candidate’s vs the skills needed for the vacant role: This is usually a simple matching of self-reported skills of candidates in their CV’s or Social Media profiles (like LinkedIn) to the skills that the hiring manager set in the beginning of the hiring process. More complex algorithms can find the skills of the past selected candidates for similar roles and look for matches of those skills even though the hiring manager hasn’t input them.

2. Relevant experience and job title match. Algorithms mostly look at simply the job title match of the candidates’ resume vs the job title of the vacant role. The years in a similar job title and the exact match of the title mostly means a higher match.

3. Other key word match. Any other key words that the recruiter or hiring manager identified are also taken into account.

4. Different than the first three criteria, which are mostly simply matching exercises, the algorithms can look for criteria that is hidden to the recruiter. As an example, if the past hired candidates are all from a specific university, the algorithms probably learns this and ranks the future candidates from that university higher than other candidates.

Possible risks with those criteria:

1. CV or social media profile design savviness become predominant for candidates to get short listed by the algorithm. The candidates’ skills in strategically placing key words in their profiles matter more than their actual skills needed for the role.

2. If an algorithm is trained on historical employment data, integrating an implicit bias that favors white men over Hispanics, then, without even being fed data on gender or ethnicity, an algorithm may recognize patterns in the data, which expose an applicant as a member of a certain protected group, which, historically, is less likely to be chosen for a job interview. This, in turn, may lead to a systematic disadvantage of certain groups, even if the designer has no intention of marginalizing people based on these categories and if the algorithm is not directly given this information (Barocas and Selbst 2016, Kochling and Wehner 2020). Example: Some algorithms decoded gender and ethnicity differences from the profile pictures of the applicants and using the past selected candidate pictures, without being detected, the algorithm can put a bias based on gender and ethnicity. Even though the gender and ethnicity information are not fed to the algorithm to avoid bias, the algorithm finds correlations. Pictures are the simplest example, but algorithms can detect differences based on language used in profiles, home addresses of applicants, application times during the day etc. Since the algorithms are mostly “black boxes”, and lack the transparency of the criteria they use, it is impossible for HR professionals to proactively address those.

3. Employees and applicants don’t see the algorithm-based hiring decisions as fair and objective, and they demand a human decision making in hiring processes (Kaibel et al. 2019; Langer et al. 2019; Lee 2018). The perceived unfairness of the hiring process has effects of employee engagement, turnover rates, individual productivity, and employer branding (Walker 2012, Lee 2018; Tambe et al. 2019; Cappelli et al. 2020)

AI for screening:

Companies increasingly use algorithms to screen the applications. After sourcing stage, companies usually end with a “long list” of applicants. The screening is the process in which the most relevant short-listed applicants are selected for hiring manager and HR interviews. The long list or the number of applicants “screened” varies between companies. It is healthy to assume that number will be somewhere between 8 to 15. Most companies have 3–5 candidates for interview process.

AI is used in two main ways here: Analyzing video recordings of the applicants as screening or using gaming as part of the screening. Most of the companies use recruiters together with the AI solution for now. In the future AI can take over the whole process.

AI in Video Recording:

There are numerous HR Tech companies focusing on Recorded Video Interviews. Applicants are given a set of questions, or they are asked by a bot a set of questions. The answers of the applicants are recorded and used to select the better fit candidates. Most of the companies still use recruiters and hiring managers to review the recordings and let them do the screening. In the past few years, AI based companies also provide analyses of the videos based not only the content of the answer but the facial reading of the applicants, the voice tones, the stress level of their voice, and similar aspects in the video. The algorithm then gives a summary of the applicant’s confidence level in the stated skills, some competencies and traits based on their facial expressions and tones.

The risks of using AI here are similar:

1. Almost always the algorithm is a black box, companies mostly don’t know how the algorithm interprets the facial expressions, or voice tone. Or the validity of the outcome.

2. Algorithms, based on the training information they are fed, can have biases towards some groups without knowing they have. Example: We know AI might be able to detect sexual orientation from faces of humans (Wang, Kosinski 2017[7]). What if the AI learns from the training data that one group of humans with a specific sexual orientation should be selected over other groups without identifying it as sexual orientation? Ethnicity characteristics are much easier to read from face recordings, what if the algorithm decides to favor a specific ethnicity based on past data.

3. Applicants and in general employees will be uncomfortable to know that AI will be decided on their competence levels and their compatibility to the job requirements.

The risks are very similar to the ones in sourcing stage, however facial expression processing (FEP) is relatively an advanced algorithm, which makes it even more difficult for humans to decipher what the algorithms looks for.

AI in Gaming:

Gaming in the screening stage has been utilized past few years in some companies for more entry level positions. The games are mostly designed to test cognitive abilities, there are some gaming solutions which also can test job-based skills and personality traits like risk aversion, attention to detail and ability to focus.

Companies like pymetri[8]cs claim that they will provide behavior insights of the candidates through gamification and AI built in that process. The gamification has been around at least for the past 5 years and now it is getting more traction.

Threats are similar, a black box AI, no links to scientific peer reviewed facts about linking gamification to psychometrics and possible hidden biases we as humans cant detect.

Summary and what I haven’t covered yet:

The AI powered matching of candidates and the unconventional assessment tools like facial expression processing are great leaps forward in hiring world. So far, biases have been a strong influencer of the hiring processes and created an accumulated unfair context for candidates. We need to be sure that the algorithms and machine learning do not amplify the injustice, but they become a force of neutrality and objectivity.

I am very hopeful of the future of hiring, powered by algorithms and partnered by humans. Just like in medicine, where we let the AI provide input to the expert radiologists and (for now) a competent human oversees the decision.

What I haven’t covered: The possible mitigations to those risks are not complex but they require investment and focus. I will clarify those in the future.

Thank you.

2. Decrease bias during the sourcing of best fit, as in theory AI should provide consistent, fair, and objective selection.

AI includes several different research areas, such as machine learning (ML), speech and image recognition, and natural language processing (NLP), face expression processing (FEP) (Kaplan and Haenlein 2019; Paschen et al. 2020). Having built logical correlations between the data and outcome, the algorithms set out to solve new cases.
