title: The Risk of Bias in AI-powered HR Tech & What You Can Do About it
content:
Over the years there’s been quite a bit written about bias in the hiring process, but not much attention has been paid to bias specifically at the top of the funnel when people are sourcing for talent.

As such, I decided to write an article about solutions such as Eightfold.ai , Entelo , Spire and SeekOut that offer configurable blind review and selection so that users are not able to view names, pictures, years of experience past 10, education and/or graduation date and many other attributes to effectively mitigate unconscious bias from creeping into sourcing and initial selection process. As a result of the article, I learned about the Unbiasify Chrome extension which you may want to check out in addition to the other solutions I listed if you’re interested in a blind review.

Using AI in search and match solutions has increasingly been sold as a way to reduce bias in the hiring process — after all, if you remove the human from the equation, you should eliminate bias, right?

Not necessarily.

In that vein, back in July of 2016, I read an article on LinkedIn that suggested a combination of data science and algorithms could be used to remove bias from the matching (searching/sourcing) process, and over the past 2 years there has been an increasing amount of content in support of that claim . However, as I commented on that article from 2016, while matching algorithms cannot, of course, be biased based on uniquely human elements such as background, cultural environment or personal experiences (all of which fuel unconscious bias), that does not mean algorithms are immune from bias. In fact, algorithms can and do unintentionally “favor” certain factors or people at the expense of others. You’ve probably already seen at least an article or two on algorithms doing an abysmal job with gender and racial bias, but most of the examples cited don’t have anything to do with sourcing or hiring.

With matching algorithms, biased results can come from the data set on which they operate (which is arguably never complete or genuinely representative of the total target talent population), and bias can also unintentionally result from whatever algorithms “learn” or come to “know” about the data set. This is especially scary because we’re talking about judging the potential match of a person between search terms or a job description and the text a person happened to share when creating their resume, social media profile, application, etc. — and the data is typically limited on both sides of the equation.

I think bias is an especially fascinating area to explore because while humans can be trained to be aware of, recognize, and mitigate unconscious bias ( although the results are not guaranteed ), algorithms cannot be “aware” of any unintended biases they may have, primarily if they are not operating with demographic data on any level, and humans are highly unlikely to be able to identify algorithmic bias within results.

As mentioned in this Wired article on AI and neural networks, “With machine learning, the engineer never knows precisely how the computer accomplishes its tasks. The neural network’s operations are largely opaque and inscrutable. It is, in other words, a black box.” If the engineer doesn’t know how the algorithm accomplishes its task, how can the user? It is indeed a challenge for humans to anticipate and factor for algorithmic bias when there is no real way to know what an algorithm will “learn” and base “decisions” on.

Perhaps unsurprisingly, some studies have already found that machine learning can amplify bias .

Algorithmic systems can develop biases as a result of pre-existing expectations of the engineers developing the systems, technical limitations of their design, user feedback, and the data the algorithms work with based on what is missing or is too abundant in the data they’re trained on.

Bias can be embedded into nearly any data set, private (e.g., your ATS) or public. You may be surprised to learn that “ Wikipedia is incredibly biased and the underrepresentation of women in science is particularly bad ” — this comes from Jessica Wade, a physicist who has personally written Wikipedia entries for nearly 300 women scientists over the past year. Wikipedia is the 5th most visited website in the world, and yet only 18% of Wikipedia biographies are of women .

Similarly, if you look to Stack Overflow to source IT professionals, you need to be aware that out of a survey of over 57,000 Stack Overflow users , only 6.9% were women. If you’re using a matching solution that leverages data from Stack Overflow or even searching it manually yourself, you need to be aware that its data set is skewed. In comparison, a recent HackerRank study surveyed 14,616 software developers, and nearly 2,000 respondents were women, nearly double the percentage of Stack Overflow.

Any solution that leverages and learns from user feedback on results faces a bias challenge because the algorithms can and will learn from unconscious biases of users. User feedback loops can produce unintentional algorithmic bias if they make use of implicit or explicit signals sent to the algorithm when users indicate results are “good” or “bad,” or that they want results “more like this” and “less like this.”

For example, what if users end up consciously or unconsciously ranking white males as good results and women and other races or ethnicities poorly? I have to say this would be almost impossible to achieve if you were using blind review and selection — which is why I believe it should be a standard feature of any solution used to find and select talent! Of course, matching algorithms don’t “know” the race or gender of results (unless, of course, the data is labeled on the back end), but that does not mean that there are not unintended consequences of the patterns of positive and negative signals being sent, essentially training the matching algorithm on what constitutes “good results.”

Yet another potential source of algorithmic bias comes from solutions that use historical data as training inputs (past interviews, hires, etc.). If the historical data itself happens to have an embedded bias (e.g., 90% of hires for a specific role were white males between 25–30 years old), there is a risk of the algorithms learning from these biased signals of “success.”

Cathy O’Neil, the author of “ Weapons of Math Destruction: How Big Data Increases Inequality and Threatens Democracy ,” believes “ When we blithely train algorithms on historical data, to a large extent, we are setting ourselves up to merely repeat the past. We’ll need to do more, which means examining the bias embedded in the data .”

In the Financial Times article, AI Risks Replicating Tech’s Ethnic Minority Bias Across Business , Michael Sippitt, a director of Forbury People; a UK based HR consultancy, says “Tech races ahead of people working out how to use it.” He predicts there will be lawsuits citing discrimination in the future because of bias in automated hiring. This is because AI algorithms learn from historic data sets, he adds, so they are more likely to hire in the image of previous staff instead of helping to tackle unfair under-representation. For example, a survey of the existing educational background, age or experience of staff in a particular industry could encourage machine learning technology to exclude candidates that did not fit a particular profile. “A lot of the CVs and historic profiles will be of one kind of candidate,” says Kriti Sharma, vice-president of artificial intelligence at Sage, the UK’s largest listed technology company. “If you were hiring a chief technology officer for a company and the algorithm was learning from historic data sets then what would you expect?”

Responsible AI matching solutions will tell you they don’t use any names, race, gender, pictures, age, etc., data in their matching processes (and they shouldn’t!), and on the surface that might make you (and them) feel comfortable about bias. However, unless you run comparative studies with a data set labeled with demographic data, there is actually no way to know if the matching algorithms do or do not produce any adverse/disparate impact — which in employment refers to selection practices that appear to be neutral but actually have a discriminatory effect on one or more protected groups.

Some talent-focused AI companies are aware of this. Pymetrics CEO Frida Polli believes, “We have to be really cautious when applying AI to hiring because untested and unchecked it can actually make diversity a lot worse.” That’s why they test their algorithm against a candidate pool of about 50,000 people for whom it has demographic data .

However, Pymetrics isn’t in the talent sourcing and matching space. Even so, it appears they have set the bar, at least publicly. If you are aware of any sourcing/matching solutions that test their algorithms against a statistically relevant set of people with demographic data to measure for adverse impact, please let me know.

If you really want to get in the weeds on this subject, you could begin to wonder (as I do) if there is any difference in the way that women write their resumes and social media profiles compared to men, or how members of a specific race or ethnicity represent themselves in their resumes and online profiles vs. other races or ethnicities. As we can see from Textio’s excellent work in the job posting space , there is a difference in how women read and respond to the text in job descriptions, and using Textio can result in a 23% increase in female job applicants. Conversely, if you’re not using Textio, it could mean that your ATS is skewed towards male applicants and not very representative of the total target talent pool.

What if we were to discover that women or people of a particular race or ethnicity tend to use fewer words and synonymous terms to describe their qualifications vs. men or another race or ethnicity? I think it would be dangerous to assume that there are no differences. If a search and match solution uses keyword/concept frequency at all, even if only as one of many factors in scoring/ranking results, this opens the door to not only algorithmic bias for AI-powered matching solutions, but also bias in a basic keyword search. Again, if you’re not evaluating results against a candidate pool with demographic data, you have no way of knowing if using your manual or automated search and match solution produces a disparate impact.

Don’t worry — the sky is not falling. I didn’t write this article to be alarmist — I merely want to call awareness to the potential risks of bias in AI-powered HR Tech solutions, as we will no doubt continue to see artificial intelligence applied to sourcing and matching and many other layers of the hiring funnel.

The use of AI in recruitment is still relatively new, so it’s not unexpected for us to always be figuring out the fair, responsible and ethical application of AI to employment and hiring, which of course starts with finding people in the first place, either through attracting applicants or through proactive sourcing.

To solve for algorithmic bias, some computer scientists believe that AI solutions can be modified to correct for bias embedded in data sets and algorithms. For example, you could attempt to correct for bias by introducing constraints so that an algorithm selects as many people from each gender or ethnicity or the same fraction of applicants in each subgroup. However, this remedy can be controversial and may be unlawful in some jurisdictions when taken to the extreme.

Wendy Hall, a professor of computer science at Southampton University and the author of a review into artificial intelligence commissioned by the UK government, mentions that “ There’s a huge problem of bias in the [technology] workforce, but if you correct for it, you are manipulating things. Dealing with this is a big issue for how artificial intelligence is designed .”

Earlier this year, some of the world’s leading researchers of algorithmic bias convened in Halifax to discuss fairness, accountability, and transparency in machine learning ( FAT/ML ), seeking to develop and promote algorithmic transparency and accountability to counter the possibility of discrimination. I believe governments, solutions providers, our industry, and the broader community must do more to encourage this kind of work, whether in exploratory stages or advanced implementations.

I commend Pymetrics for open-sourcing their Audit AI tool for detecting bias in algorithms , now available on GitHub , which can be used to mitigate discriminatory patterns that exist within training data sets which influence or improve the probability of a population being selected by a machine learning algorithm.

More broadly, Microsoft and IBM appear to be developing algorithms for detecting, rating, and correcting bias and discrimination, although not necessarily specific to hiring.

When it comes to the data algorithms are using, think about “completeness,” not just regarding whether specific fields are populated, but whether the data set is completely relative to the target population. Wherever practically possible, seek to reduce the bias embedded in the data you gather and use in sourcing, recruiting, hiring and internal mobility. As Wendy Hall notes, “ Now, with AI, we talk about bias in, bias out.” With the spread of artificial intelligence to employment functions such as recruitment, she says, bad inputs can mean biased outputs, which led to repercussions for women, the disabled and ethnic minorities .

Rachel Thomas, who works at fast.ai , a non-profit research lab that partners with the University of San Francisco’s Data Institute to provide training in deep learning to the developer community, raised a number of insightful questions to ask about AI-powered solutions during her “Analyzing & Preventing Unconscious Bias in Machine Learning” keynote presentation at QCon.ai 2018 :

I would recommend asking the above questions when evaluating and selecting any AI-powered HR technology. Also, you should ask if they can explain precisely why and how their solution ranks results in the order they are presented, how they specifically address the risk of algorithmic bias if they can verify that the use of their solution produces no adverse impact. Of course, if you’re already using such solutions, and you haven’t already asked those questions, now might be a good time.

Although there are risks of algorithmic bias when using AI for sourcing/matching, the reality is the manual search and non-AI powered methods we’ve been using for the past two decades may also be prone to unintended bias. The same applies to other applications of AI to the hiring process, such as AI video interview analysis vs. standard video or in-person interviewing. If you don’t have demographic data, there is no way to measure and say with any certainty that your baseline processes, including basic keyword search and in-person interviewing, do not, under certain circumstances, produce biased results that end up driving candidate selection and thus hiring outcomes.

At this stage of development, it is likely to be unrealistic to expect the perfection of 0% probability of adverse impact from AI-powered talent acquisition solutions, especially if we don’t inspect and expect it from all of our legacy systems and processes. However, I believe combining awareness with efforts designed to specifically address the key areas that can give rise to bias across the entire hiring funnel can easily improve diversity and inclusion above what we are achieving today, while we continue to work towards solutions that can eliminate bias altogether.

Artificial Intelligence (AI) is becoming increasingly prevalent in our every day lives, and has recently found its way into hiring practices all across the United States. In hopes of finding potential employees more efficiently, many employers are using machine-learning algorithms to search through social profiles and online resumes to find the best person for the job based on set characteristics. As objective as this algorithm may seem, it can play a very negative role.

On the surface, the use of AI in hiring practices seems nothing but helpful. After all, what’s wrong with saving some time and money? However, studies have shown that this new technology raises several ethical issues, particularity by exacerbating unjust gender and racial biases.

When it comes to applying for positions at tech companies like Amazon, women experience a fair disadvantage when it comes to applicant selection using AI. Amazon’s “AI recruitment engine” was found to direct bias against women’s applications. The engine would go through applications and penalize resumes that included the word “women’s,” as in “women’s chess club captain.” Additionally, it penalized graduates of all-women colleges, according to Reuters.

The selection of job applications using AI systems like the Amazon AI recruiter engine further promote gender bias in the workforce and exclude women from certain fields. In Big Tech companies like Microsoft and Google, women make up only a fraction of total employment, and AI involvement is only making this gender disparity worse.

Additionally, AI’s use in hiring practices may not be as efficient and helpful for applicants as it is for employers. When an applicant’s resume is processed through a tracking system or engine, AI is used to determine keywords within the resume. If the resume has words that are not search engine optimized, the resume will most likely be rejected. This selection can negatively impact job seekers if they are applying and unaware of the use of AI in their application.

A wide variety of solutions have been proposed by companies and legislators alike to counteract the negative effects of AI bias. Some companies have implemented programmed “nudges,” which are specifically implemented to remind a program that it should be considering certain groups equally. This works to correct bias, but still does not fully account for the flaws of such software, and these practices are not adopted by the majority of companies utilizing AI in hiring practices.

Illinois has been quite progressive in encouraging transparency surrounding hiring practices. Legislation “requires companies to inform applicants that AI will be used to analyze their interview videos.” (Waltz, 2019) However, it isn’t clear whether this actually protects the applicants from the bias AI has been proven to exhibit. (Jimenez, 2020) Laws also protects applicants from immediate disqualification if they don’t want their applications subject to AI examination. This legislation should absolutely be the model in order to move toward a future with more transparency and concern for the wellbeing of people affected by AI’s biases.

As dystopian as it seems, AI and machine learning is advancing our world, however leaving unerasable marks on people’s lives changing their lives many times for the worse. We must hope to make change with AI so that our globe continues to spin in the direction of prosperity and success.

title: “Until you try to regulate, you won’t learn how”: Julia Stoyanovich discusses responsible AI for The New York Times
content:
The ethical AI expert weighs in on a New York City law that will regulate the use of the technology in the hiring process

Regulating AI has proven to be quite challenging for lawmakers and AI experts alike. While governments and international organizations have developed broad frameworks and approaches for safeguarding the use of the technology in society, New York City is among the first to nail down the details.

The city passed a law in 2021 set to go into effect this July that outlines restrictions on the use of AI in hiring and promotion decisions. Companies using AI in hiring processes will now be required to notify candidates. The technology will be audited annually by an independent party looking specifically at biases in the system. Candidates can also request information about what data is collected by AI. To enforce the law companies that don’t follow these rules will face financial consequences.

The law has received criticism for being impractical and not going far enough, highlighting the challenge of striking a balance between interest groups in AI regulation. There are also concerns that certain loopholes within the law might weaken its effectiveness.

“It’s much better than not having a law,” said CDS Associate Professor Dr. Julia Stoyanovich , in a recently published New York Times article “ A Hiring Law Blazes a Path for A.I. Regulation ”. “Until you try to regulate, you won’t learn how.”

Julia’s research interests focus on AI ethics and legal compliance, data management and AI systems, and computational social choice. Through engaging in academic research, technology regulation, and speaking on the benefits and harms of AI, her goal is to make “Responsible AI” synonymous with “AI”.

In addition to her role at CDS, she is an Institute Associate Professor of Computer Science and Engineering for NYU Tandon School of Engineering and founding director of the Tandon Center for Responsible AI , which seeks to advance a socially responsible approach to the technology. Julia is engaged in technology regulation in the US and internationally, having served on the New York City Automated Decision Systems Task Force , by mayoral appointment, among other roles. A MS and PhD graduate in Computer Science from Columbia University, her work has been supported by the US National Science Foundation, Pivotal Ventures, JP Morgan Chase, and Meta Responsible AI, among others.

Julia was active in deliberations leading up to the adoption of the hiring law and carried out several public engagement activities when the law was initially proposed. Julia’s public testimony regarding the adoption of the hiring law before the New York City Department of Consumer and Worker Protection was given from CDS during a lecture for her Responsible Data Science course.

While the law only applies to companies with workers in NYC, it is expected to influence the national response to AI. California, New Jersey, New York, Vermont, and the District of Columbia are working on legislation around the use of AI in hiring, while Illinois and Maryland have enacted laws restricting the use of specific AI technologies, according to the New York Times.

As more state governments begin to address the issue of regulating AI within society, for many these new laws raise more questions than they answer. More remains to be seen about who is affected by AI technologies, the benefits and harms it produces, and the best ways to institute interventions. “Without a concrete use case, you are not in a position to answer those questions,” said Julia for The New York Times.

Julia has written extensively about data ethics having co-authored over 100 academic publications along with “Data, Responsibly” and “We are AI” comic book series. For a more detailed analysis of the hiring law, she has written about the auditing and disclosure requirements in the Wall Street Journal, “ Hiring and AI: Let Job Candidates Know Why They Were Rejected ” and The New York Times, “ We Need Laws to Take On Racism and Sexism in Hiring Technology .”

title: New Ways of Interview Process for Designers in the AI Era
content:
Too many times I’ve seen outdated processes stand in the way between talented designers and good companies. The advance of technology was already fast. With AI joining the game, companies need talents to join to catch up. However, it’s not news that portfolios take weeks or even months to be in a job-ready state.

When we think about a designer’s portfolio, it’s easy to imagine polished images and visually appealing user flows. And take-home design challenges? Often hypothetical exercises leave candidates burning hours on mockups, only to submit work that may or may not truly showcase their strengths. Yet, as long as we’ve had design careers, portfolios and take-home challenges have been standard fare in the hiring process. But in an age of rapid change — where AI can generate images, suggest UX flows, and even manage entire design systems — the approach to evaluating a designer’s skills needs an upgrade. Here’s why portfolios and take-home challenges are increasingly out of step with hiring needs and some alternative activities that can better gauge creativity, proactiveness, and other core product design skills.

For years, portfolios were central to assessing a designer’s talent. But with the speed of design evolution, they’re beginning to feel irrelevant and even misleading in evaluating a candidate’s actual abilities. Here’s why:

Portfolios are often biased toward showcasing final deliverables instead of demonstrating a designer’s process. While polished images and smooth UI animations look great, they don’t fully convey the depth of problem-solving, user research, or the often messy iterations that lead to final solutions. But in today’s world, adaptability, critical thinking, and a user-centered approach are more crucial than visual perfection alone.

Design is a team sport. Designers collaborate with engineers, product managers, and users to build impactful products. A portfolio might showcase beautiful screens, but it rarely reflects a candidate’s ability to work in cross-functional teams, navigate feedback, or handle complex stakeholder requests — all of which are essential to today’s product design roles.

AI-powered tools like Midjourney, DALL-E, and Figma’s AI features are revolutionizing the industry, transforming everything from brainstorming to rapid prototyping. AI is reshaping the “hands-on” aspect of design, making it quicker to create UI assets or wireframes. Hiring managers want to know how a designer leverages these tools for efficiency and innovation rather than only relying on their ability to create polished visuals.

Take-home challenges were introduced to see how a designer might tackle a real-world problem, but these exercises often create more frustration than insight:

A complex take-home challenge can take candidates hours, if not days, of unpaid work. For professionals balancing current jobs, families, or freelancing commitments, these challenges can feel like an unrealistic commitment, leading to an uneven playing field.

Without access to real user data or project constraints, these challenges can feel more like an academic exercise than a real-world design task. This approach doesn’t provide much insight into how a candidate works with feedback, adapts to constraints, or validates design choices based on actual user needs.

With today’s AI tools, candidates can use ChatGPT for user personas, Midjourney for image assets, and other AI-powered design tools to create polished work in minutes. This diminishes the original intent of take-home challenges, as they’re now just as much a test of AI proficiency as of creative problem-solving.

Design is all about adapting. Our field is built on a foundation of continual change and evolution, from new design tools to emerging technologies. Designers are expected to stay nimble and innovative, adopting the latest trends and frameworks at a pace few other fields experience. Yet, the hiring process evaluating us remains oddly static, especially in light of transformative advancements like AI. While our toolkits and workflows have been revolutionized, hiring practices like portfolios and take-home challenges are still the norm.

Let’s think about this for a second. AI now handles many of the data-driven aspects of design: user research, insights, iteration, and analysis. AI can even assist in crafting user personas and performing real-time A/B testing. So, if the toolkit and skills expected of designers are evolving, shouldn’t hiring methods follow suit? Portfolios can show a designer’s past work, but they fail to illustrate the candidate’s adaptability, creativity under pressure, or proactive approach to problem-solving in an AI-driven world.

As we redefine the evaluation criteria in the age of AI, here are some alternative ways to test a candidate’s core skills without relying on traditional portfolios or take-home tests:

Whiteboard exercises allow hiring managers to observe a designer’s thought process, problem-solving approach, and adaptability in real time. It gives candidates a chance to showcase their creativity and critical thinking without the pressure of creating polished visuals. A prompt like, “How might you redesign the onboarding process for a new app aimed at seniors?” can reveal how the candidate approaches empathy, user-centered thinking, and innovation.

Instead of hypothetical design problems, try asking candidates about specific challenges they faced on past projects and how they handled them. For example, questions like, “Tell us about a time when you received unexpected stakeholder feedback. How did you respond?” can give insights into a designer’s adaptability and proactiveness. These conversations highlight real-world problem-solving skills and demonstrate how well a candidate can communicate design rationale.

Inviting candidates to participate in a short workshop with the existing design team can simulate a real-world project environment. In this setting, candidates can collaborate, ideate, and iterate in real time, giving hiring managers a chance to observe how they handle collaboration, feedback, and time constraints. This setup tests both creativity and teamwork, two critical aspects of product design.

Rather than a traditional portfolio, invite candidates to present case studies from their past work and include a Q&A session. This allows them to articulate their design decisions, answer clarifying questions, and explain how they’ve iterated on feedback and learned from challenges. These discussions showcase their communication skills, depth of thought, and ability to reflect on and improve their work.

Since AI tools are increasingly integral to design, it’s helpful to test candidates’ proficiency with these tools. This might look like giving a brief, time-boxed assignment where candidates are encouraged to use AI to brainstorm and produce rapid wireframes or generate visual concepts. This test can highlight their familiarity with AI tools, as well as how they balance automation with hands-on design.

Design is about problem-solving, collaboration, and adaptability. Moving away from traditional portfolios and take-home challenges to dynamic, interactive evaluations can better represent a designer’s capabilities and align with today’s needs. As the world shifts more rapidly toward AI-driven workflows, evaluating a designer’s adaptability, creative approach, and use of AI tools is more essential than ever.

It’s time for the hiring process to embrace the future of design and let go of outdated methods that miss the mark on evaluating what really matters.

title: The Use of AI in Fintech Recruitment: Why Human Expertise Matters
content:
The wave of artificial intelligence (AI) has washed over various sectors, radically transforming processes and expectations, and in fintech recruitment it is no different. The allure of harnessing AI’s capabilities to streamline the hiring process is undeniable. It beckons with promises of efficiency and data-driven insights. Yet, a word of caution is warranted — AI, regardless of its advancement, is not a panacea for all recruitment challenges. As a staunch advocate for recruitment excellence, I stand firmly in the belief that while AI can aid the process, it cannot replace the nuanced judgment and interpersonal skills of human fintech recruiters.

Despite these benefits, integrating AI into recruitment is not without its pitfalls.

Conclusion

As fintech advances into new frontiers, the incorporation of AI in recruitment will continue to enhance capabilities. We must not neglect the profound human elements that converge to not only fill a position, but to forge a partnership that propels both individuals and fintech companies to greater heights.

title: Developing a Functional Streamlit ML app leveraging fair AI practice
content:
I t’s no secret that bias is omnipresent in our society, from the hiring process to the criminal justice system, and In reality, AI also falls prey to the same biases as humans. In my previous role as a Data Scientist at Citi Bank North America’s credit card business, a cornerstone of our operations has been the commitment to fair lending and the elimination of bias or discrimination in the credit card issuance process. We recognize the critical importance of ensuring that race, gender, and other confidential attributes do not influence lending decisions. To achieve this fairness of AI systems, open-source projects like the Fairlearn package into our data analytics and model-building processes are a relevant option. This utility allows us to thoroughly assess and mitigate bias in our machine learning models, providing a transparent and data-driven approach to evaluate and address any disparities that may arise in the credit application process. By integrating Fairlearn into our workflow, we enhance our ability to offer fair and equitable access to credit cards, fostering a more inclusive financial environment.

The purpose of this article is to show and stepwise build a fully functioning Stremlit app by leveraging Fairlearn’s capabilities in light of the possible biased AI solution. With the help of a fair AI system framework, we can identify and rectify any potential disparities in lending decisions based on confidential attributes, ultimately bolstering our commitment to fair lending practices. This approach not only aligns with regulatory requirements but also fosters the institute’s dedication to promoting diversity, equity, and inclusivity in the lending industry. It’s a testament to our commitment to creating a level playing field for all applicants and contributing to a more just financial landscape.

Table of contents

What is Fairlearn

Fairlearn is a Python package that empowers developers of artificial intelligence (AI) systems to assess their system’s fairness and mitigate any observed unfairness issues. Fairlearn contains mitigation algorithms as well as metrics for model assessment to define whether an AI system is behaving unfairly in terms of its impact on people — by focusing on the following two kinds of harm:

The approach is known as group fairness, which asks: Which groups of individuals are at risk for experiencing harm?

In general, Fairlearn tries to strike a balance between ML accuracy and parity — the acceptance/selection rates of the subjects from the multiple groups must be equal(assume group 1 is the advantageous group i.e. has a higher probability to be hired when no fairness problem is considered)and it’s one the useful tool to build Responsible AI.

To get a more details understanding please refer to the official git repo.

Streamlight app framework

Streamlit is a user-friendly, open-source Python library that simplifies the process of creating web applications with minimal effort. With Streamlit, developers and data scientists can turn data scripts into interactive web apps effortlessly, making it an invaluable tool for data visualization, data exploration, and sharing insights. Its simplicity and speed have made it a popular choice for those looking to deploy data-driven applications quickly and efficiently, even if they have limited web development experience.

Possible sources of unfairness in AI system

Unfairness in AI systems can originate from various sources and stages in the development and deployment process. Some common sources of unfairness in AI systems include:

Apart from this unfairness may come from a Lack of Transparency, Model Complexity, Data Preprocessing, etc. In the next part, I will demonstrate the unfairness in detail in light of the specific type of data bias and it’s consequences.

In this particular case study, I used the available public datasets Fairlearn - fetch_adult and the purpose is to develop an AI decision system to predict the income category(less than 50K USD/year or more than 50K USD/year ) based on customers’ demographic features.

In this dataset mainly ‘race’ and ‘sex’ are potentially sensitive features, however, to some extent, it’s possible to contribute towards unfairness with the use of features like ‘age’ and ‘native-country’ etc.This is one of the examples of potential unfairness because of data bias.

This particular feature distribution is exasperated by the significant difference in the relative distribution of the target variable -’income_category’ w.r.t. the sensitive features.

This is clear evidence of the presence of bias -data coming from the minority group is much less than those coming from the majority group, which in effect makes the AI system less likely to model perfectly the minority group.

Components- There are the following three design components in our AI app. The detailed code is in this git repository (master branch).

A) ML system : Building a binary classifier pipeline that explores various algorithms like RandomForestClassifier, SVM, Logistic Regression, and KNN while optimizing hyperparameters through 2-fold cross-validation (70:30).

At the same time a robust, reproducible pipeline offers several advantages. To start, it promotes consistency in the model-building process, making it easier to maintain and update. In this pipeline, components like SimpleImputer help handle missing data, ensuring data completeness and integrity. ColumnTransformer is instrumental for feature preprocessing, allowing the application of specific transformations to different subsets of features, which is especially valuable when dealing with a mix of numerical and categorical data.

The pipeline not only streamlines the development process but also facilitates straightforward model evaluation and comparison.

B) Fairness in AI : Incorporating the Fairlearn framework involves several key steps.

i) ’demographic_parity’, ‘selection_rate_parity’ (synonymous)- Matches the selection rate across groups

ii) {false,true}_{positive,negative}_rate_parity’- Matches the named metric across groups

iii) ’equalized_odds’- Matches true positive and false positive rates across groups

i) ’accuracy_score’, ‘balanced_accuracy_score’ -Allowed for all constraint types

ii) ’selection_rate’, ‘true_positive_rate’, ‘true_negative_rate’ -Allowed for all constraint types except ‘equalized_odds’

The complete pipeline config with fairlearn component

C) Frontend App : Streamlit offers an exceptional frontend interactive app design experience, empowering developers to create dynamic and user-friendly applications with remarkable ease. With Streamlit’s intuitive API, it becomes straightforward to integrate customizable user inputs like

there are more, allowing for a highly interactive and tailored user experience. These elements make it simple to collect user preferences and input data, which can then be used to drive the app’s functionality and visualization. What sets Streamlit apart is its rapid development capabilities, making it a preferred choice for prototyping and deploying data-driven applications. Here is the link for the shared Streamlit app , which runs the script by importing the code from my git repo .

A) Without Fairlearn

Although overall offline(statistical metrics)performance is decent, there notable bias in terms of the selection rate w.r.t. sensitive features like ‘sex’ and ‘race’ by the AI decision system, which potentially introduces a latent discrimination in a socio-demographic context. Also, the intergroup performances differ a lot.

B) With Fairlearn

It’s clearly visible that the discrimination or unfairness in the system in terms of selection rate is reduced to a great extent among the different socio-demographic groups, however with some differences. This demographic parity also brought better consistency in intergroup performances.

In this blog, I discussed the relevance and necessity of the Fairness component to design a responsible and ethical AI system. I also demonstrated possible sources of bias/unfairness components in the system in the context of a real-life use case and a possible resolution using a popular framework- Fairlearn. Finally, I also demonstrated a simple way to build a user-friendly app at the front end of this AI decision system.

Key Takeaways:

Road Ahead:

In conclusion, improving decision systems with responsible and fair AI is an ongoing journey. Utilizing tools like Fairlearn, increasing awareness of bias sources, and fostering diversity are crucial steps to make AI systems become more equitable and unbiased.

title: How to Ace the Recruiter Phone Screen: Your Roadmap to Success
content:
Virtual hiring has become a norm in the present era of remote and hybrid work. The virtual hiring process begins with a telephone conversation, followed by an interview over a video call. In this hiring journey, the recruiter’s phone screen is a pivotal step serving as your gateway to securing the role of your dreams. The telephonic conversation is usually brief but crucial, allowing you to showcase your qualifications, skills, enthusiasm, flexibility, and cultural fit. But just like other job roles, the first step towards a new job application starts with a great resume. Your resume should be able to intrigue a recruiter to pick up the phone and dial your number to discuss and dwell deep into your skills and abilities. By mastering preparation techniques, refining your communication skills, and tailoring your resume, you can confidently navigate this process and leave a lasting impression.

1. Impact of a well-crafted resume on the Recruiter Phone Screen

The recruiter’s phone screen is more than a casual conversation. Your ticket to interview is how well your resume presents you. A well-crafted resume showcases your abilities, key skills, expertise, and experience. A well-structured resume helps the recruiter assess how well your skills and experiences complement the job role. Recruiters gauge if you meet the role’s basic requirements before recommending you for further interviews.

Use Kudoswall AI Resume builder to generate resume and assess it with the help of a resume analyzer.

2. Preparing Your Personal Brand Story

A resume is not just a document but the first step towards creating a personal brand. In your CV, you set the tone of your brand. Once the tone is set, a face-to-face or telephonic interview is an opportunity to establish your brand. Your narrative — how you describe your industry experiences, achievements, and aspirations establishes your unique professional expertise. Along with an effective resume objective, prepare a concise yet impactful introduction during the interview to leave a lasting impression. Highlight your adaptability to remote or hybrid work environments.

Use tools like the interview co-pilot feature in the Kudoswall AI resume builder and prepare for your interview.

3. Research the Role and the Company

As a job seeker, you do a lot of research to generate resume. Side-by-side research about the organization will help you dive deep into the company’s culture, mission, and recent developments. Familiarise yourself with the job description and build your resume that aligns with the role’s expectations.

4. Fine-Tuning Your Remote Work Skills

Working in remote and hybrid setups requires proficiency in using tools like Slack or Trello boards. As a job seeker when you build your resume emphasize skills that demonstrate your time management skills, proficiency in communication, ability to work independently, and familiarity with these tools. The resume makes the recruiter well aware of your skills in remote work, at the time of the interview elaborate on your expertise and proficiency with these tools.

5. Mastering Common Recruiter Questions

Prepare answers for frequently asked questions, such as:

Although the recruitment process has changed cliché questions like “Tell me about yourself” are asked to date. Well, the answer doesn’t need to be a cliché at all. Structure your response which conveys your professional journey along with your soft skills.

6. Showcasing Achievements for Remote Roles

When you build your resume, use a clean layout to make it concise and crisp. A study has shown that a recruiter takes only 7 seconds to scan a resume before deciding whether you make it to the next step or not. A well-written resume will help you highlight skills that help you excel in remote roles, your drive for productivity, and self-motivating skills. Include accomplishments like:

7. Demonstrating Communication Prowess

Effective communication is the cornerstone of remote work success. During the call, speak clearly and concisely. Be an active listener, and respond thoughtfully to the questions asked by the recruiter. In the case of a telephonic interview since the recruiting officer cannot see your body language, focus on your tone of voice. Your voice and tone must be calm, and composed, and enthusiastic.

8. Asking Insightful Questions

Recruiters appreciate candidates who show genuine interest. Asking insightful questions about the organization shows your interest in the organization, your enthusiasm, preparedness, and research about the work culture, team dynamics, and expectations from remote employees.

9. Leveraging Technology like AI Resume builder to Generate Resume

Leverage Kudoswall’s AI resume-building features to craft a polished document effortlessly. The tool will help you highlight sections like “Remote Work Experience” and “Technical Proficiency” to align your resume with remote job demands. The platform allows you to generate resume that are ATS friendly ensuring your resume passes the automated screening process.

10. Maintaining Professional Etiquette During the Call

Politeness and professionalism are crucial. Begin the call with a warm greeting maintain a professional attitude throughout the call and end with gratitude. Ensure a quiet environment, free from distractions, to convey respect for the recruiter’s time.

11. Following Up with a Thank-You Note

After the interview, sending a concise thank-you email is a great gesture. Mention certain specific points discussed during the call to personalize your message. A well-crafted follow-up reinforces your enthusiasm and professionalism, eagerness to work in a new environment, and readiness for a new challenge

12. Crafting a Resume for Hybrid Work

In today’s era of AI, one resume document that fits all doesn’t work anymore. Use an AI builder that helps to build your resume highlighting key skills and experience required for hybrid or remote work mode. For hybrid work roles, tailor your resume to demonstrate versatility:

By using Kudoswall, you can generate resume that perfectly balances professionalism and customization. The platform offers multiple resume examples and actionable suggestions to make your application stand out.

13. Emphasizing Soft Skills for Telephonic Interviews

Soft skills such as adaptability, emotional intelligence, and problem-solving are highly sought after. This soft skill sets one candidate from another. Irrespective of the job role the HR team focuses on the soft skills part of a candidate. Articulate scenarios where these traits helped you succeed, particularly in remote or hybrid settings.

Conclusion: Turning Conversations into Opportunities

Excelling in a recruiter phone screen is about preparation, authenticity, and adaptability. By honing your communication skills, tailoring your resume using tools like Kudoswall, and aligning your narrative with the demands of remote work, you position yourself as a top candidate.

Seize every telephonic interview as an opportunity to showcase your value. With a builder resume and the right preparation, you’ll move closer to landing your dream role in today’s evolving work landscape.

title: How Generative AI is Transforming Recruitment & Hiring Processes
content:
All sectors and functions of business are being revolutionized by artificial intelligence (AI), and human resources is no different. Thus, among employers driving their organizations with creative ambitions, generative AI in HR is becoming a popular topic.

AI is enabling HR departments to use this cutting-edge technology to uncover new insights and efficiencies as its capabilities grow.

Adoption is still in its infancy, nevertheless.

According to recent research, there is a lot of space for growth in the application of AI in HR in the years to come.

According to a recent study by the Society for Human Resource Management (SHRM), 24% of organizations have embraced AI to revolutionize their HR processes.

This adoption spans a spectrum of HR functions, including recruitment, hiring, and various other activities. This statistic underscores the increasing recognition of AI’s efficacy in augmenting traditional HR practices.

Delving deeper, insights from Gartner reveal that while the overall adoption of generative AI in HR is relatively modest, with only 5% of HR leaders having implemented it, a significant 60% engage in discussions about its enterprise-wide application.

This indicates a growing awareness and curiosity within HR leadership regarding the potential benefits of generative AI.

Additionally, a McKinsey report highlights a compelling projection — a staggering 80% of jobs could integrate generative AI into their current activities.

This suggests a widespread applicability of AI across diverse job roles, further emphasizing its versatility in transforming the HR landscape.

Despite the current low adoption rates, the research points to a promising future for AI in HR. The disparity between the present usage and the anticipated growth underscores the untapped potential that AI holds in reshaping HR functions.

The key takeaway from this research is that while AI adoption in HR is still in its early stages, the trajectory indicates robust growth as capabilities expand.

Organizations that have already embraced AI in their HR processes are likely to be at the forefront of this transformative wave, reaping the benefits of enhanced efficiency, data-driven decision-making, and improved overall HR performance.

AI in Human Resources is a perfect integration when you consider the following stats.

24% of organizations currently utilizing AI in recruitment and hiring processes are paving the way for more efficient and unbiased candidate selection. As AI algorithms evolve, these organizations are likely to experience even greater success in identifying top talent.

The 5% of HR leaders who have implemented generative AI are trailblazers in leveraging advanced technologies for strategic decision-making. As discussions about enterprise-wide usage become more commonplace, the potential for generative AI to revolutionize leadership roles within HR becomes increasingly evident.

McKinsey’s projection that 80% of jobs could incorporate generative AI highlights the potential for a paradigm shift in how diverse job functions operate. From employee onboarding to performance management, the integration of AI could streamline processes and elevate overall organizational efficiency.

Organizations are encouraged to invest in developing and enhancing AI capabilities within their HR departments. This includes providing training programs, fostering a culture of innovation, and staying abreast of emerging AI technologies to remain competitive in the evolving job market.

The current state of AI adoption in HR reveals a landscape on the cusp of significant transformation.

While only a quarter of organizations have ventured into the realm of AI in HR, the potential benefits and widespread applicability forecast a future where AI becomes an integral part of daily HR operations.

AI in HR would be a topic that would be part of a bigger conversation when it comes to structuring HR operations for success.

As organizations navigate this paradigm shift, those at the forefront of AI adoption in HR are likely to position themselves as industry leaders, driving innovation and redefining the future of work.

The question is not whether to adopt AI in HR, but how swiftly and strategically organizations can embrace this inevitable evolution.

title: Harnessing the Power of AI in Hiring and the Promising Future of Interview Intelligence: Why We Invested in Pillar
content:
by Shawn Ellis and Carolina Rojas
Today, the hiring process is inefficient and unscientific, resulting in low retention, a bad candidate experience, and high costs. It typically takes weeks or months to hire a candidate, while the top 10% of candidates are only on the market for less than 10 days . On average, it takes 33–49 days to fill a role , and 31% of new hires turn over in the first 6 months ; a failed hire can cost a company as much as $240,000 per person . In response to this problem, Pillar has built an enterprise grade interview intelligence platform that coaches and guides teams to hire faster, better, and more equitably.

The past few years have been a time of unprecedented change in the workplace, primarily catalyzed by the COVID-19 pandemic. This significantly impacted all employment sectors, creating a noticeable gap in the labor market. According to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics , the dislocation between job openings and new hires that commenced in late 2021 has not subsided: in April of 2023 , there were 10.1 million job openings (up from 9.7 million in March), while there were only 6.1 million new hires (See figure below). Historically, when there was a rise in voluntary attrition, workers were typically leaving their jobs to pursue better opportunities elsewhere. However, the current wave of attrition is unique. Instead of switching to similar roles at different companies, employees are now leaving to take on completely different positions or even choosing to leave the workforce altogether. According to a survey by McKinsey from Q1 2022, half of the employees who left their jobs voluntarily stated that they have no intention of returning to work within the next six months, creating a challenging environment for talent acquisition.

Job Openings, Hires and Separation Levels, Seasonally Adjusted

Since COVID-19, the labor market has transitioned into a completely different structural reality, marked by significant changes in workplace priorities and expectations. With millions of job opportunities available in the United States, workers are now seeking roles that align better with their needs and preferences, such as more flexibility and work-life balance, and are leveraging their advantageous position to secure higher salaries and improved benefits. They are making it evident that they expect more from employers and feel empowered to voice their requirements. Considering these broader hiring shifts, there have been several key challenges for hiring teams and managers in 2023 including:

The utilization of artificial intelligence in HR processes is an emerging trend that’s shown to increase productivity and mitigate costs for companies. According to the Stanford Human Centered AI Index for 2023 , Global AI private investments in 2022 were $91.9 billion in 2022, almost 18x greater than 2013, and the U.S. led the charge with over $47 billion invested into AI technology. Of this general market, the AI powered HR Tech market was estimated to be $3.9 billion in 2022 and is expected to reach $17 billion by 2027, growing at a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 35.3%.

Further, virtual interviewing, an HR area that’s ripe for further AI and ML innovation, became a necessary tool for most companies when traditional, in-person job interviews were abruptly halted in 2020 due to the COVID-19 pandemic. In 2020, the use of video interviews in the hiring process more than doubled to 58% compared to 22% in 2019, primarily due to the COVID-19 pandemic. Meanwhile in 2022, 55% of respondents reported using video interviews, indicating a relatively stable adoption even after the reopening of the world in 2021. Regarding the ROI, recruiting technology and automation saves companies on average $30,000 per recruiter even before considering cost from failed hires and turnover. Overall, virtual interviewing has become an established practice in the hiring process, offering convenience and flexibility for both employers and candidates. As artificial intelligence continues to embed itself into the interviewing process, artificial intelligence will too become crucial to creating a streamlined hiring process.

In response to these behemoth labor market and hiring shifts, Pillar’s team has built an interview intelligence platform that enhances the hiring process, increasing its efficiency, impartiality, and effectiveness. Although certain hiring managers have been hesitant to adopt AI and ML enabled platforms given biases that can emerge due to biased training data,, Pillar’s software does not replace the human role that interviewers play in the candidate decision making process. Instead, interviewers leverage the technology to augment live interviews via their current video communication platforms (e.g., Zoom, Microsoft, Teams etc.), resulting in reduced time to hire and improved quality of hires. Further, given their focus on the real-time interview process, Pillar is creating a new data source for hiring. By analyzing the historical interview data and outcomes of hiring decisions, biases can be identified and addressed moving forward.

Pillar’s Interview Intelligence Platform optimizes the interview process by:

Improving Hiring Operational Efficiency:

(1) Interview Guides: Pillar can guide interviewers in real time by displaying a standardized interview guide, created in collaboration with the hiring manager.

(2) Interview Highlights: Teams can access post-interview recaps and highlights via a condensed “highlight reel” of responses, which ensures a seamless information exchange across members of the team.

(3) Interview Insights: Interviewers can access post-interview candidate sentiment analysis and interview optimization features, which allows the interviewers to gain valuable insights into areas where they may be falling short, enabling them to make necessary improvements and realign their approach.

Assisting in the Candidate Selection:

(1) Skills Comparison: Teams can compare candidates side-by-side through video and transcription highlights, and search for times that each candidate described a specific skill set, such as Leadership skills.

(2) Candidate Scoring: Pillar simplifies the candidate scoring process by enabling team members to individually evaluate and rank candidates based on their responses to essential questions.

Assisting in Internal Interviewer Training:

(1) Automated Training and Interviewer Analytics: Pillar coaches team members to improve and grow in their interviewing skills and creates interviewer specific guidelines for improvement.

We are thrilled to share our partnership with the Pillar team, which is made up of exceptional industry leaders with extensive expertise in building and expanding global SaaS businesses. Among these individuals are Mark Simpson, Pillar’s CEO, who has successfully built SaaS businesses from the ground up, achieving remarkable growth. His notable accomplishments include leading the development of Maxymiser (later acquired by Oracle) and Acoustic Insights. Additionally, we have Jordan Sherer, CTO, who previously held the position of Head of Engineering at Nativ and served as a Senior Engineering Manager at Zapier, and Withe Thompson, VP of Customer Success, who has a wealth of experience as an Account Manager at On Hiatus, a VP at Transfix, and a VP of Customer Success at Maxymiser, where he worked closely with Mark. Overall, the team has demonstrated success in building startups and achieving key business milestones. We are thrilled to work closely with Pillar as they lead the way in revolutionizing the interview sphere.

Interested in learning more and following Pillar’s story?

If you are a company, investor, or simply someone interested in the intersection of AI and employer solutions, please don’t hesitate to reach out to us at shawn@distributedvc.com and carolina@distributedvc.com .

title: Talent Retention in the Digital Age: The SkillScaler.io Advantage
content:
SkillScaler.io , a platform at the forefront of recruitment and education, offers a unique solution. It streamlines the hiring process, ensuring a perfect match between job vacancies and candidates, thus aiding companies in acquiring the right talent. Furthermore, SkillScaler.io’s emphasis on continuous learning and development, through its connection with educational opportunities, aligns with the modern workforce’s aspirations for growth and skill enhancement.

By leveraging data-driven insights, SkillScaler.io provides companies with critical information on candidate potential, enabling informed decisions about talent development and management. This approach not only enhances the recruitment process but also significantly contributes to employee retention by aligning career development with industry needs.

The integration of SkillScaler.io into a company’s talent retention strategy exemplifies a modern, data-informed approach. It not only streamlines recruitment but also fosters a culture of continuous learning and professional growth, making it an invaluable tool for businesses in the digital age.

Embracing Flexibility and Remote Work

The rise of remote work has been one of the most significant shifts in the workplace. In the digital age, employees value the flexibility and work-life balance that remote work offers. Companies that have adapted to this trend by offering flexible working arrangements have seen a positive impact on employee retention. This shift not only caters to employee preferences but also widens the talent pool, as geographical limitations are diminished.

Investing in Continuous Learning and Development

In a rapidly evolving digital landscape, continuous learning and skill development are essential. Businesses that invest in their employees’ growth through training programs, workshops, and opportunities to work on challenging projects, are more likely to retain their talent. These initiatives show employees that the company is invested in their career progression, thereby fostering loyalty.

Fostering a Culture of Innovation and Inclusion

Creating a workplace culture that values innovation and inclusivity is vital. Employees today seek environments where their ideas are heard, and they can contribute to meaningful projects. An inclusive culture that celebrates diversity not only enhances creativity but also helps in retaining employees who feel valued and understood.

Competitive Compensation and Benefits

While not the only factor, competitive compensation and benefits remain critical in talent retention. In the digital age, this extends beyond just salary. Companies are now offering creative benefits such as wellness programs, mental health support, and stock options, which resonate with the modern workforce’s values and needs.

Effective Leadership and Communication

Leadership plays a crucial role in employee retention. Leaders who communicate transparently, show empathy, and provide clear direction and support to their teams, create a sense of trust and belonging among employees. Regular feedback and recognition also contribute to a positive work environment where employees feel valued and motivated.

As the digital landscape continues to evolve, so do the strategies for retaining talent. Companies that are flexible, invest in their employees’ growth, foster an innovative culture, offer competitive compensation, and practice effective leadership, stand a better chance of retaining their top talent. These strategies not only ensure that employees stay but also that they remain engaged and committed to the organization’s success. In the end, the companies that prioritize their human resources are the ones that thrive in the dynamic digital age.

title: Wait a minute, now AI is hiring me? Some thoughts on AI, Hiring Processes and Fairness
content:
In 2019, an AI adoption survey conducted by Gartner [1] mentioned that 17% of organizations were using AI-based solutions in their human resources departments and by 2022, 30% planned to do so. For those who were using AI-based solutions:
o 62% were deployed to improve decision making

o 57% wanted to improve the employee experience

o 56% were trying to automate repetitive or manual tasks

o 51% expected to capture cost savings

Despite the multiple opportunities that are expected to open in the world of human resources (HR) for Artificial Intelligence (AI), it is important to keep in mind that projects based on AI, are NOT developed on a blank slate, they are formed in pre-existing social conditions, some of which are sometimes unfair, unequal and discriminatory.

a) What are the potential impacts?

b) Which vulnerable groups may be affected?

c) If vulnerable groups are affected, What measures could be consider to compensate the damage?

Let’s see the following example:

“Company X’s HR team has been overwhelmed with the number of applications they receive; to contain the demand, they developed an AI-based solution to identify the best candidates. To train the solution, the HR team provided dozens of resumes from the past considered suitable for positions within the company and resumes that didn’t meet the profile. Based on this input, the algorithm would learn from past applications decisions and review new applications, identifying the applicants that best met the requirements of each profile and leaving aside those that didn’t fully meet the requirements.

Three months after the solution was deployed, the HR department received several complaints for hiring more male employees than female employees [2] . Company X had made efforts in recent months to achieve equal opportunities for women. The success criteria used by the HR department was to assure that the number of employees hired between men and women had a similar proportion. The proportion of women hired from January to March had risen from 11% to 48% ( Chart 01 ) of the total positions hired. For this result, the company felt that significant improvements had been achieved in terms of equality.

“Now let’s see a different approach of the problem. Chart 02 shows the distribution of job applications by gender, more than 1,400 job applications were received in March, of which 997 were woman applicants (600 more women applications than the number received in January).”

At first glance, we can see that the increase in the number of women hired is a product of the greater increase in female applications between January and March. However, when we take a closer look at the proportion of hires based on each gender ( Chart 03 ), we can find that 35% of the total number of male applicants were hired in March, on the other hand, the proportion of female hires in the same month does not exceed 15% of the total number of female applications; in other words, almost 4 out of every 10 men who apply for a position within the company manage to be hired; while only 1 out of 10 women that applied for a job manage to be hired. This new approach results could change our perception of Company X’s achievements in reducing the gap between women and men working in the company. What could have gone wrong? Bias in the training data? Bias in the development team? Measuring the wrong form of equality?

Quoting Zoe Marks and Teddy Svoronos, public policy professors at the Harvard Kennedy School; “Just because things look “equal” doesn’t mean they are meeting goals for good, equitable outcomes. Measuring the wrong form of “equality” can confuse our understanding of the problem [3] ”

I don’t want to be misunderstood, AI is awesome, and it will always be great in helping us understand our environment and solve problems. But the way in which human beings make decisions is complex and the biases that haunt our minds sometimes are transferred to the world that we are building around AI, therefore it is important to be aware of them. This requires from those of us who work around data, to think with an open mind, always receive new data evidence and always question our findings and possible impacts:

-> Do people feel better or improve their life conditions with our products and services based on AI?

-> Do AI solutions applied to HR should only focus on efficiency? What about Diversity, Equity, Creativity?

-> What are the trade-offs of choosing only efficiency?”

Questions that are worth asking.

A similar approach of AI solutions used in hiring processes is Case Study 5: Hiring By Machine developed at Princeton University , a case study that fictitiously addresses the deployment of an AI solution to achieve efficiency on recruitment processes. The case raises interesting discussions like the “The efficiency Bias” (pursuing only efficiency in AI systems over other attributes), the preferences for homogeneity vs heterogeneity and the presence of BIAS (on datasets or development teams).

Sometimes the problems arise in our own understanding of fairness or equality definitions, we underestimate the importance of defining both concepts correctly as we develop AI solutions that interact with society. As the Princeton’s case study addresses, when people talk about “Fairness”, most of us have different approaches:

a) For some people, fairness may refer to equal opportunity conditions; that is, all individuals receive the same opportunities.

b) For others, fairness means equality of outcomes ; everything must be distributed among all equally, regardless of their individual merits or achievements.

c) Some may think fairness within a framework of social justice , which requires that efforts be made to correct inequalities.

d)Finally, for others, fairness is multidimensional (procedural, legal, interpersonal, etc.) . What an individual considers fair depends on which definition of justice they choose. Is it what I deserve? What do we deserve? What does anyone deserve?

Achieving consensus on inequality, equity or fairness definitions may anticipate that multiple definitions emerge while developing an AI solution and avoid negative outcomes in the way in which this AI solution interacts with society.

Finally, for those who are interested in experiencing the thrill of managing an AI-based solution for the HR recruitment process, I encourage you to check out Survival of the Best Fit ( https://www.survivalofthebestfit.com/ ), an educational game developed by NYU students who seeks to raise awareness about the use of AI. The game is dynamic and as you progress not everything is as it seems, and preconditions appear and participate in your decision making. This is a game for everyone, whether you are in HR, software development, AI.

Truth be told, is not necessary to be an engineer to talk and learn how technology partakes in our lives. Enjoy the game!!

References

[1] AI Shows Value and Gains Traction in HR. Gartner (2020)

[2] For academic purposes and case study, only two genders have been defined (man and woman), the article in no sense seeks to establish a position on gender options

[3] Zoe Marks and Teddy Svoronos: Evidence for Equity: Measuring and Addressing Inequalities ( https://youtu.be/1aCurM-vqMc )

title: Yes, hiring is broken — No, AI interviews won’t fix it
content:
The hiring process has always been riddled with flaws. Human recruiters routinely give résumés a mere seven-second skim ( source ), allowing personal biases and snap judgments to steer decisions. Despite countless corporate “unconscious bias” workshops, discrimination persists. In one 2003 study, applicants with white-sounding names got 50% more callbacks than those with African American-sounding names, and by 2016 that gap had soared to 150% ( source , source ). The reality is that short, superficial résumé scans perpetuate an unfair cycle.

In theory, AI seems tailor-made to sweep up this mess. Algorithms are great at scouring large candidate pools to find talent humans might miss. One study from the London School of Economics ( source ) found that employees selected by AI-based recommendations tended to perform better and move up faster than those chosen by human managers. Removing the whim of snap impressions and personal prejudice should be a slam dunk.

Yet, as large language models (LLMs) capture headlines, there’s a growing push to use AI for interviewing. Picture applying for a job, only to discover your “interviewer” is a digital avatar firing off scripted questions. If you pass this gatekeeper, then — maybe — you’ll earn the privilege of speaking with an actual human.

I’m hardly an AI skeptic; I’m building my own AI startup. But I can’t help wondering whether AI-driven interviews will really solve the problem of finding the best people. Job interviews are a two-way street. Yes, the employer needs to assess a candidate’s competence, but it’s also a rare opportunity for a hiring manager to show why this is a great place to work.

That second part — what you might call “discretionary candor” — is something no AI system can replicate. Years ago, when I interviewed for a Product Manager role at a startup, I asked the founder directly about runway and financials. Without hesitation, he pulled up slides from a not-yet-finalized Series A deck. “I probably shouldn’t be showing you this,” he admitted. “You’re not on our team yet.” But he did anyway. It was a masterstroke of transparency that instantly made me feel trusted and included — so when the offer came, I jumped on it.

Picture an AI trying something similar: it just wouldn’t feel genuine. “I shouldn’t be showing you this” coming from an LLM either comes off as disingenuous or wildly unhinged. Most crucially, top candidates with multiple offers want real conversations with people who can speak candidly about culture, growth paths, and the intangibles that make or break a job decision.

Hiring processes shape the candidate pool. If you swap out actual human interaction for an AI avatar, a lot of your best contenders may decide not to bother. Companies that go all-in on AI-driven interviews might save hours on their calendars, but they risk lowering their talent bar in the process. Sometimes, even in our shiny tech-centered world, there’s just no replacement for a human being who can lean in, share a glimpse behind the curtain, and say, “Here’s why this is a great place for you.”

title: Facts About Artificial Intelligence And ATS In Bulk Hiring
content:
Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly becoming an essential part of the hiring process, especially regarding large-scale or bulk hiring. With the help of AI, companies can streamline and automate many of the tasks involved in recruiting and selection, making the process more efficient and effective. In this blog, we’ll take a closer look at how AI is used in bulk hiring and some potential benefits it can offer.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being used in hiring software, also known as applicant tracking system (ATS), to assist with recruitment and hiring. AI can automate various tasks, such as resume screening and candidate ranking, to help HR professionals more efficiently identify qualified candidates. AI is used in ATS through natural language processing (NLP) algorithms, which can analyse resumes and job descriptions to identify relevant skills and experience. AI can also be used to match candidates to job openings based on their skills and experience and to predict which candidates are most likely to be successful in a given role.

According to a survey conducted by the Society for Human Resource Management ( SHRM ), approximately 75% of organisations use some form of ATS. The use of ATS is more common among larger organisations, with 90% of organisations with more than 500 employees reporting the use of ATS, compared to 60% of organisations with fewer than 500 employees.

The use of ATS is expected to grow in the coming years. A report from MarketsandMarkets predicts that the global ATS market will reach $6.8 billion by 2024, up from $3.6 billion in 2019. This represents a compound annual growth rate of 11.4% over the forecast period.

One of the main ways that AI is used in bulk hiring is through chatbots and virtual assistants. These tools can be integrated into a company’s career website or job application portal, allowing candidates to interact easily with the hiring process and get answers to their questions. Chatbots can be programmed to answer common questions about the company, the job requirements, and the application process, freeing HR staff to focus on more complex tasks.

Artificial intelligence is used in bulk hiring through machine learning algorithms. These algorithms can analyse large amounts of data about candidates, including resumes, cover letters, and job application answers, to identify key skills and qualifications relevant to the job. This can help companies identify the best candidates for a particular role, even if they don’t necessarily have the traditional credentials or experience that might be expected.

Another benefit of using AI is that it can help to save time and resources. Automating certain tasks, such as resume screening and initial candidate interviews, can free up HR staff to focus on more important tasks, such as conducting in-depth interviews and making final hiring decisions. This can help companies to fill open positions more quickly and efficiently. By providing candidates with a more efficient and streamlined application process, companies can improve the perception of their brand and increase the likelihood of attracting top talent.

Of course, it’s important to note that AI does not replace human judgement and decision-making in the hiring process. While it can be a helpful tool, it’s still important for HR staff to review resumes and conduct interviews to ensure that the best candidates are being selected.

In conclusion, AI plays an increasingly important role in bulk hiring, helping companies streamline and automate many of the tasks involved in the recruiting and selection process. By using chatbots, machine learning algorithms, and other AI tools, companies can reduce bias, save time and resources, and improve the candidate experience. While AI should not replace human judgement, it can be a valuable tool in hiring, especially regarding large-scale or bulk hiring.

These tools can be integrated into a company’s career website or job application portal, allowing candidates to interact easily with the hiring process and get answers to their questions. Chatbots can be programmed to answer common questions about the company, the job requirements, and the application process, freeing HR staff to focus on more complex tasks.
